title: Acoustic imaging method based on local-nonlocal attention and masked generative knowledge distillation
abstract: Deep learning (DL) has been extensively studied as a powerful data-driven method and shown encouraging results in numerous acoustic imaging-related tasks. Nevertheless, the notable improvements achieved through the advanced DL-based methods often come with increased model parameters and complexity, making the deployment of the models on devices with limited computational capabilities challenging. Knowledge distillation is an extremely promising technique for model compression, in which a lightweight student model is trained to mimic the behavior of the complex and powerful teacher model. The key idea of knowledge distillation is to leverage the supervisory information from the teacher model to enhance the overall performance of the student model without modifying its structure. Therefore, to develop lightweight models with enhanced performance in the context of acoustic imaging, a novel acoustic imaging method based on local-nonlocal attention and masked generative knowledge distillation (LNLMG-KD) is proposed. To apply the LNLMG-KD, a residual dense U-net teacher model (RDUN-T) and residual dense U-net student model (RDUN-S) are constructed. RDUN-T boasts superior performance and strong generalization ability in acoustic imaging, but it is burdened with sophisticated architecture and extensive parameters. RDUN-S is more efficient and possesses a more compact architecture with fewer parameters, but its capacity for acoustic imaging remains constrained compared to RDUN-T. During the training process of RDUN-S, LNLMG-KD is employed to transfer the knowledge learned from RDUN-T to RDUN-S. Through the local-nonlocal attention knowledge distillation, RDUN-S can effectively utilize both local and global information from RDUN-T. Additionally, the masked generative knowledge distillation enables RDUN-S to learn more robust features from RDUN-T. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through the comparisons of the proposed method with the advanced deconvolution methods using both simulation and experimental data. The results indicate that the proposed LNLMG-KD significantly enhances the performance of RDUN-S under the guidance of RDUN-T, which makes it a promising solution for deploying lightweight and superior models in embedded devices with limited computational resources for real-time and accurate acoustic imaging.

title: A defect-mode elastic metamaterial enhancing nonlinear ultrasonic signatures for fatigue crack detection
abstract: This study presents enhanced nonlinear features at the sensing terminal for improved fatigue detection through leveraging the wave control capability of metamaterials, utilizing a defect-mode metamaterial (DMM) system. Initially, an analytical investigation based on mass-spring chain models is explored to illustrate the defect cavity concept aiming at improving the current nonlinear ultrasonic sensitivity. Subsequently, by examining the complete band structure of the DMM supercell through modal analysis, distinct defect bands can be identified within a specific frequency range. Notably, one defect mode effectively localizes the antisymmetric Lamb waves, boosting the sensing signal nonlinearity. To validate the enhancement capability, harmonic analyses of both the DMM and a smooth plate system are conducted, revealing the transmitted wave energy spectrum and identifying the optimal frequency for targeting at the second harmonic component. A coupled-field transient finite element simulation follows, capturing the transient dynamic responses of both systems, and demonstrates the effectiveness of the DMM in amplifying the originally weak second harmonic signature generated by wave-crack interactions. Experimental demonstrations further substantiate these theoretical findings and numerical predictions. This approach holds promise for advancing conventional Nondestructive Evaluation (NDE) and Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) system via metamaterial enhancers.

title: Multiple moving vehicle load identification driven by measurement weights and multiple load-specific regularization parameters
abstract: In existing indirect methods for the moving vehicle load (MVL) identification from bridge responses, challenges related to the identification of multiple loads with varying magnitudes remain insufficiently explored. To address these issues, a novel two-stage identification framework is proposed by integrating measurement weights (MWs) and multiple load-specific regularization parameters in this study. Firstly, the traditional linear model is reformulated as a linear mixed model by distinguishing between the static and dynamic components of vehicle loads. Furthermore, the response normalization across multiple measurements is replaced by the known MWs derived from Morozov’s discrepancy principle for multiple-input multiple-output systems with heterogeneous measurement noise. Then, in the first stage, the static and dynamic components are roughly estimated with single regularization parameter (SRP) for the preparation of second stage. In the second stage, a group-regularized model based on multiple regularization parameters (MRPs) is formulated for the refinement of dynamic loads. The MRPs are selected from a frequentist perspective based on a novel constrained least squares model and only one tuning parameter, i.e. the residual noise from the first stage. A series of numerical simulations and comparative studies are conducted to evaluate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method under varying conditions, including multiple vehicles, vehicle speeds, vehicle-bridge interaction, noise levels and response combinations. Results show that the proposed method can significantly improve the MVL identification accuracy compared to existing approaches based on SRP. Even with inaccurate noise variance estimation, the method remains better robust and only shows performance degradation near to the SNR of 25 dB.

title: Optimized variable reluctance energy harvester with dual magnet arrays for self-powered multimodal monitoring of rotating machinery
abstract: Energy harvesting technology enables the conversion of kinetic energy into electrical power, delivering a sustainable energy supply to wireless sensing nodes. Underpinned by high power density, structural adaptability, and operational robustness, electromagnetic energy harvesting has emerged as a highly promising approach for self-powered sensing applications. This paper presents a Dual Magnet Array–Augmented Variable Reluctance Energy Harvester (DMAA-VREH), designed for rotational applications based on variable reluctance principles. Its architecture features a periodically staggered dual-magnet array alongside a toothed stator–rotor arrangement to enhance magnetic flux variation and optimize spatial utilization. A rigorous parametric analysis of critical factors, referring to air gap length and magnet dimensions, was performed to evaluate their effects on local magnetic saturation in the ferromagnetic components. Furthermore, the output performance of the DMAA-VREH was systematically investigated through theoretical modeling, finite element simulations, and experimental validation. Output power was assessed under both pure resistive and capacitance-matched load conditions across rotational speeds ranging from 150 to 600 rpm. The DMAA-VREH achieved 0.6598 W at 150 rpm and 8.6318 W at 600 rpm under pure resistance, with output increasing to 9.3750 W under capacitance-matched load conditions at 600 rpm. Notably, ranging from 150 to 600 rpm, the enhanced configuration achieves 47.52 %–55.28 % power enhancement over the counterpart configuration of a single-magnet array. The corresponding volume power density reached 3.6701 mW/cm3, and the frequency-normalized volume power density was 0.5872 mW/(Hz2·cm3), indicating excellent energy harvesting capability. Additionally, a multimodal self-powered sensing system integrating an accelerometer and camera module was demonstrated under varying speeds, load impacts, and eccentricities, confirming the device’s capability to stably power wireless sensor nodes and its suitability for multimodal condition monitoring in rotational environments.

title: Health state assessment of complex electromechanical systems based on AINN and frequency domain causal network
abstract: The reliability of complex electromechanical systems is crucial for industrial and national operations. However, accurately assessing the health state of these systems presents significant challenges due to high-dimensional data, nonstationary conditions, and limited labeled data. To address these challenges, we proposed an unsupervised health state assessment method that integrated an Autoregressive Informed Neural Network (AINN) with Generalized Partial Directed Coherence (GPDC). Our approach, AINN-GPDC, introduced an Iterative Variable Selection (IVS) strategy to establish correlation models among high-dimensional parameters and leveraged GPDC to construct frequency-domain causal networks, effectively handling nonstationary and nonlinear data. The method provided a comprehensive evaluation of system health by constructing health indicators based on graph density and graph entropy, enabling precise detection of system state changes. The proposed framework was validated on the N-CMAPSS and real-world satellite datasets, demonstrating superior performance in early anomaly detection and failure prediction. Our findings highlight the potential of AINN-GPDC as a robust tool for health monitoring, particularly in complex, unlabeled, and dynamic environments.

title: MMSE noncausal FIR based wheel force soft-sensing under Bernoulli-uniform prior
abstract: Wheel Center Load (WCL) is crucial for assessing the system durability in vehicle health monitoring. Several WCL estimation methods, such as multibody dynamics modeling (MDM), are implemented for the substitution of WCL sensors due to their high cost and complex installation. However, accurate MDM for different types of vehicles is a challenge. This paper aims to design and implement a sparse noncausal FIR based soft-sensor system to estimate WCL in real time. A minimum mean square error (MMSE) noncausal FIR estimator under Bernoulli-uniform prior is proposed in this work, which is sparse, unbiased, analytical and has minimum variance. To improve the algorithm’s efficiency, an iterative coordinate minimization algorithm is utilized to approximate the MMSE estimator. Moreover, a dynamic horizon reallocation (DHR) method is proposed to reallocate the parameter channels, which can further improve the estimation accuracy. The soft-sensor system is implemented and verified using multiple testing vehicles. The experimental results indicate that the proposed method is applicable to various types of vehicles and achieves the highest estimation accuracy with less computational resources, compared to other sparse threshold methods.

title: Nonlinear model calibration through bifurcation curves
abstract: Nonlinear systems exhibit a plethora of complex dynamic behaviours that are difficult to model and predict accurately. This difficulty often arises from a lack of knowledge of the physics that induces the nonlinear behaviours and the strong sensitivity of the nonlinear dynamics to parameter variation. We introduce in this paper a methodology to carry out nonlinear model updating based on bifurcations. The proposed approach involves minimising the distance between experimental and numerical bifurcation curves, which are key dynamic features that define stability boundaries and regions of multi-stability. For the model, bifurcation curves are computed via standard numerical bifurcation tracking analyses. In the experiment, we use control-based continuation to obtain the data. The approach is first demonstrated on a Duffing and a beam system using synthetic data, before being applied to experimental data collected on a base-excited energy harvester with magnetic nonlinearity.

title: Multi-output subspace identification of complex Bloch wavenumbers in 1D periodic structures
abstract: The experimental identification of complex dispersion curves is challenging in phononic crystals, composites, periodic, architected or metamaterials. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of subspace identification methods in determining wave propagation properties through complex wavenumbers and, consequently, in characterizing a complex structure experimentally. Still, such methods have not yet been adapted for periodic structures with periodic sampling limitations. This work relies on full-field vibration measurements which provide multiple data points per unit cell to statistically reduce the negative impact of having a limited number of unit cells. We propose a subspace identification framework based on a state-space representation of the wave finite element method. A symplectic state-space model is formulated and mathematically proved to represent the original system. Eventually, the proposed method enhances complex wavenumber estimates when a small number of unit cells is available. In addition, a general-purpose, adaptive spectral mask is introduced to rejectphysically irrelevant identification results, enabling straightforward denoising of the identified dispersion curves. The proposed approach is validated through numerical and experimental applications.

title: Fast variational Bayesian inference for structural finite element model updating
abstract: Bayesian inference has been widely used for updating structural finite element models. However, the high computational cost of evaluating the posterior distribution in conventional Bayesian model updating (BMU) frameworks significantly limits their applicability. In this study, a novel fast variational Bayesian inference method is introduced to reduce the computational cost of BMU. The core of the method is to decouple the joint optimization problem of model parameters and noise parameter, and accomplishes the optimization through the iterative solution of two analytically tractable subproblems. Specifically, an explicit update equation for the optimal parameter distribution is derived by linearizing the structural response with a first-order Taylor expansion, thus avoiding the need for expensive Monte Carlo sampling. The accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method are validated through numerical case studies on an 18-story steel frame and an arch bridge structure. The results demonstrate significant improvements of the proposed method in both parameter identification accuracy and computational efficiency compared to conventional methods such as Gibbs sampling and Laplace approximation. This establishes the proposed method as an efficient and practical solution for structural model updating.

title: Enhancing spatial resolution in sparse array ultrasound imaging using nonlinear beamforming: Simulation and experimental validation
abstract: Sparse array ultrasound imaging offers a cost-effective and scalable solution for nondestructive testing (NDT). However, the reduced number of transceiver elements typically compromises resolution and contrast. To address this limitation, this study proposes a novel nonlinear apodization method, null subtraction imaging (NSI), integrated with the total focusing method (TFM-NSI). This approach effectively suppresses side lobe and grating lobe artifacts, thereby improving lateral resolution and contrast without increasing computational complexity. Numerical simulations and experimental studies on steel samples show that TFM-NSI achieves a 36–96 % improvement in lateral resolution and a 71% reduction in artifacts. Notably, TFM-NSI with an 8-element array achieves image quality comparable to conventional TFM with 64 elements, highlighting its superiority in array utilization. Further experiments on reinforced concrete (RC) slab confirm the potential of TFM-NSI for concrete NDT, enabling accurate measurements of rebar size and embedded defects. These results demonstrate TFM-NSI as a promising tool for advanced NDT applications in various engineering domains.

title: A chassis performance enhancement method for wheeled engineering vehicles: Road profile estimation and active suspension control
abstract: To improve the chassis performance of wheeled engineering vehicles, this paper proposes a control strategy that combines tire trajectory inner road profile estimation (TTIRPE) and active suspension preview control (ASPC). The highly accurate and timely TTIRPE method consists of two main components: the generation of a high-precision map, the generation and filtering of the road profile within the wheel–ground contact trajectory. The ASPC method is proposed for an active suspension actuator’s position tracking problem, including feedforward compensation and feedback control. Feedforward compensation is designed to mitigate the effects of road disturbances by combining the dynamics of the active suspension with the previewed road profile information. Based on the hybrid sensitivity robust control method, the feedback control is developed to ensure the robust stability of the active system and realize the precise position tracking. Experimental validation was conducted using a real vehicle platform. The results show that, compared with the passive suspension system, there are significant improvements in terms of chassis attitude stability, ride comfort, handling stability, and tire-road contact performance.

title: Multimodal algorithm-optimized chirped ultrasound thermography for enhanced quantitative detection of metal fatigue cracks
abstract: Metal fatigue cracks under cyclic loading conditions cannot be ignored. Ultrasound-induced thermography has been emerged as an effective technique for crack detection, however, single-frequency ultrasound excitation often produces weak thermal signals, especially for small or shallow cracks, limiting identification accuracy. To overcome these challenges, Multimodal Algorithm-enhanced Chirped Ultrasound-Induced Thermography (MA-CUIT) was proposed for quantitative crack characterization. Firstly, metal cracks three-dimensional thermal-wave model under chirp excitation was established to analyze temperature distribution and thermal diffusion. Subsequently, a comprehensive feature extraction framework integrating frequency-domain, time-domain, and machine learning methods was developed under chirp ultrasound excitation, with systematic optimization of frequency modulation parameters to determine optimal excitation ranges. MA-CUIT experimental platform was established for quantification of real crack defects. The results indicate that MA-CUIT, achieved exceptional crack sizing accuracy with relative errors of 5.9% (FFT phase optimized), 6.7% (PLSR 1st coefficient optimized), and 6.3% (DOD phase optimized), establishing MA-CUIT optimized by FFT phase analysis as the most precise quantification method.

title: Novel S-type inertial nonlinearities and their effects on dynamic vibration responses
abstract: This paper reveals significant inertial nonlinearities using a unique X-mechanism, validated through experiments. The system features a local rotating unit connected to a specially designed X-mechanism via a four-bar linkage, leading to the discovery of novel symmetric and asymmetric S-shaped inertial nonlinearities. These have not been reported before and allow the resonant frequency to be tuned as low as 1 Hz. An innovative modification of the classic harmonic balance method is proposed to obtain the nonlinear dynamic response of the system, enabling analytical solutions without polynomial fitting.Key findings include (a) New S-type inertial nonlinearities can lower the resonance frequency/peak with a higher decay rate while suppressing potential saddle-node bifurcation; (b) Symmetric S-shaped nonlinearity achieves the highest decay rate, maintains good high-frequency performance, and adapts well to varying excitations; (c) Nonlinear inertia equivalence is revealed which means that the rotation unit’s nonlinear inertia is equivalent to a linear motion oscillator, a novel discovery; (d) Adjustability of the X-mechanism allows for large relative motion and independent tuning of high-frequency vibration isolation and resonance peaks; (e) Special nonlinear dynamics are also unveiled, including nonlinear energy transfer and band-stop properties, effectively achieved with the proposed X-mechanism. The study advances the understanding of nonlinear inertia, inspiring new technical innovations in vibration control, energy harvesting, motion control of robots, and the design of novel robotic systems.

title: Contact-Induced vibration in ball screw feed driver: A moving nut FEM model and ball recirculation characterization method
abstract: Dynamics of ball screw feed driver are nonlinear and position-dependent. It is a challenging task to accurately predict the nut vibration response as it moves along the screw. This paper introduces the dynamic modeling technology to describe the nut continuous motion using discrete FEM. The length of beam elements located on both sides of nut is time-varying at a specific speed. Ball contact geometry within the screw-nut interface is obtained by shape function interpolation, and contact loads are assigned to adjacent nodes by the inverse matrix. Moreover, the position of all moving balls including unloaded balls in the returner is registered based on the original equal perimeter transformation, ball recirculation motion is originally characterized, and the impact when ball comes in contact with raceway is introduced. Combined with the elastic deformation of the ball bearing and the base, multi-body dynamic equations are established. Model effectiveness is verified by dynamics tests, and frequency shift phenomena are observed experimentally. The dynamics ball load distribution and the nut vibration response are analyzed. This paper can be used to reveal the dynamic error mechanism.

title: A quasi-probabilistic brushing-based acoustic source localization technique for both burst and continuous sources
abstract: This study proposes a quasi-probabilistic brushing-based acoustic source localization technique for both two-dimensional and three-dimensional structures, capable of localizing burst and continuous sources. Acoustic signals are captured by distributed sensors attached to the structure’s surface, and then segments are determined for subsequent calculations. This technique employs generalized cross-correlation functions to compute quasi-probabilistic curves from the segmented data, effectively addressing signal distortion issues—particularly attenuation, dispersion and reflection effects that become pronounced during long-distance propagation in large-scale structures. In contrast to conventional methods solely relying on time difference of arrival, this technique utilizes complete time-difference information from the entire quasi-probabilistic curve (rather than just peak values) to configure the quasi-probabilistic brushes. The source position is determined by identifying the point with maximum color intensity in the brush-generated map, thereby mitigating localization errors caused by time-difference deviations or false peaks in conventional methods. The proposed technique is experimentally validated on a square plate, a gas containment, and a liquid tank, demonstrating high localization accuracy. It achieves 98.46 % accuracy for burst sources within 30 mm and 100 % accuracy for both simulated and actual continuous sources in the same range. These results confirm its feasibility for practical engineering applications, particularly in structural health monitoring (SHM) and early leakage detection in safety–critical infrastructures such as nuclear containments and storage tanks, where preventing catastrophic failures is paramount.

title: Data-driven modeling of hydroelectric turbine startup fatigue load spectra
abstract: Startup transients significantly impact hydroelectric turbine runner fatigue. Due to the high cost and extreme conditions associated with experimental measurements, the number of startup schemes that can be tested is limited, restricting optimization and fatigue assessment capability. Moreover, the complexity of dynamic strain behavior during startup presents a significant challenge for modeling such signals. This paper proposes a methodology aimed at preserving fatigue loading cycles, represented specifically as a rainflow-based loading spectrum. The approach integrates the rainflow reconstruction technique with a signal envelope estimator, enabling the generation of strain signals from vane opening and rotational speed signals collected during startups. Data from an actual hydroelectric prototype was used for training and evaluation, resulting in accurate estimations with minimal calibration, even for extreme values associated with the highest fatigue damage.

title: A novel high-velocity impact testing system based on multi-stage electromagnetic coil accelerator and in-situ monitoring signals
abstract: The impact resistance of aluminum alloys critically influences the service reliability of key load-bearing components in aerospace and automotive industries. However, the unclear micro-failure mechanisms under high-velocity impact loads severely limit lifespan improvements. This study developed a compact desktop-level electromagnetic ejection-based high-velocity impact in-situ testing system through systematic optimization of excitation current parameters, coil geometry, and multi-stage configuration. The system integrates a nine-stage electromagnetic coil acceleration module achieving 62 m/s impact velocity and an in-situ monitoring unit combining infrared thermography, high-speed imaging, and acoustic emission signal. Multi-angle impact experiments enabled synchronized monitoring of dynamic mechanical responses, micro-damage evolution, and transient temperature fields. Experimental results demonstrate that increased impact angles reduce impact load, shift plastic flow from radial uniformity to shear dominance, expand transient thermal zones, and transition acoustic emission signatures from low-frequency plasticity to shear-induced frequencies.

title: The analysis of compression system instabilities using approximate entropy for centrifugal blower
abstract: This paper examines the early-stage nonlinear disturbances that preceded deep surge in a centrifugal compressor and proposes the use of Approximate Entropy (ApEn) as a diagnostic indicator in a novel combination with its derivative (DApEn). ApEn, a statistical measure of time-series irregularity, is applied to pressure signals acquired from multiple locations within the system. Results reveal that as the flow becomes increasingly unstable, the regularity of the pressure signal deteriorates, resulting in elevated ApEn values. Moreover, the emergence of sharp variations in differential Approximate Entropy (DApEn) serves as a sensitive marker for the onset of flow instabilities, including inlet recirculation and surge. The findings, obtained on a low-speed centrifugal compressor, demonstrate the method’s ability to capture subtle changes in system dynamics and indicate its potential for wider turbomachinery applications that will require future validation.

title: Frequency band recalibration spectrogram
abstract: Extracting valuable features from a signal’s Region of Interest (ROI) is critical for advanced signal analysis. However, existing methods often require domain-specific design assumptions and fixed filter structures, limiting their adaptability and generalization. To address these limitations, this paper proposes the Frequency Band Recalibration Spectrogram (FBRS), a novel time–frequency analysis method based on the wavelet packet energy distribution. FBRS adaptively optimizes filter bandwidth and dynamically generates filter distributions based solely on a signal’s intrinsic frequency characteristics. By iteratively reconstructing wavelet packet components and refining frequency resolution, FBRS adaptively constructs a signal-driven time–frequency representation by dynamically recalibrating frequency bands based on intrinsic energy distribution. While this results in improved resolution in important regions, the core contribution lies in its adaptive and data-driven spectrogram generation mechanism. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, extensive experiments were conducted on simulated signals and three real signals from multiple practical application scenarios. The experimental results demonstrate that FBRS is theoretically innovative and exhibits strong adaptability and descriptive resolution in various signal analysis scenarios. The adaptability and flexibility of the proposed method enable it to cross different domains, providing a new perspective and a powerful tool for signal analysis. The code of the proposed method has been made public in https://github.com/Qinr1026/Frequency-Band-Recalibration-Spectrogram.

title: An anti-swing trajectory tracking approach for quadrotor tethered transportation systems: Self-regulating time-varying gain and underactuation control
abstract: In the presence of unknown disturbances, parametric uncertainties, and unmodeled dynamics etc., this paper proposes a finite-time disturbance estimator-based anti-swing trajectory tracking controller for underactuated quadrotor tethered transportation systems. The disturbances and uncertainties are dealt with by an introduced lumped disturbance term, which can be compensated online during transportation through a designed disturbance observer. Together with the observer, a varying gain anti-swing trajectory tracking controller is proposed. The closed-loop system is proven to be finite-time stable after rigorous theoretical analysis. The effectiveness of the designed observer and controller is validated through a series of hardware experiments.

title: Thermal network modeling and analysis of bi-directional sliding guide system for CNC machine tools
abstract: The thermal stability of bi-directional sliding guide systems directly impacts the machining accuracy and operational reliability of CNC machine tools. However, existing research remains insufficient in modeling their thermal behavior under multi-heat-source coupling and complex contact conditions. To enhance thermal stability during machining, this paper proposes a more comprehensive fully-coupled thermal network model for bi-directional sliding guide systems based on thermal network analysis. This model captures key heat sources and heat transfer pathways within the system, comprehensively describing thermal conduction and feedback relationships. Experimental validation confirms the model’s ability to accurately predict temperature distributions and thermal deformation patterns under various operating conditions. Further analysis reveals that motor speed, lead screw length, and contact interface parameters significantly influence the system’s thermal response. Among these, lead screw length and rotational speed are key determinants of thermal deformation, while lubricant viscosity has a relatively minor effect. This study not only validates the importance of real-time heat source updating mechanisms in reflecting transient thermal behavior but also uncovers the influence patterns of multiple parameters on the thermal performance of guide systems. These findings provide theoretical support and methodological references for thermal error modeling and structural optimization of sliding guide systems in CNC machine tools.

title: Stator current AM-FM model and signature analysis for induction motor eccentricity detection
abstract: Induction motors are widely used in many electromechanical systems, and their stator currents contain rich information about the system health condition. Therefore, current signature analysis provides an effective alternative approach to detect electromechanical system fault. However, rotor eccentricity inevitably exists in induction motors, and may interfere with diagnosis of other faults in both drive motors and driven machines. Therefore, it is essential to thoroughly understand rotor eccentricity signatures in current signals. To this end, an amplitude modulation and frequency modulation (AM-FM) current signal model is derived through mechanical-magnetic-electric interaction analysis of induction motors, giving an insight into the modulation mechanism of stator currents due to rotor eccentricity. Furthermore, the explicit equations of Fourier spectrum, amplitude and frequency demodulation spectra are derived, thus revealing the rotor eccentricity signatures analytically. To avoid possible misleading results due to asymmetrical and intricate sidebands, a joint analysis method based on Fourier, amplitude and frequency demodulation spectra is proposed, thereby extracting the rotor eccentricity fault characteristic frequency effectively. The theoretical derivations and proposed method are validated through lab experiments of an induction motor – planetary gearbox drivetrain, and the rotor eccentricity is successfully detected.

title: Two heuristic-optimization-based frameworks for tailoring signal decomposition methods
abstract: Signal decomposition can break down a complex signal into multiple simpler signal components. Thus, it received considerable attention and has been widely applied in various fields. However, many existing signal decomposition methods, such as empirical mode decomposition and variational mode decomposition, can only decompose a signal into several predefined general signal modes, so their performance in analyzing specific signal components of interest is always restricted by their general decomposition paradigms. Thus, a naturally arising question is how to design signal decomposition methods tailored for analyzing specific kinds of signal components of interest. To answer this question, based on heuristic optimization that does not require gradient information and exhibits great adaptability to various statistical optimization objective functions, this short communication proposes two heuristic optimization-based signal decomposition frameworks: the concurrent decomposition framework and the successive decomposition framework. Once a proper statistical objective function that can quantify certain features of signal components is designed, it can be used in the proposed new frameworks to form new signal decomposition methods to extract signal components having the concerned features. To validate the proposed new frameworks, new concurrent impulsive mode decomposition, impulsive mode decomposition, and new concurrent and successive time–frequency sparsity mode decompositions are demonstrated and effectively applied to the analysis of rotating machinery fault vibration signals and ECG signals. Variational mode decomposition, empirical wavelet transform, and Autogram are used to demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the tailored SD methods based on the two new frameworks. In the future, based on the newly proposed frameworks, many new signal decomposition methods can be tailored to analyze signal components of interest.

title: Theoretical and experimental analysis of the characteristics of a novel tilting-pad bearing with preload effects
abstract: Tilting-pad journal bearing is the key component of rotor system and its preload factor has drastic effect on its operating characteristics. Under different structures and operating parameters, the effects of preload factor on the vibration of rotor system and on the characteristics of oil film are not clear. A fluid domain model and rotor system model are established. The effects of preload factor on the static and dynamic characteristics and corresponding vibration of rotor systems under different parameters are analyzed. The mechanisms of above variation laws are revealed. The results show that the increasing preload raises maximum pressure and dynamic coefficients while reducing film thickness and eccentricity. The effect of preload factor on bearing dynamic characteristics intensifies with higher support factors and larger bearing widths. An increase in both the load-bearing angle and pad number leads to elevated maximum pressure as well as increased Kyy and Dyy values. The suppression effect of bearing preload factor on rotor system vibration displacement and velocity becomes more pronounced with higher support factors, rotational speeds, bearing widths, or lower applied loads. The results can provide theoretical basis for the design of such bearings.

title: From laboratory experiments to in-service tests: Learning embeddings for damage identification in structural health monitoring
abstract: In-situ nondestructive structural tests provide invaluable insight into structural behavior under service conditions, but often are not directly applicable to damage detection in-service. We address the generalization gap between laboratory and in-service structures through (i) development of a neural network damage model learned from various laboratory test structures and (ii) identification of damage progression using this model for an in-service structure. We generate cepstral coefficients from accelerometer time histories across laboratory test structures and damage scenarios, which are classified by a time-delay neural network (TDNN) architecture to determine feature patterns associated with particular damage expressions. Classification of various damage classes over a large laboratory test structure corpus (the LANL SHM dataset, the IASC-ASCE benchmark, the U. Nevada & UCSD Seismic Bridge Columns test, the U. Houston NEESR Reinforced Columns test, the U. Illinois Urbana-Champaign 144-DoF Truss, and the Purdue Truss) provides the model a diversity of scenarios to cover the span of damage phenomena. Generalization of the damage model to in-service structures is performed through clustering of embeddings from this TDNN, which are more-general representations of damage in the laboratory structure domain. A model of the priors for labeled damage scenarios and corresponding embeddings is generated via probabilistic linear discriminant analysis (PLDA). We assess these techniques on the Z24 Bridge Benchmark and obtain strong results for both ambient and forced vibration tests, in (i) a-posteriori diagnosis of previous in-service damage to demonstrate the extent of separability through supervised clustering and (ii) hypothesis testing of the deviation of an unseen queried condition, from the baseline condition in the PLDA, spanned purely by laboratory test damage classes. Explainability is also investigated via the association of in-service damage with seen laboratory test structure damage conditions, demonstrating feasibility for interpretable output-only structural health assessment. • Lab test vibration measurements can serve as a basis for in-service damage detection. • A TDNN classifier is trained on lab damage cases as a damage-sensitive feature generator. • A PLDA model of lab TDNN DSFs allows hypothesis testing for DSFs of unseen structures. • The TDNN-PLDA system developed only on lab structures detects Z24 Bridge damage cases. • Diagnosis of in-service damage is possible using PLDA clusters of lab damage cases.

title: Uncertainty-aware fault diagnosis of unknown faults using ensemble-based NODE residuals
abstract: This paper presents an uncertainty-aware approach to fault diagnosis using ensembles of neural ordinary differential equations for residual generation. The proposed method leverages physical insights in the design of the NODE models and employs bootstrap ensembles to quantify prediction uncertainty and adapt detection thresholds. The adaptive thresholds enable robust detection and isolation of faults in scenarios with limited training data. The methodology is validated on real-world data from an internal combustion engine test bench, providing insights into how training data quality and residual design impact uncertainty-aware fault diagnosis.

title: A unified equivalent model of the l 0 minimization model for structural damage identification
abstract: Sensitivity analysis-based structural damage identification can be transformed into solving the l0 minimization model (the original model) because damage typically occurs in a few sections or members especially at the early stage, making it spatially sparse. Many existing approximation models have approximately solved the original model because it is NP-hard, by replacing the l0-norm with continuous sparsity-promoting functions, which inevitably reduces the accuracy of damage identification in theory. A unified nonconvex model, where sparsity base function fθ (θ>0 controls the tightness of approximation) replaces the l0-norm of the original model, is theoretically equivalent to the original model when parameter θ satisfies certain conditions. Inspired by this, this paper firstly proposes a unified equivalent model (named sparsity base function minimization model) for structural damage identification to theoretically eliminate the reduction of damage identification accuracy caused by approximately solving the original model. Secondly, a general optimization algorithm based on the Difference of Convex functions Algorithm and the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers is designed to solve the proposed unified equivalent model, and a novel parameter selection strategy is proposed to select θ. Finally, the results of numerical simulations and experimental studies demonstrate that six specific forms of the proposed unified equivalent model outperform the l1 regularization model, the elastic net, and the l1/2 regularization model in terms of damage localization and quantification accuracy, respectively.

title: A physics-driven DT framework for fault diagnosis based on frequency-domain simulation
abstract: The performance of dynamic models deeply depends on a suitable parameter selection. To address this, a digital twin (DT) model of planetary gear system is developed based on a rigid-flexible coupling dynamic model. A two-stage decoupling optimization framework is proposed for the iterative updating of dynamic model parameters. Based on the theoretically derived system frequency response function, model responses are simulated by a frequency-domain solution method to reduce computational time. Guided by gear vibration mechanisms, model responses and sensing data are then aligned in an order feature space for a less signal interference. Finally, a simplified numerical fault model is developed to represent the meshing stiffness under different health conditions. The severity of gear localized faults can be assessed by an identification of fault model parameters. Experimental results demonstrate that the DT model requires 5h to converge, achieving a 97 % faster computation speed compared to the model based on the numerical integration method (183h). The DT model exhibits a vibration magnitude that closely matches the test data and achieves high similarity (0.86), which enables it to effectively distinguish between normal, gear crack, and tooth break states. Therefore, this study provides a new paradigm for DT modeling and its diagnostic applications in planetary gear systems.

title: Independent determination of compactometer value from a compaction roller
abstract: Continuous Compaction Control (CCC) enables near-continuous monitoring of the compaction process during earthwork construction by instrumenting a compaction roller with sensors. One of the most widely used CCC measurements is the Compactometer Value (CMV), due to its historical significance and relatively straightforward calculation procedure, which involves performing spectral analysis of the compaction drum’s vibratory response. In practice, CMV measurements from commercial CCC systems are typically black box in nature, as they report only the final values—without disclosing the raw acceleration data or the calculation steps performed by the CCC system. As a result, most CCC technologies remain closed and proprietary. This paper presents a methodology to independently calculate CMV using data collected from a compaction roller equipped with both an aftermarket CCC retrofit kit and a secondary accelerometer. This setup allowed for direct comparisons between independently measured CMV values and those reported by the CCC retrofit kit. Data was collected from the construction of a full-scale earthen embankment compacted in multiple lifts. Results from this study showed that independently measured CMV values were within 1% of CMV values measured from the retrofit kit. These results provide a practical, transparent workflow for researchers and practitioners interested in replicating CMV measurements, ultimately contributing to the development of more open-source CCC solutions.

title: Blade tip-timing based surge prevention method for axial compressors: from warning to frequency identification
abstract: Surge is a highly destructive phenomenon in the operation of axial compressors such as aero-engines, inducing severe blade vibrations and significantly reducing blades life severely. To address this, this paper proposes a novel method named surge warning to frequency identification (SWFI). This method introduces a dual-characteristic fusion mechanism of phase and amplitude, resolving the false alarm problem of surge warning in traditional methods. Furthermore, by combining the blade vibration differential equation with the All-phase Fast Fourier Transform (AP-FFT) phase spectrum, the method derives an accurate differential frequency correction method, eliminating the interference of frequency aliasing and leakage. To validate the effectiveness of the SWFI method, a numerical model incorporating mistuning and coupling effects was established. The results indicate that the SWFI method achieves a warning response time of less than 0.015 s; its maximum frequency identification error is 0.11 %, which much better than the 0.3 % error level of traditional method. Experimental studies were conducted on a high-speed academic impeller test bench and an industry scale experiment bench. The results demonstrate that the SWFI method eliminates false alarms associated with synchronous resonance responses, exhibiting accuracy and real-time capability; its maximum error for non-synchronous frequency identification is less than 1.57 %. This holds significant practical value for real-time surge warning in compressors and the frequency identification.

title: A novel frequency-domain control strategy for semi-active suspensions with reduced hardware demands
abstract: The widespread adoption of high-performance semi-active suspensions in vehicles remains limited by relatively high costs. Cost-effective semi-active suspensions with reduced performance specifications have consequently emerged as a promising alternative. However, the development of control algorithm for such systems with limited hardware capabilities has received little research attention. Based on the suspension frequency–response characteristics, this study proposes a novel multi-objective frequency-domain control (FDC) strategy, which is applicable to the suspension systems with limited adjustment bandwidth. The FDC is established through a two-degree-of-freedom (2-DOF) suspension model and consists of a three-step control architecture utilizing short-time Fourier transform (STFT) for real-time signal processing. Numerical simulations based on practical two-wheeler parameters validate the algorithm effectiveness through comparisons with five classical semi-active control algorithms. The simulation results show critical performance degradation in classical methods when controller execution frequency for adjusting the control damping decreases from 100 Hz to 10 Hz and 1 Hz, while the proposed algorithm maintains consistent stability. The FDC achieves significantly control performance improvements of at least 31.6 % in sprung mass acceleration (SMA), 46.3 % in suspension working space (SWS), and 20.7 % in dynamic tire deformation (DTD) over classical strategies. By using a magnetorheological (MR) damper, a vertical vibration table testing was conducted for algorithm’s validation. The experimental results validate the near-optimal SMA performance of FDC across different road conditions compared to other controllers at a 1 Hz control frequency.

title: Analysis and control of the unfolding motion of the foldable-leg mechanism of an unmanned deformable vehicle
abstract: The reconfiguration of the unmanned deformable vehicle investigated during this study between its vehicular state and its humanoid state is primarily achieved by the unfolding motion of two foldable-leg mechanisms installed on the chassis of the vehicle. Smoothness and synchronization are not only important performance indicators for this unfolding motion but are also key factors that affect the stability of the reconfiguration process. Therefore, it was necessary to conduct motion analyses and control research regarding the foldable-leg mechanism. In this study, a kinematic model of the unfolding motion was developed based on the homogeneous coordinate transformation theory, and a Lagrangian dynamic model of the system reconfiguration process was established using analytical mechanics. Smoothness rules were designed for the unfolding motion of the foldable-leg mechanism. LuGre friction models were established for the foldable-leg joints, and the flower pollination algorithm was used to identify the model parameters. Based on these models, a cross-coupling control strategy was designed to compensate for synchronization deviations between the left and right legs during the unfolding motion. The effects of the interference caused by the slider motion on the smoothness of the unfolding motion and the effects of leg-joint friction on the synchronization were considered. A fuzzy proportional-integral (PI) controller was designed to track the angle and angular velocity of each joint motor in the foldable-leg mechanism. Simulation and experimental verifications demonstrated that the smoothness and synchronization control strategy designed for the foldable-leg mechanism significantly improved the synchronization and smoothness of the unfolding motion, and it thereby further enhanced the reconfiguration stability of the unmanned deformable vehicle.

title: Two-dimensional multi-scale graph direction dispersion entropy and its application in mechanical fault diagnosis
abstract: The vibration signal of mechanical faults is characterized by distinctly nonlinear and non-stationary feature. Traditional complexity measurement methods can quantify its nonlinear characteristics, but the main challenges faced by this method include its limited capacity to represent the overall complexity and dynamic behavior of intricate structures, lack of sensitivity to directional patterns and low robustness in the presence of noise. To address these challenges, an effective measurement method for characterizing the complexity of vibration signals in multi-directional dimensions termed two-dimensional multi-scale graph direction dispersion entropy (MGDDE2D) is proposed, and a fault diagnosis approach for rolling bearings based on MGDDE2D and reformed whale algorithm optimized support vector machine (RWOA-SVM) is constructed. First, aiming at the deficiency of the original signal in structural modeling and local dynamic characterization, a time-series weight dynamic visibility graph (TWDVG) is proposed to enhance the modeling ability of impact faults. Second, MGDDE2D is utilized to directionally encode local neighborhoods within the graph signal across multi-scale. Subsequently, the RWOA-SVM multi-fault classifier is employed to further improve the classification accuracy and generalization performance of pattern recognition. Finally, the proposed method is validated based on public and self-constructed rolling bearing data sets, and comparisons are made with five entropy-based algorithms and four SVM optimization classifiers. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method exhibits superior stability and performance in fault diagnosis.
keywords: Two-dimensional multi-scale graph direction dispersion entropy
Reformed whale algorithm optimized support vector machine

title: Research on identification of marine coupled mechanical vibration source and vibration-sound transmission path based on a novel operational path analysis method
abstract: To address the limitations of vibration transfer path analysis for mechanical equipment in practical applications, this study derived the operational transfer path analysis (OTPA) method based on the characteristics of ship-coupled mechanical vibration sources and explored four key challenges in its practical implementation. First, by integrating independent mechanical equipment operations with auxiliary artificial excitation and using system identification to extract vibration source signals while eliminating cross-coupling, a novel SOM-OTPA method was proposed to identify cross-coupled vibration sources and transfer paths in ship mechanical systems. Second, a regularized TLS Lagrangian objective function was developed by incorporating convexification techniques, adaptive regularization parameter adjustments, and a conjugate gradient iterative method with a restart mechanism to effectively resolve the ill-posedness problem in OTPA. This led to the development of an OTPA approach based on iterative weighted TLS-Tikhonov regularization, ensuring that the complex transfer function matrix solution converges to the global minimum. Numerical simulations and experimental validation demonstrated the high computational accuracy and robustness of the proposed algorithm. Additionally, a Partial Coherence Analysis-based method (PCA-MCF) was introduced along with key implementation conditions, enabling the optimal selection of vibration source input measurement points while minimizing the risk of omitting major vibration sources. The effectiveness of the proposed OTPA method was validated through underwater cylindrical shell vibration experiments and shipboard vibration transfer path tests. By employing noise frequency domain cloud maps, vibration source and transfer path comparisons, noise contribution vector diagrams, and weighted contribution calculations, the new OTPA method successfully identified the localized ship-coupled mechanical vibration sources and their transfer paths, providing strong technical support for controlling ship mechanical noise at both the source and transfer path levels.

title: Determination of defect depth of barely visible impact damage using local defect resonance frequency equation for arbitrary delamination
abstract: In this paper, local defect resonance (LDR) frequency for an arbitrary sized delamination has been derived from Fourier series expansion and shown its usefulness in defect depth detection. Clamped boundary conditions have been used for shallow defects. The Fourier series are used to take the shape variation from an equivalent circle of defect size. Perturbation of governing differential equations as well as frequency parameters has been carried out for that purpose. The LDR frequency formula is first verified with numerical results from ANSYS using super circular boundary conditions. Thereafter, the LDR frequency and area of barely visible impact damage (BVID) has been obtained from a laser doppler vibrometry experiment. The defect boundary is fitted with Fourier series to determine the Fourier coefficients, and the equivalent radius is found using the defect area. Now, the LDR frequency and the determined Fourier coefficients are used to evaluate the defect depth. The defect depth calculated in this process is validated with X-ray computed tomography results and found to be in good agreement. The defect depth variation is also calculated for artificial delamination. The present formulation opens a way for defect depth detection of arbitrary shaped delamination.

title: A comprehensive evaluation of the influence of cracks with breathing behavior on dynamic characteristics in rolling bearings
abstract: The breathing behavior of cracks exhibiting periodic transitions between open and closed states under alternating load serves as one of the driving mechanisms for crack propagation. The breathing behavior of cracks in bearing outer rings under cyclic stress directly induces parametric resonance through periodic time-varying stiffness, thereby inducing abnormal multi-peak vibrations. Traditional static crack fault models considering constant transient excitation fail to elucidate this catastrophic mechanism. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a fault modeling method for cracks with breathing behavior. The dynamic stress intensity factor (DSIF) is computed via the displacement extrapolation method, with breathing characteristics incorporated into finite element model. In the fault dynamic model, by introducing time-varying contact stiffness, the mapping between stiffness loss and vibration response is established to elucidate the mathematical mechanism by which breathing behavior induces multi-peak response. The model is validated using practical cases of bearing degradation and through comparisons with existing models. The results demonstrate that crack size governs the saturation characteristics of stiffness loss, whereas the opening angle dictates linear growth of stiffness loss. The time span of breathing behavior correlates directly with crack size, thereby offering an optimization criterion for methods predicting remaining life on crack propagation law.

title: Nonlinear feature extraction in a mechanical system using kernel PCA and output-only data: Experiment and physical insights
abstract: Identifying features in nonlinear structures, especially when they already exhibit inherent nonlinear behavior in the undamaged conditions, remains a significant challenge in structural health monitoring (SHM), particularly when the damage mechanism is also nonlinear. This complexity further increases in field applications, where controlling and measuring excitation is particularly challenging. Traditional methods, which rely on frequency response functions (FRFs), are unsuitable for nonlinear structures because they require knowledge of the excitation source and cannot effectively separate inherent nonlinearities from structural changes. This paper presents an output-only approach that combines transmissibility functions and kernel principal component analysis (KPCA) for damage detection in structures with nonlinear behavior caused by cubic stiffness and breathing crack effects. A numerical validation on a nonlinear multi-degree-of-freedom (MDOF) system with multiple resonances, followed by an experimental application on a nonlinear flexible beam, was performed to demonstrate the method’s generalization and practical relevance. The experimental beam exhibits cubic nonlinearity in the undamaged condition, while the simulated damage, a breathing crack, introduced additional quadratic stiffness effects. KPCA successfully separated cubic and quadratic nonlinear effects by analyzing transmissibility functions between accelerometer pairs, enabling accurate damage detection. This framework addresses the limitations of FRF-based methods, providing a straightforward and valuable tool for practical applications in SHM that does not rely on complex machine learning techniques.

title: Grain size estimation in additively manufactured metal thin-wall using noncontact laser ultrasonic and zero-group-velocity Lamb waves
abstract: Grain size is a critical factor influencing the performance of fabricated structures, particularly their elastic modulus and yield strength. In metal additive manufacturing (AM), unique thermal properties such as thermal accumulation, thermal gradients, and cooling rates can lead to grain size variations throughout the structure. This study proposes a grain size estimation technique for additively manufactured metal thin-walled structures. The developed technique employs pulsed and continuous wave (CW) lasers to generate and measure zero-group-velocity (ZGV) Lamb waves. By extracting ZGV resonance frequencies from the measured waves, Poisson’s ratio is determined and correlated with grain size using a pre-established model. The developed technique offers several key advantages: (1) Localized ZGV Lamb wave modes enable precise, localized grain size estimation. (2) The advanced and localized nature of the technique allows it to accommodate the complex geometries of compact and lightweight AM designs. (3) As a non-contact and non-destructive measurement method using lasers, it is suitable for both in-situ monitoring and post-processing investigation. The technique was experimentally validated on additively manufactured stainless steel 316L thin-walled samples, demonstrating its feasibility for real-time in-situ grain size monitoring in AM.

title: Research on a magnetic rolling pendulum-based multi-stable electromagnetic generator with dual-path transition mechanism
abstract: A magnetic rolling pendulum-based multi-stable electromagnetic generator (MRP-MEMG) is designed and investigated in this paper for low-frequency energy harvesting. The multiple stable equilibrium positions are realized by coupling the magnetic repulsion and gravitational forces. The circumferential configuration of the proposed system provides a special dual-path transition mechanism, which realizes additional transition pathways between potential wells through alternative energy barriers. This mechanism enables larger displacement response and enhanced kinetic energy accumulation, thereby improving the dynamical and electrical performances compared to conventional multi-stable generators. The dynamical and electrical models of the system are theoretically derived, along with nonlinear magnetic force and magnetic flux analyses. The prototype of the MRP-MEMG is fabricated for parameter identification and experimental work, which confirms the effectiveness of the theoretical models. The rich dynamical behaviors of the system and parametric influences on the system’s energy harvesting performance are analyzed through numerical simulations, and a comparative discussion with a conventional quad-stable energy harvester is provided. Energy harvesting experiments are further conducted to evaluate the energy harvesting potential of the MRP-MEMG. It is found that a peak output power of 66.23 mW is achieved across a single coil under a harmonic excitation with amplitude of 2.5 g and frequency of 8.5 Hz. This work presents a novel multi-stable architecture with dual-path transition mechanism, and provides guidelines for the design and optimization of the proposed MRP-MEMG, which has considerable potential for practical application in low-frequency vibration energy harvesting.

title: Interpretable stacking-SHAP prediction model for dam deformation during long term operation
abstract: Accurate prediction of dam deformation is crucial to ensure the structural safety of hydraulic engineering. An innovative Stacking-SHAP model is proposed to indicate the nonlinear coupling effect of complex environmental factors in this study. Firstly, an integrated model of stacking is constructed, regarded RF, SVR, GBDT, LGBM and XGBoost as the base learners, and the MLP meta-learner is used to realize the nonlinear fusion. The hyperparameters of each base learner and meta-learner are all optimized by the ISRES algorithm to improve the optimal performance of the whole stacking integration architecture. Secondly, the interpretability of the prediction results of the stacking model is carried out through the SHAP method. It can thoroughly investigate differential contributions of the environmental factors to the dam deformation and influence weights of each base learner on the prediction. The SHAP dependency graph can further indicate the complex nonlinear relationship among the environmental factors and the dam deformation. Finally, the proposed model is validated and applied using the measured time series of a concrete hyperbolic arch dam. Compared with various single models, the Stacking-SHAP model can significantly improve the prediction accuracy and clearly indicate the mechanism of the differential influence of the environmental factors to the dam deformation. Moreover, it can provide interpretable insights for dam temperament analysis during long term operation.

title: An analytical calculation method for whole workspace position-dependent natural frequencies and mode shapes of machine tool
abstract: Determining the position-dependent natural frequencies and mode shapes is essential for optimizing machining performance of machine tools throughout their workspace. However, obtaining comprehensive modal data for heavy-duty machine tools through conventional modal testing is challenging, limiting the applicability of data-driven methods. Meanwhile, numerical methods like finite element modeling (FEM) are computationally intensive for large-scale machine tools, reducing their practicality. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a novel analytical method based on a rank-modified eigenpair-solving strategy, significantly enhancing computational efficiency and accuracy by directly updating modal parameters using previous mode shapes and frequencies. Specifically, the proposed method decomposes the machine tool into lumped-mass substructures and characterizes their positional changes as structured rank modifications to stiffness matrices. Consequently, position-dependent modal analysis is transformed into an analytically solvable eigenpair updating problem, maintaining clear physical interpretations. Simplified analytical formulas derived from this approach explicitly reveal the relationship between structural parameters and modal variations, providing deep theoretical insights for dynamic optimization. A systematic, three-stage experimental validation—including substructure, subassembly, and full-machine modal tests—was conducted on a CH5120 vertical lathe. Analytical predictions exhibited excellent agreement with measured natural frequencies and mode shapes across multiple positions, confirming the method’s robustness and accuracy. Furthermore, machining experiments using a highly rigided workpiece verified that even when natural frequencies vary minimally (less than 5%), the position-dependent variations in mode shapes can still lead to significant differences in the critical cutting depth that determines machining stability. These findings clearly demonstrate that position-dependent modal characteristics play a critical role in determining machining performance. The proposed analytical framework provides a powerful tool for dynamic performance optimization and structural design of machine tools across their entire workspace.

title: A theoretical and experimental study on the vibration control of a coupled beam system using a series-coupled dual oscillator system model
abstract: The coupled beam system (CBS) is widely found in various engineering fields. During their operation, they are inevitably subjected to vibration excitation caused by the working environment, power equipment, and other factors. Long-term vibration can lead to structural fatigue and damage in CBS, which affects the stability, reliability, and safety of the system. To effectively suppress the adverse vibration of CBS, a new series-coupled dual oscillator system (SCDOS) model is proposed in this study and introduced into CBS. Then, theoretical and experimental studies are conducted on CBS equipped with the SCDOS. The theoretical study demonstrates that the reasonable use of SCDOS can suppress vibration in each sub-beam of CBS without altering the original vibration characteristics of CBS. The theoretical research guides the experimental study and evaluates the vibration control capability of the SCDOS on CBS. The experimental results show that the actual designed model of the SCDOS exhibits significant nonlinear mechanical properties. In addition, the experimental results confirm that the SCDOS is capable of simultaneously suppressing the vibration of each sub-beam of CBS, and can reduce or even eliminate the complexity of non-monocyclic responses. In summary, this research proposes a novel model for vibration control, offering a new approach and solution to the nonlinear vibration control of elastic coupled beam structures in engineering.

title: Torque fault signal extraction in hybrid electric powertrains through a wavelet-supported processing of residuals
abstract: • Development of an innovative Torque FD Technique based on shaft angular speed monitoring only, suitable for HEPS. • The ODE-RLS-DWT framework overcomes the fault masking effect and the limitations of data-driven methods. • Experimental Validation across various hybrid operating modes on the HEPS Test Bench. • Consistency of the technique even under non-ideal conditions, including measurement noise and model parameter variations. • Performance metrics show an average ACC of 98.88 %, a FAR of 0.63 % and an average processing time of 0.7 ms across 97 tests. The growing implementation of Hybrid Electric Propulsion Systems (HEPS) in the aeronautic field introduces new challenges for health monitoring and fault detection (FD). This is due to different motor dynamics and limited sensor accessibility. Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) torque represents one of the most critical quantities for monitoring HEPS reliability. This work proposes a non-invasive torque FD framework that couples physical modelling and signal processing approaches. It addresses the previously mentioned issues, supervising the angular speed measurement only. The residual, obtained from the difference between measured and model-predicted shaft speeds, is refined through a Recursive Least Squares estimator to enhance the adaptability of the proposed modelling approach. A Discrete Wavelet Transform isolates transient features associated with ICE characteristics. This enables the extraction of torque-fault signatures from non-ideal conditions and overcomes the fault-masking effect of adaptive estimators. Experimental validation on a dedicated HEPS test bench confirms consistent performance of the method under various hybrid operating conditions, parameter deviations, and measurement noise. The proposed method achieves an average accuracy of 98.88%, a false alarm rate of 0.63%, and an average processing time of 0.7 ms.

title: Review of fault diagnosis for rotating machinery: Prior knowledge integration in data-driven methods benefits model interpretability and generalizability
abstract: Fault diagnosis for rotating machinery has always been a hot research topic in both academia and industry. This review provides a holistic and concise overview of relevant studies that are categorized into three main research directions: fault mechanisms, signal processing, and machine learning. It is found that studies on intelligent fault diagnosis (IFD) today face two significant challenges: model interpretability and generalizability. Model interpretability refers to the degree to which humans can understand the decision process in IFD models; generalizability refers to the performance decrease that IFD models exhibit when tested on samples with different data distributions from the training samples. These two challenges are especially critical, given the risk-sensitive nature of machinery fault diagnosis and the ever-increasing demand for responsible artificial intelligence. At the same time, it is also observed that prior knowledge derived from fault mechanisms and signal processing is not fully utilized in most IFD studies. As a result, although many methods have been proposed to address the two challenges, the final outcome is still not satisfactory. Recently, much attention has been paid to integrating prior knowledge derived from studies of fault mechanisms and signal processing into IFD models. This integration is effective and enlightening. However, prior knowledge and integration techniques are diverse and not systematic. Therefore, we provided a clear taxonomy and an in-depth discussion at the end of this paper to support the development and application of prior knowledge integrated IFD.

title: Dynamic modeling of rod-fastening rotor systems with rub-impact and rod loosening
abstract: Rod-fastening combined rotor (RFCR) systems are extensively utilized in aerospace and industrial machinery due to their high strength and modular design. However, the compact configuration of gas turbines makes rotor–stator rub-impact more likely to occur during operation. Moreover, the relaxation of interfacial preload under cyclic loading further exacerbates the situation by introducing structural looseness. These combined effects give rise to complex nonlinear dynamic behaviors, such as bifurcations, subharmonic resonances, and instability near critical speeds. To investigate these phenomena, this study develops a detailed dynamic model of the RFCR system, incorporating tie-rod preload detuning and rub-impact effects using Timoshenko beam theory and finite element discretization. The system response is analyzed using the Newmark-β numerical method, and the nonlinear dynamic characteristics such as bifurcations, subharmonic resonance, and fractional frequency components are examined. Simulations reveal that preload detuning induces higher-order periodic responses, reduces the threshold for quasi-periodic motion, and broadens the vibration instability region. These findings are further validated through experimental tests on a custom RFCR test bench. The results demonstrate a strong correlation between preload degradation and the evolution of nonlinear behaviors, such as early-onset rub-impact and critical speed shifts. This study provides a theoretical and experimental framework for understanding and diagnosing preload-induced faults in rotor systems, offering valuable guidance for structural health monitoring and reliability design in turbomachinery applications.

title: Traversal Weighted Envelope Spectrum (TWES) towards the passive acoustic detection of underwater propeller
abstract: Underwater propeller noise is the primary source of radiated noise from surface ships and underwater vehicles. Demodulation techniques such as Detection of Envelope Modulation On Noise (DEMON), narrowband demodulation, and cyclostationary analysis are the prevailing methods for detecting modulation frequencies associated with propeller rotation. However, capturing these characteristic modulation frequencies can be challenging, as the actual acoustic signals are always under extremely low Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) due to far-field measurement and intense interference noise. To tackle this challenge, this paper proposes the enhanced demodulation method—Traversal Weighted Envelope Spectrum (TWES), tailored for the passive acoustic detection of underwater propellers. First, the cyclostationary model for underwater propellers is presented, and its cyclostationary signature is derived in detail. Second, two distinct types of weighting functions are designed elaborately based on the crucial indicator—Frequency-domain Correlated Kurtosis (FCK): one that relies on prior knowledge of the target frequency, and another that operates without it. On this basis, the Adaptive Traversal Weighted Envelope Spectrum (ATWES) and the Optimal Traversal Weighted Envelope Spectrum (OTWES) are constructed correspondingly for situations without or with prior knowledge of target frequency, respectively. Ultimately, the effectiveness of ATWES and OTWES is validated by simulation signals and experimental data from the jet pump in water tunnel and the propeller in open-water area, and the comparison with state-of-the-art demodulation methods verifies the superiority of the proposed TWES.

title: Mapping model of structure nonlinearity and feedrate for predicting chatter stability in robotic milling
abstract: The study presents an innovative method for predicting stability lobe diagrams (SLDs) by explicitly incorporating the nonlinear dynamics of robotic milling systems. A frequency-domain decomposition (FDD)-based technique has been devised to systematically identify a comprehensive set of nonlinear frequency response functions (FRFs), from which a systematic mapping relationship between modal parameters, cutting forces, and feedrate is developed. Through this mapping, the complex governing equation of robotic milling is subsequently transformed into a more tractable form to predict SLDs. The significant advancement lies in that a decoupled formulation between modal parameters and excitation forces is established for the first time, thereby simplifying SLD analysis. It also offers the following two advantages over existing methods: (i) enhanced sensitivity in identifying the feedrate-dependent transition between regenerative chatter (RC) and low-frequency chatter (LFC), and (ii) substantial enhancement in the prediction accuracy of SLDs. Experimental results demonstrate that increasing feedrate shifts the RC-LFC transition point toward higher spindle speed regions, with more distinct variation patterns under strong-stiffness conditions. The proposed method achieves an average prediction accuracy of 89.48%, thereby effectively verifying its capability to enhance both the sensitivity and reliability of SLD predictions in robotic milling processes.

title: Optimal design of a tuned rotational inertial damper for mitigating torsional vibrations in offshore floating wind turbine drivetrains
abstract: The expansion of offshore floating wind turbines (OFWTs) into deeper waters exposes drivetrain systems to harsher environmental excitations and stronger platform-shaft couplings. Under these conditions, mitigating torsional drivetrain vibrations becomes essential to reducing operational stresses and preventing costly failures. This study integrates a tuned rotational inertia damper (TRID), inspired by passive tuned mass damper principles, into a coupled aero-hydro-elastic-servo model for the OC3-Hywind spar-type OFWT to control the drivetrain torsional loads. The TRID’s performance is evaluated across different installation positions, inertia ratios, and empirical formulas, while robustness is further assessed under both diverse wind and wave conditions and wind and wave misalignment scenarios. The results reveal that installing the TRID near the generator, where torsional energy is concentrated, achieves optimal vibration reduction. An inertia ratio of approximately 2% proves most effective overall, enhancing damping in high- and intermediate-speed stages, while higher ratios offer stability benefits in the low-speed stage. The study on different formulas indicates that, compared to the gear loads in the low-speed and intermediate-speed stages, the high-speed stage gear loads are more sensitive to adjustments in TRID parameters. Furthermore, the TRID consistently exhibits robust suppression under both diverse wind and wave conditions and wind and wave misalignment scenarios. Near rated wind speeds, it achieves the most notable load reductions. Under large wind and wave misalignment angles, the mitigation effect becomes more pronounced.
