Order spectra and Fourier analysis were conducted at key operational points, and orbit patterns were visualized through whirl plots to capture changes in rotor motion across a full range of speeds. The results reveal that elevated oil temperature markedly lowers the bifurcation threshold, causing nonlinear instabilities—marked by earlier onset of complex, multi-loop orbits—at reduced speeds. These transitions are dominated by two principal subsynchronous spectral components, Sub 1 (cylindrical and conical modes) and Sub 2 (translational and bending modes), whose evolution is mapped in detail using both spectral and orbit-based methods. A distinctive trend toward thermal saturation in the lubrication system was identified, as outlet oil temperature increases plateau at higher inlet temperatures, indicating a thermal energy absorption limit. Comparative analysis demonstrated that the system’s dynamic response is highly sensitive to both viscosity and supply pressure, with higher temperatures and lower viscosities amplifying instability and orbit complexity. Filtered vibration signals provided consistent results with displacement data, validating their use for practical bifurcation detection. By combining advanced order-domain diagnostics with direct orbit visualization, this study establishes clear experimental benchmarks for understanding turbocharger instability mechanisms, justifies the focus on the dominant subsynchronous modes, and highlights the importance of oil rheology and thermal effects in governing rotor dynamics. These insights support the development of improved predictive models and informed maintenance or control strategies for higher efficiency and reliability in turbocharger systems.

title: Wearable up-frequency energy harvester based on a novel unidirectional excitation mechanism
abstract: A novel unidirectional excitation mechanism (UEM) operating under harmonic excitation is proposed in this paper, which has two advantages, one is the long effective working time, and the other is to overcome the deceleration process of harmonic motion. The UEM mainly consists of a belt drive and a lead screw nut drive. Thus, this paper adopts the coupling method of the gear drive and the belt drive to realize frequency increase, which actualizes the up-frequency conversion from the slow swing to the high-speed rotation. Based on different movements of the UEM-based energy harvester (UEMEH) under the excitation of the human arm swing, the dynamic piecewise model is established and makes the calculation results more accurate. To investigate the effect of the wearable energy harvester on the human body, the reaction torque of the harvester driving by the upper arm swing is calculated. Since the reaction torque is far less than the output torque of the upper arm swing, the results show that the UEMEH is much more suitable for human motion, even strenuous motion. Comparing the output characteristics of the UEMEH with the None-UEM frequency-up energy harvester (NUEH), it is proved that the UEMEH has better power generation performance under harmonic excitation. Finally, the power generation efficiency of the UEMEH is tested under human walking and running. When the subjects are in a running state, the average output power of UEMEH could reach 20.52 mW, and the maximum energy conversion efficiency is as high as 70.88%.

title: Full-cycle self-sustaining wireless jet engine shaft monitoring via rotor-conformal thermoelectrics
abstract: Self-sustaining monitoring of jet engine shafts revolutionizes efficiency by eliminating power and wiring constraints. Among self-sustaining power sources, thermoelectric generators can harvest waste heat both during operation and after shutdown, enabling all-state monitoring. However, thermoelectric energy harvesting remains inadequate under geometric constraints and thermal fluctuations induced by the operation-to-shutdown transition, hindering reliable full-cycle monitoring. Here, we propose a full-cycle self-sustaining rotor monitoring concept that combines a sail-shaped rotor-conformal thermoelectric generator (SR-TEG) for enhanced thermal harvesting with an energy-scalable sampling scheme for stable operation. The SR-TEG is integrated into the shaft to efficiently capture low-grade heat energy consistently during engine operation or idle. The sensing and wireless transmission modules are simultaneously powered, forming the rotor-conformal thermoelectric-powered wireless monitoring system (RT-WMS). Furthermore, a fluid-thermal-electrical multi-physics coupling model for the SR-TEG is developed to reveal the enhanced energy harvesting mechanism. Simulation results show a 108% increase in power output by introducing the sail-shaped thermal structure. The energy-scalable sampling system adjusts monitoring frequency according to the available energy to ensure prolonged operation in dynamic thermal conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that the RT-WMS not only enables wireless temperature/pressure monitoring during the engine operation, but also sustains the post-shutdown operation for up to ∼ 1000 s, even as the available temperature gradient decreases to 4°C. This study demonstrates an integrated thermoelectric energy harvesting system with autonomous power regulation, enabling self-sustaining monitoring of critical jet engine components across full operational cycles.

title: Multiple Rotary Nonlinear Energy Sinks for vibration control of flexible beams
abstract: Nonlinear Energy Sinks (NES) are known to dissipate energy through a nonlinearly coupled secondary mass, providing vibration mitigation over a broad frequency range. Among various NES configurations, a rotary NES is a horizontal pendulum that introduces nonlinear inertial coupling to the primary structure. Here, the use of multiple rotary NES devices is employed for passive vibration control of a simply supported beam. The beam undergoing bending motion is a flexible structure representative of a wide range of engineering applications. The reduced equations of motion derived via the Galerkin method are employed for numerical investigations. Reference NES designs are obtained through an optimization scheme for one to three devices attached to the beam. The results indicate that the rotary NES can achieve multi-mode vibration control, with performance improving with increasing number of devices. The three-RNES design could reduce peak vibration by over 80\% for a reference beam resonance. The full dynamic characterization shows that although the devices can exhibit complex, aperiodic oscillations, they remain robust in mitigating vibrations across a wide range of initial conditions.

title: Bearing fault diagnosis via topological data analysis: Strategic feature selection and algorithm-dependent performance under sample-size constraints
abstract: Vibration-based bearing fault diagnosis under severe sample-size constraints (n < 100) presents fundamental challenges in feature extraction and classification. This work develops a systematic methodology combining topological data analysis (TDA) with classical time-domain features, validated on laboratory (n=51, 30 kHz, SKF 6206) and industrial (Paderborn, 64 kHz, FAG 6203) datasets under strict bearing-wise generalization. Strategic 8-dimensional Classical+H 0 feature selection achieves perfect classification (100.0% ± 0.0%) on the laboratory dataset using Support Vector Machines with radial basis function kernel, significantly improving over classical features alone (94.2%, p = 0 . 046 , Cohen’s d = 1 . 21 ). Cross-dataset validation confirms consistent performance trends, with SVM achieving 73.3% accuracy under industrial conditions, outperforming metric learning (Metric LDA: 46.7%) and tree-based ensembles. Kernel ablation experiments demonstrate algorithm-dependent exploitation of topological features, with nonlinear kernels achieving up to 40% higher accuracy than linear classifiers. Correlation analysis quantifies partial redundancy between classical and topological features ( r = − 0 . 883 ), yet residual geometric information remains discriminative under nonlinear projection. Multi-window extraction stabilizes feature estimation, reducing classification variance by 14 × . Results establish practical deployment strategies for small-sample diagnostics, demonstrating that topological features provide complementary geometric invariants exploitable by appropriate nonlinear classifiers.

title: A bidirectional transfer learning method for tool life prediction in machine tools and robots based on the spatio-temporal features of multi-modal sensors and physics-informed constraints
abstract: Accurate prediction of remaining tool life is essential for developing intelligent machining systems in robotic milling. To address the challenges posed by pose variations, cross-equipment heterogeneity, and multi-modal signal integration, we propose a fine-tuning-based transfer learning framework named M−BLCAP−FTN, which integrates adaptive feature selection and physical information constraint mechanisms. The framework first enhances data quality using a combination of interquartile range analysis and wavelet soft-threshold denoising. Discriminative features are then selected via the maximum relevance and minimum redundancy algorithm. A BiLSTM model with Channel Attention is constructed to extract deeply coupled spatiotemporal features from multi-sensor signals. Furthermore, the incorporation of physical consistency and monotonicity loss terms ensures that model outputs adhere to underlying tool wear laws. By leveraging fine-tuning-based transfer learning, the proposed method enables effective knowledge migration from the CNC machine tools to robotic machining platforms. Without compromising robotic flexibility and while maintaining low implementation costs, our approach achieves high-accuracy cross-domain tool life prediction. Experimental results on public milling datasets and a robotic milling platform validate the effectiveness and superiority of the method. The RMSEs on public milling datasets, pose-varying robotic trials, and cross-equipment bidirectional transfer are as low as 0.0111, 0.0286, and 0.0277, respectively, demonstrating robust predictive performance.

title: Offline real-time hybrid testing based on adaptive-force-correction multitask time-history iteration
abstract: Real-time hybrid testing (RTHT) is a reliable and efficient experimental method for evaluating the dynamic performances of engineering structures. However, it exhibits contradictory problems associated with the real-time loading of experimental substructures and non-real-time high-accuracy calculation of numerical substructures. Offline RTHT based on time-history iteration (THI) has recently been proposed to solve these problems. However, this method becomes unstable when the experimental substructure contributes a high proportion of the system’s damping and stiffness, especially if multiple experimental substructures are involved. To solve this problem, this paper proposes an offline RTHT based on adaptive-force-correction multitask THI (AFCMTHI). The proposed method updates the damping and stiffness of the surrogate model using all previously measured data after each iteration of loading and then progressively corrects the equations of motion based on the velocity and displacement differences between the numerical and experimental substructures. Furthermore, this method realizes the individual loading of multiple experimental substructures by performing multiple rounds of the overall restart technique on a single agent specimen. The accuracy and convergence of the proposed method are validated through numerical simulations and experimental tests on a typical three-story steel-frame structure with multiple dampers. The results show that, when the experimental substructure’s contribution to the structural response is relatively low, the offline RTHT based on AFCMTHI achieves a higher convergence efficiency when compared to the offline RTHT based on THI. Specifically, the numerical simulation results show that the number of iterations required for achieving a root mean square deviation (RMSD) below 0.1 decreases, from more than five to only three, for the offline RTHT based on AFCMTHI. The experimental results demonstrate that, to achieve an RMSD below 0.2, the offline RTHT based on AFCMTHI requires one less iteration than the offline RTHT based on THI, across different conditions. When the experimental substructure accounts for a large proportion of the structural response, the offline RTHT based on THI becomes unstable, whereas the offline RTHT based on AFCMTHI maintains stable convergence, with response correlation coefficients exceeding 95%, under all conditions.

title: Rayleigh distribution-driven adaptive Gaussian colored noise filtering method
abstract: Advanced denoising methods primarily emphasize the regularity of fault signals under varying operating conditions, whereas background noise is generally characterized by its randomness, thereby limiting denoising performance. To address this limitation, a statistical criterion is established to demonstrate that sufficiently narrowband Gaussian colored noise (GCN) follows a Rayleigh distribution. Driven by this criterion, an adaptive GCN filtering method is proposed, comprising a spectrum segmentation module, a distribution discrimination module (DisDM), and a filtering module. The spectrum segmentation module adaptively provides narrowband sub-signals, while the DisDM integrates locally weighted regression, linear transformation, and a chi-square test to robustly identify Rayleigh-distributed noise components. Finite impulse response filters are then constructed to remove the identified GCN components. The advantages of the proposed method are verified through simulation signals and three cases. Results demonstrate that the noise reduction effect reaches 67.45% for a simulated signal with a signal-to-noise of −8 dB. In the vibration, acoustic and acoustic emission signals, the proposed method can accurately retain the fault information while mitigating narrow-band noise interference. Compared with the advanced denoising methods, the proposed method has a larger SNR and a higher spectrum peak.

title: Higher-order transmissibility and its linear approximation for in-service crack identification in train wheelset axles
abstract: In-service structural health monitoring is a so far rarely exploited, yet potent option for early-stage crack detection and identification in train wheelset axles. This procedure is non-trivial to enforce on the basis of a purely data-driven approach and typically requires the adoption of numerical, e.g. finite element-based simulation schemes of the dynamic behavior of these axles. Damage in this particular case can be formulated as a breathing crack problem, which further complicates simulation by introducing response-dependent nonlinearities into the picture. In this study, first, a new crack detection feature based on higher-order harmonics of the breathing crack is proposed, termed Higher-Order Transmissibility (HOTr). Next, a reduced-order model is developed by introducing a first-order perturbation-based approximation of the essentially nonlinear crack contact forces. This yields a sequence of linear frequency-domain problems that approximate the higher-order harmonic response with substantial computational speedup, while retaining the damage-sensitive nonlinear features required for crack identification. The accuracy of the proposed method in reproducing the delivered HOTr is compared against the nonlinear simulation model. The obtained results suggest that the approximation of the HOTr can significantly reduce the computational burden by eliminating the need for an iterative solution of the governing nonlinear equation of motion while maintaining a high level of accuracy when compared to the reference model. Finally, the robustness and effectiveness of the proposed indicators are systematically demonstrated through noise-contaminated simulations. Results advocate the great potential of the proposed method for adoption in in-service damage identification for wheelset axles, feasibly within a near real-time context.

title: Fast and accurate decomposition of overlapping Lamb wave modes in metallic and composite structures
abstract: Accurate separation of overlapping guided wave modes is critical for reliable predictions by most damage detection algorithms for ultrasonic guided wave (UGW)-based structural health monitoring (SHM) of thin-walled structures. This article introduces a novel, computationally efficient method for automatic separation and accurate reconstruction of individual wave modes, isolation of damage-scattered wave packets, and elimination of boundary reflections from multimodal UGW signals in plates, actuated and sensed by surface-mounted piezoelectric wafer active sensors. The proposed methodology leverages the time–frequency precision of the synchrosqueezed wavelet transform (SWT) and integrates it with an image smoothing process involving Gaussian filtering, morphological operations, and the watershed segmentation to automatically identify individual mode boundaries in the time–frequency representation. The segmented wave modes are then isolated using a simple yet effective binary masking technique and reconstructed via inverse SWT. This method eliminates the need for predefined threshold parameters and significantly reduces computation time. For complex signals exhibiting strong interference among multiple modes and reflections, it achieves accurate results in just 8 s compared to 766 s with a region-growing approach. Numerical and experimental studies on aluminium and laminated composite plates, with and without damage, confirm the method’s robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, making it highly suitable for real-time guided wave analysis in practical SHM applications.

title: Actual kinematics-based identification of tool runout parameters in milling using measurable tooth-level responses
abstract: Tool runout alters the actual tool rotational center, which influences both the rotational radius and angular spacing of teeth relative to the spindle center, thereby changing the material removal process and significantly affecting both processing quality and tool lifespan. Traditional techniques for determining tool runout, regardless of whether they rely on static measurements or force analysis, often assume uniform pitch angles around the geometric axis and thus neglect the pitch-angle variations caused by actual rotational kinematics. This study presents a method for identifying tool runout parameters by considering the spindle-centered pitch distribution, utilizing measurable tooth-level responses, including actual tooth rotational kinematics, single tooth milling-based pitch measurements, and maximum rotational radii identified from slot milling tests. A kinematic model is developed to relate the theoretical pitch angle (with respect to the tool center) and the measured pitch angle (relative to the spindle center), along with rotational radii, through a geometric triangular configuration. Based on this model, analytical equations are derived linking the tool’s theoretical radius, maximum rotational radius, and runout offset, resulting in an explicit solution for identifying tool runout parameters. The maximum rotational radius is determined from slot widths measured during slot milling operations, while actual pitch angles are extracted by correlating tooth positions with their corresponding force signals in single-tooth milling tests. Experimental validations in both micro- and conventional-milling processes demonstrate that the identified tool runout parameters exhibit strong consistency with traditional methods. This validates the precision of the proposed approach and highlights its independence from specific cutting force magnitudes, ensuring robustness and applicability across various milling scenarios.

title: Acoustic-force fusion with stacking ensemble learning for wear recognition of pyramid abrasive belts under variable grinding conditions
abstract: In recent years, pyramid-structured abrasive belts have gained widespread application in the precision grinding of complex free-form surfaces, such as the edges of aircraft engine blades, owing to their excellent self-sharpening properties and heat dissipation capabilities. However, during operation, the belt wear condition undergoes continuous evolution, exerting a cumulative impact on machining quality. Currently, achieving accurate identification of the belt wear state remains challenging under complex combinations of process parameters. To address this challenge, this study develops a mechanism-informed acoustic–force fusion framework specifically tailored to the wear evolution of pyramid-structured abrasive belts, employing stacking ensemble learning for decision-level integration. Through full-life-cycle experiments on TC4 titanium alloy, the percentage of mass loss was determined as the quantitative indicator for the pyramid belt wear, and statistical features sensitive to belt wear were extracted from acoustic and force signals. The proposed model achieved an average recognition accuracy of 97.93% across the eight wear stages defined under fixed process parameters, surpassing the performance of both single base learners and single-signal models. In cross-process parameter validation experiments involving varying normal forces and belt speeds, the model maintained a minimum accuracy exceeding 75% under unknown conditions, serving as a conservative lower bound for generalization and providing preliminary reference and risk indication for new operating regimes. Furthermore, a parameter-distance approach was employed to analyze the quantitative relationship between process parameter variations and model accuracy degradation.

title: A hybrid two-stage Model Order Reduction framework for large-scale structural problems
abstract: This paper presents a hybrid two-stage Model Order Reduction framework tailored for large-scale industrial finite element problems in structural dynamics. The proposed approach combines a preliminary reduction step using a Component Mode Synthesis (CMS) method with a second reduction stage employing a state-space based approach. By leveraging the complementary strengths of these families of techniques, the framework ensures accurate preservation of input/output behavior, making it particularly well-suited for applications like transfer path analysis and control system design. For the CMS stage, the study investigates the classical Craig-Bampton method and the Enhanced Craig-Bampton technique, introducing an alternative primal assembly strategy to enable the use of the latter method with separate finite element models of substructures. The state-space reduction stage explores both modal truncation and balanced truncation, with the latter demonstrating superior performance in representing critical input/output dynamics. This hybrid scheme is designed for industrial scenarios requiring reduced-order models of large-scale structures as a prodromal step for controller design or transfer path analysis. The hybrid framework is finally applied to a large-scale finite element model derived from the European Space Agency’s Micro Vibration Measurement System facility, showcasing its effectiveness and practical applicability.

title: A new refined modeling method for rotating inter-shaft elastic support considering preload effects: Theoretical and experimental validation
abstract: The rotating inter-shaft elastic support effectively mitigates strain energy concentration at critical speeds in flexible dual-rotor systems. In-depth research on the modeling of such systems is therefore of significant importance. To address this, the influence of preload force is analyzed, and the characteristic matrix of the rotating inter-shaft elastic support is derived using Hamilton’s principle. Based on the Lagrange equation, a dynamic model of the dual-rotor system with the rotating inter-shaft elastic support was established. The dynamic characteristics were then investigated using a combination of analytical calculation methods and Newmark-β numerical method, and the model’s validity was further verified through experiments. The results show that under normal circumstances, the rotating inter-shaft elastic support provides an additional stiffness to the dual-rotor system. In the case of unidirectional preload loss, the translational stiffness of the rotating inter-shaft elastic support decays, and the generalized force term is introduced in the angular freedom. This causes a change in the fundamental frequency amplitude of the rotor in the dual-rotor system, and the change is significant in the critical speed state. The error between the calculated and experimental values of the critical characteristics of the dual-rotor system with rotating inter-shaft elastic support is less than 3%, offering improved accuracy over the conventional single-stiffness modeling approach. As the pretension loss rate increases, the amplitude of the low-pressure (LP) rotor vibration response in the critical state shows a trend of first decreasing and then increasing. The study reveals the dynamic mechanism of the rotating inter-shaft elastic support, providing a theoretical basis for the dynamic design of flexible dual-rotor systems.

title: Corrigendum to “FD-MVLLM: Fault diagnosis based on multimodal vibration data and large language model for bearing system” [Mech. Syst. Sig. Process. 239 (2025) 113226]
Deep learning-based dynamic load reconstruction and localization: A novel multi-task learning framework with physical distance-aware graph attention
abstract: Direct measurement of dynamic loads is often infeasible due to deployment constraints or harsh environments, necessitating indirect inference through responses. Traditional methods face limitations due to reliance on precise modal parameters, while existing data-driven approaches often decouple reconstruction and localization tasks, ignoring their inherent coupling. This paper proposes a novel multi-task learning (MTL) framework for dynamic load identification that synergizes graph attention network (GAT) with physical distance-aware attention mechanism. The graph structure representing the dynamic load identification issue is constructed and the GAT layer-based shared feature encoder is introduced to process spatially distributed sensor response as node features. This design utilizes task-specific attention weights that facilitates cross-task knowledge transfer while preserving the uniqueness of each task, reconstruction and localization. Furthermore, physical distance between the sensor and the load locations is embedded as constraints of attention weight learning, which leads to the adaptive narrowing of solution space and the improvement of localization accuracy. A series of numerical and experimental scenarios are designed to validate the performance of the method. The findings demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve satisfactory outcomes in both reconstruction and localization tasks while circumventing the intricate process of modeling dynamic characteristics. Moreover, the proposed method is insensitive to sensor arrangement and can function even when the response data sources of the training and testing phases are different, rendering it practical in engineering scenarios.

title: A multi-directional magnetorheological semi-active inerter with self-powering capability
abstract: Semi-active inerters can modulate inertance and are effective for vibration control under time-varying excitation frequencies. However, conventional inerters and semi-active inerters are predominantly single-axis devices, whereas real structural vibrations occur simultaneously in multiple directions. This mismatch reduces effectiveness under multi-directional excitation and often requires multiple uncoupled devices. In addition, most semi-active vibration control systems rely on external power sources, limiting applicability in power-loss scenarios such as earthquakes or remote installations. To address these limitations, this paper presents a multi-directional magnetorheological semi-active inerter capable of generating tuneable inertial forces with self-powered semi-active control. The inerter employs a gimbal structure to convert planar translation into orthogonal rotational motion of two variable-inertia flywheels, enabling multi-directional modulation of inertance. Meanwhile, two energy harvesting units are also integrated into the inerter, enabling self-powered semi-active operation. A nonlinear two-degree-of-freedom inertance model is derived using the Euler–Lagrange formulation and combined with a bilinear hysteresis representation of the MRVIF. Harmonic characterisation experiments confirm directional invariance and controllable inertance modulation along both axes, with harvested energy sufficient to switch inertance states. Vibration control demonstrations under multi-directional random excitation show reductions in peak relative displacement and RMS acceleration compared with passive configurations. The results demonstrate a self-powered, multi-directional, semi-active inerter exhibiting configuration- and state-dependent inertial behaviour, contributing to the emerging class of nonlinear and variable inertial elements in structural dynamics.

title: Robust momentum conjugate gradient filter with M-estimation for nonlinear active noise control
abstract: The conjugate gradient (CG) filter exhibits great potential for nonlinear active noise control (ANC) due to its efficiency and convergence properties. However, its performance may deteriorate under nonlinear dynamics and non-Gaussian impulsive noise. To address these issues, this paper proposes a M-estimate-based modified CG method within the filtered-s framework, employing a functional link artificial neural network (FLANN) as the nonlinear modeling module. The proposed method, termed as the FsMCG algorithm, makes three major contributions: (1) integration of the M-estimate robust cost function with the Huber weighting strategy to enhance robustness against impulsive noise, (2) incorporation of a momentum term into the filter weight update process, which accelerates convergence and reduces the risk of being trapped in local minima by leveraging past gradients, and (3) introduction of a Sigmoid-inspired nonlinear modulator during the gradient update process, adding nonlinearity to enable more robust filter weight adjustments, particularly in non-Gaussian or nonlinear environments. Simulation results confirm that the proposed FsMCG method achieves significant improvements in convergence speed, robustness and nonlinear noise reduction capability compared to existing techniques.

title: Editorial Board
Efficient model-assisted probability of detection in guided-wave structural health monitoring systems
abstract: Traditional methods for obtaining probability of detection curves in structural health monitoring systems are often costly in terms of budget, and time. To address these limitations, we propose a novel computational framework that uses gradient- and Hessian-enhanced surrogate modeling for estimating model-assisted probability of detection curves in guided-wave structural health monitoring systems. The framework leverages the hypercomplex automatic differentiation method combined with the spectral finite element method to compute highly accurate derivatives of wave propagation phenomena with respect to model parameters. These derivatives form the basis for two derivative-enhanced surrogate modeling approaches. The first, Taylor series expansion, approximates model-assisted probability of detection curves under nominal conditions, offering a computationally efficient alternative to traditional simulations. The second, gradient-Hessian Enhanced Kriging, constructs a surrogate model capable of predicting model-assisted probability of detection curves under varying operational conditions, enabling efficient transfer of probability of detection curves across scenarios without additional simulations. Two application examples are presented: an academic example with a detailed step-by-step description, and an application study of a plate with a localized through-thickness defect detected using two piezoelectric transducers in a pitch-and-catch configuration. Our framework significantly reduces the computational cost by over 30% in obtaining model-assisted probability of detection curves while maintaining equivalent accuracy to traditional methods. Additionally, incorporating gradient and Hessian information improves surrogate model accuracy and reduces training sample requirements by a factor of two compared to derivative-free models. This approach offers an efficient solution for generating model-assisted probability of detection curves and facilitates the development of probability of detection transfer functions with negligible additional computational cost.

title: Physics-guided neural network for force identification in component-based transfer path analysis
abstract: In component-based transfer path analysis (TPA), the accuracy of estimated results depends on the treatment of accelerance matrix inversion for equivalent force identification. However, the measured accelerance often exhibits significant uncertainty, even though it should satisfy the reciprocity condition, which substantially degrades TPA accuracy. Conventional regularization methods, which use uncertain accelerance, mainly focus on mitigating ill-conditioning without effectively resolving the problem. In this study, an innovative physics-guided neural network model was proposed to replace the conventional matrix inversion process in component-based TPA. The proposed model acts as a trainable version of TPA capable of compensating for uncertainties in nondriving-point accelerance. Its architecture is designed to identify the equivalent forces at the hidden layer, and tailored training strategies improve estimation accuracy. Physical information, such as the driving-point accelerance and noise transfer function, is incorporated into the model to preserve the physical characteristics of the system during training. In addition, the output layer is virtually expanded by exploiting the property that the equivalent forces remain invariant to modifications in the passive part stiffness, thereby improving the accuracy of the estimated forces. The proposed method was validated through a numerical simulation in which intended uncertainty was imposed on the known accelerance, and the estimated equivalent forces closely matched the references despite the uncertainty. Furthermore, the application of a road noise vehicle experiment revealed that the suggested neural network-based method surpasses conventional inversion-based methods in accuracy and offers a reliable framework for component-based TPA in practical applications.

title: Head-tracking active road noise control by real-time path adaptation using neural networks
abstract: Conventional active road noise control (ARNC) with virtual sensing requires accurate secondary path estimates and observation filters. However, these paths are dependent on the listener’s head position, and the use of fixed models results in modeling errors and consequent degradation in control performance. To overcome this limitation, this study proposed a head-tracking ARNC (HARNC) framework that uses neural networks (NNs) to update secondary path estimates and observation filters in real time based on the listener’s head position. In addition, a prefilter-based initialization scheme was introduced to accelerate the convergence of the control filter after head movements. NN models for estimating secondary paths and observation filters were trained using a dataset measured at multiple listener head positions and integrated into a virtual sensing ARNC algorithm. The proposed HARNC framework was validated through simulations and experiments, including a comparative assessment of prefilter initialization and path update strategies. Simulation results evaluated over 30–500 Hz showed that compared with conventional ARNC using fixed paths, the proposed HARNC achieved an additional noise reduction of 3.02 dBA on average. It was also compared with look-up table and interpolation-based updating strategies and outperformed them in terms of path estimation accuracy and noise attenuation in ARNC simulations. The framework was further validated through real-vehicle experiments, confirming its effectiveness in achieving robust ARNC performance under realistic driving conditions.

title: Electric bus loudness time-series prediction via singular value decomposition and Hash-based long short-term memory with enhanced features
abstract: To address the issue that traditional offline prediction methods struggle to capture the dynamic characteristics of sound quality during continuous conditions, this paper employs loudness as the fundamental psychoacoustic parameter and constructs a six-dimensional loudness feature vector as the model input. The multi-scale vector derived from the original signal, global frequency-domain enhanced signal and time–frequency enhanced signal, with the latter two generated by combining Laplacian operator with prominence ratio. To further improve the loudness time-series prediction accuracy and efficiency, an improved long short-term memory (LSTM) based on singular value decomposition (SVD) and Hash mapping (SVD-Hash-LSTM) is proposed. This approach is achieved by performing low-rank compression via SVD on the input weights and applying Hash mapping with linear reconstruction for dimension reduction to the hidden-state weights, while theoretically explaining its gradient propagation mechanism and computational complexity reduction. Electric bus interior noise tests demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms traditional LSTM and SVD-LSTM in terms of prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. Consequently, the low computational error observed in the parameter transfer from loudness to sharpness validates its effectiveness in multi-parameter collaborative assessment, thereby providing a feasible technical approach for the objective analysis of time-series data in vehicle sound quality.

title: Energy finite element method-based topology optimization for aircraft control surfaces under thermo-vibrational coupling with experimental validation
abstract: The investigation of high-frequency dynamic optimization for high-speed aircraft structures operating under coupled thermo-vibrational conditions continues to represent a critical research frontier in contemporary aerospace structural engineering. The energy finite element method (EFEM) has established itself as a predominant computational technique for high-frequency vibration analysis in complex structural systems, owing to its computational efficiency and its ability to provide clear representations of energy density distributions. A substantial scientific gap remains in practical applications, as the combination of the EFEM and topology optimization has yet to be achieved for mitigating high-frequency vibrations in thermally loaded structures. To address this research gap, the present study develops an EFEM-based topology optimization framework specifically designed for mitigating high-frequency vibrations in typical control surface structures operating under thermal environments. Fundamental techniques, including thermo-vibrational coupling, solution algorithms, optimization models, and sensitivity analysis, were investigated under thermal conditions. For the first time, the proposed coupled thermo-vibrational topology optimization framework is applied to optimize typical control surface structures. The analysis shows that the method enhances the dynamic performance of the typical control surface structures by 11.28% to 66.08% under thermal conditions, with experimental validation confirming its efficacy in improving structural dynamics. The proposed framework exhibits strong extensibility, allowing other researchers to apply it to curved surfaces, complex spatial structures, or composite materials in various engineering fields.

title: Physics-guided generative data augmentation for vision-based signal processing under class-imbalanced conditions in directed energy deposition monitoring system
abstract: • Addresses signal processing limits from class-imbalanced DED molten pool signals. • Physics-guided CVAE-GAN synthesizes high-fidelity visual signals. • Thermodynamic losses enforce spatial and spectral signal consistency. • Augmented data improves decision boundaries for rare defect detection. • Validated on a real-world aerospace component with complex geometry. Vision-based signal processing is critical in metal additive manufacturing (AM), particularly within Directed Energy Deposition (DED), for capturing the rapid thermo-fluid dynamics essential for detecting process instabilities and ensuring structural integrity. While DED operates as an open, inherently non-stationary system and molten pool visual signals carry rich spatiotemporal information, effective processing is fundamentally constrained by the scarcity of anomalous events relative to stable deposition. This data sparsity leads to imbalanced training sets that fail to represent the full spectrum of transient process dynamics, causing classifiers to misclassify rare but critical failure modes and degrading overall monitoring performance. Crucially, conventional data augmentation techniques, being agnostic to the underlying physics, often introduce signal artefacts that violate governing thermodynamic constraints, thereby degrading the physical validity of the training data. To bridge the gap between data-driven feature learning and physical principles, this study proposes a physics-guided generative data augmentation framework based on a Conditional Variational Autoencoder–Generative Adversarial Network (CVAE-GAN). The framework explicitly learns the intrinsic physical manifold of the process, incorporating thermodynamically motivated loss functions to ensure the synthesis of high-fidelity, physically coherent molten pool visual signals. Validation through both spectral analysis and downstream classification confirms that the augmented signals preserve essential morphological and textural properties while significantly improving the decision boundaries of sequence classifiers. A case study on a complex aerospace component demonstrates the framework’s practical utility in enhancing robust in-situ monitoring under varying geometric conditions. By addressing the sparse representation of critical dynamics through a physics-aware methodology, this work offers a reliable pathway for advanced signal processing in data-scarce engineering systems.

title: A method for discontinuous data repair and precise health monitoring of rolling bearings integrating particle filtering and digital twin
abstract: In real-time data acquisition systems for bearings, sudden temperature surges and mechanical shocks under high-speed operating conditions tend to cause intermittent sensor failures, leading to critical data loss. Prolonged data loss not only reduces the accuracy of feature extraction but may also lead to misjudgments of health status, endangering equipment safety. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel digital twin modeling method for rolling bearings. This method integrates the Particle Filter Model (PFM) with digital twin technology to repair missing data and accurately monitor bearing health status. Specifically, a high-fidelity bearing dynamics model is constructed to fully characterize its evolution throughout the life cycle, providing a data foundation for the PFM. Based on this, a defect prediction method for discontinuous data is proposed. Relying on the particle filtering framework, this method can effectively integrate historical states and available observations when measurement data are missing or intermittent to accurately predict defect propagation trajectories. Furthermore, a digital twin framework based on Time-cycle-Wasserstein-GAN (TCW-GAN) is designed. By establishing dynamic mappings between measured and virtual data domains, this framework drives the digital twin model to adaptively match bearing condition features under discontinuous operating conditions, significantly enhancing adaptability and enabling precise real-time health monitoring. Experimental validation shows that the proposed method successfully addresses the issue of temporal discontinuity, restores physical continuity, and that the resulting high-fidelity digital twin model provides reliable support for bearing health monitoring.

title: Nonlinear behavior of passive heave compensator: modeling, experiment validation and investigation
abstract: Passive Heave Compensators (PHCs) decouple payload motion from the carrier vessel, expanding the operational weather window and reducing operation risk in ocean engineering. Their reliability, however, hinges on predictive models that capture nonlinear dynamics. Existing models often overlook key hysteresis sources, and are rarely validated comprehensively. Moreover, the errors introduced by commonly used pneumatic state models are seldom quantified, undermining response prediction and parameter optimization. To address these gaps, we develop a nonlinear coupled dynamic model that consistently reproduces the hysteresis observed in both motion and pressure responses of PHCs. The model integrates the effects of sealing friction, inertial throttling of the working fluid, and gas diversion with compressible pneumatic behavior, thereby linking the physical mechanisms responsible for hysteresis to the measurable system outputs. This explicit coupling, together with a systematic audit of alternative modeling assumptions, directly targets the principal error sources that limit prior approaches and strengthens the basis for design and optimization. An extensive experimental campaign under harmonic excitations with varied amplitudes and frequencies validates the model. Simulations closely match measured responses, achieving accuracy above 90%, and faithfully reproduce hysteresis loops and nonlinear parameter trends. The study further clarifies how excitation conditions and design parameters shape compensation performance, highlighting the necessity of stiffness–damping matching. Notably, we identify “critical design zones” prone to resonance or performance degradation, which should be avoided to ensure robust, high-performance PHC operation across sea states. This work provides validated models and data to guide engineering design and enhance adaptability in complex offshore environments.

title: A thermal-aware, data-driven strategy for optimal sensor layout in cutting tools
abstract: Effective temperature monitoring of cutting tools is essential for machining precision and tool life, yet it is often constrained by limited options for sensor placement. This paper proposes a thermal-aware, data-driven method for optimizing sparse sensor layouts to monitor temperature fields. The approach first extracts low-dimensional feature modes of the field via proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), and then integrates them using a thermal-aware strategy that jointly considers nodal mean temperature, temperature gradient, and modal spatial coefficients. This enables adaptive prioritization and spatial constraints for sensor placement, ensuring focused coverage of thermally critical regions such as high-temperature and high-gradient zones. Comparisons with genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, and greedy POD methods demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves higher reconstruction accuracy and robustness with the same limited number of sensors. Furthermore, by dividing the tool surface into three characteristic thermal zones, the study clarifies spatial placement priorities and quantifies the impact of protective distance on reconstruction error. Results indicate that 2–3 sensors are sufficient for effective field reconstruction, provided that at least one sensor is placed near the core heat source. The proposed framework offers an intelligent layout solution for tool temperature monitoring and can be extended to state estimation and field reconstruction in other complex systems.

title: Decoupling the feature manifold structure: a domain incremental method for mechanical fault diagnosis under variable rotational speeds
abstract: Fault diagnosis of typical rotating machinery is of great significance for ensuring the safe and reliable operation of mechanical equipment. Machine learning-based intelligent diagnosis methods have achieved significant progress, but most existing approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting and lack the ability to incrementally adapt to new operating conditions. To address this challenge, a domain-incremental fault diagnosis method with decoupled feature manifold structures (DFMS) is proposed for mechanical equipment operating under variable rotational speeds. In the proposed framework, although the physical fault types remain unchanged, vibration signals corresponding to the same fault exhibit significantly different data distributions under different rotational speeds, which can be interpreted as domain-dependent latent manifolds. To explicitly model these variations, vibration signals are first transformed into feature representations, and fault features acquired under different operating conditions are then mapped into fault-domain-specific latent subspaces using an autoencoder-based manifold representation. The reconstruction error is employed as a distance metric to characterize the proximity between an input feature and the corresponding fault-domain manifold. Furthermore, an adaptive weighted confusion contrast loss is designed to reduce classification ambiguity caused by manifold overlap across different domains. To alleviate catastrophic forgetting during incremental learning, a knowledge distillation loss with dynamic parameter adjustment is introduced to preserve the reconstruction-error distributions of previously learned fault-domain manifolds, and a feature distillation loss is employed to stabilize latent representations across incremental stages. The proposed DFMS method is applicable to fault diagnosis tasks under quasi-stationary operating conditions, such as constant-speed or piecewise constant-speed scenarios. Extensive experiments conducted on a gear transmission test rig and a high-speed wheelset bearing test rig demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed method for domain-incremental fault diagnosis of typical rotating machinery under variable rotational speed conditions.

title: Fault-induced dynamic response and structural reconfiguration mechanism of a six-wheeled suspension system under actuator degradation
abstract: Multi-axle ground vehicles are prone to enhanced nonlinear coupling and stochastic dynamic characteristic drift under suspension actuator degradation, leading to load redistribution imbalance and increased rollover risk. To overcome the limitations of existing fault-tolerant approaches that mainly focus on single-layer control compensation with limited cross-layer coordination, this paper proposes an adaptive dynamic framework featuring cross-layer signal-control-structure coordination to preserve stability and restore structural resilience of a six-wheeled unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) under stochastic suspension degradation. First, a stochastic actuator degradation model coupling exponential gain decay with Gaussian drift is constructed. Based on this, a dynamic fault-aware load transfer ratio (DFALTR) is proposed as a unified signal-level index. A sliding-window statistical mechanism is introduced to quantify risk progression and non-stationary load asymmetry, enabling DFALTR to serve as a risk criterion for triggering attitude control and structural-level reconfiguration. A Lyapunov-guided adaptive parameter learning mechanism (LG-APLF) is further designed to achieve risk-driven attitude control self-adjustment. Simultaneously, a risk-aware optimal force allocation (RAOFA) strategy is proposed to complete multi-objective attitude compensation under physical invariant-set constraints. When control redundancy becomes insufficient, a structural-level reconfiguration mechanism combining Variable-Scale Lightweight Particle Swarm Optimization (VSLPSO) and limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS) hybrid search is activated to dynamically adjust the middle-axle position and track width, thereby expanding the feasible dynamic domain. Simulation and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) experiments demonstrate that the proposed cross-layer framework effectively suppresses fault-induced vibrations, improves load redistribution, and restores attitude stability across multiple degradation and extreme fault scenarios, confirming its robustness, real-time feasibility, and engineering applicability in nonlinear stochastic systems.

title: Mode-Switchable acoustic metamaterial for Low-Frequency broadband absorption
abstract: Conventional impedance-based calculation models assume quasi-1D cavities and can become inaccurate in complex geometries. To address this, we propose an Effective Propagation Length Optimization (EPLO) model. By introducing a correction factor related to the actual maximum propagation path of sound waves and integrating it into the classical impedance formulation, the model enables precise prediction of the absorption spectra in irregular cavities. It also improves the calculation accuracy for conventional cavities, reducing the error from 2.69% to 0.54%. Based on this theory, we further design and fabricate a mode-switchable acoustic metastructure with serial–parallel tunability. The structure allows switching between cavity configurations, enabling a serial mode optimized for low-frequency absorption and a parallel mode achieving broadband absorption. Experimental results show that a 29 mm-thick sample (approximately 1/44 of the wavelength at 270 Hz, the lower limit of the target band) achieves efficient sound absorption across a wide frequency range of 270–960 Hz.

title: Unsupervised deep learning framework for damage identification under ambient excitations: trait of damage localization and demonstrative applications
abstract: Developing unsupervised deep learning-based damage identification (uDLdi) under ambient excitations is crucial for civil engineering but remains hindered by insufficient feature extraction from complex original acceleration responses and a lack of damage localization capabilities. To address these issues, this study proposes a novel framework of uDLdi under ambient excitation (F-uDLdi-ae) by adopting the following innovative techniques: (1) a cube-shaped sample set is constructed to theoretically protrude damage information while suppressing interference information; (2) a self-attention module dedicated to protruding damage feature so as to largely identify damage samples is constructed; and (3) an uncertainty-weakened damage probability strategy for localizing damage accurately and reliably is proposed. Validation using a numerical steel truss bridge and a laboratory three-story frame structure demonstrates the superior damage discrimination and localization performance of the proposed framework. Specifically, in the numerical case under a high-noise environment (SNR = 5 dB), F-uDLdi-ae achieves an F‑score of 91.98%, outperforming several advanced unsupervised methods by 6.27% to 20.65%. In the three-story frame structure, F-uDLdi-ae achieves an F‑score of 100%. Furthermore, the framework is applied to a long‑span cable‑stayed bridge, Yonghe Bridge, where it achieves an F‑score of 99.17% and successfully localizes the damage via the maximum damage probability. The proposed F-uDLdi-ae overcomes the limitations of existing uDLdi, holding the promise for viably and intelligently identifying damage in practical engineering structures.

title: Guided wave detection and localisation of weld defects in circumferentially periodic thin-walled structures
abstract: Weld regions in regenerative cooling thrust chambers are highly susceptible to cracking under thermo-mechanical cyclic loading, posing a risk of catastrophic rocket engine failure. While the inspection of these thin-walled, circumferentially periodic structures is critical, conventional non-destructive evaluation (NDE) methods are ill-suited for rapid, remote screening. This study introduces an axial-guided-wave-based technique for rapid detection and localisation of weld defects in complex cylindrical thin-walled structures. The core of this approach is a novel, unit-cell-based modelling strategy developed within the Semi-Analytical Finite Element (SAFE) framework, which incorporates pointwise constraints to accurately capture the modal behaviours and wave structures of existing guided wave modes in circumferentially periodic waveguides of arbitrary cross-section. From this model, we establish a systematic, mode-selection workflow for selecting guided wave modes with enhanced detection sensitivity to localised weld defects. This workflow, encompassing dispersion analysis, energy localisation, mode-shape evaluation, and excitability assessment, provides a physics-based alternative to traditional, ad-hoc mode selection. Through comprehensive three-dimensional finite element (FE) simulations and experimental validation, a specific longitudinal type L(0,1)-like guided wave mode is identified as optimal, exhibiting concentrated wave energy at the vicinity of the weld seam, minimal dispersion, and high excitability. Furthermore, we provide a direct basis for localising defects via time-of-flight and assessing their significance via reflection-coefficient analysis. The proposed methodology establishes a versatile new framework for applying axial guided waves, paving the way for quantitative integrity monitoring of complex, circumferentially periodic engineering components.

title: A dynamic model for instantaneous angular speed jitter in low-speed rolling element bearing to mimic natural spalling zone on outer race
abstract: The instantaneous angular speed (IAS) is well suited for diagnosing bearing faults in low-speed conditions because it is synchronized with shaft rotation and can reveal the dynamic behavior of rollers when they enter and leave a spalling zone. Prior studies have emphasized vibration responses at medium and high speeds and often idealized spalling as rectangular notches, which overlooks natural spalling morphology and the torque produced by rough surfaces. We develop a dynamic IAS model for rolling element bearings (REBs) with a spalling outer race (OR) that combines a displacement-gradient representation of natural spalling with a time-varying additional torque and friction model, and that accounts for stiffness variation as well as entry and exit excitations. Simulations and experiments validate the model and explain IAS jitter near the natural spalling zone at low speed. The approach enables estimation of spall width on the OR. The results clarify the mechanism of IAS jitter under realistic operating conditions and provide guidance for dynamic modeling methods that use IAS.

title: A non-smooth nonlinear energy sink
abstract: As a wide-band vibration reduction strategy, nonlinear energy sink (NES) has been a research hotspot in recent years. Although many theoretical studies have ignored the linear stiffness of NES, it is difficult to avoid the linear stiffness of NES in practical engineering. The vibration reduction efficiency of a NES is greatly affected by linear stiffness, which hinders the engineering application of NES. A non-smooth NES with piecewise cubic stiffness and piecewise linear stiffness is proposed. The mechanical model of the forced vibration of a linear oscillator coupled with a non-smooth NES is established. The vibration reduction performance of the non-smooth NES is investigated through theory, optimization and experiments. Compared with the smooth NES with linear stiffness, the non-smooth NES has better vibration reduction efficiency. The change of parameters will cause global bifurcation of non-smooth NES. The change of mass ratio has little effect on the vibration reduction efficiency of non-smooth NES. With the change of excitation intensity and linear stiffness, the non-smooth NES has better vibration reduction efficiency in most cases. Adjusting the size of piecewise gap can make the non-smooth NES adapt to more vibration conditions. The particle swarm optimization algorithm is used to optimize some parameters. Finally, the vibration control effect of non-smooth NES is verified in terms of mass ratio, excitation intensity and piecewise gap through experiments. This paper provides a new strategy to solve the problem of linear stiffness affecting the vibration reduction efficiency of NES.

title: Load condition monitoring of the large-scale bearing via smart roller
abstract: Large-scale bearings are widely used in wind turbines, tunnel boring machines, rolling mills, and other applications. The load status of large-scale bearings directly determines the operational stability and service life of the equipment. The traditional method of affixing strain gauges to the outer ring fails to realize overall load condition monitoring of the bearing. To solve the load condition monitoring problem of large-scale bearings, this paper proposed a method for monitoring the conditions of the roller and bearing using a smart roller. The smart roller primarily consists of a sensing system, a lithium battery, and a wireless data transmission module. The smart roller can sense the contact pressure in the line contact area through the strain gauge adhered to the inner wall of the hollow roller and achieve wireless signal transmission. The deformation of hollow rollers contains contact deformation and bending deformation. The equivalent elastic modulus of hollow rollers can be calculated using Hertz contact theory and the Energy method. The deformation and load distribution of hollow rollers can be calculated using the equivalent elastic modulus. Training the finite element simulation deformation dataset can obtain a nonlinear fitting algorithm for roller deformation. Fitting the deformation values of the measured data by the trained algorithm can obtain the roller deformation values. The static calibration experiment results show that the smart roller has a high linearity under different loads. To determine the dynamic monitoring characteristics of the rollers, the planar thrust cylindrical roller bearing experiment bench is established. A cosine fit can be performed on the roller load distribution on different roller positions to determine the bearing’s load distribution. The deformation value of the rollers at the maximum bias load position of the bearing can be analyzed to determine the bias load angle and position of the bearing under different working conditions. When the rotation speed is 60 rpm and the load is 240 kN on the plain thrust cylindrical roller bearing, the bias load occurs at the position of 139° with a bias load angle of 0.0359°. The acquired data can also be fitted to determine the slip rate of rollers. Strain gauge information within the smart roller enables determination of the slip rate and load distribution of the roller, as well as the load distribution and bias load of bearing conditions. This method is of great significance for studying the mechanical behavior of bearings, predicting fatigue life, optimizing structural design, enhancing reliability, and digital twins.

title: Modeling approach for asymmetric evolution of outer-race defects in ceramic bearings and analysis of vibration signal characteristics
abstract: This study investigates the asymmetric evolution of local spalling defects on the outer ring of Si3N4 ceramic bearings and proposes a defect-geometry evolution model incorporating the tilt angle and an asymmetry quantification parameter. A coupled geometric–dynamic modeling framework is developed by integrating the proposed evolution model with a three-stage displacement excitation function, enabling accurate characterization of the entry, traversal, and exit behaviors of rolling elements across the defect. Simulation results demonstrate that asymmetric evolution gives rise to uneven impact amplitudes and modulation sidebands in the frequency domain, whereas symmetric evolution produces only uniform periodic impacts. The predicted tilt angle and asymmetry parameter show strong agreement with experimental measurements, effectively reproducing both the geometric evolution trend and the associated vibration characteristics under various operating conditions. The findings indicate that incorporating asymmetric evolution significantly enhances the physical fidelity of ceramic bearing fault modeling and improves the interpretability of vibration features, offering important benefits for early fault diagnosis.

title: Non-deterministic approach for identification and isolation of ultrasonic guided wave modes for structural health monitoring
abstract: Ultrasonic inspection techniques have shown great promise for monitoring progressive damage in thin-walled structures. The ultrasonic signals contain damage fingerprints that can be used for assessment of structural damage and degradation. The signal features are inherently linked to the physical behaviour of fundamental guided wave modes. This study presents a novel signal reconstruction and modal identification approach for experimentally measured ultrasonic signals with composite waveguide dispersion models and harmonic wave propagation functions. The modal amplitudes and dispersion characteristics have been calibrated accurately using both a deterministic approach and a Bayesian joint parameter estimation technique. The latter quantifies the uncertainties in both experimental measurements and latent dispersion parameters. The modal identification is regularized by physics-informed models of waveguide dispersion. The reconstructed signals show excellent agreement with the experimental measurements over a broad frequency range. The calibrated parameters were subsequently used to investigate progressive structural degradation arising from displacement-controlled compressive fatigue loading. A probabilistic Bayesian joint parameter estimation framework effectively captured direction-specific signatures and quantified uncertainty in parameter estimation, revealing distinct directional and modal sensitivities to fatigue damage. This achievement underscores the efficacy and reliability of the calibrated ultrasonic guided wave modes as reliable identifiers of damage with potential for further description, characterization, and sentencing.

title: Vibration reduction analysis method for permanent magnet coupling considering anisotropic magnetic stiffness coupling effect
abstract: Permanent magnet coupling (PMC) enables noncontact power transmission through the magnetic field in a shaft system and has great application potential in the ship field. However, the anisotropic magnetic stiffness of the PMC is coupled with each other. The traditional analysis method of vibration characteristics considers only the stiffness in a single direction and disregards the coupling effect of the anisotropic stiffness, which leads to inaccurate analysis of vibration energy transfer and restricts the design of the PMC with high vibration reduction characteristics. In this paper, considering the coupling effect of anisotropic magnetic stiffness, a magnetic‒dynamic joint analysis method (MDJAM) is proposed. A three-dimensional (3D) magnetic force model of the PMC is constructed, and the fluctuation values of the force and torque are calculated according to the changes of offset and deflection angle. The influence factors of each matrix element in the stiffness matrix are calculated via an energy ratio method, and anisotropic magnetic stiffness that has a significant impact is screened via comparing with the threshold, and the equivalent stiffness matrix is constructed. The dynamic model of magnetic‒solid coupling rotor is constructed in light of the strong coupling effect of anisotropic magnetic stiffness, and the natural frequency and vibration level difference of the PMC are calculated by using the equivalent stiffness matrix as input. The experimental results show that this method can accurately analyze the vibration energy transfer of the PMC, and provide guidance for the optimal design of magnetic components with high vibration reduction characteristics.

title: Eulogy – Professor Dr.-Ing. Michael Link
A mixed-norm regularized time-domain inverse framework for localizing and quantifying rotor noise sources
abstract: Conventional source identification methods for rotating machinery are generally formulated in the frequency domain under the assumption of steady or quasi-steady sources, which limits their ability to resolve temporally evolving source behaviour. Time-domain approaches such as the rotating source identifier and virtual rotating arrays allow source localization at individual time instances but are often inadequate for quantifying the evolving strength of unsteady rotating sources. In this study, a time-domain inverse method is developed based on the integral solution of the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings equation with quadrupole source terms being neglected. An equivalent source model is employed to establish a time-resolved mapping between measured acoustic pressures and source strengths. A mixed-norm regularization scheme is introduced to incorporate prior knowledge of the spatiotemporal characteristics of the source field, enabling stable and accurate reconstruction of time-varying source strengths. The method is validated through numerical simulations over a range of rotational speeds and signal-to-noise ratios, as well as the rotor noise experiments of an unmanned aerial vehicle conducted in a semi-anechoic chamber. The results demonstrate that the method can localize rotor noise sources, capture their temporal evolution, and accurately predict radiated sound fields across a range of operating conditions.

title: Designing out manufacturing uncertainty: Interface topology optimization for lap joint structures
abstract: Bolted connections are ubiquitous in mechanical and aerospace engineering. However, these connections introduce significant uncertainties in vibration responses. The primary source of uncertainty in a jointed connection is due to manufacturing tolerances resulting in a non-flat interface. Topological features on the order of 50μm can significantly affect the natural frequency and damping capacity of a large-scale structure, even shifting linear natural frequencies by 10%. With recent improvements in physics-based modeling of jointed structures, it is now possible to robustly optimize the topology of a jointed interface to be insensitive to manufacturing variability. The present work presents a novel framework for the robust optimization of a jointed interface. The framework is demonstrated on a three-bolt lap joint benchmark structure commonly referred to as the Brake–Reußbeam. The gap profiles arising from manufacturing imperfections were measured from existing joint specimens and approximated using analytical sinusoidal expressions. These representations were employed to perturb baseline interface designs in the context of robust optimization. Based on sensitivity analysis and optimization results, two candidate interface topologies were selected for fabrication. Experimental testing of these manufactured interfaces demonstrates that the proposed approach enables the design of predictable joint behavior that is robust to mesoscale manufacturing deviations. Overall, this study highlights the influence of machining-induced variability on the dynamic response of jointed structures and presents a viable pathway to mitigate its effects through informed surface design.

title: Stability and Hopf bifurcation analysis for a vertical active magnetic bearing system with dual feedback delays
abstract: In magnetic bearing control systems, Hopf bifurcation induced by signal time delays can significantly affect system stability. However, existing studies seldom consider models with both position and velocity time delays, which limits the applicability of related theories to practical systems. This paper focuses on the impact of dual time-delay feedback variables on Hopf bifurcation in a vertical active magnetic bearing (VAMB) system. A magnetic levitation system model incorporating dual time delays in displacement and velocity is developed, through which the bifurcation behavior arising from delay coupling is systematically investigated, extending beyond the scope of traditional single-delay models. Furthermore, to address the engineering challenge where exact solutions rely on complex implicit equations, a novel explicit algebraic criterion for critical delay estimation is proposed. This method not only significantly reduces computational complexity but also provides a transparent physical meaning for rapid parameter tuning. The Hopf bifurcation type is determined using the method of multiple time scales, with the theoretical results validated by numerical simulations, followed by an investigation of the effects of global bifurcations on the system dynamics under coupled dual delays. The study shows that, under dual time-delay feedback, Hopf bifurcation impacts the rotor’s dynamic behavior in an interdependent manner, exhibiting more complex evolutionary patterns than single time-delay systems. This provides a new perspective for the controller design and stability analysis of VAMB systems.

title: Robust online monitoring of aircraft modal parameters using data fusion-based mode tracking
abstract: Accurate real-time identification of modal parameters of aeroelastic systems, such as aircraft during flight vibration testing (FVT), remains a major challenge, e.g., due to low signal-to-noise ratios, variations in aerodynamic excitation, and the time-varying nature of flight conditions. This paper presents a robust methodology for online monitoring of aeroelastic systems using output-only modal analysis and data fusion techniques. A clustering-based Automated Modal Analysis framework enables the combination of time-domain (Stochastic Subspace Identification) and frequency-domain (Least-Squares Complex Frequency) methods, providing real-time uncertainty estimates for each identified mode. These results are fused across methods and over time using a Kalman filter, allowing for improved mode tracking and significant reduction of uncertainty. The proposed approach is validated using simulated data, wind tunnel experiments, and flight test data from a modified business jet. Results from wind tunnel testing demonstrate a reduction of the identification errors by up to 63% for eigenfrequency and 33% for the damping ratio. In addition, the results from the flight test demonstrate that the fusion of multiple identification methods with real-time uncertainty assessment and Kalman filtering enhances the robustness and resolution of aeroelastic parameter tracking — enabling more reliable real-time monitoring even under challenging operational conditions. • Real-time modal parameter monitoring for flight vibration tests. • Fusion of time-domain and frequency-domain identification methods. • Fusion of subsequently identified modal parameters.

title: Dual-learning framework: Integrating deep and reinforcement learning for optimizing bio-inspired Helmholtz-porous acoustic metamaterials for railway noise mitigation
abstract: Urban railway noise pollution poses significant public health challenges, necessitating advanced mitigation solutions. This study presents a novel dual-learning framework to optimize bio-inspired Helmholtz-porous acoustic metamaterials (HPAM) for railway noise absorption between 500–2000 Hz. The framework uses a highly accurate surrogate model, ESKAN (Echo-state module with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks), which achieved an R 2 of 0.987. To find the best material designs, a Q-learning enhanced Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) optimization algorithm efficiently explores complex 14-dimensional parameter spaces. This method successfully identifies optimal configurations for various material thicknesses (20–120 mm) and types, including porous materials like melamine sponge and rockwool, and shell materials ranging from soft polymers to rigid metals. Experimental tests on 3D-printed ABS prototypes confirmed the framework’s accuracy. The fabricated samples demonstrated excellent broadband absorption (SAC > 0.8) across the 480–2000 Hz range. This research introduces a generalizable method for designing next-generation metamaterials, overcoming previous optimization limitations while respecting manufacturing constraints.

title: Inverse modeling with physical constraints and uncertainty correction for mesh stiffness identification in gear crack fault
abstract: Gears play a key role in mechanical transmission systems, e.g., wind turbine drivetrains and helicopter gearboxes, etc. Identifying the health status of gears is crucial for ensuring equipment safety and achieving refined operation and maintenance. Mesh stiffness is the most principal internal excitation in the process of gear meshing, which is the pivot parameter to characterize the gear state. However, it is challenging to directly monitor. Therefore, an inverse modeling with physical constraints is developed to identify the mesh stiffness of gears in crack fault for strong interpretability. A sparsity-assisted energy alignment method is proposed to quantify the fault characteristics. Then, a nonlinear method with physical constraints is proposed to map the fault features to the mesh stiffness. After that, a dual-loop Bayesian inference model is proposed to modify the mapping error for uncertainty correction. Finally, the fault severity degree is estimated using the corrected identification results of mesh stiffness. The analysis and verification by simulation signals and experimental signals show that the method proposed can obtain superior results in stiffness identification and estimation of fault severity degree.

title: Dynamic responses of gear-linkage mechanism considering mixed clearances: Simulation and experiment
abstract: Clearances, resulting from assemblage, manufacturing errors and wear, always lead to undesirable vibrations due to impact forces in clearance joints. Usually, there are inevitably clearances between bearing and shaft in revolute joints as well as tooth backlash in gear pairs of gear-linkage mechanism system, which is widely used in mechanical engineering. However, in dynamics analysis of gear-linkage mechanism, it is usually assumed that the coupling relationship between the revolute clearance joint and backlash of gear pair is ignored. In this work, the effects of multiply clearances on the dynamic responses of planar gear-linkage mechanism system are investigated using computational and experimental methodology. Firstly, the mathematic models of the radial clearance in revolute joint and tooth backlash in gear pair are established considering the coupling relationship between radial clearance and tooth backlash.
