abstract: Health indicators (HI) rooted in signal probabilistic distribution models have received extensive application and development in bearing degradation monitoring. However, a promising HI in this category, which enables direct parameter-oriented degradation characterization, along with sufficient sensitivity to early faults and remarkable robustness under time-varying conditions, remains to be further explored. To tackle these issues, a new HI derived from the generalized pareto distribution (GPD) is proposed in this study. Initially, it is revealed by investigations that the GPD offers a highly appropriate and intuitively interpretable probabilistic model for the feature signals obtained via the advanced squared envelope-derivative technique, wherein the critical shape and scale parameters are directly indicative of the bearing degradation condition at different phases. On this basis, the intrinsic GPD entropy (GPDE) is extracted to achieve dual-parameter synergistic representation of the bearing degradation behaviors. Afterwards, an enhanced HI based on the GPDE is further produced via exponential transformation and fusion with a designated speed-based linear mapping model to alleviate the effect of variable-speed operating conditions. Furthermore, an EVT-based joint fault alarm threshold is developed for early fault recognition. Finally, comprehensive investigations using both experimental and industrial wind turbine generator bearing run-to-failure datasets, including analysis of the overall degradation trend, early fault detection, and ROC curve-based quantitative evaluation, fully demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed HI for bearing degradation monitoring.

title: Semi-analytical modeling and attenuation vibration control of composite joint plates under a uniform thermal field
abstract: As a crucial component of spacecraft, during the on-orbit operation, the satellite solar panel not only faces the impact of the thermal environment, but also, due to the low damping characteristics of its own structure, the free attenuation vibration (FAV) generated after being disturbed is difficult to attenuate autonomously and rapidly. This issue seriously affects structural stability. To address these practical engineering challenges, this study simplifies the satellite solar panel as composite joint plates (CJPs). The research is dedicated to developing a corresponding semi-analytical modeling method and, with the help of active control technology, solving the complex problem of suppressing its FAV. Firstly, the non-uniform distribution of contact pressure at the bolted interface is effectively simulated by surface spring and surface damping with power law attenuation characteristics. The influence of the uniform thermal field is characterized by introducing temperature-dependent material parameters and thermal strain energy. In combination with the piezoelectric effect, a dynamic model of the CJPs with piezoelectric materials under a uniform thermal field is constructed. Leveraging the results derived from COMSOL and experimental tests, the validity of the model proposed in the present work for capturing the natural properties and vibration responses of structures under both room temperature and thermal operating conditions is thoroughly confirmed. Secondly, a Hilbert transform-positive position feedback controller (Hilbert-PPF) is designed. By extracting the frequency and damping ratio of the FAV in real-time, the control parameters of the PPF are dynamically adjusted to enhance the adaptability of the control system. The test results show that the suppression rate of the controller for the first-order FAC of the CJPs exceeds 90% at room temperature and 75℃, and it still maintains a suppression rate of 76% in a high-temperature environment of 125℃. Finally, the influences of parameters such as the fiber angle, the transverse position and thickness of the lap plate on the natural frequency and the damping ratio of the FAV are discussed. Moreover, the temperature effect is further coupled to explore the relevant variation trends, providing an essential theoretical reference for the optimised design of the structure.

title: Design and experiment of an in-plane low-frequency vibration isolator with quasi-zero-stiffness supports
abstract: Multi-directional in-plane low-frequency vibration exerts a substantial impact on the precision of instruments. The in-plane stiffness is always reduced to isolate low-frequency vibration, while sacrificing the load-bearing capacity out of plane. To ad-dress such a challenge, this paper proposes an in-plane low-frequency (IPLF) vibration isolator with quasi-zero stiffness (QZS) supports. Firstly, the QZS support is designed using three-segment flexible beams, and its shape and geometry is optimized to fulfill quasi-zero stiffness. Subsequently, the QZS support structure is integrated with linear springs to construct the IPLF vibration isolator. Both the static and dynamic analyses of the IPLF vibration isolator are conducted to reveal its in-plane and out-of-plane stiffness properties and vibration isolation performance. Finally, a prototype of the IPLF vibration isolator is fabricated, and experiments are conducted to validate the design concept and theoretical predictions. The results demonstrate that the initial vibration isolation frequency of the IPLF vibration isolator is 8 Hz, which is far lower than 57 Hz exhibited by the isolator consisting of only linear springs with equivalent support stiffness. This significant frequency reduction indicates that the IPLF isolator exhibits desired low in-plane stiffness and superior load-bearing capability, and also highlights the unique advantage of the IPLF isolator in low-frequency scenarios. Therefore, the IPLF vibration isolator integrates excellent low-frequency vibration isolation performance with sufficiently high load-bearing stiffness, thereby providing a viable solution for in-plane low-frequency vibration isolation.

title: Time-reassigned synchrosqueezing frequency-domain chirplet transform for multicomponent signals with intersecting group delay curves
abstract: To analyze signals with rapid frequency variations or transient components, the time-reassigned synchrosqueezing transform (TSST) and its variants have been recently proposed. Unlike the traditional synchrosqueezing transform, TSST squeezes the time-frequency (TF) coefficients along the group delay (GD) trajectories rather than the instantaneous frequency trajectories. Although TSST methods perform well in analyzing transient signals, they are fundamentally limited in processing multicomponent signals with intersecting GD curves. This limitation compromises the accuracy of both feature extraction and signal component recovery, thereby significantly reducing the interpretability of time-frequency representations (TFRs). This is particularly problematic in broadband signal processing systems, where the linearity of the phase response is critical and precise measurement of group delay dispersion (GDD) is essential. Motivated by the superior capability of frequency-domain signal modeling in characterizing rapidly frequency-varying signals, this paper proposes a novel three-dimensional time-frequency-group delay dispersion (TF-GDD) representation based on the frequency-domain chirplet transform. A subsequent time-reassigned synchrosqueezing frequency-domain chirplet transform (TSFCT) is introduced to achieve a sharper TF-GDD distribution and more accurate GD estimation. For mode retrieval, a novel frequency-domain group signal separation operation (FGSSO) is proposed.The theoretical contributions include a derivation of the approximation error for the GD and GDD reference functions and an establishment of the error bounds for FGSSO-based mode retrieval. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed TSFCT and FGSSO effectively estimate GDs and retrieve modes--even for modes with intersecting GD trajectories.

title: Virtualization of sensors using laser vibrometer-based sensor synthesis
abstract: Effective application of ultrasonic guided waves in structural health monitoring requires systematic selection and placement of elastic wave transducers, acting as actuators and sensors, to maximize sensitivity of the system while minimizing the number of its elements. Non-contact space–time wavefield measurements performed using scanning laser Doppler vibrometry (SLDV) are often utilized to replace physical sensors in sensor network optimization studies. However, on their own, these measurements do not accurately represent the characteristics of complex transducers, which are commonly used in guided waves-based applications. In this work, we propose two methods for constructing virtual sensors that can be applied to space–time wavefield measurements to accurately represent elastic wave transducer behavior in sensing. These methods, namely, direct matrix inversion (DMI) and directional filter (DF), estimate a set of weighting coefficients that describe the directivity pattern of the required arbitrary physical transducer for a given excitation. The DMI method involves inversion of transducer’s constitutive equations, while the DF method implements a directional filter in the wavenumber domain. In this paper, the effectiveness of both the proposed approaches is investigated using three different types of complex transducers, with numerical simulations and subsequent experimental validation using SLDV measurements. The results show that the responses predicted by the proposed methods have high agreement with those of the physical transducers; with the DMI method achieving higher accuracy and the DF method offering lower computational complexity.

title: A novel parallel feature fusion strategy-based machine learning approach for accurate prediction and early warning of wind-induced vibrations of solar towers
abstract: Solar towers are highly flexible structures prone to wind-induced vibrations, which can significantly reduce the operational efficiency of concentrated solar power (CSP) plants and, more critically, may jeopardize the structural integrity. With the growing maturity of structural health monitoring (SHM) technologies and the increasing availability of multi-source sensing data, data-driven prediction has emerged as a key method for real-time evaluation and early warning of wind-induced vibrations. However, conventional machine learning models often exhibit some randomness in their predictions and struggle to accurately predict wind-induced vibration responses arising from strong fluid–structure coupling, which is particularly pronounced in solar towers. In addition, these models typically require extensive hyperparameter tuning, leading to high computational cost and reduced prediction efficiency. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel data-driven prediction method based on a parallel feature fusion strategy. The model integrates Long Short-Term Memory Network(LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit(GRU), and improved Transformer within a dual-branch architecture, leveraging gated mechanisms and multi-head attention for multi-scale feature extraction. Then, an Extreme Learning Machine (ELM)-based hierarchical feature fusion module is designed to achieve efficient integration of multi-source features from both branches. The proposed approach is validated through wind tunnel experiments on a scaled aeroelastic model and tested against field measurements from a full-scale operational tower. Finally, an early warning system based on the model is developed and shown to be reliable for real-world wind hazard mitigation in CSP plants.

title: A Bayesian compressive sensing – Stochastic harmonic function based random field simulation method incorporating with Gaussian mixture model to consider fusion of multi-groups of spatial data
abstract: In engineering applications, random fields provide a robust probabilistic framework for characterizing properties that exhibit spatial and temporal variations. In practice, however, data sets for random field modeling are often collected sequentially. Consequently, rationally fusing these multiple data sets requires further investigation to maximize data utilization. Previous studies have demonstrated the excellent performance of the Bayesian compressive sensing – stochastic harmonic function method in representing random fields based on a single set of data. In this study, this method is combined with a Gaussian mixture model to further extend its capability to represent random fields using multiple data sets. Specifically, the high-dimensional probability distribution of the wavenumber spectral density function can be obtained using the Gaussian mixture model. As a result, the convergence property of the proposed method is verified, and the method is applied in some engineering problems to validate its performance.

title: A convex optimization difference analysis model for intelligent fault detection and diagnosis of gearboxes
abstract: Data-driven artificial intelligence diagnostic methods have been widely applied in the intelligent operation and maintenance of wind turbine transmission systems. However, the transmission system and its key components typically remain in a healthy and stable operating state for a long period of time. Traditional supervised learning methods based on prior knowledge and multi-fault mode training are difficult to efficiently extend to practical applications. To address the issues of scarce fault data for gearboxes and bearings, as well as the difficulty of effective modeling based on data from a single healthy state, this paper proposes a Convex Optimization Difference Analysis Model (CODA Model). Within the bispectrum framework based on demodulation of natural and harmonic frequencies, the difference analysis mechanism is introduced to discretize complex modulation features and achieve decoupling of modulation information among multiple components. A vibration signal training set under normal operating conditions of healthy gearboxes and bearings is constructed and mapped into an ultra-high-dimensional physical feature space to establish a convex optimization model based on one-class data, which enhances the discriminative capability of the bispectrum framework in the feature representation space. The bispectral domain differences between unknown samples with anomalous labels, as identified by the CODA Model, and healthy samples need to be analyzed by constructing a contribution rate spectrum. Subsequently, weighting factors are constructed using adaptive thresholds to enhance fault features of anomalous samples in the bispectrum, suppressing the interference of gear meshing and background noise present under normal operating conditions, and reducing signal complexity. The feasibility of the proposed method was validated using simulation data, and fault data of gearboxes and bearings were processed and analyzed under two different experimental operating conditions. The results show that, even without fault samples included in the training, the CODA Model can still effectively perform fault detection and diagnosis, demonstrating strong generalization capability and practical application potential. Under a health data-driven modeling framework, this method demonstrates the advantages of unsupervised diagnosis for complex mechanical systems, providing a novel technical approach and theoretical support for health state modeling and anomaly detection in the intelligent operation and maintenance of wind turbine transmission systems.

title: Dynamic modeling and vibration mechanism analysis of cracked complex blade using pseudo-rigid body beam method
abstract: Blade crack often occurs in rotating machineries such as aero-engine, gas turbine and steam turbine, thus investigating the vibration mechanism of cracked blades is critical for the design, diagnosis, and maintenance of rotating machineries. In this paper, a novel dynamic model of cracked complex blades based on pseudo-rigid body beam method is developed, in which the mapping relationship between blade structure stiffness and crack parameters is established. By employing the slicing, thickness equivalence, and angle equivalence method, the effects of the blade’s complex cross-section, varying thickness, and pre-twist angle are comprehensively incorporated. This involves slicing the complex cross-section to compute sectional properties, and determining blade stiffness and inertial parameters using the thickness and angle at the left end and intermediate points of the pseudo-rigid body beam. The effectiveness of the slicing method, thickness equivalence method, and angle equivalence method is validated by comparing results with those from ANSYS and existing literature, meanwhile, modal tests on normal and cracked blades are conducted to verify the validity of the complex blade dynamic model. Based on the validated model, effects of geometric parameters of the blade (thickness variation rate and pre-twist angle) and crack parameters (position and depth) on the natural frequency of the complex blade are analyzed.

title: Prediction of response and damage localization in monitored torsional buildings through an evolution of deconvolution-based seismic interferometry
abstract: The detection of a possible global damage state is now within the reach of current methods of structural health monitoring (SHM) of buildings. However, despite the large number of studies published on the subject, a reliable and simple localization of damage represents an objective not yet achieved; as well as an evaluation of damage severity and safety of monitored structures. Unfortunately, both of the currently most widespread types of approach to SHM, model-driven and data-driven, provide inaccurate results and/or represent a process that is too long and costly, if not practically impossible due to the lack of necessary data. In this work, two innovations are presented that constitute the fundamental components of an integrated and developing approach, aimed at verifying the safety and performance of a monitored structure: (1) a method for predicting the seismic response of torsional structures. (2) a new procedure for damage localization. Both methodologies are developed starting from the theoretical foundations of seismic interferometry. To allow an accurate and simple procedure for damage localization, the author has combined the concepts of impulse response function (IRF), which characterizes the dynamic behavior of a building, and interstory drift ratio (IDR), a physical quantity strongly correlated to the performance or damage of the structural element to which it refers, to define the IRFs in terms of IDR (IRFs-IDR). It has been found that the values of the peaks of the IRFs-IDR related to a given floor of the building increase when transitioning from a reference state to a damage state of that floor; it has also been found that this increase becomes larger as the severity of the floor damage increases. In order to obtain numerical values that allow to objectively indicate the location of the damages, as well as to estimate their severity, the author has defined a new structural parameter, the relative variation of the peaks of the impulse response in terms of IDR, δPIR-IDR, to be calculated, at each floor, by comparing the reference state with the damaged state. Moreover, the prediction of the response at each point of the monitored building to a generic seismic input, necessary for the evaluation of its safety, is present in the literature related to seismic interferometry only for the ideal case of purely translational structure. In this way, the overload, often strong, of stresses typical of the response of most real structures, generally torsional (with torsion coupled to translation), is neglected. To predict the response at each point of the floor of a torsional structure, the author has developed a method based on the definition of six IRFs for each floor. The approach is validated on simulated and full-scale test data and shows promising potential for SHM applications, notably due to its simplicity of implementation and the encouraging level of agreement observed in the investigated cases, supported by a comparison with three alternative localization approaches on the same benchmark structure. Furthermore, the proposed formulation extends interferometry-based response prediction to torsional coupling effects under the linearity assumption: this provides a basis for future developments toward performance-oriented assessment of the components of monitored buildings.
keywords: Prediction of the response of monitored buildings
Relative variation of the peaks of the impulse response in terms of interstory drift ratio ()

title: A Conditional constraint Generative adversarial networks model for predicting high cycle and very high cycle fatigue life of titanium alloy
abstract: Fatigue life prediction of aero-engine has been an important research topic in the aerospace industry. This study focuses on predicting the high cycle and very high cycle fatigue (HCF/VHCF) life of aero-engine titanium alloys under small-sample conditions. First, based on the test results and empirical phenomena, a dimensionless constraint index (δ) was designed to assign values to the test type (Typ) and fracture conditions (Fc), and life mapping characteristic variables were introduced to establish a foundation for subsequent data augmentation and predictive modeling. Second, a Kernel density estimation-Synthetic minority over-sampling technique (KDE-SMOTE) data enhancement method is proposed, which expands the dataset while preserving feature-variable correlations. Then, a Conditional constraint Generative adversarial network (C-cGAN) model was built by embedding δ and Fc computation as explicit constraints in the loss and implicitly guiding attention learning with adversarial training. Finally, under the conditions of high-density distribution test validation (Test set 1) and random test validation (Test set 2), the C-cGAN model shows better prediction results at 3–5-fold dispersion bands (satisfying 5-fold dispersion band) by training on KDE-SMOTE enhanced data, and extends to the fatigue life prediction studies of a variety of titanium alloys, which suggests that the model has a potential reference value.
keywords: High cycle and very high cycle fatigue (HCF/VHCF)

title: Uncertainty law for modal identification using free vibration data
abstract: Making inference about the ‘modal properties’, e.g., natural frequency and damping, is becoming a basic task in modern instrumentation of engineering structures such as vibration diagnosis or more generally structural health monitoring (SHM). In the context of modal identification with data modelled in a probabilistic manner, ‘uncertainty law’ aims to capture the mathematical relationship between the ‘posterior’ (i.e., given data) uncertainty and test configurations, e.g., data length, sensor quality (noise), number and locations, by investigating its leading order term under asymptotic conditions such as long data and small damping. In addition to providing a fundamental understanding of identification uncertainty, the uncertainty law formulae allow one to plan vibration tests in a quantitative manner. Further to existing work on ambient and forced vibration tests, this work develops the uncertainty law for free vibration tests where inevitable contributions from ambient vibration and instrument noise are modeled. In addition to the uncertainty law formulae, the work reveals a definition of the ‘free/ambient ratio’ that quantifies the relative strength of the free and ambient vibration in regards to making inference about modal parameters. The theory is verified using synthetic data and applied to field vibration data of a footbridge.

title: A two-stage approach for predicting tribological variables via latent-regularized blind denoising and machine learning in microscratch testing
abstract: The development of predictive models in tribology has emerged as a tool for predicting key process variables. Penetration, tangential force, volume removed, coefficient of friction, and specific energy are critical parameters for minimizing energy consumption and reducing losses due to friction and wear. This work proposes a two-stage methodology that integrates signal denoising and predictive modeling. In the first stage, a recurrent autoencoder with contrastive learning and temporal smoothness constraints is employed to enhance the quality of force and position signals in a blind, unsupervised manner. In the second stage, a Random Forest (RF) model estimates tribological variables while integrating mechanical properties of the materials to improve generalization. The methodology was validated through microscratch tests performed on four steels (AISI 303, 304, 310, and H13) under normal loads between 40 and 100 mN, enabling analysis of material-dependent tribological responses at the microscale. Compared to conventional filters (Savitzky–Golay, moving average) and data-driven baselines (EMD, DAE), the proposed latent-regularized blind denoising autoencoder (LR-BDAE) achieved the highest signal preservation, with mean SNR improvements of 18.5dB and Pearson correlation exceeding 0.93 across materials. When integrated into the predictive stage, this denoising enhanced model consistency and reduced mean squared error by up to 42.3% for tangential force, 36.6% for penetration, 25.2% for the friction coefficient, and 20.8% for removed volume, with a minimum gain of 5.1% for specific energy. Incorporating material properties further increased R2 for specific energy by 26.2%, demonstrating robustness across distinct steels and supporting the general applicability of the framework to other tribological systems with noisy multi-sensor data. This proposal represents a step forward in integrating signal processing and machine learning techniques for tribological systems, providing a physically interpretable and scalable framework for industrial applications.

title: Learning to predict and control with sparse model discovery and deep temporal difference reinforcement learning
abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has demonstrated remarkable success in complex decision-making tasks, yet its application to predictive control remains challenging due to high sample requirements and limited long-horizon generalization. Model-based DRL methods promise improved sample efficiency by leveraging learned dynamics, but their performance is often restricted by inaccuracies in online model learning, which degrade control quality. This work introduces the Model-Agnostic Predictive Temporal Difference (MAP-TD) framework, a deep reinforcement learning approach capable of controlling systems with unknown physics. MAP-TD employs a pre-trained, interpretable, and parsimonious dynamics model discovered offline using Sparse Bayesian Learning (SBL), which is used for long-horizon trajectory prediction within the DRL architecture. This parsimonious model enhances predictive capability and enables the DRL agent to learn superior control strategies. The optimal control policies are learned by accumulating rewards and value functions along predictive trajectories, supported by a jointly trained terminal value function. For faster learning, we propose a hybrid strategy that periodically switches between fine and coarse solvers. MAP-TD delivers accurate long-horizon predictions while eliminating the need for online adaptation of approximate models. Numerical simulations on benchmark control tasks, including active vibration control of discrete and continuous structural dynamical systems, demonstrate that MAP-TD offers a computationally efficient and robust solution for predictive control.

title: A stability-switch analysis framework for virtual shaker voltage-based fixed frequency continuation test
abstract: Existing nonlinear model updating predominantly relies on a constant-force level swept frequency test, which captures only stable solutions. Recently, shaker voltage-based fixed frequency continuation has been proposed as an experimental method capable of acquiring unstable responses without additional feedback devices. However, current research has not thoroughly investigated its underlying dynamical mechanisms, treating it merely as an experimental technique with limited unstable solution regions. To probe the deeper principles of shaker voltage-based fixed-frequency continuation and expand its applicability, this paper proposes a stability-switch analysis framework. This framework enables quantitative analysis of this continuation method and enhances optimization efficiency. Virtual testing is conducted on a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) system with nonlinear stiffness coupled to a shaker, replicating fixed frequency voltage continuation. The coupled system exhibits a characteristic force drop-out phenomena and is validated against published experimental literature, showing excellent agreement with published experimental trends. Subsequently, stability-switch analysis elucidates stability differences and connections between the shaker-coupled system and the SDOF system. Crucially, this study reveals that adjusting stinger stiffness expands the range of force levels over which multi-valued responses are all stable in the SDOF system. This adjustment transforms previously unstable responses into stable states. Under these conditions, new force jump and force drop-out phenomena emerge during voltage continuation. This research provides valuable references for designing nonlinear dynamic experiments.

title: Calculation method for evaluating interface slip and preload optimization design strategy for bolted connections of turbine rotors in thermal environments
abstract: As the core power unit of aircraft engines, bolted turbine rotors must operate under complex thermal and mechanical loads. The reliability of bolted connections is subject to stringent testing. To investigate the dynamic characteristics and interface behavior of bolted turbine rotors in thermal environments, this paper establishes a dynamic model of bolted turbine rotors in thermal environments based on finite element theory. A nonlinear contact mechanics friction model was used for the bolt connection interface. A process for determining the viscous-slip state of bolts at various locations in the motion state of the rotor system was given. The judgment process was applied to the finite element theoretical model. For the first time, quasi-static experiments were used to obtain the mechanical parameters of the bolt connection interface under thermal conditions. The correctness of the model was verified by the test results of bolted turbine rotors. Evaluation calculations of the interface slip of bolted turbine rotors under different temperature and speed conditions were carried out. The nonlinear dynamic response caused by the slip phenomenon at the connection interface of bolted turbine rotors was analyzed. The preload results for bolted turbine rotors to avoid interface slip under different temperatures and speeds were discussed, and a preload optimization design strategy was proposed. The dynamic analysis model of bolted turbine rotors under thermal conditions and the preload optimization design results established in this study can provide a theoretical basis for the preload design of bolted connections under thermal conditions.

title: Damage detection using autocovariance functions
abstract: • ACFs are proven to be valid features for damage detection. • ACFs are particularly advantageous in wireless sensor networks. • A method is proposed to identify which changes are detectable. • Variations in excitation statistics do not affect detectability. • A diagram is presented to assist in selecting key parameters of the SHM system. Using wireless sensor networks in structural health monitoring systems is cost-efficient, because cables are not needed. On the other hand, issues occur with time synchronization between sensor nodes and transmission of long data records. To address these issues, autocovariance functions (ACFs) are proposed as damage-sensitive features, because they can be estimated independently in each sensor node and time-synchronization is not necessary. Data transmission to the central data repository is also more efficient, since ACFs are much shorter than the measurement period. The application of ACFs for damage detection lacks both theoretical justification and practical implementation guidelines. The objective of this paper is to prove the validity of ACFs for damage detection and provide practical instructions on choosing values for two design variables: the number of sensors and the number of time shifts given the number of active modes. Their values determine which changes are detectable. With appropriate design variables, data redundancy can be achieved, and damage can be detected using subspace methods. A diagram is provided to assist in selecting these two parameters. It is also proved that with a proper choice of design variables, the variability of the excitation statistics has no effect on redundancy. The use of ACFs for structural change detection was experimentally validated with a laboratory structure and the KW51 Bridge. A subspace-guided damage detection procedure was applied, in which it is not necessary to determine the subspace dimensions.

title: Variable-scale adaptive stepwise denoising for vehicle response enhancement in drive-by bridge inspection
abstract: In indirect bridge measurement, vehicle response signals are often contaminated by multiple sources of interference, including environmental noise, sensor errors, and road roughness. These disturbances obscure the structural vibration characteristics, thereby masking bridge modal features and limiting the use of vehicle-based data in structural damage identification. To address the limitations of traditional techniques in handling complex, non-stationary signals, a Variable-Scale Adaptive Stepwise Denoising (VSASD) method based on proxy reference signals is proposed. First, adaptive wavelet threshold denoising is employed to suppress measurement noise. Subsequently, both the vehicle-bridge contact-point and vehicle response signals are reconstructed through inverse analysis. Traversal-based variational mode decomposition, guided by a dual-domain energy factor, is then performed to optimize parameter selection. Following this, the preliminarily denoised signal is paired with the reconstructed signal to establish accurate reference filter pairs. Finally, an evolutionary infinite-impulse-response (IIR) adaptive modal filtering framework is introduced to achieve precise, mode-level noise reduction. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed VSASD method adaptively eliminates broadband noise and enhances weak yet structurally meaningful modal components. Furthermore, the method is shown to outperform three conventional denoising approaches. Overall, the proposed strategy improves the reliability of bridge modal identification and offers a robust signal-processing framework for bridge health monitoring.

title: Sparse time-domain synchronous averaging with adaptive bandwidth for rotating machinery fault diagnosis under speed fluctuation conditions
abstract: Speed fluctuation is a prevalent phenomenon in modern rotating machinery. Under time-varying speed conditions, the signals generated by the mechanical system exhibit complex features, including the smearing of characteristic frequencies and component coupling, which pose significant challenges for feature extraction and fault diagnosis. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a sparse time-domain synchronous averaging method with adaptive bandwidth (STSA-AB) for fault diagnosis of rotating machinery that involves speed fluctuation. Specifically, a morphological component analysis model is established to adapt to the phenomenon of speed fluctuation, in which the range of speed fluctuation serves as a strong prior, constructing a dynamic adaptive model weight vector. In addition, unlike conventional signal processing that directly resamples for signal with speed fluctuation, this model allows for a certain level of speed fluctuation. It facilitates the direct use of raw sampled signals for analysis, and introduces an indicator to quantitatively distinguish between different levels of speed fluctuation, thus enabling adaptive selection of the weighting mode. The proposed sparse model is solved by the fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (FISTA), and its resolved results can be applied to both bearing diagnostics and gear diagnostics. Through simulations and power transmission system diagnosis cases for both bearings and gears, the robustness of proposed method in fault diagnosis with varying degrees of speed fluctuation is validated. The health and fault signals are compared through performance evaluation indicators, and the results are further evaluated against those obtained by prevalent methodologies.

title: Probabilistic machine learning aided acoustic emission source localization in mode-I fracture test of multi-layer engineered wood
abstract: The mode-I fracture test is an important technique to evaluate materials’ fracture toughness and behaviors, where tracking the crack front is essential. This is usually done by visual inspection or computer vision, which could be problematic due to the large process zone and the difficulty of determining the onset of material cracking. Source localization via acoustic emission (AE) offers an alternative solution to this challenge. Locating AE sources in homogeneous materials is intuitively straightforward by leveraging phase differences from the measured time of arrival and potentially angle- or path-dependent velocity models. But it becomes complicated and intractable once the material heterogeneity comes into play. This is especially true for multilayer engineered wood, like laminated veneer lumber (LVL), where natural and manufacturing defects (knots, voids, discontinuity, and non-uniform textures) impose great challenges for 2D AE source localization. To cope with this problem, this study proposes probabilistic machine learning models, namely the Student-t process regression and the Gaussian process regression, for the 2D AE source localization on two LVL samples. To enhance prediction performance, both the multi-output Student-t and Gaussian process regression are developed. These probabilistic machine learning models are first trained and verified via pencil lead break tests and then applied to locate the crack tips in two mode-I fracture tests. Meanwhile, the Gaussian mixture models, along with Laplacian scores, are considered to identify AE events related to crack tip locations. The results suggest that the Student-t process can outperform the Gaussian process both in pencil lead break tests and mode-I fracture tests. The multi-output models can further enhance the prediction performance compared with the single-output processes. The multi-output Student-t process and the multi-output Gaussian process can support similar prediction performance when the degree of freedom of the Student-t process is large enough, and therefore, both are recommended for AE source localization in complex heterogeneous media like engineered wood.

title: Process uncertainty in Kalman filtering: A novel adaptive filter for vehicle dynamic state estimation
abstract: This paper introduces an Automatic process noise covariance matrix Kalman Filter (AQ-KF) that adaptively estimates the process noise covariance based on innovation statistics, without requiring manual tuning of the full process noise covariance matrix. Using a short observation window (typically 0.2 s), the method reduces the tuning effort to the selection of a single scalar parameter corresponding to the number of observations used for innovation covariance estimation. When applied to vehicle dynamics estimation, the AQ-KF outperforms the conventional Kalman Filter with inaccurate noise assumptions and achieves results comparable to the ideal case with exact noise statistics. In addition to its accuracy, AQ-KF remains computationally efficient and robust to variations in process uncertainties, ensuring reliable state estimation over time. Its simplified tuning also makes the method accessible to less experienced designers. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through both simulation and real-world experiments.

title: Estimating first-passage probabilities of stochastic dynamical systems: A POD–GPR based approximate Bayesian active learning approach
abstract: Evaluating the first-passage probabilities of stochastic dynamical systems is often required for assessing the safety and performance of modern engineered systems. However, despite significant progress, this task remains rather challenging both analytically and numerically. To address the challenge, this work presents a novel method—proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and Gaussian process regression (GPR) based approximate Bayesian active learning (ABAL), referred to as POD–GPR–ABAL. First, POD is employed to obtain an optimal low-rank representation of the stochastic dynamical response of interest using a compact set of basis functions and coefficients, and the POD coefficients are subsequently approximated by independent GPRs. Second, the integral of the first-passage probability is interpreted as a Bayesian inference problem by leveraging the Bayesian formulation of the combined POD–GPR model. Further, an approximate Bayesian inference scheme is developed, which avoids the computational intractability of the exact Bayesian inference. In this context, the mean of an approximate posterior first-passage probability is derived, which can be used a Bayesian estimator for the first-passage probability. In addition, we derive an upper bound on the standard deviation of the approximate posterior first-passage probability, which provides a uncertainty measure for the estimator. Third, based on the posterior statistics, a new stopping criterion is proposed to determine when the active learning process should terminate and a novel learning function is also developed to identify the best next evaluation point when the stopping criterion is not satisfied. Three numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed POD–GPR–ABAL method for evaluating the first-passage probabilities in stochastic dynamical systems. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves accurate first-passage probability estimates using only a small number of time-history analyses.

title: PrecisionPINN-ABKDE: uncertainty-weighted physics-informed neural network with adaptive bandwidth kernel density estimation for milling surface roughness prediction
abstract: Surface roughness critically determines the quality and performance of machined workpieces. Predicting the surface quality of key components in manufacturing systems is inherently a risk-sensitive task where both prediction accuracy and stability are pivotal metrics. To enhance physical interpretability and quantify prediction uncertainty in surface roughness modeling, this study proposes a novel framework integrating uncertainty estimation with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). The proposed approach employs an improved physical model that incorporates normalized cutting parameters and cutting forces to guide the training of a customized CNN-BiLSTM-attention network. Further, the prediction uncertainty is quantified using quantile regression with adaptive bandwidth kernel density estimation (QR-ABKDE). The QR-ABKDE uncertainty evaluation strategy quantifies both the local probability density and global error variance. It integrates locally adaptive noise (LAN) loss with a dynamically weighted loss function that adaptively balances the variance in prediction accuracy between the physics-based and data-driven models. Experimental validation through milling surface roughness monitoring demonstrates that the proposed method significantly improves the prediction accuracy and stability compared with existing approaches, achieving a 4.99% increase in R2 (0.8962 vs. 0.8536) and 15.08% reduction in root mean squared error (RMSE; 6.36 nm vs. 7.49 nm) over the baseline, while delivering near-perfect prediction coverage (prediction interval coverage probability, PICP, of 98.46%) with relatively small interval widths. These capabilities make the proposed framework well-suited for real-time surface quality monitoring and risk-aware process control in precision manufacturing environments.

title: A weighted likelihood exponential degradation model by kernel function smoothing for RUL prediction
abstract: Degradation process modeling is the cornerstone of reliable remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, a critical task in prognostics and health management (PHM). Conventional modeling approaches often assign uniform weights to historical observations, thereby failing to capture time-varying degradation dynamics and resulting in suboptimal fitting for recent trends. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes a weighted likelihood exponential degradation model. By integrating a kernel function into a likelihood within a Bayesian framework under the assumptions of Gaussian and Brownian motion errors, the model achieves adaptive weighting of historical data . Specifically, the kernel function attenuates the influence of distant observations, enabling a more precise characterization of recent degradation trajectories. We derive closed-form analytical solutions for posterior distribution parameters and show that the proposed model generalizes the classical Bayesian RUL prediction framework from a kernel smoothing perspective. Experimental validations on real-world bearing and gearbox datasets confirm that the proposed model effectively mitigates regression bias and achieves a superior balance between prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification in RUL prediction compared to the classical Bayesian RUL prediction model.

title: Neural operators for ultrasonic full waveform inversion: A next-generation ultrasonic NDT with improved fidelity, efficiency, and robustness
abstract: Full waveform inversion (FWI), a computational wave imaging technique that fully incorporates the physics of wave propagation, enables high-resolution quantitative reconstruction of inhomogeneous media and promotes effective application in non-destructive testing (NDT). However, its widespread adoption is hindered by the intrinsic challenges of solving a nonlinear, ill-posed inverse problem, resulting in a high computational cost considering the iterative implementation, sensitivity to the initial model, and the possible convergence to a local minimum solution. Recent advances in data-driven FWI frameworks using neural networks have improved both accuracy and efficiency, yet challenges in robustness and generalization persist. Neural operators, an emerging paradigm in scientific machine learning, aim to learn mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces, offering superior generalization and scalability for complex physical systems. Motivated by this, we propose a neural-operator-based framework for direct inversion of ultrasonic full-waveform data based on the Unet Fourier Neural Operator (U-FNO), extending the neural operator paradigm to ultrasonic NDT. By leveraging parameterized Fourier kernels to globally capture intricate wave physics, U-FNO demonstrates improved inference efficiency relative to classical FWI, and improved fidelity and robust reconstruction compared with representative data-driven models and total focusing method (TFM). Numerical and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a promising direction for next-generation computational wave imaging technology in ultrasonic NDT.

title: Bayesian active learning for Bayesian model updating: The art of acquisition functions and beyond
abstract: Estimating posteriors and the associated model evidences, with desired accuracy and affordable computational cost, is a core issue of Bayesian model updating, and can be of great challenge given expensive-to-evaluate models and posteriors with complex features such as multi-modalities of unequal importance, nonlinear dependencies and high sharpness. Bayesian Quadrature (BQ) equipped with active learning has emerged as a competitive framework for tackling this challenge, as it provides flexible balance between computational cost and accuracy. The performance of a BQ scheme is fundamentally dictated by the acquisition function as it exclusively governs the active generation of integration points. After reexamining one of the most advanced acquisition function from a prospective inference perspective and reformulating the quadrature rules for prediction, four new acquisition functions, inspired by distinct intuitions on expected rewards, are primarily developed, all of which are accompanied by elegant interpretations and highly efficient numerical estimators. Mathematically, these four acquisition functions measure, respectively, the prediction uncertainty of posterior, the contribution to prediction uncertainty of evidence, as well as the expected reduction of prediction uncertainties concerning posterior and evidence, and thus provide flexibility for highly effective design of integration points. These acquisition functions are further extended to the transitional BQ scheme, along with several specific refinements, to tackle the above-mentioned challenges with high efficiency and robustness. Effectiveness of the developments is ultimately demonstrated with extensive benchmark studies and application to an engineering example.

title: Physics-guided residual correction model for monitoring machining deviations of complex thin-walled parts considering spatial–temporal dynamics
abstract: Machining deviation of complex thin-walled parts critically affects the product performance and stability. However, accurate deviation monitoring is significantly challenged by the complexity of the processing environment. Traditional theoretical models are computationally expensive, while existing deep learning methods often operate as black-box models with limited interpretability. To address these challenges, this study proposes a spatial–temporal physics-guided residual correction model (ST-PGRC), which integrates the theoretical machining deviation model with a Transformer-based learning module. Initially, a theoretical deviation model is established through machining dynamics and kinematics analysis. A spatial–temporal mapping module links vibration signals with the toolpath, converting temporal information into spatially meaningful features. Ultimately, the Transformer encoder learns the residuals between theoretical results and experimental results through its global attention mechanism, capturing the interactions between the theoretical model and spatial–temporal features and subsequently correcting the theoretical deviations. Experiments on thin-walled workpieces demonstrate that ST-PGRC achieves an RMSE of 0.0069 mm and reduces monitoring error by at least 22.5% compared with physics-guided neural networks, residual networks, and purely data-driven neural networks. The proposed method offers a reliable and interpretable solution for machining deviation monitoring.

title: Signal processing and force control for precision machining with grinding system integrating an aerostatic suspension compact pneumatic actuator
abstract: Signal processing is the core component of precision machining, where reliable contact force signals underpin monitoring, control, and quality assurance. Pneumatic actuators are highly favored in grinding applications due to their compliance, but friction and stick–slip phenomena distort force signals and degrade closed-loop performance. This study developed an aerostatic suspension compact pneumatic actuator (ASCPA) that suppresses friction at its source and compares it with traditional pneumatic actuators (TPA) and commercial low-friction pneumatic actuators (LFPA). Through piston-level fluid dynamics simulation, a balance between radial load capacity and air consumption was achieved, enabling prototype manufacturing and friction validation testing. From a manufacturing-oriented signal perspective, the adaptive state-space force signal recognition method EM-KF-RTS was proposed. This method integrates a Kalman filter with a Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother and employs an expectation maximization algorithm for online parameter adaptation. Using only standard force values and air supply pressure measurements from the test bench, this estimator significantly enhances resistance to vibration, electromagnetic interference, and sensor noise, enabling precise force reconstruction. The actuator-algorithm stack was evaluated under constant, sinusoidal, and variable-amplitude frequency-modulated conditions, as well as during sudden external contact and inter-chamber pressure changes on the dynamic grinding test bench. Results demonstrate that the EM-KF-RTS method achieves stable force recognition under constant, sinusoidal, and variable amplitude-frequency reference signals, as well as during sudden external contact and inter-chamber pressure changes. It exhibits superior dynamic response performance, lower root mean square error, and stronger interference suppression capabilities.

title: Development of an asymmetric magnetorheological suspension towards improved ride comfort
abstract: Under rough road conditions, the suspension system requires asymmetric damping characteristics on the damper. However, conventional magnetorheological dampers (CMRD), constrained by their symmetric flow-channel structure and high static friction, not only struggle to meet the differentiated performance demands in the compression and rebound stroke, but also induce pronounced stick–slip behaviour, thereby degrading riding comfort. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel asymmetric magnetorheological damper (NAMRD). By incorporating an adaptive pressure-relief channel in parallel with a check valve, the proposed structure fully decouples the compression and rebound flow paths, thereby enabling controllable asymmetric damping characteristics while significantly reducing system static friction. To accurately describe the dynamic behaviour of the check valve, an HB-CM model is developed, based on which a prototype NAMRD is manufactured and subjected to mechanical testing on an MTS test platform to validate the model’s accuracy. The static friction of the damper is also tested. Experimental results show that, compared with a traditional CMRD, the critical gas pressure of the NAMRD is reduced from 3 MPa to 1.5 MPa, and the static friction force is reduced by 45.87%. Furthermore, to achieve operating-condition-adaptive damping, an extended Kalman filter −based (EKF) road excitation estimation method is introduced, and the system-level validation of the control strategy, together with the NAMRD device, is carried out on a quarter-car vibration test platform. The results demonstrate that the proposed system achieves significantly improved vibration isolation performance and riding comfort under rough road conditions.

title: Using implicit correlations among synchronized vibration signals from pixels to improve the accuracy of structural damage detection
abstract: In recent years, deep neural networks have been used increasingly to process vibration signals for detecting structural damage. However, the effectiveness of deep neural networks relies on having many vibration signals, which are difficult to acquire in practical engineering scenarios. To address this limitation, a phase-based motion estimation (PME) technique has been introduced, which treats each pixel as an independent sensor, enabling the extraction of millions of vibration signals from a single video. PME not only provides sufficient training data for deep neural networks but also ensures that the signals obtained from multiple pixels are perfectly synchronized in the temporal domain. The implicit correlations among synchronized signals from multiple pixels (i.e., pixel-dependencies) have the potential to enhance damage detection. However, it remains challenging to use the pixel-dependencies effectively to facilitate damage detection. To address this issue, a multi-feature-attention network is proposed. Innovatively, the contribution of pixel-dependencies to damage detection is quantified. By assigning greater attention weights to pixel-dependencies with greater contributions, the network achieves a substantial improvement in damage detection performance. The effectiveness of the proposed method was validated by successfully detecting subtle bolt looseness in a steel structure, showcasing its superior performance in structural damage detection tasks.

title: Elastic metasurfaces for broadband Rayleigh wave attenuation in layered half-spaces with irregular interface
abstract: Elastic metasurfaces offer a promising route for attenuating and manipulating Rayleigh waves in foundations. However, most existing studies rely on idealized site assumptions and largely overlook complex geological conditions commonly encountered in practice, such as irregularly layered media. To address this gap, we propose a multiple scattering framework to explore the performance of elastic metasurfaces atop irregularly layered half-spaces, and to further optimize the metasurface, thereby facilitating broadband Rayleigh-wave mitigation under realistic geological settings. We systematically investigate the effects of upward- and downward-inclined layered interfaces on the wave mitigation performance of a uniform metasurface. Compared to horizontal stratification, these configurations exhibit distinct influence mechanisms: upward-inclined interfaces shorten the reflection paths of converted bulk waves, while downward-inclined ones guide the incident bulk waves to strongly interfere with the converted bulk waves. As a result, both lead to surface-energy accumulation and repropagation in the near field, significantly degrading attenuation performance and bandwidth. Additionally, we then jointly optimize the mass and resonance frequency of the units within the metasurface. By realizing randomly distributed tuning coverage within the target band, these optimized metasurfaces promote multidirectional diffuse scattering and suppress highly directional coherent interference. This mechanism effectively mitigates near-field surface-energy focusing and enhances broadband Rayleigh-wave attenuation, substantially outperforming the conventional classic/inverse metawedges. This work provides theoretical guidance for achieving broadband Rayleigh-wave attenuation in complex geotechnical environments.

title: Virtual time reversal-enhanced nonlinear Lamb wave tomographic approach for local thermal damage imaging
abstract: Ultrasonic guided waves combined with the reconstruction algorithm for probabilistic inspection of damage (RAPID) can be used to produce clear visualizations of damage regions. However, conventional RAPID methods generally rely on comparing signals against undamaged baseline and exhibit limited sensitivity to capture the subtle nonlinear acoustic responses. This paper introduces a baseline-free framework via internal path self-referencing for imaging localized thermal damage in metal plates. We integrate a virtual time reversal (VTR) procedure with a nonlinear ultrasonic technique, which effectively enhances the visibility of subtle nonlinear responses induced by damage. This method constructs the damage image using the VTR-enhanced amplitudes of second harmonics generated along propagation paths. To eliminate the influence of the accumulation effect of second harmonic generation, a path-length stratification strategy is adopted to define the damage index. We validate this framework through finite element simulations and flame-damaged experiments on an aluminum plate. Compared with conventional RAPID, the proposed method reduces imaging artifacts, removes reliance on undamaged baselines, and improves sensitivity to microstructural changes. This approach shows strong potential for in-service inspection of thermally loaded components.
keywords: Reconstruction algorithm for probabilistic inspection of damage (RAPID)

title: Unveiling the masking effect of unbalance force on incipient bearing cracks in flexible rotor systems: dynamic modeling and physics-guided VMD-TEO diagnosis
abstract: While localized bearing defects have been extensively modeled in isolation, their dynamic interaction with flexible rotors under heavy unbalance—and the resulting signal masking—remains underexplored. This paper investigates the nonlinear dynamic evolution and signal detectability of inclined raceway cracks in a coupled rotor-bearing system. A refined dynamic model is established, incorporating time-varying stiffness (TVS) and displacement (TVD) excitations within a Timoshenko beam finite element framework. A critical “masking effect” is revealed: under large eccentricity, the massive centrifugal load pins the journal and linearizes the system stiffness, completely submerging the crack-induced nonlinear signatures. To overcome this detectability challenge, a Physics-Guided Variational Mode Decomposition and Teager Energy Operator (PG-VMD-TEO) strategy is proposed. Unlike purely data-driven methods that easily trap into unbalance-dominated local optima, this strategy utilizes high-fidelity simulation priors to pinpoint sensitive frequency bands. Experimental validations confirm that the proposed method accurately decouples weak fault features from severe synchronous interference. This study provides a rigorous theoretical basis for compound fault diagnosis and offers robust engineering guidelines for heavy rotating machinery.

title: Feedforward-feedback control method for stick-slip piezoelectric actuators: wear allocation and self-updating of contact force database
abstract: In the stick–slip piezoelectric actuator, friction always exists between the driving foot and the slider, leading to a severe degradation of the actuator’s performance over time. This study is a follow-up research on the closed-loop control method of contact force with multiple feedback parameters. To improve the stability of the stick–slip piezoelectric actuator throughout its whole life cycle, a combined control method integrating feedforward control (based on a contact force database) and feedback control (based on the driving characteristic surface) is proposed in this study. The prediction and update of the contact force database degradation over time are realized through a wear allocation method. This method can maintain the long-term stability of the contact force feedforward control effect and effectively improve the full-life-cycle stability of the actuator. The proposed feedforward-feedback control method can effectively enhance the linearity of the actuator’s displacement output and improve its ability to maintain driving characteristics under external disturbances. The control method proposed in this study effectively improves the driving stability of the stick–slip piezoelectric actuator in the full working range and throughout the whole life cycle, which is of certain significance for the industrial application of stick–slip piezoelectric actuators.

title: Nonlinear vibration suppression of a beam subjected to concentrated mass loads with an X-shaped local isolator
abstract: The truss girder structure of the spacecraft optical platform is a critical component for supporting precise optical payloads. Its dynamic design and analysis significantly affect the overall orbital stability of the spacecraft. This study establishes a mechanical model for a beam subjected to concentrated mass with X-shaped local isolators to explore the system’s dynamic stability and nonlinear vibration characteristics. The governing equations of the system are derived and discretized using the assumed modes method and Hamilton’s principle. A parametric analysis reveals the variation of the system’s natural frequencies, and numerical calculations of the amplitude-frequency response curves are performed using the arc-length continuation method. The numerical results show that under a given excitation, the proposed isolators may exhibit rich nonlinear dynamic responses, such as hardening nonlinearity, jump phenomena, and superharmonic resonance. Compared to traditional isolators with linear spring compensation, the proposed device has a lower resonance frequency. These findings provide important theoretical and reference support for the dynamic optimization design and stability control of spacecraft optical platforms.

title: A hidden failure state identification method for steel-spring floating slab track isolators using MVFuseNet
abstract: Isolators in steel-spring floating slab track (SS-FST) systems can suffer from hidden failures, such as fractures and fluid leakage, which may lead to safety risks like train derailments. However, research on fault modeling and failure state identification is limited. This paper proposes MVFuseNet, a fault-diagnosis framework for identifying failure states of steel-spring isolators. The framework constructs a dataset from multi-source vibration signals generated from field wheel-drop tests and simulations, ensuring high-quality data for classification. In addition, a novel time–frequency feature extraction method based on phase-coupled time–frequency analysis (PC-TFA) enhances damage-sensitive features, while a multi-channel phase-enhanced variational decomposition (MC-PEVD) method generates robust inputs for deep learning. Finally, an improved deep residual network is used for high-precision classification of failure states. Experimental results show that MVFuseNet outperforms existing methods in feature representation and classification accuracy, providing valuable support for the safe operation of SS-FST systems.

title: Surrogate-based optimization of electromagnetic converter for an airfoil-based torsional flutter energy harvester with structural nonlinearity and turbulent wind inflow
abstract: A previous pilot study proposed a novel airfoil-based stall-flutter energy harvester equipped with an electromagnetic induction converter for wind energy harvesting. While the feasibility of the device was demonstrated, its efficiency under optimized electromagnetic circuitry and the combined effects of structural nonlinearity and turbulent wind inflow remains largely unexplored. To address these gaps, this study advances the information processing, necessary to optimize the previous design. In particular, the electromagnetic converter is optimized using a surrogate-based global optimization approach employing radial-basis-function stochastic response surface models, yielding up to a 503% increase in average electrical output power compared to the non-optimal circuit used in earlier work. The effects of structural nonlinearity and turbulent inflow are also examined. For the open-circuit configuration, turbulence is found to have a secondary influence on the harvester response, confirming previous wind tunnel observations. For the closed-circuit configuration, turbulence across different intensities similarly produces only modest changes in output energy. By contrast, structural nonlinearities, theoretically modeled using hybrid Duffing-van der Pol oscillators, have a beneficial impact, enhancing performance by nearly an order of magnitude. With the optimal electromagnetic circuit and appropriately tuned structural nonlinear parameters, the harvester achieves a maximum average output power of 64.32 mW for simulated operational conditions at a representative deployment site. These findings demonstrate feasibility of this compact harvester and highlight the critical role of electromagnetic and structural optimization in maximizing energy generation, offering guidance for future prototype and field deployment.

title: Active Double Glazing With In-Cavity Compensated Microphones
abstract: This study investigates an active noise control method to improve the transmission loss of double-wall partitions at low frequencies, with an application example of double-glazing partition. The approach involves integrating loudspeakers and microphones into the cavity of the partition and using a novel control strategy to enhance the attenuation at low frequency and consequently the transmission loss of double-wall partition. Specifically, it introduces a method to learn optimal filters that compensates in-cavity microphone signals to replicate the performance obtained by minimizing downstream microphone signals. Simulations and experiments were conducted on a 2.1 m×0.85 m double-glazed prototype using 8 loudspeakers and 8 microphones under harmonic and broadband excitations, comparing the optimal attenuation of active noise control strategies using either uncompensated downstream microphones, uncompensated in-cavity microphones, or compensated in-cavity microphones. Results with uncompensated downstream microphones, show that optimal commands achieved attenuation averaging 31 dB under harmonic excitation and 8.2 dB for broadband noise (100–500 Hz). Concerning in-cavity microphones, the compensated method yields to attenuation averaging 21 dB under harmonic excitation and 5.5 dB for broadband noise (100–500 Hz; which is consistently better than the uncompensated method, for harmonic (13 dB) or broadband control (3.1 dB). It highlights the essential role of using compensated in-cavity microphones to attenuate the acoustic pressure transmitted through double-wall partition.

title: Similar transformation method of ship frame structures explosion shock scaled model based on exponential diffeomorphism mapping
abstract: For the scale model experiments of ship structures under underwater explosion loads, the traditional similarity theory generates distortion effects as it fails to meet the complete similarity criteria under the conditions of multi-physical field coupling. Moreover, the dynamic response of underwater explosion ship structure presents transient strong nonlinear and non-stationary dynamic behavior, which makes it difficult to construct an accurate similarity transformation relationship between existing scale model experiment data and prototype structure response. This paper proposes a similarity transformation method based on nonlinear dynamics theory. The response evolution of ship structure under transient strong nonlinear impact is revealed by phase space reconstruction and symbolic dynamics theory, and then the similarity transformation equation of the system is constructed by combining parabolic mapping and topological semi-conjugate theory. Firstly, this paper designed scale experiments of a typical hull structure under different impact factors. The results show that the dynamic response of the system presents nonlinear and nonstationary characteristics of chaos and period interweaving. Furthermore, based on topological semi-conjugacy theory, this paper constructed a similarity transformation equation with an exponential function as diffeomorphism mapping. The quantitative transformation from model experiment data to prototype structure is realized. By introducing symbolic sequence complexity metrics to validate the conversion results, it is demonstrated that the conversion error can be controlled within 15%. Compared with traditional similarity theory methods, the proposed framework improves the conversion accuracy by approximately 30%–40%. This similarity conversion framework provides a new perspective for understanding the similarity mechanisms of nonlinear dynamic responses in ship structures under blast impact.

title: Dynamic characteristics analysis of shaft-mounted labyrinth-brush composite seal rotor system
abstract: Labyrinth seal and brush seal are currently the most widely used seal technologies in large rotating machinery, each with its own advantages and disadvantages in complex working conditions. Brush seals can adapt to rotor motion to form dynamic seal with minimal leakage, but direct contact between bristles and seal disc generates friction. Labyrinth seals have a long service life but suffer from significant leakage due to seal clearance. At present, most of the research on rotor seal systems analyzes a single seal with a fixed stator installation, the direct contact between the seal and the rotating shaft will cause frictional heat loss on the shaft. Based on this, this study proposes a dynamic model of a shaft-mounted labyrinth-brush composite seal rotor system, which is causing the centrifugal effect. Using bifurcation diagrams, axis trajectory diagrams, and frequency spectra, the nonlinear dynamic characteristics of the system are analyzed. In addition, the influence of composite seal parameters such as rotational speed, axial pressure drops, and seal length on the nonlinear response of the system are studied. The discovery that rotational speed can cause the timing of chaos in the system to occur earlier. Additionally, a higher axial pressure drop reduces the rotational speed at which chaos occurs. However, this also results in a decrease in the maximum vibration displacement of the system. The system state changes have become more complex. Through the research in this article, new ideas are provided for the analysis and optimization of seal structures, and a theoretical basis is provided for the stability research of rotating machinery.

title: Wave-PINN: a wavelet-based physics-informed neural network for continuous pavement roughness evaluation from vehicle dynamics
abstract: Automated pavement monitoring across pavement networks generates large volumes of high-frequency data that are typically non-stationary, multi-scale, and incomplete, making accurate, physically consistent, and robust prediction challenging. This paper presents Wave-PINN, a hybrid framework that integrates wavelet-based multiscale signal representation with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). Using the International Roughness Index (IRI) of asphalt pavements as a representative application, longitudinal pavement elevation profiles from more than 11000 pavement sections in the Long-Term Pavement Performance (LTPP) database were collected and analyzed. In the proposed framework, longitudinal pavement elevations and vehicle dynamic responses are projected into the wavelet domain, and the quarter-car model is embedded in the loss function via staged physics-informed training. Results demonstrate that Wave-PINN achieves high predictive accuracy (R2 > 0.999) while substantially improving physical consistency, with physics loss reduced by more than 80% as the training data fraction increases from 20% to 80%. The hybrid strategy maintains test accuracy comparable to purely data-driven models while, relative to purely physics-driven models, reducing physics loss by nearly 50% and lowering the coefficient of variation of physics loss by more than 44%. Compared with time-domain neural networks, Wave-PINN provides superior interpolation and extrapolation performance, with relative L2 errors consistently below 0.016. Under incomplete-data conditions, it improves prediction reliability over conventional IRI computation and remains applicable in extreme scenarios where the conventional method becomes inapplicable. These results support Wave-PINN as a robust and effective framework for continuous pavement-signal modeling and network-level pavement-condition assessment.

title: Uncertainty laws of modal identification under free vibration
abstract: Aiming at understanding the identification uncertainty in modal identification, uncertainty laws have been developed in the context of ambient vibration test and shaker-based forced vibration test. Similar laws are developed in this paper for the case of free vibration test, which is widely used in structural condition assessment. More specifically, the asymptotic coefficient of variation of modal parameters (natural frequencies, damping ratios and mode shapes) is derived for the structural vibration excited by known/unknown initial conditions. The derivation is based on the Fisher information matrix (FIM) evaluation, under the assumptions of long data and small damping, and the inversion of FIM, analytically obtained with the tool of asymptotic decoupling. Assumptions and theoretical results are intensively validated using synthetic, laboratory and field test data. The derived uncertainty laws reveal the governing factors of identification uncertainty, including the damping ratio, the bandwidth factor, the modal signal-to-noise (s/n) ratio, and the effective data length. Compared with existing uncertainty laws, it is shown that the free vibration test can achieve similar identification precision as the forced vibration test, and both are better than the ambient vibration test, provided that the modal s/n ratio remains the same in the equivalent sense. The developed uncertainty laws provide a scientific basis for planning and managing identification uncertainties in practical free vibration tests.

title: Modeling and experimental study of rotor drop dynamics in maglev rotor systems with caged deep-groove ball touchdown bearings
abstract: Active magnetic bearings (AMBs) require touchdown bearings (TDBs) to protect the rotor–stator system in the event of failure. To describe the detailed dynamics during rotor drop, a dynamic model of a caged deep-groove ball TDB is developed by explicitly considering the motions of the inner ring, outer ring, cage, and rolling elements. The effects of TDB clearance and initial drop position on ball slip, ball load, and post-drop rotor response are investigated. The results show that smaller clearances reduce ball–raceway slip. In the non-full-rub whirl state, the ball load is minimized at a clearance of -5μm, whereas under full-rub whirl conditions, larger clearances lead to lower ball loads. Both negative clearances and excessively large positive clearances increase the likelihood of full-rub whirl. The initial drop position strongly affects the rotor response at intermediate rotational speeds and may also trigger full-rub whirl. High-speed rotor drop experiments under different TDB clearances, initial drop positions, and rotational speeds are conducted to validate the model and the main findings.

title: Inverse design of nonlocal lattices with arbitrary multiband dispersion relations
abstract: We present a numerical algorithm to implement arbitrary multiband dispersion relations in one-dimensional periodic lattices with N-degree-of-freedom unit cells using nonlocal interactions. First, we present a general model to calculate the dispersion relation for periodic lattices with N-DOF unit cells with linear, mass–spring–damper-type interactions. We show that the dispersion relation is obtained from a quadratic eigenvalue problem, in which nonlocal interactions yield wavenumber-dependent mass, stiffness, and damping matrices via a Fourier series. In principle, because these properties can be specified at every wavenumber, nonlocal interactions can yield any set of dispersion curves.
