The method is first demonstrated using a numerically simulated Duffing oscillator with negative linear stiffness, positive nonlinear stiffness, and sinusoidal forcing. The method is then applied to experimentally measured responses of a Duffing oscillator with unknown stiffness and damping excited by a nonlinear external force through a magnetic stinger and a modal shaker.

title: Offline synchronization framework based on signal decomposition techniques for accurate modal analysis
abstract: Structural health monitoring (SHM) through modal analysis of dynamic responses has garnered significant interest in bridge and building engineering due to its ability to provide in-depth monitoring of structural conditions, facilitate early detection of potential issues, and enhance structural reliability and safety. In addition, extensive studies indicate that wireless sensor networks (WSNs) or low-cost sensing systems (LCSs) offer significant cost-effective advantages for monitoring civil engineering structures; however, they also introduce issues related to asynchronous sensing. Asynchronicity can immediately degrade modal analysis and hinder subsequent damage detection, quantification, localization, and assessment. Therefore, verifying synchronicity across all channels and performing time correction are essential steps before further analysis. Given the difficulties in implementing synchronization functionalities in hardware or firmware, offline synchronization can effectively achieve synchronous measurement via model-driven or signal-driven methods. Compared to the other one, signal-driven methods rely on decoupled modes in structural responses; thus, no dynamic models or identification processes are required beforehand, and less computation is needed. In this study, the impacts of asynchronous sensing are first introduced to demonstrate their influence on the performance of structural modal analysis. Asynchronization can substantially alter analysis results for each mode, especially when delays coincide with modal cycles, and eventually deteriorate condition assessment and damage evaluation. Subsequently, an offline synchronization framework based on signal decomposition techniques is developed, and various techniques are employed to compare results for monitoring structures using low-cost sensors. The proposed three-step framework—comprising time-domain signal decomposition, cross-correlation evaluation, and optimized delay search—is initially examined using a numerical model subjected to ambient vibrations to evaluate its performance, followed by a discussion comparing different techniques. To further validate the proposed framework, after the numerical study, laboratory and field experiments are conducted using free-vibration and forced-vibration tests, respectively. Apparently, the experimental study evidently demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework, yielding reliable and accurate results for modal analysis.

title: Homotypic multi-source joint representation with dynamic hierarchical feature tracing in hybrid Walsh–frequency domain for prior knowledge-constrained fault diagnosis of multi-cylinder drilling pumps
abstract: Fault diagnosis in multi-cylinder drilling pumps is fundamentally challenged by homotypic multi-source mixing, where identical mechanical mechanisms generate overlapping spectral signatures that obscure early fault indicators. Contemporary state-of-the-art methods often falter in these complex environments, lacking the stability to maintain performance across varying pressure levels and the sensitivity to quantify the severity and urgency of developing faults. To address these limitations, this study proposes the Homotypic Multi-source joint Representation with Dynamic Hierarchical Feature Tracing (HMR-DHFT) framework. The methodology integrates a prior-independent energy-kurtosis screening mechanism for adaptive mode reconstruction, a hybrid Walsh–frequency feature space to resolve spectral blurring, and a matrix-free dynamic ridge tracking algorithm to extract fault evolution patterns. Experimental validation confirms that the proposed framework achieves superior diagnostic resolution and reliability when compared to recent state-of-the-art approaches and domain-specific baselines. Key results demonstrate that HMR-DHFT not only achieves superior fault isolation accuracy across four distinct operating pressure regimes but also successfully characterizes the severity and urgency of failures—capabilities that are notably absent in existing signal processing baselines. These findings establish the framework as a robust solution for monitoring complex mechanical systems under diverse hydraulic operational conditions.

title: Nonlinear dynamic analysis of stretchable inorganic electronics in three-dimensional serpentine configuration
abstract: A three-dimensional (3D) serpentine configuration is widely used in stretchable inorganic electronics, whose dynamic behaviour is essential in various service environments. In this study, a nonlinear dynamic model of a buckled 3D serpentine structure under base excitations is derived from the extended Lagrangian principle, with consideration of the specific local deformations. The obtained first order resonance frequency is consistent with previous results. The symplectic Runge-Kutta method is used to simulate the system, which has both high accuracy and long-term numerical stability. Rich nonlinear dynamic behaviours are revealed, including coexisting periodic and chaotic vibrations. Particularly, an essential structure parameter is identified as the ratio of the length of the unit cell to that of the serpentine configuration, which can effectively regulate the mechanical characteristics of the potential well of the structure. Various nonlinear dynamic behaviours under different applied loads and different structure parameters are found through calculating the fraction of initial conditions leading to chaos. The key geometric parameter can significantly affect the tendency of the serpentine interconnections to generate chaotic vibrations, and the change of this parameter will expand or shrink the chaos region in the phase space of the structure, indicating that complex dynamical behaviours in the buckled serpentine configuration can be tuned by the simple structure parameter. Consequently, the results of this investigation are useful for understanding complex dynamics of the buckled serpentine configuration, and for tuning the sensitivity of novel 3D serpentine-structured devices.

title: A novel method to identify weak fault features in strong composite noise by enhanced cyclic correlation entropy with truncated nuclear norm LRSD
abstract: Rolling bearings are utilized extensively to support rotating parts. However, under long-term operating conditions, bearings are prone to failure. Moreover, their initial failure is very weak and would be buried in strong Gaussian and impulse noise. When impulse noise and strong Gaussian noise coexist, the majority of signal processing methods degrade to varying degrees. To solve this issue, the enhanced cyclic correlation entropy (CCE) algorithm based on truncated nuclear norm (TNN) low-rank sparse decomposition (LRSD) is proposed to accurately identify weak fault characteristics under strong composite noise situation. Firstly, the Gaussian kernel function is introduced on the basis of cyclostationary analysis to obtain the two-dimensional cyclic correlation entropy spectrum (CCES) matrix to suppress the interference of impulse noise. Then, considering the low-rank and sparse properties of the noise-contaminated signals within the two-dimensional f-α matrix, the spectral matrix is further noise-reduced and feature-enhanced by a sparse decomposition method based on the improved TNN. Finally, a full-band integration process is performed to obtain the enhanced envelope spectrum (EES). Validation is then carried out using simulated fault signal and two bearing datasets, and the analysis results demonstrate that, unlike most existing fault diagnosis methods which are severely impaired or rendered ineffective by mixed noise, the proposed method can still reliably extract fault features while significantly mitigating noise interference.

title: Parametric study and design for quasi-static-toggling electromagnetic energy harvester
abstract: The quasi-static-toggling (QST) electromagnetic energy harvester (EMEH) is an established solution for motion-powered wireless remote switches. These devices generate sufficient electricity for wireless transmission under low-speed actuation. Despite their extensive application as engineered products, the fundamental operating principles of QST EMEHs have only recently attracted attention from the research community. This paper conducts a parametric analysis to optimize the mechanical input energy of a bistable QST EMEH. The input energy is defined as the potential energy stored in the energy-buffering spring before toggling. The magnetic attracting force is a key factor affecting the input energy amount. It is proportional to the square of the total magnetic flux through the iron bar mover. Major geometric parameters’ influencing the total magnetic flux are first evaluated via finite element method (FEM) simulation. The optimization process also involves two other parameters: the mover’s stroke distance between two magnetic poles, and the energy-buffering spring stiffness. The theoretical lumped-parameter model is simulated with a multi-field-coupled numerical simulator. Experimental results obtained from several prototypes with different geometries indicate that the trend of the force–displacement curve and the harvested energy are consistent with theoretical and simulation predictions. The discussion provides the optimal parameter region for achieving the maximum output electrical energy in practical design. This understanding is valuable for a rational optimization of QST EMEH.

title: Nonlinear dynamic characteristics analysis of aerostatic spindle with active control
abstract: Aerostatic spindle is primarily used in precision machining applications, where its vibration characteristics directly determine machining accuracy. Closed-loop active control serves as an effective measure to enhance precision by suppressing vibration deviations while maintaining operational stability. This paper proposes a real-time active control approach that utilizes signal conversion to achieve compensation and vibration suppression. Real-time control excitation is determined through a proportional-differential-integral control strategy. Dynamic air film excitation is derived by employing air film mesh node partitioning to calculate the instantaneous air film thickness under vibration influence. Accounting for deflection angle variations yields instantaneous mass eccentricity excitation incorporating centrifugal effects and vortex-induced vibrations. Analyzing the coupled dynamics under multiple load excitations, a dynamic model of the spindle system incorporating active control is constructed. The closed-loop solution approach for vibration characteristics under active compensation is proposed, enhancing theoretical analysis accuracy. Closed-loop active control is achieved by collecting vibration signals and utilizing piezoelectric actuators for real-time compensation of vibration displacement. The validity of the coupled theoretical model is verified through experimental and simulation signal comparisons, and active control effectively reduces response amplitude and suppresses vibration. Vibration behavior under different parameter conditions is simulated to investigate the influence of active control on nonlinear characteristics, providing theoretical references for control parameter selection.

title: Simultaneous displacement and rotation estimation for flexible structures through millimeter-wave radar and inertial sensor fusion
abstract: Structural displacement and rotation are critical metrics in structural health monitoring, yet their simultaneous estimation remains a significant challenge. This study proposes a novel technique that fuses measurements from the collocated inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor and frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) millimeter-wave radar to estimate both parameters. Initially, Line-of-Sight (LOS) displacement is derived from radar measurements in the presence of structural rotation. Subsequently, the initial rotation is estimated using IMU acceleration data, with radar measurements utilized to decouple translational components. A calibration algorithm is then applied to convert the LOS displacement into actual structural displacement. Furthermore, an error-optimization-based fusion of initial rotation and angular velocity data of the IMU sensor is proposed to enhance rotation estimation accuracy. The proposed technique was validated through laboratory-scale experiments. The conversion factor was successfully calibrated under rotational motion, and displacement was accurately estimated with an error of less than 0.3 mm, even in the presence of structural rotations up to 6.5°. Additionally, the proposed technique reduced rotation estimation errors by over 88% compared to existing methods.

title: Experimental and theoretical approach for determining ball-interface sliding in rotor-bearing systems and its application in control moment gyroscopes
abstract: The operational precision and service life of rotor-bearing systems are critically threatened by interfacial sliding, which may result in excessive wear, localized temperature rise, and cage deformation. However, direct characterization of such micro-phenomena remains challenging as the relative sliding behavior is intrinsically coupled with the balls’ spatial motion. Thus, this paper presents a methodology for the in-situ measurement of bearing ball spatial motion and the subsequent derivation of interfacial sliding features. First, binocular vision is employed to reconstruct the balls’ three-dimensional position and orientation. The interfacial sliding parameters are then calculated for the contact zones between the balls and the inner/outer raceways as well as the cage pockets. These parameters encompass micro-translational sliding, spin sliding, and the related skidding rate. Lastly, the control moment gyroscope, a sample rotor-bearing system, is used to test and validate the proposed technique. An in-situ measurement rig is constructed. The results demonstrate that when the gimbal speed increases, the balls’ orbital speeds decrease and their rotation speed increase, thereby significantly intensifying both translational and spin sliding. Crucially, gimbal motion exerts the most detrimental effect on the ball-cage interface, providing a quantitative basis for bearing reliability optimization.

title: An optimal sensor placement framework for iFEM-based shape monitoring using Fisher information matrix
abstract: High-accuracy shape monitoring is essential for ensuring the performance and safety of aerospace structures. The inverse finite element method (iFEM) has shown substantial potential due to its real-time capability and its independence from load and material parameters. However, achieving high reconstruction accuracy requires a sufficiently fine inverse element discretization, with strain rosettes installed on both surfaces of each element. This large sensor demand constrains broader adoption of iFEM in aerospace engineering. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a Fisher information matrix (FIM) based optimal sensor placement (OSP) method for shape monitoring using iFEM. This study is the first to directly incorporate FIM into iFEM for OSP. Two optimization criteria are introduced. The first, the FIM criterion, constructs a FIM to quantify and maximize the amount of information in the reconstruction equation, leading to spatially continuous sensor placement. The second, the divergence criterion, enhances the representativeness of measurement points under various deformations. The simultaneous optimization of these two criteria enables the OSP under multiple load conditions. The proposed method was first validated on plate structures with different dimensions and load conditions, and subsequently applied to a complex wing box structure subjected to aerodynamic loads to verify the accuracy, efficiency and robustness. Finally, an experimental investigation was conducted on a wing-shaped sandwich plate with a triply periodic minimal surface core. The results demonstrated that the method can reduce the number of sensors by approximately 67% while maintaining a maximum reconstruction error of about 11%.

title: Snap-bounded FIR-based global trajectory smoothing via alternating minimization under axial kinematic constraints
abstract: In high-end semiconductor manufacturing equipment, maximizing throughput while suppressing motion-induced vibrations is a critical yet inherently conflicting requirement. To meet these competing demands, advanced trajectory planning that generates high-order smooth motion profiles is essential. Although Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filtering offers an effective pathway for synthesizing such smooth and frequency-suppressed motion profiles, its application to global trajectory planning is hindered by the complex coupling between filter-induced delays, corner blending errors, and strict axial kinematic constraints. To address this issue, this paper proposes a unified global smoothing and optimization framework for snap-bounded motions. At the core of the framework is an alternating minimization algorithm that solves the highly coupled non-convex optimization problem of dwell times and velocity profiles, thereby improving execution efficiency under strict axial kinematic constraints. To support this optimization, a precise corner blending error evaluation method is developed based on the exact superposition of velocity pulses, which provides an accurate geometric basis for tight constraint enforcement. In addition, a geometry-regularized pre-processing scheme is introduced as an auxiliary module to regularize the reference path before optimization, thereby reducing unnecessary conservativeness in the subsequent optimization and further improving execution efficiency. Experiments on a high-precision motion stage and additional evaluations on various path geometries demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for high-precision repetitive motion tasks where offline planning is acceptable.

title: Open-set domain generalization residual feature reconstruction network for intelligent fault diagnosis under unknown time-varying working conditions
abstract: Currently, deep learning has garnered significant attention for addressing fault diagnosis challenges. However, in real-world industrial settings, the complexity of equipment and diversity of operating conditions can lead to unknown faults occurring under target conditions. Consequently, open-set domain generalization fault diagnosis (OSDGFD) has emerged as a critical research direction. However, existing open-set domain generalized fault diagnosis suffers from negative transfer, drastic changes in feature distributions under non-stationary time-varying rotational speed conditions, and insufficient revelation of fault features. These issues severely hinder performance research in open-set domain generalized fault diagnosis. Therefore, this paper proposes the Residual Feature Reconstruction Network for Intelligent Fault Diagnosis in Unknown Time-Varying Conditions (RFR-OSDG). First, a compact and reconstructable latent representation for known-class features is learned using known-class feature distribution mechanisms, while KL divergence constrains the normality of the latent distribution. Unknown classes, failing to conform to this distribution, exhibit larger reconstruction errors and are thus preliminarily distinguished. Building upon this foundation, an adaptive domain-aware class boundary loss constructs a dynamic decision boundary. This boundary constrains intra-class samples to remain within the boundary region while excluding out-of-class samples, thereby enhancing the model’s boundary recognition for known classes and reducing cross-class confusion and misclassification of unknown classes. By minimizing the triplet loss, the aggregation of similar features and the separation of dissimilar features are enhanced. An entropy-enhanced category-aware mechanism is designed to address the issue of inconsistent data distribution between the source domain and the target domain. Finally, experimental results under non-stationary time-varying speed show that the proposed method, RFR-OSDG, has better clustering and classification performance as well as superior generalization.

title: Fixed-point constrained maximum total generalized correntropy: Convergence analysis and low-complexity algorithms
abstract: In recent years, robust linearly constrained adaptive filtering has gained increasing attention, and the constrained generalized maximum correntropy (CGMC) works well in some impulsive noise situations. However, when the input signal contains some noise, the performance of CGMC is greatly affected. To solve this problem, we first propose a fixed-point constrained maximum total generalized correntropy (FP-CMTGC) algorithm based on the errors-in-variables (EIV) model. According to the Banach fixed-point theorem, we have conducted the convergence analysis for FP-CMTGC. To improve its performance in practice, we further apply the gradient and recursive methods to FP-CMTGC, yielding two kinds of online versions, i.e., the CMTGC and recursive CMTGC (RCMTGC) algorithms. Moreover, combining the weighting method and the leading dichotomous coordinate descent (DCD) strategy, we have proposed a low-complexity version of RCTGMC, namely DCD-RCTGMC. In addition, we derive the equivalence analysis between DCD-RCTGMC and the original RCTGMC. Finally, the validity of the convergence and the superiority of the proposed algorithms are verified by several simulations.

title: Adaptive sparse matching squeezing chirplet transform for multi-component time-frequency feature extraction of non-stationary signals in rotating machinery fault diagnosis
abstract: Thanks to time–frequency analysis (TFA), the time–frequency features in non-stationary mechanical vibration signals are effectively represented. However, many existing TFA methods based on linear chirplet transform (LCT) face issues such as energy diffusion, interference components between features, and ridge breakage in the time–frequency representation (TFR) when processing time-varying multi-component instantaneous frequency (IF) features. Additionally, at the same instant, the unclear matching mechanism for multi-component IFs leads to the problem of uninterpretable parameter determination criteria. Therefore, taking the interpretability of feature sparsity measures as the core idea, this paper proposes a novel TFA method based on adaptive sparse matching squeezing chirplet transform (ASMSCT). First, a new higher-order kernel function is proposed to extend the conventional linear modulation kernel function, enabling the chirp rate (CR) to match multi-component IFs accurately. Second, the sparse mechanism underlying the optimal matching between CR and IFs is clarified mathematically, and a unified and interpretable sparsity measure optimization framework is constructed for CR determination. Finally, the Hoyer index is used to generate a TFR with high energy concentration, and an improved local squeezing operator is employed to achieve refined feature focusing. Furthermore, by adjusting the new kernel function and sparsity measure criterion, ASMSCT can extended to other advanced LCT-based methods, making it a more fundamental time–frequency transform framework. Simulated signals verify the significant advantages of ASMSCT in terms of time–frequency energy concentration, feature distinguishability, noise robustness, and signal reconstruction. Real signals demonstrate the applicability of ASMSCT in fields of mechanical fault diagnosis and biological time–frequency feature extraction.

title: General contact point response estimation approach for vehicle scanning via Bayesian filtering and smoothing
abstract: Contact point response signals offer competitive advantages for bridge modal identification in vehicle scanning. This study proposes a general framework to estimate all time derivatives (displacement, velocity, and acceleration) of the contact point response across different vehicle types, bridge types, and contact models. The proposed framework consists of (i) a novel state-space model that links contact point response to the flexible modal response of the vehicle while accommodating various vehicle measurement scenarios, and (ii) a joint input-state estimation algorithm (via an Augmented Kalman Filter (AKF) and a Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother). In this context, the unknown input accounts for the contact point response with a kinematic relationship instead of the conventional random walk model. Subsequently, the residual contact point response is obtained by post-processing the contact point response. Using first numerical simulations, the study demonstrates the applicability of the proposed approach and investigates the influence of contact model, vehicle speed, bridge and vehicle types, road roughness, sensor noise, and modeling errors on estimation accuracy. Then, the study further validates the proposed framework by means of a laboratory experiment.

title: Optimization of non-periodic P(VDF-TrFE) piezoelectric transducers for high-purity selective transduction of Lamb waves: Analytical, numerical, and experimental analysis
abstract: Surface-mounted polymer piezoelectric transducers offer attractive design flexibility for guided-wave structural health monitoring (SHM), yet broadband methods for mode-selective Lamb-wave excitation remain limited. In this work, we investigate non-periodic annular P(VDF-TrFE) transducers for high-selectivity Lamb-wave transduction by combining analytical modeling, numerical optimization, and experiments. A line force model is first extended to concentric annular electrodes and assessed against fully coupled finite-element simulations and broadband measurements. The model is shown to capture the overall tuning behavior and to predict the peak and null frequencies of the two fundamental modes with good accuracy, making it suitable for fast design optimization. Based on this model, a broadband optimization framework is developed by minimizing the wave-packet energy of the undesired mode relative to that of the desired mode over the full tone-burst bandwidth. The optimized transducers achieve high selectivity with compact geometries, a small number of electrodes, and a single driving signal. The underlying mechanism is clarified by showing that the introduced non-periodicity clusters neighboring nulls in the source influence spectrum and creates an effective rejection band over a finite frequency range. Comparisons with conventional tuning and a phased-array approach further highlight design flexibility and robustness for various signal bandwidths. Experiments on two fabricated optimized transducers confirm the predicted selective behavior, although the measured suppression levels remain lower than the theoretical ones. These results provide a computationally efficient route to compact broadband transducer design for SHM applications.

title: Nonlinear vibrations and chaotic dynamics of a rotating cable in a wind turbine with transverse modal coupling
abstract: The nonlinear dynamic model of the rotating cable system is established for the first time to enhance the design reliability of cable-stayed wind turbines. First, the governing equations of the system are derived using Hamilton’s principle. Subsequently, the partial differential equations of the system are discretized based on the assumed mode method and Galerkin method. The model order is reduced via the degree-of-freedom condensation method. Finally, the analytical and numerical solutions are obtained by combining the Method of Multiple Scales and the Runge-Kutta method. The proposed dynamic model is validated experimentally under wind turbine shutdown conditions. Parametric studies are subsequently conducted to evaluate the influence of key parameters on the centrifugal static displacement and natural frequencies. Furthermore, the system’s nonlinear response characteristics are investigated under the 1:2 internal resonance condition in the vicinity of the primary resonance, revealing the intrinsic relationships among rotational effects, modal coupling, and nonlinear resonance. Notably, rotation-induced centrifugal stiffening significantly alters the static displacement and tension distribution along the cable, while the natural frequencies of the system are shown to increase with angular velocity. Additionally, rotation induces strong coupling between in-plane and out-of-plane modes, altering both the modal sequence and mode shapes. Near the primary resonance, the system exhibits pronounced hardening nonlinearity, multi-stability, jump phenomena, hysteresis, Hopf bifurcations, and chaotic behavior. Ultimately, these findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for the dynamic design and optimization of rotating flexible cable structures.

title: Development of a camera-laser-IMU system for non-contact transverse displacement estimation using an adaptive extended Kalman filter
abstract: Monitoring lateral displacement in railroad bridges is important because excessive displacements can increase derailment risk during train crossings. Traditional displacement measurement systems require invasive installations, posing safety and operational challenges. To overcome these limitations, this study developed a non-contact, sensor-fusion-based system that combines a laser, camera, and inertial measurement unit (IMU) through an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF), designed for future deployment on an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV). The EKF used in this study incorporates an innovation-based adaptive mechanism that dynamically adjusts process and measurement noise covariance, allowing the system to respond to changing sensor uncertainties during UAV-induced motion. A controlled indoor UAV flight was conducted under a motion capture system to inform the design of subsequent laboratory tests. Given the importance of UAV rotational motion for measurement accuracy, a six-degree-of-freedom (6DOF) platform was used to simulate UAV dynamics through combined translational and rotational movements. The system was evaluated under four motion scenarios. Estimated displacements were compared against two contact and non-contact ground truth measurements, as well as a previously developed camera-laser system by other researchers. The developed system outperformed the camera-laser method, reducing peak errors by 69.1% and Root-Mean-Square Error by 68.3%. The fusion approach was particularly effective under yaw-dominated motion. Correlation and phase-shift analyses showed that error magnitude increased when translational and rotational motion were misaligned, while phase-aligned conditions yielded the lowest average error. The current validation was performed in a controlled laboratory setting to evaluate the system and algorithm as a foundation for future field deployment.

title: An improved stochastic harmonic function representation for stochastic processes based on starting time of phase evolution
abstract: Simulations of stochastic processes using traditional spectral representation (SR) methods typically involve high-dimensional random variables. Although advanced dimension-reduction SR methods such as the stochastic harmonic function representation (SHF) have been proposed in recent years, the challenge of ’curse of dimensionality’ still remains open. To address the challenge, this study proposes an improved stochastic harmonic function representation (iSHF) based on the concept of starting time of phase evolution, by which the independent random phases in original SHF can be modeled as a coupled function of random frequency and a large-scale time argument. This treatment successfully reduces the dimension of random variables by half. Rigorous theoretical derivation proves that the iSHF can not only accurately reproduce the target power spectral density with controllable precision, also feature Gaussian properties. To define the ranges for starting time of phase evolution, the power spectral densities of Gaussian white noise processes and stochastic excitation processes such as earthquake ground motions, turbulent wind, and ocean waves are explored. For illustrative purposes, the sampling discrepancy analysis of the proposed method and stochastic response analysis of a 9-story nonlinear shear frame structure subjected to stochastic ground motions are conducted by introducing the generalized F-discrepancy and the probability density evolution method. Numerical example reveals that the iSHF can effectively reduce the sampling degradation associated with high-dimensional problems and improve sample uniformity, compared to the original SHF, demonstrating its credible applicability and effectiveness.

title: Domain interference suppression for reliable fault diagnosis under unseen operating conditions
abstract: Fault diagnosis under varying operating conditions remains challenging due to the entanglement of fault-related information and condition-related variations in measured signals. In practical industrial scenarios, continuously varying operating conditions such as speed changes can induce significant intra-class variability within the same operating state, which in turn leads to unstable feature representations and compromised diagnostic reliability under unseen conditions. Motivated by the observation that fault-related and condition-related information are entangled in measured signals, this paper models them as coexisting structures within a shared representation space, where condition-related variations act as structured interference when performing domain generalization based fault diagnosis. Accordingly, a domain interference suppression (DIS) framework is proposed to mitigate condition-related interference while preserving fault-discriminative representations. Instead of pursuing strict feature disentanglement, the proposed framework learns a shared representation and encourages functionally differentiated features with different degrees of domain sensitivity, so that condition-related variations can be modeled in a complementary manner without undermining robust fault diagnosis. To further stabilize representation learning and avoid feature collapse, a teacher-student strategy is introduced, where the teacher network provides domain-supervised structural guidance, enabling the student network to learn more consistent feature representations without increasing inference complexity. The proposed framework is evaluated on two public bearing fault diagnosis datasets under continuous speed variation and unseen operating conditions. Under the unseen target domain setting, the proposed method achieves average accuracies of 98.96% and 90.59% on two benchmark datasets, outperforming the second-best method by 2.86% and 0.82%, respectively. The code of DIS is available at https://github.com/jshzh163com/DIS.

title: Uncertainty-aware adaptive Bayesian inference method for structural time-dependent reliability analysis
abstract: Time-dependent reliability analysis is critical for assessing the safety of structures throughout their full life cycle. Bayesian active learning methods have recently gained attention in reliability analysis, demonstrating more attractive features than existing active learning methods, e.g., the capability of providing and utilizing the probabilistic uncertainty measures over the failure probability. However, they are only investigated in the context of time-invariant reliability analysis. This study proposes a novel Bayesian active learning method termed ‘Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Bayesian Inference’ (UABI) for time-dependent reliability analysis with small failure probabilities. The time-dependent failure probability integral is first interpreted from a Bayesian inference perspective to quantify the uncertainty arising from the discretization error. The posterior mean and upper-bound posterior standard deviation of time-dependent failure probability are then derived to facilitate the construction of adaptive strategies. Besides, a new hyper-ring decomposition importance sampling technique is developed to numerically approximate the posterior statistics, which can greatly reduce the required sample size. Furthermore, a learning function and two stopping criteria are proposed based on the concept of reducing and judging the numerical uncertainty of the time-dependent failure probability, thereby enabling active learning. The performance of the proposed method is verified by five examples. The proposed method is shown to be able to accurately estimate the time-dependent failure probability, while requiring fewer limit state function calls and less computational time than other state-of-art active learning methods.

title: AFAO: adaptive feature adjustment optimization for long-tailed distributed wear fault diagnosis of hydrodynamic mechanical seal
abstract: In third-generation nuclear power units, hydrodynamic mechanical seals (HDMS) in reactor coolant pumps often fail due to wear, and collecting fault data is challenging because of the high reliability requirements and low failure probability. This results in long-tailed distributions in failure datasets, with sparse tail classes and highly similar signals. To solve these issues, we propose the adaptive feature adjustment optimization (AFAO) method for HDMS wear fault diagnosis. AFAO first expands the decision boundary by broadening the clusters of training sample features, which inversely compresses the test sample clusters and reduces the chance of actual samples crossing the decision boundary. Then, it assesses the similarity between fault types using a pre-trained model. Based on this, AFAO adaptively adjusts sample point margins according to the classifier’s weight parameters and assigns different weights to each fault type based on their frequency. This improves the classifier’s learning effectiveness across various fault types. AFAO is a plug-and-play module that can be integrated with classic backbones to enhance long-tailed learning capabilities. Experimental results show that our method performs as well as or better than other long-tailed learning methods.

title: A hypergraph-enhanced state space model-Mamba framework for cross-domain response reconstruction guided by physical information
abstract: In data-driven structural response signal reconstruction tasks, the scarcity of high-quality, well-marked batch response data and the ambiguous spatial dependency patterns between response data constitute critical bottlenecks that constrain the performance of response reconstruction models. To address this challenge, this work proposes a novel cross-domain response reconstruction method based on a Hypergraph-enhanced Mamba (State Space Model) network (HeMamba) — a dual-stream framework that simultaneously processes temporal and spatial information. Specifically, the method utilizes the Mamba to capture long-term dynamic dependencies in multi-sensor signals, employs hypergraphs to model the higher-order spatial relationships among sensors, incorporates a designed two-layer Hypergraph Convolutional Network (HGCN) to capture their spatial dependency patterns, and additionally introduces a physics-based loss function derived from Power Spectral Density (PSD) to constrain the training process. Furthermore, a physics-informed transfer learning paradigm is introduced, wherein the model is pre-trained using finite element numerical simulation data. By freezing the spatial encoding module, the knowledge of structural physical response laws and intrinsic patterns learned by HeMamba is transferred to scenarios with limited real measured data for fine-tuning, thereby guiding the Mamba model to perform response signal reconstruction in the measured domain under physical constraints. Experiments on a tower steel structure indicate that the proposed method effectively alleviates the reconstruction accuracy degradation caused by data scarcity. With fine-tuning on a small amount of measured data, the reconstructed signals achieve an R2 value of 0.9798 and exhibit high-precision response reconstruction across the full frequency band, significantly outperforming baseline models trained directly. Notably, even under structural damage conditions, the proposed method still can transfer physical knowledge learned from the source domain to response reconstruction in the target domain. This study provides a feasible technical pathway for high-precision cross-domain response reconstruction under small-sample conditions.

title: Suppression of nonlinear friction-induced vibration in high-pressure water-lubricated interfaces via interfacial shear hysteresis: modeling, simulation, and experimental validation
abstract: Friction-driven self-excited vibration is a persistent instability in high-load water-lubricated contacts, where strong load support is often accompanied by limited intrinsic dissipation. Rigid designs mainly mitigate instability by reducing friction, but provide limited energy dissipation. Soft liners add damping but may lose dimensional stability under high pressure, leaving an unresolved load–noise conflict. To address this challenge, we embed constrained-layer damping (CLD) into a CFRPEEK-NBR-17-4PH water-lubricated bearing. The layered architecture introduces an interfacial shear-hysteresis dissipation pathway while maintaining high load support. A nonlinear rotor–bearing model is developed that couples water-film forces, the Stribeck friction effect, and viscoelastic damping. Multi-condition rig tests are conducted to validate the mitigation mechanism in time-domain statistics, frequency-domain responses, and full-band energy. The CLD bearing reshapes the vibration statistics, with the measured PDF peak increasing from 0.199 to 0.216 (about 8.5%). It reduces the dominant 3X pulsation component by 3.6 dB. Above 4000 Hz, the maximum overall acceleration level decreases by 6.5 dB, corresponding to an amplitude reduction of about 53%. These results identify interfacial shear hysteresis as an effective dissipation pathway for suppressing pulsation–friction-coupled vibration under high-pressure water lubrication.

title: An improved multi-sensor rail damage detection method based on geometric-numerical adaptive weight fusion and exponential Gini entropy
abstract: Railway transportation is a critical pillar affecting the economy, and the timely detection of potential rail damage is essential for its operational safety. However, most existing methods rely on a single sensor, which leads to a limited detection range and poor signal quality stability. This in turn reduces accuracy and reliability, especially when multiple damages are involved. To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes an improved acoustic emission (AE) testing method based on multi-sensor signal geometric-numerical adaptive weight fusion (GNAWF) and exponential Gini entropy (EGE). GNAWF mitigates inter-channel attenuation biases and waveform distortions by combining geometric attenuation weight derived from the attenuation effect model with numerical similarity weight based on similarity metrics, thereby enhancing signal confidence and damage-related information. By combining the Shannon entropy-based distribution sensitivity factor with the Gini index to compute the EGE feature, dual sensitivity to spectral variations is achieved, thereby enhancing detection accuracy. The proposed method is validated using a vehicle-mounted rail damage detection experimental platform. It is also compared with mainstream signal fusion, feature extraction, and damage detection methods. The results demonstrate that the proposed method exhibits significant superiority across all evaluated metrics.

title: Spin induced topological phase of ultrasonic guided wave in corrugated structure
abstract: Ultrasonic guided waves are widely used in structural health monitoring (SHM) and nondestructive evaluation (NDE). However, commonly used phase features, such as time-of-flight (TOF) shifts and single-channel phase measurements, are often sensitive to temperature variation, mechanical loading, and sensor coupling. This work introduces a geometry-based alternative: the geometric phase accumulated when guided-wave polarization slowly rotates while crossing a corrugated plate, and this phase is shown to be governed by the wave’s spin (local polarization rotation), making it less sensitive to absolute timing and amplitude variations than conventioanl phase-based methods. Starting from a continuum decomposition of total angular momentum, closed-form expressions for guided wave spin densities and spin field linked to energy transport by separating the Poynting vector into orbital and spin contributions are derived. Unlike bulk media, guided waves are shown to support multiple mixed spin states (similar and hybrid contributions), which provide additional pathways for geometry-driven polarization evolution and can enhance sensitivity to small boundary changes. Three practical geometric-phase estimation approaches are investigated: a k -space Berry-phase formulations, a field-space topological metric, and a real-space spin-trajectory construction. Among these the field-space metric is adopted because of its robustness to amplitude/timing drift. Time-domain finite-element simulations on corrugated aluminum plates (corrugation coefficient ∊ ∊ , periodicity P ; tone bursts 400–1200 kHz) show that near each tone-burst central frequncies the phase curves collapse across ∊ ∊ and P indicating low sensitivity. Away from that band they tilt and separate, while Δ ϕ approaching π and polarization flips relative to a flat-plate baseline. The full-field spin maps reveal counter-rotating layers through the thickness and localized repeating spin packets as P increases, coinciding with regions of highest Δ ϕ sensitivity. The time–marching 3D simulations also show that the spin field changes it shape over time, but keeps a clear mirror symmetry about the mid–plane due to symmetric geometry and loading scenario. The out–of–plane spin component s 3 can reverse between snapshots, indicating time–dependent switching of the local particle–rotation caused by wave mixing and scattering in the corrugated wave guide. Overall, a chain is demonstrated between geometric phase and spin, suggesting a robust geometry-linked feature for guided-wave propagation.

title: Bow drill-inspired vibration modulation strategy for efficiently exploiting low-quality vibration energy
abstract: Road vibration energy is one of the most important power sources for implementing in-situ power supply to distributed electronics. However, the low efficiency in harvesting energy from road vibrations is primarily from the lack of a high-performance vibration modulation strategy (VMS), due to the road vibration’s low-quality characteristics of ultra-low frequencies (≤ 5 Hz) and small amplitudes (≤ 5 mm). To solve this issue, we propose herein a bow drill-inspired VMS (BD-VMS) that can convert each small-amplitude vibration to high-speed one-way rotation (OWR) through a displacement amplification unit, a bow drill-like flexible driving unit, and an OWR unit. Attributed to the unique modulation principle of the BD-VMS, the measured OWR speed reaches 2418 rpm under low-quality vibration (3 Hz, 3 mm), achieving a rotational speed amplification of 75.5 times as compared with that (32 rpm) enabled by the conventional rack-pinion mechanism. Moreover, by leveraging the rotary inertia of a rotator, the OWR can be maintained even under 0.01 Hz ultra-low-frequency vibration. In addition, an energy harvester designed with the BD-VMS can deliver electric outputs at 241 Hz and harvest as much as 395.4 mW electrical energy from a low-quality (3 Hz and 3 mm) vibration, which is 564.9 times higher than that (0.7 mW) generated by an energy harvester constructed with the rack-pinion mechanism. As a distinctive and efficient approach for modulating and exploiting low-quality vibration energy, the BD-VMS may greatly promote the practical application of energy harvesting technologies in self-powered distributed electronics.

title: R1CSS: a novel method for completely separating REB fault responses based on rank-1 characteristic subspace
abstract: Accurate separation of complete Rolling Element Bearing (REB) fault responses can help to accurately monitor REB fault conditions. Existing separation methods can only remove noise and other vibration sources to a certain extent, but cannot accurately separate the complete single fault response, and the existing methods generally lack a clear physical explanation and have poor adaptability to noise. In this paper, based on the Rank-1 property of the REB fault response characteristic matrix and sparse modelling of impulsive noise, an accurate and efficient optimal separation model is proposed: Rank-1 Characteristic Subspace Separation (R1CSS). R1CSS introduces a discrete low-rank sparse model and constructs a Rank-1 characteristic subspace with clear physical significance based on the theoretical fault characteristic frequency, to constrain the separation of the target REB fault response. The corresponding closed-form solutions are derived to develop the alternating minimisation heuristic algorithm. Through simulation and real experiments, the proposed R1CSS can more accurately and adaptively separate the complete REB fault response from common interference than the existing typical methods. The R1CSS also achieves good separation results for amplitude modulation phenomena and random fluctuation phenomena.

title: An efficient computational framework for the dynamics simulation of elastic wheels on deformable terrain
abstract: Dynamic evaluation of crewed lunar rovers operating on loose, rugged regolith requires a wheel–terrain interaction model that can account for wheel compliance, evolving contact geometry, and terrain deformation with acceptable computational cost. However, high-fidelity wheel–soil interaction simulations often incur prohibitively high computational overhead for system-level multibody integration, whereas conventional quasi-static terramechanics approaches are insufficient for transient elastic wheel behavior. To address this issue, this study proposes an efficient computational framework for simulating the interaction between elastic wheels and rugged deformable terrain. A reduced-order discrete multibody wheel model is developed by discretizing the metallic tread into lumped-mass nodes connected by multidirectional spring–damper elements. The model captures the dominant compliant characteristics of the wheel, including radial, circumferential, and lateral deformation coupling, as well as equivalent bending effects of the tread surface. An extended terramechanics formulation is further introduced to evaluate interfacial forces over the actual deformed contact patch. By computing stresses at the element level and accounting for time-varying and interrupted contact, the method can handle irregular and discontinuous wheel–terrain interaction on rough terrain. The proposed framework is validated through single-wheel soil-bin tests with a prototype wheel under crater and rock crossing crater-traversal and rock-crossing conditions, and is further integrated into an 18-degree-of-freedom dynamic model of a crewed lunar rover. Results show that the method can reproduce the main mobility and ride-dynamics responses of elastic wheels on rough soft terrain with acceptable accuracy and high computational efficiency. The proposed framework therefore provides a practical tool for system-level dynamic analysis of crewed lunar rovers under specified operating conditions.

title: Dynamic modeling and decoupling control of a clear-aperture tip-tilt-piston piezoelectric platform with high bandwidth and large stroke
abstract: Stable optical link establishment requires three-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) compensation for both beam pointing errors (tip/tilt) and defocus drift (piston), demanding both high natural frequency (> 1 kHz) and high positioning accuracy (μrad/nm-level). However, small or nonexistent clear apertures in existing platforms restrict their integration into the primary optical path. This work proposes a 3-DOF piezoelectric platform featuring a large clear aperture and a decoupling control strategy, enabling unobstructed high-precision beam transmission. The mechanism utilizes three sandwich-type piezoelectric actuators (SPAs) coupled to a central mirror seat via flexible hinges to generate decoupled rotation about the x/y-axes and translation along the z-axis. Integrated strain sensing beams monitor SPA deformation in real-time, facilitating precise calculation of angle and displacement. Through kinematic analysis and static modeling, the functional relationship between driving signals and motion outputs is established, achieving 3-DOF decoupling. A dynamic model based on the pseudo-rigid-body method further characterizes its vibrational behavior. In terms of bandwidth and decoupling ability, compared with existing tip-tilt-piston platform that exhibit first-order natural frequencies below 1 kHz and cross-axis coupling above 1.8%, this work achieves a first-order natural frequency of 5075 Hz and cross-axis coupling below 1.64%. Experimental validation using the strain sensing system demonstrates strokes of 1.64 mrad (x-axis), 1.89 mrad (y-axis), and 13.62 μm (z-axis), with resolutions of 2.66 μrad, 3.08 μrad, and 21.9 nm, respectively. Closed-loop control suppresses hysteresis within 1.57%, eliminates creep, and maintains steady-state errors within ± 8 μrad. High-frequency beam steering validates its effectiveness for angle error compensation, while defocus drift compensation in microscopy improves image sharpness by at least 12.6%.

title: Editorial Board
Active suppression of line spectrum vibration in electro-hydraulic pumps using harmonic current injection
abstract: The electro-hydraulic pump (EHP), serving as the core power unit of an electro-hydrostatic actuator (EHA), exhibits pronounced line spectrum vibration in the low- to mid-frequency range that is difficult to attenuate using conventional vibration isolation. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an active suppression strategy using harmonic current injection (HCI). The dominant excitation sources are analyzed, while the relationship between injected current harmonics and mounting feet vibration is derived, establishing the preconditions for HCI-based suppression. Further, a controllable harmonic alignment design (CHAD) is introduced via motor–pump co-selection of key parameters, intentionally aligning the pump characteristic frequency with the controllable band of current harmonics. Finally, an HCI control algorithm is developed, prototype EHPs are fabricated, and experiments are conducted to validate the proposed approach. Compared to conventional designs, the co-designed EHP achieves considerable line spectrum vibration suppression, thereby reducing the pump-dominated characteristic line by above 96% and decreasing the total vibration energy in the 0–200 Hz band by 86.7%. This study provides a novel approach for mitigating line spectrum vibration in EHPs and demonstrates considerable engineering potential.

title: Box-Cox sparsity measure-based impulse extraction for gearbox condition monitoring
abstract: Vibration impulses from gearboxes are crucial for fault diagnosis but are often obscured by strong meshing components and background noise. This paper proposes Box-Cox Sparsity Measure-Based Impulse Extraction (BCIE), which advances beyond the existing Optimal Weighted Impulse Extraction (OWIE) method by: (1) generalizing the kurtosis criterion in OWIE to Box-Cox sparsity measures (BCSM) parameterized by λ, where λ=1 corresponds to the original OWIE formulation; and (2) introducing an optimized window-length selection strategy absent in OWIE. The efficacy of the proposed BCIE is validated through both numerical simulation experiments and gearbox run-to-failure datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed BCIE exhibits strong sensitivity to incipient gear faults and is well-suited for gearbox impulse extraction and health monitoring, particularly when λ=0 (negative relative entropy), which optimally balances early fault detection sensitivity with false alarm suppression. Parameter analysis reveals: (1) large λ values (λ⩾2) increase false alarms while showing minimal BCSM changes during faults; and (2) small λ values (0<λ⩽0.2) yield insignificant fault indications while weakening healthy-state signals.

title: Generative digital twin: A Sparse-xLSTM based self-evolution hybrid modeling approach for complex equipment
abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into digital twins (DTs) offers transformative potential for characterizing the non-linear dynamics of complex equipment. However, realizing high-fidelity, self-evolution generative DTs remains challenging due to the computational prohibitiveness of Transformer based architectures and the insufficient long-term memory of traditional recurrent networks. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel generative digital twin (GDT) method driven by a Physics-Guided Sparse-xLSTM. First, we construct a Sparse-xLSTM architecture designed to model high-dimensional temporal dynamics efficiently. By leveraging exponential gating and matrix memory, this architecture achieves linear computational complexity while effectively capturing long-range dependencies, overcoming the quadratic bottleneck of conventional attention mechanisms. A sparse attention strategy is further incorporated to extract distinct state features from noisy sensor data, enhancing representation robustness. Second, to ensure physical consistency and generalization, a hybrid modeling mechanism is devised. Physical priors are embedded as input feature, and governing equations are integrated into the optimization objective as physical constraints, effectively confining the generative solution space to physically valid trajectories and mitigating model hallucinations. Third, addressing the imperative for continuous adaptation, a low-rank adaptation (LoRA)-based self-evolution engine is developed. This mechanism enables the GDT to perform online updates using limited streaming data by fine-tuning low-rank matrices, ensuring rapid synchronization with the time-varying states of the physical entity without catastrophic forgetting. Experimental validation on CNC machine tool wear datasets demonstrates that the proposed approach significantly outperforms advanced baselines in both prediction accuracy and adaptation efficiency, providing a robust paradigm for intelligent predictive maintenance of complex equipment.

title: Dual-domain fusion and dual-path information extraction network for rapid high-resolution distributed fiber-optic sensing
abstract: Distributed Brillouin-based optical fiber sensing is widely employed for structural health monitoring of large-scale infrastructure and for early disaster warning. However, it is necessary to acquire and average a substantial number of time-domain Brillouin signals to suppress noise, followed by time-consuming Lorentzian curve fitting to extract the Brillouin frequency shift (BFS). Here, we propose a Dual-Domain Fusion and Dual-Path Information Extraction Network (D2IENet) to extract BFS with high accuracy and at high spatial resolution. The D2IENet consists of a feature-reconstruction network, a denoising path, and a frequency-shift fitting path. The feature-reconstruction network extracts features separately in the spatial and frequency domains and adaptively fuses them to obtain multi-scale and low-redundancy representations, which are then split to the denoising and frequency-shift path to perform BGS denoising and along-fiber BFS extraction. In the experiments, the D2IENet increased the signal-to-noise ratio by approximately 13 dB compared with the existing denoising algorithms. It reduced the required number of average times from 1000 to 5, a decrease of two orders of magnitude. A 98200 set of BGSs over 9.82 km of sensing optical fiber was measured, and the simultaneous BGS denoising and BFS fitting were completed in only 19 s, representing a 90% reduction in processing time. The BFS standard deviation was reduced to 0.073 MHz, an improvement of one order of magnitude. The D2IENet does not compromise high spatial resolution while maintaining strong stability and robustness. We believe that, without requiring additional hardware devices, D2IENet offers a solution for distributed optical fiber sensing that integrates high accuracy, high spatial resolution, and rapid processing.

title: A fragmental prediction framework for the prognosis of rolling bearings based on in-line oil debris monitoring
abstract: In-line oil debris monitoring (ODM) provides an effective health indicator (HI) for rolling bearings, thanks to the high robustness to environmental and measurement noise, and the high monotonicity regarding the degradation process. However, the trajectory of ODM-based HI is generally complex or even irregular, which brings a great challenge for the remaining useful life (RUL) prediction. For this issue, this study proposes a novel fragmental prediction framework. Given the difficulty of the RUL prediction of the whole life cycle, as a trade-off, this framework truncates and translates the HI first, and only conducts the RUL prediction at the last degradation stage. Specifically, this framework introduces a stage threshold to identify whether the degradation reaches the last stage. Then, a probabilistic retrospective analysis is designed to find the stage transition point of the last stage. After the truncation and translation operation on the HI, the RUL can be predicted with a fragmental linear degradation model. A set of numerical and real-world experiments are conducted. The results show a significant improvement in the proposed framework compared to the state-of-the-art RUL prediction models. This study provides a novel strategy for accurate RUL prediction of safety-critical assets with complex degradation behavior.

title: A new approach to the analysis of erosion-emulated damage in wind turbine blades: An experimental study
abstract: Wind turbine blades (WTBs) govern both the aerodynamics and the structural response of wind turbine generators (WTGs). Leading-edge erosion (LEE) alters local surface roughness and geometry, degrading lift-to-drag characteristics and reducing energy capture, while mass loss and stiffness changes may shift the rotor’s dynamic behavior. We present an integrated workflow that emulates LEE on a 1 kW WTB and quantifies its impact on aerodynamic and structural performance. Tip-section erosion is parameterized in QBlade® (BEM) to evaluate Cp and power output; modified geometries are then analyzed via FEM and validated experimentally through modal testing. Results show measurable aerodynamic damage (up to 15% power loss) and consistent shifts in the first (flap-wise) natural frequency as erosion severity increases. FEM and experiments agree within 10% across the first three modes. The study proposes vibration-based indicators as early, low-cost SHM features for WTBs and demonstrates a practical QBlade® –FEM–EMA pipeline for LEE assessment.

title: Effects of preload degradation on hysteresis nonlinearity of silicone foam–metal interfaces: Experimental and numerical investigations
abstract: Silicone foam is widely used as a vibration-damping material in critical equipment, where the mechanical properties at the foam–metal interface significantly influence the structural response. This paper establishes constitutive models that describe the hyper-viscoelasticity of silicone foam and velocity-dependent interfacial friction behavior. A continuous testing method for foam–metal interfacial mechanical properties is designed, enabling simultaneous acquisition of both joint normal stress and tangential stick–slip friction responses. An identification method for obtaining self-consistent material–interface parameters is proposed, avoiding parameter incompatibility arising from uncertainties in the foam/interface mechanical properties. Based on these developments, refined finite-element simulations of silicone foam connection areas are conducted. The simulations showed well agreement with the experimental results, validating the effectiveness of the proposed methodology. The findings reveal the influence of preload degradation on the interfacial tangential hysteresis response under cyclic shear, providing support for evaluating the performance of vibration-damping structures incorporating silicone foam damping layers.

title: ReNo: Optimal regularized normalization with endogenous distribution matching under low-quality data for remaining useful life prognostics
abstract: Predictive maintenance and reliability analytics are emerging as key paradigms for sustaining complex engineered systems, with remaining useful life (RUL) prediction as a core task for health management and intelligent decision-making. In practical industrial scenarios, time series signals are often affected by noise and exhibit low-quality characteristics. As a widely adopted preprocessing technique, normalization aims to eliminate dimensional differences and improve the comparability of data in the input space. However, traditional methods such as min–max and z-score normalization rely on fixed statistics and often fail to maintain scale consistency under noise-dominated conditions. In this paper, we propose ReNo, an Optimal Regularized Normalization with Endogenous Distribution Matching. We first analyze the failure modes of conventional normalization under low-quality data and unify them within a latent optimization formulation. Building on this insight, we endogenously construct the discrepancy between the observed distribution and a reference distribution as a KL-divergence–based regularization term, thereby suppressing scale estimation bias without resorting to explicit noise separation. Additionally, we introduce a general RUL prediction framework and design a simple yet effective Degradation-Aware Representation Amplifier (DARA) as an instantiation of the time series encoder, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple public datasets. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that ReNo yields consistent improvements across various backbone models, validating its effectiveness as a general and robust normalization method for data-driven predictive maintenance in complex industrial systems.

title: Fatigue crack monitoring in L-shaped structures using AHBMP and enhanced RAPID imaging
abstract: Fatigue cracking in L-shaped aerospace components is a major safety concern. Ultrasonic guided waves can monitor this, but the complex geometry causes multimodal conversion and scattering, which creates noise and hides damage signals. We propose a visualization method combining the Adaptive Hybrid Backward Matching Pursuit (AHBMP) algorithm with an enhanced Reconstruction Algorithm for Probabilistic Inspection of Damage (RAPID) framework. We use AHBMP to decouple overlapping signals and isolate the A0 mode, as it is highly sensitive to cracks. This data is then processed by an enhanced RAPID algorithm that introduces a third focal point to refine the probability distribution. This approach significantly betters damage localization and resolution. Experiments show the method tracks the full fatigue lifecycle, from initiation to propagation. In the stable propagation phase, crack length estimation error remained below 5%, proving its practical engineering value.

title: A large-linear-stroke magnetic negative-stiffness mechanism for quasi-zero-stiffness vibration isolation
abstract: Quasi-zero-stiffness (QZS) vibration isolators provide excellent low-frequency isolation but are often limited by the limited linear stroke and pronounced stiffness nonlinearity of negative-stiffness mechanisms. This study proposes a large-linear-stroke magnetic negative-stiffness mechanism (LLS-MNM) that generates negative stiffness via attraction between annular permanent magnets and a profiled iron case. A physically motivated conceptual model is developed to elucidate the negative-stiffness formation mechanism. A surrogate-assisted multi-objective optimization framework combining finite-element analysis (FEA), an ANN surrogate model, and NSGA-II is employed to maximize linear stroke and negative-stiffness magnitude while minimizing nonlinearity. The optimized mechanism achieves a 55 mm linear stroke with an equivalent negative stiffness of −1.02 N/mm and a nonlinearity index of 1.78%. Quasi-static experiments confirm a 54 mm linear stroke with δ<1.7%. Dynamic tests (0.5–6 Hz) demonstrate a reduced resonance frequency and markedly suppressed transmissibility compared with a linear isolator, and up-/down-sweep responses remain overlapped without jump phenomena up to 10 mm excitation.

title: A CRLB-based statistical framework for interpreting diffraction-limited localization in Lamb wave array imaging
abstract: Ultrasonic phased array imaging based on Lamb waves offers accurate defect localization in non-destructive testing, where multimodal dispersion improves responsiveness to structural anomalies. As the classical technique, the delay-and-sum (DAS) beamforming algorithm is distinguished by its computational efficiency and robustness to noise; it is further improved by the total focusing method (TFM) which synthetically focuses at every point in the imaging region, thereby maximizing spatial resolution and defect detectability across the entire field. However, the resolution of TFM imaging, as with any other array imaging, is fundamentally constrained by the diffraction limit, prescribed by Rayleigh’s criterion. Moreover, its effectiveness may be obscured by the multi-mode propagation of Lamb waves which introduces mode interference and overlapping wavefronts. Seeking to understand and quantify the fundamental factors governing imaging resolution and the inherent limitations in Lamb wave-based beamforming detection is therefore crucial to enhance TFM defect localization performance. In this study, we derive the Cramér–Rao lower bound (CRLB) for defect localization under a classical envelope-based, group-delay Lamb-wave DAS/TFM model. The resulting bound is interpreted as a statistical, model-conditioned benchmark for localization uncertainty of guided-wave imaging. Notably, under the adopted imaging formulation, the CRLB is found to follow the same principal wavelength-aperture trends with diffraction-limited point spread function (PSF) broadening, thereby providing an interpretable basis for comparing the localization behaviors of multi-modal Lamb wave. Extensive numerical simulations and experimental study are conducted; the results are observed to be consistent with these theoretical derivations. Particularly, the effect of different modes, including multi-modes, on the imaging resolution is studied; it is found that the introduction of the A1 mode of Lamb waves provides the most substantial improvement in resolution, possibly because the A1 mode exhibits higher group velocity, combined with its steeper dispersion curve slope, thereby enabling more precise and clearer resolution in detecting defects. Overall, this work contributes to a novel rigorous quantitative framework for understanding the resolution constraints in Lamb wave-based TFM and potentially in broader array imaging. The applicability of this work and further study needed in future research are also discussed.

title: Dynamics-guided disentangled hypersphere prototype for rotor system fault diagnosis under variable operating conditions with limited data
abstract: Rotor systems are fundamental components of rotating machinery, and their accurate fault diagnosis is the cornerstone of equipment safety. However, in practical industrial scenarios, existing data-driven methods are challenged by the coupling effect of variable operating conditions and limited training data. The feature variations induced by variable operating conditions typically require massive data for complex distribution fitting, which inherently conflicts with the reality of limited data. To address this dilemma, a dynamics-guided disentangled hypersphere prototype (DG-DHP) framework is proposed, which integrates physics-based dynamics modeling with data-driven representation disentanglement and prototype learning. First, a dynamic model of the rotor system is constructed to simulate a large amount of diverse data, and real-world noise patterns are injected to enhance data fidelity, thereby alleviating the scarcity of training data. Second, a representation disentanglement mechanism based on Brownian distance covariance is proposed to extract fault-related representations that are invariant to variable operating conditions via an explicit statistical regularization. Finally, adaptive hypersphere prototype learning is developed to replace traditional classifiers for fault diagnosis, thereby simultaneously facilitating the fitting of complex distributions and rapid adaptation to limited real-world samples. The proposed DG-DHP framework is validated on two rotor systems, demonstrating its superiority in rotor system fault diagnosis under variable operating conditions with limited data.

title: Modeling and analysis of nonlinear dynamic buckling-type vibrations in an auxetic rotating polygonal metamaterial
abstract: Auxetic rotating polygons are instrumental for programmable design of metamaterials with tunable proprieties. Their particular configuration leads to a sudden but controlled transformation between different states. However, opposed to the conventional perspective of the static stability in the pre-buckling state, a dynamic buckling-type phenomenon is observed in experiments based on a finite rotating-polygonal network. Under harmonic excitations much lower than the static buckling limit, global longitudinal motions and local rotations contribute to the buckling-type deformation of the system. In this paper, we report this phenomenon and we develop an analytical discrete nonlinear model to understand this phenomenon. The discrete model parameters are rigorously identified and validated against finite element simulations, achieving good agreement in both static force–displacement responses and linearized modal analyses. Based on the analytical discrete model, the phenomenon is reproduced in dynamic simulations with nonlinear jump resonances on both ends of the rotation-excited branch where the global longitudinal mode is coupled with the local rotational mode. Our work not only unveils a previously overlooked dynamic instability mechanism in buckling-based materials, but also provides an analytical framework for predicting and designing auxetic rotating polygonal metamaterials, with implications for future applications in vibration control and soft robotics.

title: A cointegration-driven auto-adaptive neural network strategy for strain-based structural health monitoring of masonry structures and its application for damage detection in full-scale experimental testing
abstract: Strain is a highly effective damage-sensitive feature for Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) of masonry structures. However, Environmental and Operational Variations (EOVs), such as air temperature changes, can induce drifts in strain time series that mask damage-related patterns, requiring compensatory techniques for reliable novelty detection. This paper proposes a cointegration-driven, auto-adaptive neural network strategy for strain-based SHM in masonry structures, a field where effective approaches remain limited. The methodology integrates nonlinear cointegration principles with a customized Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) regressor at the sensor level. Unlike standard implementations, the MLP captures time dependency through a modified input matrix that incorporates historical information, enabling damage-sensitive features cleansed of EOV effects. Novelty analysis then combines stationarity assessment with statistically robust control charts for damage detection. A Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) validates the proposed time-dependent MLP model, and a Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) is adopted as a benchmark to assess novelty detection against an established deep-learning paradigm. A case study consisting of a full-scale masonry building monitored through smart bricks and subjected to varying damage scenarios under real environmental conditions demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. Results show that the time-dependent MLP achieves higher computational efficiency than the RNN while maintaining accuracy, that the nonlinear cointegration approach overcomes key limitations of linear methods in EOV compensation and damage detection, and that the proposed framework matches the CAE in novelty detection at a markedly lower computational cost. Overall, this supports a broader and more effective application of strain-based SHM in masonry structures.

title: Three-dimensional vibration analysis of a aperiodic truss lattice cylindrical shell protective structure
abstract: This paper addresses the random vibration problem of aperiodic truss lattice (ATL) cylindrical shell protective structures in aerospace vehicles by developing a dynamic modeling and parameter identification approach that integrates the spectral-geometric method with particle swarm optimization (PSO) inversion. Due to the curvature and aperiodic distribution of the structure, conventional homogenization methods based on periodic boundary conditions are less applicable. To overcome this, the study employs three-dimensional (3-D) elasticity theory, a modified Fourier series to represent the displacement field along the wavenumber direction, and an artificial virtual spring technique to simulate arbitrary boundaries, thereby establishing a vibration model for multilayer cylindrical shells. The PSO algorithm is then used to inversely identify equivalent orthotropic material parameters of the lattice core by minimizing the natural frequency discrepancy between a detailed finite element method (FEM) model and a homogenized analytical model, eliminating reliance on structural periodicity. Numerical simulations and experimental tests validate the method’s convergence, accuracy, and computational efficiency. The main contribution of this work lies in a dynamic modeling and inversion framework suited to aperiodic, curved lattice sandwich shells, which overcomes limitations of traditional homogenization regarding unit-cell aperiodicity and shell curvature. Coupling wavenumber-spectral expansion with intelligent optimization significantly enhances computational performance. The results provide a practical strategy for vibration analysis and lightweight design of aerospace support structures under random excitation.

title: A broadband piezoelectric-electromagnetic hybrid energy harvester based on a multi-magnetic coupling structure
