abstract: This paper introduces a broadband piezoelectric-electromagnetic hybrid energy harvester based on a multi-magnetic coupling structure. This research conducts theoretical analysis and performance evaluation of this energy harvester. The test experiments adopt the variable-control method. In this experiment, the parameters of the magnetic coupling and limiters were changed to explore the output performance of this energy harvester. The test results show that by adjusting the magnetic coupling parameters, the bandwidth of this energy harvester is increased from 4 Hz to 9.5 Hz. Compared with the piezoelectric energy harvester without magnetic coupling, the bandwidth of this energy harvester has increased by 171.4%. By changing the parameters of the limiters, the maximum peak-to-peak voltage generated by this energy harvester is increased from 22 V to 27.6 V. In addition, with an external load of 16 KΩ, the maximum root mean square power of this energy harvester is 13.1 mW. Application experiments prove that this energy harvester can continuously power 80 LED lights or an electronic thermometer. This shows that the output performance of the energy harvester proposed in this paper can meet the power supply needs of some low-power devices.

title: Discussion on the convergence of the matrix power control algorithm
abstract: Multi-input multi-output random vibration tests require control of response spectral densities through a closed-loop equalization process. Various correction algorithms have been developed for this purpose, including the commonly used matrix power control algorithm. Recently, Manring et al. introduced an optimized moving-average method to enhance both the control performance and convergence behavior of this algorithm. Although many studies have practically employed this control algorithm, a theoretical proof for its convergence remains unaddressed. This brief discussion provides a theoretical analysis of the matrix power control algorithm, detailing its derivation process, inherent limitations, and convergence characteristics.

title: A graph attention network framework utilizing Kolmogorov–Arnold networks for dynamic analysis of complex structures in unseen scenarios
abstract: The rise of deep learning (DL) has greatly improved the analysis of complex structural responses. However, traditional DL models are limited by their dependence on large datasets, which hampers generalization to unseen scenarios and adaptability to various structural forms. To address these challenges, this paper introduces GATKAN, a novel graph attention network framework based on Kolmogorov–Arnold networks (KAN). GATKAN models complex structures as graphs, integrating spatial topology into the training process. Utilizing a multi-head attention mechanism, it captures temporal response patterns and aggregates data from each graph node. The Kolmogorov–Arnold network updates potential states and projects data into the desired dimensions. Experimental results show that GATKAN generalizes well across unseen scenarios, particularly for complex systems with varying structural forms. The model’s robustness is further validated by noise introduction and sensitivity analyses. Comparison with baseline models demonstrates GATKAN’s superior prediction accuracy, especially in handling node features and dynamic system responses. Moreover, it reduces training data requirements while maintaining high accuracy, making it a promising tool for practical engineering applications.

title: Reinforcing metamaterial-based wave attenuation through integration of negative capacitance with graded piezoelectric inductive shunts
abstract: Piezoelectric inductive-shunt-based metamaterials for wave attenuation is generally limited by the narrow bandgap, primarily due to the weak electromechanical coupling of piezoelectric transducers. While recent investigations into graded metamaterials with spatially varying unit cells have indicated promise of bandgap broadening, the actual attenuation strength may be compromised, and experimental validation remains inconclusive. In this research, we investigate a graded piezoelectric metamaterial beam with identical transducers series-connected individually to graded inductive shunts that are further enhanced by negative capacitance (NC) elements, and provide a first-of-its-kind experimental validation of the design. The unit cells are synthesized based on the LC resonance of piezoelectric inductive shunts, which are fully adaptive upon tuning the synthetic inductors (SIs). Meanwhile, op-amp-based NC elements are incorporated to enhance electromechanical coupling. Our correlated analytical and experimental studies reveal that such an integration can significantly reinforce wave attenuation as a performance multiplier. Particularly, while the graded LC resonances broaden bandgaps, the NC elements further extend the attenuation zone and concurrently reduce the transmission ratio (TR) within it. These advancements can enhance wave attenuation, especially for practical situations where only a finite number of unit cells are deployed. The effects of structural damping and circuitry resistance on wave attenuation performance are assessed systematically. Guidelines for graded inductance tuning with proper frequency spacing are developed, and insights into the experimental implementation of SI-NC network are provided. This research lays down a solid foundation for fully unleashing the potential of piezoelectric metamaterial-based wave attenuation by means of advanced circuitry synthesis.

title: Experimental identification of a bistable device for seismic energy dissipation
abstract: This work describes a novel method for experimentally measuring and identifying dynamic parameters of bistable systems. The investigated samples are physical models of unit cells of mechanical metamaterials used for seismic energy dissipation. In order to identify this type of nonlinear systems, the paper proposes a new instantaneous probabilistic algorithm, which is capable of extracting the causal components of the dynamic response from the random ones. This is especially relevant for nonlinear systems exhibiting abrupt transitions between dynamical regimes, whose frequency content can evolve significantly over time. In particular, the approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) approach is extended to the time-frequency representation of non-stationary dynamic responses typical of bistable systems. The method was tested on experimental measurements of 3D-printed bistable samples with the final goal of estimating the instantaneous energy dissipated under different external excitations, proving the device's effectiveness.

title: A novel adaptive maximum correntropy extended Kalman filter for structural input-state-parameter identification under non-Gaussian measurement noises
abstract: Traditional extended Kalman filter (EKF) typically rely on the Gaussian-noise assumption, which limits their effectiveness in complex real-world conditions where disturbances are often non-Gaussian. To address this issue, we propose an adaptive maximum correntropy extended Kalman filter with unknown input (AMCEKF-UI). The proposed framework integrates a fixed-point iterative optimization scheme and leverages correntropy-based criteria to improve robustness against non-Gaussian measurement disturbances while maintaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, to enhance multi-kernel maximum correntropy filtering, we develop a novel adaptive kernel-size optimization strategy that dynamically regulates kernel widths, thereby avoiding performance degradation caused by excessively large kernel sizes and promoting stable convergence. The feasibility and effectiveness of AMCEKF-UI are evaluated through a series of numerical studies, including linear and nonlinear hysteretic shear structures subjected to unknown external or seismic excitations. The results indicate that GEKPF-UI exhibits relatively poorer identification performance and significantly higher computational cost. In contrast, the AMCUKF-UI method, which incorporates the adaptive maximum entropy criterion into the UKF-UI framework, achieves an identification accuracy comparable to that of the proposed AMCEKF-UI. In addition, the identification performance benefits from increased sensor density. Finally, shake-table experiments further demonstrate the practicality of the proposed method for real structural systems.

title: A Class-Aware Supervised Contrastive Graph Network for CNC machining condition monitoring with class-imbalanced data
abstract: Machining state monitoring plays a critical role in ensuring quality, productivity, and reliability in CNC manufacturing. However, real-world industrial scenarios are often characterized by severe class imbalance and limited annotated data, which significantly challenge the robustness and generalization of existing learning-based approaches. To address this issue, we propose a Class-Aware Supervised Contrastive Graph Network (CSCGN), a unified framework that rethinks imbalanced industrial signal learning from a representation-centric perspective. Instead of treating signal segments independently, the proposed approach explicitly models the intrinsic structural relationships of one-dimensional sensor signals through a dynamic graph mechanism, while incorporating class-aware contrastive learning to enhance discriminative representation under imbalance. By jointly integrating multi-view signal representations, physics-informed topological modeling, and imbalance-aware optimization, the proposed framework effectively captures both structural dependencies and minority-class characteristics in noisy industrial environments. Extensive experiments on representative CNC machining tasks, including chatter detection and tool wear monitoring, demonstrate that CSCGN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across various imbalance settings. The results highlight its strong capability in minority-class recognition while maintaining overall robustness, indicating its potential for reliable deployment in real-world industrial systems.

title: SEE–GROW: Reliable exploration and boundary-aware learning for open-set single-domain generalization in fault diagnosis
abstract: Reliable fault diagnosis for rotating machinery under industrial condition monitoring is challenged by (i) limited labeled data, (ii) distribution shifts induced by unseen operating conditions, and (iii) previously unseen fault types at test time. Most existing methods address only part of this coupled setting, leading to degraded performance when open-set uncertainty and condition shift occur simultaneously. This paper proposes SEE–GROW, an interleaved training scheme for open-set single-domain generalization (OS-SDG) that alternates between reliable known-class diversification with pseudo-unknown synthesis and boundary-aware representation learning, thereby consolidating closed-set decision boundaries while strengthening open-set rejection. SEE constructs two training resources in a controllable and reliable manner: it first expands the known-class manifold through discrepancy-driven feature perturbations while filtering unreliable variations to avoid semantic drift, yielding a diversified yet label-consistent safe-known set; it then generates boundary-adjacent pseudo-unknowns by searching for minimally crossing samples near a jointly calibrated one-vs-all rejection boundary, providing boundary-aware unknown exposure. Built on these resources, GROW shapes a representation space that is robust to domain shifts and sensitive to open-set inputs in a coherent attraction–repulsion–calibration pipeline: reliable samples dominate prototype shaping for stable known-class discrimination, boundary-weighted Open-Push repels pseudo-unknowns to form a structured open-space margin, and uncertainty distillation aligns the multi-class head with the rejection behavior for better confidence calibration. Extensive experiments on bearing and planetary gearbox datasets demonstrate that SEE–GROW consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior harmonic-mean performance between known-fault recognition and unknown-fault detection under unseen operating conditions.

title: Deep Learning-Accelerated inverse design of NURBS-Based phononic crystals with customized bandgaps
abstract: Phononic crystals (PnCs) enable effective control of elastic wave propagation through the formation of frequency bandgaps, but their design is computationally demanding due to the complex relation between geometry and dynamic behavior. To address this challenge, this study proposes a deep learning–accelerated inverse design framework for non-uniform rational B-spline (NURBS)-based phononic crystals. In the proposed approach, a NURBS parameterization scheme is employed to represent the unit-cell geometry using control points and weights, enabling smooth, fabricable, and highly flexible curved-edge design. A deep neural network (DNN) is trained to accurately predict the full dispersion relations of PnCs, replacing finite element (FE) analysis with millisecond-level inference. The trained model is integrated with an improved real-coded genetic algorithm (IRGA) to perform global optimization under multiple objective functions, including single-bandgap maximization, dual-bandgap enhancement, target-frequency bandgap control, and dispersion customization. The results demonstrate that the DNN surrogate achieves an R2 of 0.996, with 84.2% of test samples exhibiting a mean relative error below 4.5%. The DNN–IRGA framework efficiently identifies optimized geometries that exhibit desired bandgap properties, validated by FE simulations and a 3D-printed experimental specimen showing strong attenuation (up to − 85 dB) within the predicted bandgap. This work establishes a unified framework that bridges geometric parameterization, deep learning prediction, and inverse optimization, providing a powerful tool for rapid and customizable bandgap design of two-dimensional NURBS-based phononic crystals.

title: Full-stroke constant-zero stiffness vibration isolation enabled by a stiffness-programmable dual-bar spring module
abstract: Quasi-zero stiffness (QZS) isolators have received extensive attention due to their advantageous performance in terms of low-frequency vibration isolation. However, the inherent stiffness nonlinearity of conventional QZS designs can amplify the jump phenomenon and introduce stability concerns, in particular when subject to high excitation levels. To address this issue, this paper presents a dual-bar spring vibration isolator that enables a full-stroke constant-zero stiffness (CZS). A dual-bar spring mechanism is formulated as a stiffness-programmable module capable of exhibiting constant positive stiffness (CPS), constant negative stiffness (CNS), and QZS characteristics through parametric design. Based on the programmed stiffness modes, the corresponding stiffness components are combined in parallel to synthesize full-stroke constant-zero stiffness. An analytical model of the equivalent restoring force and stiffness characteristics of the stiffness-programmable dual-bar spring module is established based on a static mechanical analysis. The dynamic isolation performance of the synthesized full-stroke CZS configuration is subsequently investigated to evaluate its low-frequency vibration isolation capability. A functional prototype that exhibits full-stroke CZS characteristics is manufactured, and static and dynamic experiments are conducted for performance validation. Experimental results demonstrate force equilibrium at multiple positions and effective vibration isolation at frequencies as low as 2 Hz under harmonic, frequency-sweep, and stochastic excitations. The results indicate that the proposed isolator provides an effective passive solution for ultralow-frequency vibration isolation, and its full-stroke CZS characteristics further support stable operation under high excitation levels.

title: Data-informed simulation of temperature effects in finite element models for structural health monitoring using inverse surrogate modeling
abstract: This work presents a data-informed framework to simulate temperature effects in a finite element model (FEM) for structural health monitoring (SHM), enabling realistic generation of synthetic modal data for both healthy and damaged states. A challenge in vibration-based SHM is that real damaged data are rarely available, so damage detection and classification methods are often validated using FEM simulations. However, temperature strongly affects modal data through changes in stiffness, connections, and boundary conditions, and these effects are difficult to reproduce realistically using standard thermo-mechanical assumptions, especially when only few temperature measurements are available. The proposed approach combines field monitoring data with an updated FEM through inverse surrogate modeling. First, an inverse surrogate model is trained on FEM simulations to recover temperature-sensitive mechanical parameters (e.g., Young’s modulus of elasticity) from modal frequencies. Then, this surrogate is applied to long-term monitoring data to estimate how these parameters evolve with temperature. A second regression model then learns a direct mapping from temperature to FEM parameters. Injecting these temperature-dependent parameters into the FEM allows simulation of realistic temperature-frequency trends, for both healthy and damage scenarios. The method is demonstrated on a numerical truss and on the KW51 railway bridge. Results show high accuracy in modal frequency prediction and consistent anomaly detection performance, indicating that the framework reproduces in-situ thermal effects without requiring explicit thermo-mechanical modeling, while preserving damage detectability under temperature variations.

title: Enhanced time-frequency representation of blade tip timing signals via group sparse modelling
abstract: High-speed rotating blades in aero-engines operate under extreme mechanical and thermal conditions, where high-cycle fatigue caused by low-amplitude, high-frequency vibrations is a primary source of structural failure. Reliable and accurate vibration monitoring is therefore essential for maintaining blade integrity and preventing catastrophic incidents. Blade Tip Timing (BTT) provides a non-intrusive alternative to strain measurement. Achieving a precise time–frequency representation of BTT signals is crucial for non-contact blade vibration monitoring and for the early detection of structural degradation, such as fatigue cracks. However, BTT measurements are non-uniform and undersampled, resulting in poor time–frequency concentration, susceptibility to noise, and frequency coupling among adjacent blades. To address these challenges, this paper introduces an enhanced time–frequency reconstruction framework based on group sparse modelling, which leverages the inherent continuity of blade dynamic frequencies. The framework explicitly encodes the intrinsic group sparse structure of blade vibration time–frequency characteristics. It formulates the reconstruction problem as a row-LASSO optimization model, which enforces group sparsity in the coefficient matrix. This approach simultaneously enhances time–frequency concentration, suppresses noise and spurious frequency components, and preserves the continuity of modal frequency trajectories. An efficient Alternating Direction Method (ADM) is further developed to solve the resulting convex optimization problem. Extensive numerical simulations and high-speed rotor experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves substantially improved time–frequency concentration and reconstruction accuracy compared with standard LASSO and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP). When applied to blades containing fatigue cracks, the method accurately tracks dynamic frequency shifts caused by crack initiation and clearly distinguishes crack-related signatures from coupled components. These results confirm that the proposed group sparse encoding framework provides an effective method for blade vibration monitoring and early crack diagnosis.

title: Decoupling compound faults under data imbalance: A multi-task dynamic balanced learning network for gearbox fault diagnosis
abstract: Gearbox is a core component in mechanical transmission systems, and its accurate fault diagnosis is critical for ensuring operational safety of mechanical equipment. Although intelligent diagnosis methods have achieved promising results, they still face significant challenges. First, gearbox is a complex system with tightly coupled components (e.g., gears and bearings). Most existing methods focus on diagnosing isolated components, failing to effectively decouple and identify multi-component compound faults. Second, in actual engineering, fault data is usually scarce and severely imbalanced compared to normal data, which significantly degrades the performance of conventional data-driven models. To address these challenges, a multi-task dynamic balanced learning network is proposed for compound fault decoupling diagnosis with imbalanced data. Specifically, gearbox compound fault diagnosis is reformulated as a component-level multi-task diagnosis problem. First, a shared backbone network is designed to extract common features from vibration signals, followed by two kernel-adaptive task-specific branch networks that hierarchically disentangle component-level fault features for different tasks. Then, an adaptive balance loss is utilized to reweight training samples and alleviate the class imbalance influence. Finally, a task dynamic balancing strategy is incorporated to dynamically coordinate and optimize multiple diagnostic tasks during training. Extensive experiments are conducted on both real-world engineering and public datasets. The results show that the proposed method still achieves over 98% diagnostic accuracy on both gear and bearing diagnosis tasks even under severe class imbalance condition, demonstrating its superiority and robustness compared to other advanced methods.

title: Fast variational Bayesian inference method for nonlinear finite element model updating
abstract: It is challenging to apply Bayesian model updating to nonlinear structures. This is because Bayesian updating usually necessitates numerous forward model evaluations, for which nonlinear finite element analysis is employed. This can lead to convergence issues, complicating likelihood evaluations in Bayesian frameworks. This paper presents a fast variational Bayesian inference (FVBI) approach for updating nonlinear finite element models. The method derives the analytical form of the evidence lower bound (ELBO) under the assumption of a multivariate Gaussian posterior distribution. The closed-form update formulas for the posterior mean and covariance are then obtained by maximizing the ELBO, after which an iterative linearization strategy is introduced. At each iteration, the nonlinear structural response is locally approximated by its first-order expansion around the current estimate, with the posterior mean and covariance updated sequentially. Numerical studies on a multi-degree-of-freedom Bouc-Wen frame, a three-span, three-story steel structure, and a reinforced concrete building are presented to demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method. The results show that the FVBI method accurately identifies the nonlinear parameters, while the computational cost is much lower than that of traditional Laplace approximation methods.

title: Corrigendum to “Non-contact 3D displacement measurement of structure based on the fusion of millimeter wave radar and digital image correlation” [Mech. Syst. Sign. Proc. 255 (2026) 114436]
Upper approximation bounds for neural oscillators
abstract: Neural oscillators, originating from second-order ordinary differential equations (ODEs), have demonstrated strong performance in stably learning causal mappings between long-term sequences or continuous temporal functions, as well as in accurately approximating physical systems. However, theoretically quantifying the capacities of their neural network architectures remains a significant challenge. In this study, the neural oscillator consisting of a second-order ODE followed by a multilayer perceptron (MLP) is considered. Its upper approximation bound for approximating causal and uniformly continuous operators between continuous temporal function spaces and that for approximating uniformly asymptotically incrementally stable second-order dynamical systems are derived. The established proof method of the approximation bound for approximating the causal continuous operators can also be directly applied to state-space models consisting of a linear time-continuous complex recurrent neural network followed by an MLP. Theoretical results reveal that the approximation error of the neural oscillator for approximating the second-order dynamical systems scales polynomially with the reciprocals of the widths of two utilized MLPs, thus overcoming the curse of parametric complexity. The convergence rates of two established approximation error bounds are validated through four numerical cases. These results provide a robust theoretical foundation for the effective application of the neural oscillator in science and engineering.

title: Interpretable physics-guided modelling and energy-efficient disturbance-compensated control for magnetorheological suspensions of off-road vehicles
abstract: Magnetorheological (MR) dampers are widely recognized as an effective solution for vibration attenuation in off-road vehicles, while their inherent nonlinearity and hysteresis pose a significant challenge for precise force tracking and real-time control. To address this problem, this paper proposes a novel control framework that integrates a Physics-Guided Differentiable Optimization-based Inverse Model (PG-DOIM) within a composite Active Disturbance Rejection Control (ADRC) architecture for the control of MR suspension. Initially, a modified Bouc-Wen forward model is identified based on the dynamic test data to characterize the intrinsic properties of the damper. Unlike conventional black-box data-driven approaches, the proposed PG-DOIM reformulates force tracking as a regularized differentiable optimization layer that calculates the required command voltage. This inverse solver is embedded in a composite ADRC control architecture, augmented by an extended state observer and an energy-efficient event-triggering mechanism to compensate for modelling error and external disturbances. Quarter-car simulations and on-road experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms other representative control strategies in suppressing body acceleration and decreasing suspension deflection. Notably, the introduction of the event-triggering mechanism reduces the control update frequency by 46.4% while maintaining comparable vibration isolation performance. Further analyses of power spectral density demonstrate a substantial reduction of vibration energy within human-sensitive frequency ranges, leading to improved ride comfort for passengers.

title: Considering labyrinth type seals in dynamic response of heavy-duty gas turbine by full length equivalent model: Influence of different seals
abstract: Investigating the nonlinear dynamic behaviors of heavy-duty gas turbines is crucial for ensuring operational stability, yet challenging due to the complex coupling of structural irregularities and fluid-induced forces. This paper establishes a full-length equivalent model (FLEM) of a heavy-duty gas turbine shaft system, integrating a nonlinear short bearing model and a versatile interpolation database method (IDM) for sealing forces. Validated against experimental data, the model utilizing the equivalent mass method effectively captures excitation frequency of nonlinear oil film than previous method. A comparative study is conducted on the system’s nonlinear responses under four sealing conditions: without seal, labyrinth Seal (LS), diaphragm labyrinth seal (DLS), and hole diaphragm labyrinth seal (HDLS). The results demonstrate the comprehensive superiority of HDLS, which reduces the vibration amplitude at the first critical speed by 28.07% compared to traditional LS, and suppresses the maximum response by 11.08% across the broad operating range. Furthermore, complex nonlinear phenomena, including bifurcation, quasi-periodic motions, and chaos induced by oil-film instability, are revealed. Notably, distinct mode-locking behaviors (e.g., period-8 and period-15 motions) embedded within quasi-periodic regions are identified as characteristic Arnold tongues, resulting from the interaction between operational and inherent system frequencies.

title: The main factors determining the friction force reduction in sliding motion at tangential vibrations of elastic support
abstract: The main purpose of this work was to investigate the effectiveness of the friction force reduction in sliding motion under the influence of forced, tangential vibrations of an elastic support, depending on the direction of these vibrations and their parameters, at different sliding velocities and different stiffness of the contact zone of the sliding body and the support. Experimental and simulation analyses were carried out for two materials of friction pairs, such as steel and Teflon, for homogeneous: steel – steel and Teflon – Teflon, and mixed: steel – Teflon connections. In numerical analyzes an original computational model was applied, based on dynamic equations of motion of a shifted body. This model uses dynamic friction models taking into account the compliance of the contact zone of the sliding body and the ground. It has been shown that the main factors determining the effectiveness of the friction force reduction under the influence of vibrations are: (i) the normalized amplitude κ of the vibration velocity and (ii) the angle γ between direction of vibrations and direction of sliding. The highest effectiveness of this reduction can be achieved with longitudinal vibrations, but only after meeting the condition that the vibration velocity amplitude va is greater than the slip velocity vd, i.e. when κ = va/vd > 1. If this condition is not met, the reduction of the friction force at longitudinal vibrations will not occur. There are no such constraints for transverse and diagonal vibrations at which the reduction of the friction force occurs also when va < vd.

title: Compound elastic concentrator for achromatic superfocusing and amplified energy harvesting over an ultra-broadband spectrum
abstract: Elastic metasurfaces offer a compact route to manipulate wavefronts, yet their focusing performance is intrinsically chromatic because the retarded phase varies strongly with operating frequency. This spectral dispersion induces chromatic aberration and deteriorates energy capture, which limits ultra-broadband elastic-wave concentration and reliable piezoelectric energy harvesting in practical plate-based systems. Here, we propose and demonstrate a compound elastic concentrator that integrates a thickness-programmed elastic metasurface with a conformally mapped gradient-index concentrator, enabling achromatic superfocusing over an ultra-broadband spectrum. A central advance is a unified, analytically tractable unit-cell platform grounded in Reissner–Mindlin plate theory, which allows both components to be designed and fabricated by modulating only the local plate thickness. In this two-stage architecture, the metasurface provides high numerical aperture steering and compact pre-focusing, while the gradient-index concentrator continuously recaptures and confines the diffracted waves, thereby suppressing the chromatic aberration inherent to elastic metasurfaces. Numerical and experimental validations verify diffraction-limited, frequency-stable superfocusing in the compound elastic concentrator over the 40–100 kHz operating band, together with substantial intensity enhancement compared with standalone configurations. When a piezoelectric energy harvester is positioned at the confocal hotspot, the concentrated elastic-wave energy converts efficiently into electrical output, yielding markedly enhanced output power across the operating band. These results establish a design- and fabrication-friendly, thickness-only pathway toward ultra-broadband elastic-wave concentration for self-powered sensing, structural health monitoring, and vibration-energy harvesting.

title: Stability analysis and multi-sensor placement optimization for dynamic load identification using the Kalman filter method
abstract: Dynamic load identification is an inverse problem in structural dynamics aimed at recovering the loads acting on a structure. Determining sensor locations to ensure stable and accurate identification has long been an important research topic. Kalman-filter–based methods can identify dynamic loads while simultaneously estimating the state vector, enabling online identification from multiple types of sensor measurements. Although these methods offer clear advantages over traditional approaches, they also place stricter demands on algorithmic stability—a fundamental requirement for reliable performance. However, the algorithmic stability from the perspective of sensor placement has not been systematically investigated. This paper presents a theoretical derivation of practical and easy-to-implement stability criteria in both the physical and modal state-space frameworks. Then, an optimal sensor placement (OSP) strategy is proposed, which explicit clarifies the different roles of sensor types in the adopted estimation algorithm. Infeasible sensor configurations are first excluded according to the invertibility and stability requirements, and the optimal configuration is then selected from the remaining feasible candidates by minimizing the trace of the input covariance matrix. Simulation studies verify that the proposed OSP strategy can determine the optimal sensor layout under single-point excitation, multi-point excitation, and complex structural systems, while exhibits a certain degree of robustness. Finally, dynamic load identification experiments on a simply supported beam are conducted, and the accurate identification results further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed OSP strategy.

title: Robust fuzzy control for in-wheel motor drive vehicle nonlinear suspensions under denial-of-service attacks based on dynamic output feedback
abstract: Because of the open network environment of intelligent ground vehicle, the vehicle suspension system is vulnerable to the denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Therefore, this paper investigates a robust fuzzy control method for the in-wheel motor drive vehicle suspension systems under DoS attacks. First, to save communication resources and maintain acceptable signal transmission performance under DoS attacks, a switched event-triggered scheme with two variable thresholds is proposed to optimize the communication scheduling via an acknowledgment character technology. Second, to construct the closed-loop suspension control system model under DoS attacks, an augmented interval type-2 fuzzy model is developed to unify the suspension nonlinear dynamics and dynamic output feedback controller. Third, to ensure the suspension control system satisfy the exponential stability and performance requirements, a novel collaborative design method is proposed for the robust controller and event-triggered scheme with a piecewise Lyapunov function. Finally, the experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed control approach compared to existing methods under DoS attacks.

title: Dual-function of isolation and energy harvesting via a spatial cam-induced multi-region quasi-zero-stiffness mechanism
abstract: With the rapid development of smart industrial systems, low-frequency vibration isolation and energy harvesting have attracted increasing research interest. Inspired by spatial cam mechanisms, this study proposes a dual-functional integrated design that simultaneously achieves low-frequency vibration isolation and piezoelectric energy harvesting. The proposed device combines a spatial cam, piezoelectric flexible beams, and linear springs to realize quasi-zero-stiffness (QZS) behavior. Owing to the multi-periodic profile of the spatial cam, the structure exhibits multiple QZS intervals, enabling effective low-frequency isolation under varying payloads and alleviating response coupling and alignment issues commonly encountered in series-type QZS configurations. The piezoelectric beams undergo controllable deformation imposed by the cam profile, allowing efficient conversion of low-frequency vibration energy into electrical energy while preventing excessive stress in the piezoelectric material. In addition, tailoring the Poisson’s ratio of the piezoelectric beam substrate further enhances the harvested power. Theoretical analysis clarifies the effects of the spatial cam contour and the structural parameters of the piezoelectric beams on the static characteristics of the proposed CS-QZS-VIEH, establishing the conditions required to achieve multiple QZS regions. A nonlinear electromechanical coupled dynamic model is developed to investigate the system response, revealing how key mechanical and electrical parameters jointly govern vibration isolation and energy-harvesting performance. The negative Poisson’s ratio configurations of three piezoelectric beams are optimized using a genetic algorithm and experimentally validated. Static experiments demonstrate QZS behavior at loads of 6.6 N and 14.0 N. Under a displacement excitation of 6 mm, the CS-QZS-VIEH exhibits initial isolation frequencies of 2.6 Hz and 2.3 Hz for the two loading conditions, representing reductions of 56.8% and 47.7%, respectively, compared with an equivalent linear isolator. The corresponding peak transmissibility is reduced by 35.5% and 16.7%. Moreover, stable energy-harvesting performance is maintained within the isolation band, and the peak output power of the negative Poisson’s-ratio piezoelectric beams is increased by 65.6% relative to the conventional configuration. Both theoretical and experimental results indicate that the proposed CS-QZS-VIEH effectively integrates low-frequency vibration isolation and piezoelectric energy harvesting, offering a promising solution for vibration mitigation in marine, terrestrial, and aerial platforms, as well as for self-powered microsensing applications, and providing useful guidance for the design of multi-load QZS systems.

title: Efficient prediction of extreme buffeting responses of an offshore long-span HSR bridge considering multi-dimensional mean wind uncertainty via a novel PEM-Kriging hybrid strategy
abstract: The accurate prediction of long-term buffeting responses is pivotal for ensuring the structural safety of long-span high-speed railway (HSR) bridges. Conventional wind-resistant design typically relies on deterministic wind parameters, often neglecting the stochastic nature inherent in wind characteristics. While advanced reliability-based frameworks address this limitation through full-probabilistic methods, the associated long-term extreme value analysis is frequently impeded by prohibitive computational costs. To address these challenges, this study proposes an efficient strategy for predicting extreme buffeting responses, accounting for multi-dimensional mean wind field uncertainties. First, a three-dimensional Joint Probability Density Function (JPDF) model comprising Mean Wind Speed (MWS), Mean Wind Direction (MWD), and Angle of Attack (AOA) is established using in-situ measurements. Subsequently, a hybrid framework integrating the Pseudo-Excitation Method (PEM) with Kriging surrogate modeling (PEM-Kriging) is developed to alleviate the computational burden of high-dimensional stochastic analysis. Finally, the mechanisms governing extreme response variations with respect to mean wind uncertainty—particularly AOA—are elucidated. The results indicate that: (1) PEM-Kriging strategy significantly reduces computational costs while preserving high prediction accuracy; (2) the sensitivity of short-term extreme buffeting responses exhibits distinct anisotropy, wherein lateral responses are primarily dominated by MWS, while vertical and torsional responses show strong nonlinear sensitivity to AOA; and (3) simplified low-dimensional models overestimate long-term extreme lateral responses but significantly underestimate vertical and torsional responses with 100-year return period by approximately 55% and 35%, respectively. The proposed framework effectively captures critical multi-dimensional scenarios in realistic wind environments, providing an effective tool for the refined wind-resistant design of long-span bridges.

title: Nonlinear viscoelastic isolation performance of a quasi-zero-stiffness flywheel isolator
abstract: Achieving low-frequency vibration control in flywheel rotor systems under harsh aerospace conditions poses a substantial engineering challenge. This paper introduces a viscous quasi-zero-stiffness (QZS) isolator with an exceptionally minimalist design. Notably, a broad QZS region can be attained simply by adjusting the length ratio and inclination angle of two straight beams, while the structure remains straightforward to manufacture and install. A prototype is manufactured using the viscoelastic material thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), and its dynamic performance is experimentally investigated. Subsequently, a high-fidelity viscoelastic model is established and validated through dynamic experiments. This study also explores the nonlinear dynamic response characteristics of viscous QZS isolators under various excitation conditions. Results indicate that the viscoelastic properties of TPU suppress structural nonlinearity, contributing to the maintenance of low-frequency isolation performance in complex environments. Flywheel vibration isolation experiments verify that the proposed isolator achieves effective vibration isolation across wheel speeds ranging from 300 to 3300 RPM, with an average isolation of −15.72 dB and a peak isolation of −47.36 dB. Consequently, the design methodology and modeling framework presented in this study offer a viable technical pathway for enhancing the performance of flywheel vibration isolators.

title: Addressing data loss in blade tip timing: A SpatioTemporal-guided Robust Compressed Sensing method
abstract: Blade Tip Timing (BTT) is a widely used non-contact technique for monitoring blade vibration in turbomachinery. However, practical applications often suffer from data loss due to sensor contamination and other issues, which limits the accuracy and robustness of traditional reconstruction methods. To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes a three-stage SpatioTemporal-guided Robust Compressed Sensing (ST-RCS) approach for BTT data reconstruction and parameter identification with data loss. First, a robust compressed sensing method is introduced to enhance resistance to outliers and non-Gaussian noise. Second, temporal stability and spatial correlation are formulated as physical priors and embedded into the compressed sensing model. Third, an iterative reweighted optimization strategy is developed to jointly estimate the signal components and adaptively adjust sample weights, which also allows for visual localization of missing data. Extensive simulations and experimental validations demonstrate that ST-RCS significantly outperforms existing methods in both reconstruction accuracy and frequency identification, particularly under high data loss rates. Tests conducted on a high-speed rotor blade test rig confirm that ST-RCS can accurately reconstruct blade tip displacement and detect both natural frequencies and harmonic components. These results highlight the method’s robustness and its potential for real-world BTT applications.

title: Sensor fusion for track geometry monitoring: integrating on-board condition monitoring and degradation models via Kalman filtering
abstract: Track geometry monitoring is essential for maintaining the safety and efficiency of railway operations. While Track Recording Cars (TRCs) provide accurate measurements of track geometry indicators, their limited availability and high operational costs restrict frequent monitoring across large rail networks. Recent advancements in on-board sensor systems installed on in-service trains offer a cost-effective alternative by enabling high-frequency, albeit less accurate, data collection. This study proposes a method to enhance the reliability of track geometry predictions by integrating low-accuracy sensor vibration signals with degradation models through a Kalman filter framework. An experimental campaign using a low-cost sensor system mounted on a TRC evaluates the proposed approach. The results demonstrate that incorporating frequent sensor data significantly reduces prediction uncertainty, even when the data is noisy. The study also investigates how the frequency of data recording influences the size of the credible prediction interval, providing guidance on the optimal deployment of on-board sensors for effective track monitoring and maintenance planning.

title: A reverse modeling direct method for remaining useful life prediction of nonlinear stochastic degrading device
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge that the existing data-driven methods struggle to accurately and efficiently estimate the probability density function (PDF) of the remaining useful life (RUL) for complex nonlinear stochastic degrading devices. To overcome this limitation, a direct RUL prediction method based on reverse modeling is proposed, which operates through a two-stage framework comprising offline training and online updating. In the offline training stage, a reverse degradation model incorporating both deterministic and stochastic terms is established. Specifically, the deterministic term is modeled by a deep neural network (DNN), while the stochastic term is characterized by a truncated normal distribution. Subsequently, the DNN is trained using reverse degradation data of historical devices to determine the network structure and corresponding parameters. The variance of the stochastic term is then estimated via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) based on the prediction residuals of the deterministic component. In the online updating stage, the dynamic time warping distance (DTWD) between the monitoring data of the in-service device and those of historical similar devices is calculated. The historical devices exhibiting the smallest DTWD is selected to fine-tune the pre-trained DNN. Consequently, by substituting the failure threshold directly into the trained and updated reverse degradation model, the PDF of the RUL is derived without complex transformations. Finally, the feasibility, convenience, and effectiveness of the reverse modeling-based direct RUL prediction method for nonlinear stochastic degrading devices are validated by milling cutter flank wear data and lithium-ion battery capacity degradation data, respectively.

title: Chatter suppression in robotic milling of thin-walled workpieces using horseshoe lattice-based acoustic metamaterials
abstract: To address the multi-frequency chatter issue in robotic milling of thin-walled workpieces (caused by the dual low-rigidity of robots and workpieces), this study proposes a novel acoustic metamaterial-based strategy, aiming to improve machining stability by leveraging the vibration-suppressing bandgaps of metamaterials. Specifically, a Horseshoe Lattice-based Acoustic Metamaterial (HL-AM) was proposed—integrating horseshoe lattices with high-mass local resonators. To realize its complex integrated structure, 3D printing was employed, enabling precise fabrication of intricate lattices (difficult via traditional machining) and simplifying assembly. To verify its vibration suppression capability, theoretical modeling and finite element analyses were conducted to characterize the HL-AM’s bandgap properties, confirming that its bandgaps cover the typical chatter frequency range in robotic milling. In practical application, the HL-AM was directly mounted onto thin-walled workpieces, acting as a core device for chatter suppression. Moreover, comparative robotic milling tests were conducted (vs. unmodified thin-walled workpieces and those with resonator-equivalent masses). The results confirmed that the HL-AM significantly improved machining stability. Notably, obvious chatter frequencies were only detected in the two control groups, further verifying the HL-AM’s effectiveness.

title: A physics-guided evolutionary digital twin for progressive fault diagnosis in T0 neutron choppers
abstract: Reliable fault diagnosis of T0 neutron choppers is critical for the operational safety of large-scale neutron scattering facilities, yet practical deployments face two compounded challenges: extreme scarcity of labeled fault samples and progressive data availability that violates the static assumptions of conventional diagnostic frameworks. This paper proposes a Physics-Guided Evolutionary Digital Twin (PG-EDT) framework that addresses both challenges through three tightly coupled components. A lumped-parameter model generates high-fidelity physical priors that encode fault-discriminative dynamics of the chopper bearing system before any real fault data is available. A residual adversarial calibration module then bridges the sim-to-real domain gap while preserving the physically meaningful fault signatures through a physical consistency constraint. An evolutionary diagnostic strategy progressively transitions the system from Day-1 zero-shot anomaly monitoring under normal-only data to fine-grained few-shot fault classification as real fault observations accumulate stage by stage. Experimental validation on a real T0 neutron chopper dataset demonstrates that PG-EDT achieves near-perfect diagnostic accuracy from as few as one labeled sample per fault class, consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art generative sim-to-real adaptation methods in the early-stage regime, and achieves complete zero-shot separation between healthy and unseen fault distributions on Day-1 without any exposure to fault signatures.

title: Development and testing of a novel multi-dimensional force sensing intelligent toolholder for milling process monitoring
abstract: Cutting force measurement plays a crucial role in the visual monitoring of smart factories. This study presents a novel intelligent toolholder that enables real-time monitoring and wireless transmission of multi-dimensional cutting force during milling, drilling, and other machining processes. Utilizing 3D printing technology, the integrated manufacturing of the intelligent toolholder was achieved, providing advantages such as a simplified structure and ease of processing. A novel parallel cutting force sensing unit was constructed in the toolholder, and 16 high-precision strain sensors were used to detect tiny deformations to calculate the cutting force. The mapping relationship between the original strain signal of the cutting force sensing unit and the multi-dimensional cutting force was determined through multi-dimensional force joint loading calibration, thus achieving accurate calculation of multi-dimensional cutting force. All sensors and electronic components, including signal acquisition, conditioning, and wireless transmission modules, were integrated into the toolholder as a cohesive system. Cutting and drilling experiments were conducted to evaluate the stability and practicality of the system’s dynamic force measurement capabilities. The results demonstrate that the proposed intelligent toolholder can precisely measure the six-component force. Compared to the commercial dynamometer, the relative deviation is below 5%. In addition, the experimental results also shown that the intelligent toolholder can reliably and conveniently identified the tool wear condition, providing an intelligent solution for monitoring the milling process.

title: Resonator-based mass density identification in nanoplates
abstract: In this paper, we present a methodological and computational study of an inverse eigenvalue problem with finite data arising from the determination of a distributed mass added to a uniform rectangular nanoplate acting as a mass resonator. The nanoplate is modeled within a simplified strain-gradient theory in linear elasticity, under the Kirchhoff–Love kinematic assumptions and with simply supported boundary conditions. The identification method relies on the lowest (Formula presented) eigenvalues and is based on an iterative procedure that approximates the unknown mass density by means of a truncated generalized Fourier series computed on a specific family of test functions. The added mass is assumed to be small compared to the total mass, and its support is confined to a quarter of the rectangular domain. Numerical simulations show that the reconstruction of smooth mass distributions with connected support of diameter larger that (Formula presented) the average side of the nanoplate domain is quite accurate, even when the mass perturbation is not necessarily small. The identification of discontinuous mass densities is less accurate, and a Gibbs-like phenomenon occurs near the jumps. The accuracy of the reconstruction degrades progressively as the number of the connected components of the added mass support increases. Numerical tests show that the identification method remains stable in the presence of errors on the data, provided that such errors are, on average, significantly smaller than the natural frequency-changes induced by the added mass.

title: Research on the dynamic properties of the ball bearing considering cage flexibility under acceleration conditions: ball skidding behavior and cage whirl mechanism
abstract: Frequent operation under variable speed conditions significantly intensifies ball skidding and flexible deformation of the cage, this intensified excitation can potentially trigger dynamic instability of the cage, ultimately resulting in bearing failure. A dynamic model of the Four Point Contact Ball Bearing considering cage flexibility and transient collision effect of ball-pocket is proposed in this paper. The cage is discretized into several discrete elements to represent its flexible characteristics, and the collision effect among the ball, flexible cage, guiding ring are comprehensively considered. The precision and reliability of the model are experimentally verified, and the accuracy and superiority of the flexible cage model are compared with the conventional rigid cage model, the differences in estimating ball skidding behavior and cage whirling performances under acceleration and uniform speed are examined and analyzed. The discussions present that the ball skidding rate and cage whirling instability can be effectively diminished by the appropriate preload, and the cage clearance further optimize the cage motion performance and reduce cage pocket wear. This research contributes novel insights into the skidding control and structural optimization for the bearing.

title: Metamaterial shaft with stiffness-adjustable resonators for low-frequency torsional vibration isolation
abstract: Traditional metamaterial shafts require structural redesigns to modify their working frequency in response to varying conditions. In turn, it also limits their application in areas where variable bandgap is required. To solve this problem, a metamaterial shaft with the stiffness-adjustable resonator, whose local resonant band gap can be tuned by adjusting the nut, is proposed to suppress low-frequency torsional vibrations. This tunability eliminates the need for structural redesigns, thereby reducing costs, improving efficiency, and enhancing design flexibility. Firstly, a static model of the stiffness-adjustable torsional local resonator (TLR) is developed to investigate its nonlinear mechanical properties. Subsequently, a dynamic model is established, and the nonlinear dispersion relation for the infinite periodic system is derived using the homotopy analysis method (HAM). The transmissibility curves of a finite-length metamaterial shaft are then numerically analyzed using the Runge-Kutta method, which validates the theoretical predictions of the band gap. By systematically investigating the influence of the structural parameters and the pre-deformation of the stiffness-adjustable TLR on the bandgap characteristics of the proposed metamaterial shaft, the mechanisms and guidelines for achieving the desired low-frequency band gap are revealed. Finally, a prototype of the metamaterial shaft is fabricated, and its vibration isolation performance is experimentally validated.

title: Analysis of bearing dynamics for disturbance mitigation in spacecraft flywheel assemblies
abstract: This article develops a simulation model for the dynamic analysis of disturbances in a flywheel bearing assembly, based on the dynamics of rolling bearings. The model accounts for the non-rigid installation of the flywheel bearing assembly and the nature of its disturbance output. It examines how rotational speed, preload force, and bearing structural parameters affect the disturbance force and moment generated by the assembly. The study explores the inherent relationship between the disturbance characteristics of the flywheel bearing assembly and the dynamic properties of the bearings, elucidating the mechanisms behind disturbance generation through relevant experimental validation. The findings suggest that, as a multi-component system, the operational behavior of the ball and cage within the bearing significantly influences the assembly’s disturbance characteristics, contributing to both disturbance force and moment. Properly selected preload forces and optimized bearing structural parameters can improve bearing stability and effectively minimize the external disturbances produced by the flywheel bearing assembly.

title: Negative amplitude position code-enabled CDMA to break through the Lamb wave multi-user information mapping limit
abstract: Wireless communication within enclosed metallic structures–a critical capability for aerospace and industrial systems–is fundamentally precluded by electromagnetic shielding. Lamb wave, which utilizes the structure itself as a transmission medium, offers a viable alternative. However, its practical application has been stymied by severe channel distortions that cripple information mapping efficiency and prevent robust multi-user networking. Here, we introduce a negative amplitude position code (NAPC)-enabled code division multiple access (CDMA) system that overcomes this long-standing barrier. Our approach is founded on a novel ultra-multi-ary information mapping scheme, NAPC, which achieves high-fidelity 32-ary information mapping by synergistically encoding data in both pulse position and a unique quaternary amplitude representation that incorporates negative values. When coupled with orthogonal CDMA, this integrated system effectively suppresses both inter-symbol and inter-user interference. We demonstrate a nearly order-of-magnitude increase in system performance, expanding the synchronous user capacity from 3 to 16 and elevating the total system bit rate from 278.7 kbps to 1851.2 kbps. The system achieves a bit error rate four orders of magnitude lower than comparable frequency-division multiple access schemes, thereby breaking a critical performance ceiling and establishing a clear technological pathway for high-capacity, networked systems embedded within metallic media.

title: Design and dynamic analysis of high-speed over-constrained deployable mechanisms with low load sensitivity
abstract: High-speed deployable mechanisms often utilize the flexible deformation of components to assist in overcoming mechanical dead points. However, under uncertain external loads, the deformation behavior of conventional flexible deployable mechanisms often exhibits a strong dependency on external loads. This paper proposes a flexible deployable mechanism based on over-constrained design. First, a flexible multibody dynamic model based on the Absolute Nodal Coordinate Formulation (ANCF) is established and validated. The study elucidates the guiding role of the over-constrained design on the deformation path of the leading-edge flexible link, forcing the mechanism’s deformation behavior to depend primarily on driving parameters, thereby significantly reducing its sensitivity to external load fluctuations. Dynamic simulations indicate that this configuration effectively eliminates motion lag and enhances locking reliability, while reducing the transient locking impact by over 40% and increasing the fundamental frequency of the locked configuration from 36 Hz to over 90 Hz. Finally, scaled prototype experiments confirm the feasibility of regulating flexible deformation through geometric parameters. This study provides a new design approach for high load adaptability high-speed deployable mechanisms.

title: A KOA optimized maximum L-kurtosis deconvolution method with adaptive spectrum segmentation strategy for compound faults in bearings
abstract: Rolling bearings are critical components of rotating machinery, which are prone to compound faults due to prolonged exposure to mechanical loads and frictional forces. The maximum L-kurtosis decomposition (MLKD) method effectively recovers periodic fault impulses. However, its decomposition performance is prohibitively susceptible to wideband noise and filter length. To solve the limitation, an optimized maximum L-kurtosis deconvolution (OMLKD) method with adaptive spectrum segmentation strategy is proposed. Firstly, the Fourier model-fitting method is employed to extract spectral trends to improve the capability against noise. Secondly, average dual-domain autocorrelation (ADDA) index is introduced, which can enhance the accuracy of fault identification and determine the final components. Finally, a fusion index quantifies the trade-off between decomposition performance and computational efficiency, which developed as an optimization objective function for the Koala optimization algorithm (KOA) to adaptively optimize the MLKD filter length. Tests on simulated noise data demonstrate the robustness of OMLKD under strong noise. Additionally, experiments on a test rig further confirm that OMLKD method the accuracy of separating and extracting individual fault components from the compound fault signals of rolling bearings.

title: Operational modal analysis of a rotating blade using continuously scanning laser Doppler vibrometer measurements
abstract: Operational modal analysis (OMA) is a powerful technique for identifying the dynamic characteristics of rotating blades under operating conditions. One limitation of standard OMA approaches, however, is that linear time invariance is assumed, which is not the case for wind turbines with rotating blades. Traditional vibration measurement techniques face limitations due to the challenges of capturing high-resolution modal data on rotating blades and possibly not detecting problems in all parts of the blade. This paper presents an extended harmonic power spectrum method for OMA using a continuously tracking and scanning laser Doppler vibrometer (CTSLDV) system, which enables measuring with a wind turbine in operation. A test rig with a small wind turbine is used in this work to evaluate the proposed measurement and analysis methods. The CTSLDV system continuously scans on the central axis of the blade under operational conditions and the mode shapes are successfully estimated using different scan frequencies. The results highlight the advantages of using a continuous scanning and extended harmonic power spectrum method for full-field vibration analysis of the linear time-periodic systems, which can enhance structural health monitoring and predictive maintenance of rotating machinery under operational conditions.

title: Non-fragile H2/H∞ mixed control for electromagnetic hybrid suspension system with uncertainties
abstract: The uncertainty problem of suspension system has been a key constraint for their performance improvement. In order to improve the overall vibration isolation effectiveness of electromagnetic hybrid suspension (EMHS) system under complex and variable conditions, this study proposes a non-fragile H2/H∞ mixed control strategy for uncertain EMHS system. The parameter disturbances and controller gain perturbations of the system are thoroughly analyzed, and the uncertainty model of the EMHS system is constructed accordingly. An advanced non-fragile H2/H∞ mixed control condition is designed by fusing the non-fragile control and the H2/H∞ mixed control. To further optimize the control effectiveness, sensitive parameters closely related to the performance index are innovatively introduced as free matrix variables in the controller design, which achieves the optimization of the uncertainty matrix structure and significantly reduces its conservatism. Based on the full consideration of the suspension performance output relationship, the performance function model of the EMHS system is successfully constructed, the dynamic response characteristics and perturbation performance of the system are analyzed. The results show that the proposed non-fragile H2/H∞ mixed control strategy can effectively improve the overall performance of the uncertain EMHS system.

title: Localized mass and stiffness effects on beam natural frequencies and modal node-antinode analysis
abstract: Traditional musical instrument making relies on empirical mastery to tune modal frequencies through structural modifications, a process fundamentally rooted in mechanical impedance matching. This study seeks to bridge the gap between artisanal practice and academic theory by providing a scientific framework for these intuitive techniques. Using rectangular wooden beams for analytical simplicity, the research validates the decoupling of localized mass and stiffness effects on natural frequencies through experimental modal analysis. The experimental methodology involved applying incremental mass additions and subtractive drilling at specific nodal and antinodal locations across the first four flexural vibration modes. Results demonstrate that mass changes have a maximal impact at vibration antinodes, while stiffness modifications are most influential near nodes. By identifying these strategic locations, the research establishes a predictable, laboratory-verified approach to instrument tuning that avoids the risks of trial-and-error material removal. This Nodal Sensitivity approach is applicable to passive vibration control in engineering structures or Tuning of Resonators. This foundational work provides a simplified alternative to complex computational modeling, offering practical guidance for luthiers to achieve precise acoustic outcomes.

title: Assembly-dependent backlash in gear systems: Coexisting dynamics and high-frequency impact prediction
abstract: In the realm of multi-state dynamics of gear systems, the characterization of backlash often leans towards theoretical simplification, predominantly treating it as a constant deterministic parameter. Moving beyond this idealization, this paper establishes an assembly-dependent backlash model that incorporates center distance offset. By modulating the operating center distance during the simulated assembly process, the theoretical backlash is dynamically adjusted, which in turn dictates the meshing path, the phase relationship between the drive and back sides, meshing stiffness characteristics, and friction torque. A prediction method for the unit-cycle backlash impact frequency is proposed based on the proximity of phase trajectories to critical boundaries, based on which a three-dimensional curtain plot is constructed to rapidly identify hazardous operating zones characterized by high-frequency impacts under two-parameter conditions. Through local analysis utilizing assembly center distance and meshing frequency as control parameters, three different Poincaré cross sections are defined to investigate periodic states and vibro-impact properties of the system via bifurcation diagrams and the largest Lyapunov exponent. Comparative results indicate that, unlike traditional models based on manufacturing-induced backlash, the proposed assembly model exhibits complex coexistence dynamics, whose bifurcation paths and evolutionary laws are revealed through bifurcation dendrogram and basins of attraction. Furthermore, it is found that the surge in impact phenomena correlates with limit cycles grazing against backlash boundaries. As working parameters evolve, the drift of limit cycles and attractors is observable in phase portraits. When these attractors drift near the hazardous boundary, the resulting grazing induces non-smooth bifurcation phenomena—such as periodic oscillations, jumping bifurcations, and grazing bifurcations—while simultaneously affecting the convergence speed of the dynamic system. Center distance offset serves as a critical backlash regulation strategy that does not rely on customized gear profiles; however, its strong correlation with other parameters significantly influences the internal mesh excitation. Ultimately, this study provides a theoretical reference for backlash regulation and system stabilization to avoid high-frequency impacts.

title: Active equilibrium control of a rhombus QZS Isolator: A hybrid strategy for payload compensation and resonance elimination
abstract: While passive Quasi-Zero-Stiffness (QZS) isolators are effective for low-frequency vibration suppression, they suffer from two key limitations: performance degradation under variable payload conditions and the presence of a residual resonance in the ultra-low frequency range. This paper presents a hybrid control strategy for a QZS isolator, based on a rhombus mechanism with vertical and horizontal springs, to overcome these limitations via active modulation of the horizontal spring length. The practical vibration isolation effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical and experimental investigations. A theoretical model is first developed that incorporates a static control law to maintain the QZS state against payload variations, and a dynamic control law to actively suppress the resonance caused by base excitation. Additionally, a stability analysis of the controlled system is performed. It is shown that modulation of the horizontal springs reinforces the energy barrier of the double-well potential, enhancing the system’s robustness against escape to instability under external excitations. The effectiveness of the proposed hybrid control is then validated experimentally on a prototype. Experimental results confirm that the static control effectively compensates for mass variations, thereby preserving the QZS characteristics. Furthermore, the application of the dynamic control law is shown to suppress the residual ultra-low frequency resonance, validating the proposed approach as a robust solution for QZS systems operating under non-stationary loading conditions.

title: Editorial Board
Corrigendum to “Three dimensional total focusing imaging of volumetric defects using laser diffuse ultrasonic phased arrays” [Mech. Syst. Signal Process. 230 (2025) 112673]
Experimental study on composite traveling wave resonance of high-speed thin-web spur gear of turbofan engine with a newfound phenomena
abstract: Gear traveling wave resonance (TWR) is characterized by random occurrence, strong concealment and severe harmfulness, and has become one of the primary factors threatening the operational safety of aero-engines. In this study, the high-speed thin-web spur gear of the turbofan aero-engine accessory casing transmission system is taken as the research object. The TWR experiment of the aviation high-speed thin-web spur gear is carried out based on the multi-parameter test of vibration, noise and stress. The TWR mode, dynamic response characteristics and stress distribution of the aviation high-speed thin-web spur gear are studied and analyzed. Through experimental investigation, the phenomenon of multiple TWR coexisting within the operating speed range of aviation high‑speed thin‑web spur gears is observed for the first time, and the frequency formula for gear composite TWR is derived. The two traveling waves of the composite TWR can be the forward traveling wave (FTW) and backward traveling wave (BTW) of different nodal diameter (ND), or the arbitrary superposition of the FTW and BTW of the same ND. This discovery further improves the gear TWR theory. The composite TWR at high speed is the main reason for the fatigue fracture fault of aviation high-speed thin-web spur gear. Increasing the web thickness of the gear can eliminate TWR under high-speed operating conditions, thereby effectively reducing the risk of gear fatigue fracture.

title: Gaussian-process-based sensor placement and uncertainty quantification for dynamic response reconstruction in flexible aeroelastic structures
abstract: Accurate sensing of dynamic aeroelastic response is crucial for the safety and performance of flexible aircraft. Although a variety of data-driven neural-network approaches, in-situ inverse estimation schemes, and modal-analysis-based identification methods have been investigated for aeroelastic shape reconstruction, existing approaches still lack providing globally consistent deformation fields with quantified uncertainty prediction under realistic sensor sparsity and complex loading. This work introduces a Gaussian-process-based fiber optic sensing framework for aeroelastic measurement and flexible structural health monitoring that links fiber optic sensing placement to the spanwise uncertainty distribution. The fiber optic sensing placements are modeled as Gaussian process models with closed-form posterior mean and variance for each deformation degree of freedom, using nonstationary hyperparameters informed by Lipschitz-regularized aerodynamic loading to capture spatially varying correlations and provide credible uncertainty estimates at both instrumented and uninstrumented locations. Continuous sensor paths on shell structure surfaces are parameterized in a reduced-order form using conformal mapping and non-uniform rational B-splines. Path design is then formulated as a posterior uncertainty minimization problem to identify information-optimal paths for shape reconstruction. Simulation and wind tunnel tests on a flexible wing prototype demonstrate a significant reduction in posterior uncertainty relative to straight and sinusoidal baselines, together with substantial improvements in displacement and rotation reconstruction accuracy.

title: A self-supervised learning approach for intelligent surface roughness monitoring in thin-walled component machining
abstract: Surface roughness monitoring is essential for process quality control in intelligent manufacturing, yet reliable prediction in thin-walled component milling remains challenging because roughness labels are sparse and multi-channel vibration responses are spatially and dynamically heterogeneous. This study proposes a spatially aware self-supervised contrastive learning framework using six-channel spindle–worktable vibration signals. The task is formulated as sparse-label anchor-bag roughness regression: only the bag corresponding to the central small region in each large region is assigned a measured roughness label, whereas the remaining small-region bags are used as unlabeled data for representation learning. The framework integrates a multi-channel vibration encoder, a physics-guided gated bag aggregation module, and a spatially aware weighted InfoNCE objective. Bag-level self-supervised pretraining enables the model to learn transferable representations while reducing excessive separation between physically related neighboring bags; the pretrained encoder and aggregation module are then fine-tuned using only labeled anchor bags. Experiments on two thin-walled helical milling datasets, Ti2AlNb and GH4169D, demonstrate robust performance under sparse annotation and material variation using a workpiece-level evaluation protocol. The proposed method achieves R2 = 0.9431 ± 0.0337 and RMSE = 0.0274 ± 0.0145 μm on Ti2AlNb, and maintains strong performance on GH4169D with R2 = 0.9246 ± 0.0424, RMSE = 0.0171 ± 0.0093 μm. Comparative and ablation analyses support the effectiveness of self-supervised pretraining, spatially aware contrastive learning, multi-channel fusion, and the anchor-bag supervision setting, providing a label-efficient route for surface quality monitoring in intelligent manufacturing.

title: Stochastic model updating through Sliced-Normal maps
abstract: Stochastic model updating plays a crucial role in minimizing the discrepancies between the computational model and measurement observations through a calibration of model input parameters. This paper introduces a novel methodology called Sliced-Normal maps that enables model updating using only one set of model evaluations and reduced parameter tweaking to invert complex nonlinear input/output joint distributions. The core approach of Sliced-Normal maps involves reweighting a subjective joint input distribution towards the joint target distributions using the Radon–Nikodym ratio. This ratio connects the subjective (epistemic) output distribution to the underlying (aleatory) distribution of actual observations. Since these distributions typically rely on finite samples, both are estimated using Sliced-Normal distributions, which efficiently model complex, multimodal probability density functions using only a single hyperparameter. Sliced-Normal maps is applied to a two-degree-of-freedom shear building model with two updating tasks, resulting in both bimodal and dependent unimodal target distributions using only a single set of Monte Carlo evaluations and two hyperparameters to reweight the subjective input distribution.

title: Characterization of BVID in CFRP via adaptive modulation signal bispectrum sideband estimator
abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer composites are susceptible to barely visible impact damage, which necessitates reliable detection and quantitative assessment of damage severity. Air-coupled ultrasonic testing (ACUT) provides a non-contact sensing modality that avoids secondary contamination or specimen damage. However, in ACUT-based nonlinear cross-modulation measurements, the extraction of nonlinear features is frequently compromised by carrier amplitude fluctuations resulting from transducer positioning offsets and by the obscuration of weak sidebands by background noise. This study developed a feature extraction framework termed the Adaptive Modulated Signal Bispectrum Sideband Estimator (MSB-SE). The bispectrum was utilized as the analytical foundation to suppress random noise and identify phase-locked nonlinear components. To address carrier-induced interference, an MSB-SE estimator was implemented by incorporating a carrier power spectrum normalization operator into the bispectrum calculation, which mathematically decoupled nonlinear features from variations in carrier energy. Furthermore, a Spectrum Amplitude Modulation mechanism was integrated to enhance sensitivity to micro-damage.
