The proposed annular ABH metasurface achieves enhanced broadband attenuation through the synergistic coupling between ABH-induced wave focusing and radially expanding periodicity. This coupled mechanism results in wider bandgaps, stronger energy localization, and more effective vibration suppression. Increasing the circumferential order shifts the characteristic frequencies toward higher values, while the axisymmetric mode dominates the global response. The key geometric parameters governing the bandgap performance are identified, while damping layers can further enhance broadband energy dissipation through the coupling between ABH-induced energy focusing and material damping. Finally, dynamic transmission experiments verify the theoretical and numerical predictions, and confirms the effectiveness of the proposed metasurface for broadband vibration suppression.

title: A novel sticky Bayesian nonparametric approach for bearing damage state tracking using acoustic emission
abstract: Acoustic emission (AE) technology holds considerable potential in bearing fault diagnosis and condition monitoring. Existing diagnostic approaches provide insufficient analysis of the morphology of amplitude distribution (MAD) characteristics in AE signals and overlook the deeper state information contained within MAD. Moreover, current research lacks an integrated inference framework capable of efficiently merging temporal evolution patterns with feature trajectories. To address these gaps, an intelligent diagnostic strategy founded on signal MAD characteristics and damage state persistence modeling is introduced, forming a complete analytical chain from feature extraction through state discovery and continuous tracking. Initially, a parameterization approach for AE signal MAD is established using the Generalized Extreme Value distribution together with a multi-region weighted loss optimization procedure, generating shape scale location feature vectors that capture heavy-tailed features of damage impulses, energy strength, and amplitude variability. Subsequently, a sticky mechanism is incorporated to construct a sticky hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov model that supports the modeling of state persistence, allowing persistent and dynamic unsupervised inference of damage states. An end-to-end intelligent diagnostic framework is then developed through in-depth integration of extracted features and probabilistic models. Experimental studies conducted on a standard test rig and a full-scale high-speed train rolling test platform with various damaged bearings demonstrate the method’s strong diagnostic capability and resilience under challenging operating environments. This research provides a novel pathway for utilizing AE in advanced fault diagnosis and condition monitoring of industrial bearings.

title: Cross-condition tool wear prediction via feature decoupling and domain-adaptive representation learning
abstract: Tool wear prediction across varying operating conditions is challenging because wear-related degradation information is usually entangled with condition-dependent variations, which degrades prediction accuracy and cross-domain generalization. To address this issue, this paper proposes a cross-condition tool wear prediction framework based on feature decoupling and domain-adaptive representation learning. A multimodal adversarial autoencoder is first developed to learn a structured latent space, in which wear-related and condition-related information are explicitly separated. This design suppresses condition interference and yields more transferable degradation representations. A domain-adaptive prediction model with domain-aware contrastive learning is then constructed to align wear-relevant features across domains while preserving discriminative structure, thereby mitigating negative transfer caused by feature entanglement and distribution shift. Experiments on the Jilin University turning dataset and the NASA milling dataset demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms representative methods under cross-condition settings and achieves superior prediction accuracy, robustness, and generalization. The results indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective solution for tool wear prediction in complex manufacturing environments.

title: DRN-PISSM: a pitch bearing fault diagnosis network integrating dilated residual convolution and a Physics-Informed State-Space model
abstract: Pitch bearings in wind turbine equipment operate for long periods under extremely low rotational speeds and time-varying loads. Under such conditions, fault-induced impulses are weak and span long periods, while diagnostic information is easily masked by background noise. As a result, conventional signal-processing methods and purely data-driven models often show insufficient stability under strong noise and cross-load conditions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Dilated Residual Network with a Physics-Informed State-Space Model, termed DRN-PISSM. The proposed method first uses a one-dimensional dilated residual convolutional network to extract multiscale temporal features, thereby enhancing the perception of weak fault information in low-speed heavy-load bearings. A physics-informed state-space recurrent branch is then designed to explicitly strengthen the modelling of periodic information associated with fault characteristic frequencies, improving both physical interpretability and feature discriminability. Finally, adaptive gated fusion, together with joint constraints of physical consistency and noise invariance, is used to improve robustness and generalization under strong noise and load variations. Experimental results show that the proposed method maintains high diagnostic accuracy under different noise intensities and outperforms several comparison models in cross-load transfer tasks with noise disturbance, demonstrating good robustness and generalization capability.

title: Assessment of bridge end-support degradation from loaded frequency variation by dual-vehicle cooperative scanning: theory and experiment
abstract: Bridge bearings are critical to structural safety, yet their hidden role in substructure forbids direct inspection. This paper proposes a dual-vehicle cooperative scanning strategy for assessing bridge end-support stiffness based on loaded frequency variations. A heavy loading vehicle is employed to amplify the variations in dynamic behavior of a bridge with bearing damages, and a light measuring vehicle to duly capture the bridge’s modal information. First, analytical expressions were derived for the elastically supported beam under measuring and/or loading vehicles, that offers an explicit relation between the bearing stiffness ratio κ, asymmetry ratio α, and the bridge’s loaded frequency. Because of the “soft-end amplification effect”, the loaded frequencies show high sensitivity to bearing asymmetry. Based on this, design criteria for the dual-vehicle system are formulated to ensure damage sensitivity and identification stability. Inversely, the stiffness parameters κ and α are estimated using the natural frequency and loaded frequencies of the bridge with the loading vehicle parked at each of the two ends. Numerical simulations demonstrate the feasibility of the method in identifying end bearing stiffnesses against road surface roughness, system damping, and vehicle speed. Scaled models with adjustable bearings were tested. Through five progressive bearing damage scenarios, the effectiveness and applicability of the method were verified. This work provides a loaded-frequency-based dual-vehicle scanning framework for evaluation of asymmetric end-support stiffness degradation for small- and medium-span bridges.

title: Multiscale microstructures fabrication on mold steel by elliptical vibration cutting equipped with fast tool servo
abstract: Microstructures have numerous applications in fields such as optics and energy. However, during the microstructure machining of mold steel, chemical reactions are prone to occur between mold steel and diamond tools which leads to severe tool wear. To address this issue, a high frequency elliptical vibration cutting equipped with fast tool servo composite system (HFEVC‑FTS) was developed in this study. In this system, the high frequency elliptical vibration unit operates at 110 kHz with vibration amplitudes of 2.5–1 μmp-p in bending and longitudinal directions and weighs only 100 g, making it well‑suited for integrated system applications. By combining high-frequency elliptical vibration with fast tool servo, multiscale microstructures were fabricated on the surface of mold steel. The primary microstructures were generated using the slow tool servo machining strategy, whereas the FTS was employed to fabricate the secondary microstructures. High-frequency elliptical vibration was continuously imposed on the diamond tool throughout the machining process to protect the cutting tool. This strategy verifies the effectiveness and flexibility of the composite system in manufacturing multiscale microstructures on the surface of mold steel. The wettability test of the multiscale microstructure proves that the microstructures are capable of transforming the originally hydrophilic surface into a hydrophobic surface.

title: Slow-sound compression and aero-acoustic performance of rainbow-trapping silencers under low-speed grazing flow
abstract: Slow-sound mechanisms are often invoked to explain broadband dissipation in rainbow-trapping silencers (RTSs), yet their robustness under grazing flow and their quantitative scaling remain largely unexplored. This study establishes a theoretical framework, assessed against numerical approaches and measurements, to elucidate slow-sound propagation and aero-acoustic performance in RTSs under low-speed grazing flow. Without flow, three wave regimes are identified – stiffness-controlled slow sound, inertial wave trapping, and fast-sound transition – governed by the effective compressibility of the resonant cavities. Closed-form asymptotic expressions derived at the quarter-wave resonance and compliance-cancellation frequencies reveal how cavity depth and visco-thermal losses enhance slow-sound or fast-sound effects across regimes. When grazing flow is introduced, near the quarter-wave resonance, interaction between convection and compressibility regularized by viscous losses reduces the expected convective shift in phase-speed, whereas near the compliance cancellation frequency, a stretching effect amplifies it. The Mach-number scaling of the slow-sound compression effect is validated on an optimized RTS prototype against the transfer matrix method, finite difference time domain model, flow-coupled finite-element method and wind-tunnel measurements up to Mach 0.09 under upstream (UPC) and downstream (DPC) propagation conditions. UPC broaden the high-dissipation plateau toward lower frequencies and DPC shift it upward. A key outcome is that the flow-induced losses further compress the UPC–DPC difference in slowed phase speeds beyond convective effects. Overall, the RTS slow-sound and dissipation performance stay robust to low-speed flow conditions. Beyond performance characterization, this work provides predictive scaling laws for the slow-sound-based optimization of compact RTSs operating under flow.

title: High-fidelity random micro-vibration reproduction via a stinger-free magneto-pneumatic platform and multi-resolution adaptive FD-ILC
abstract: High-fidelity broadband random micro-vibration reproduction is a fundamental prerequisite for vibration-isolation performance evaluation and metrological calibration of ultra-precision equipment. Unfortunately, conventional ground excitation systems generally rely on mechanical stingers for force transmission, which tend to introduce parasitic stiffness and nonlinear friction. Moreover, under random vibration conditions, standard control algorithms inherently suffer from noise amplification and steady-state overlearning, severely constraining the signal-to-noise ratio and metrological reliability of micro-vibration testing. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel non-contact, direct-drive ground excitation platform based on a stinger-free magneto-pneumatic hybrid suspension. The platform combines magnetic coupling from a voice-coil motor with air-floating guidance to establish a high-purity dynamic environment characterized by low friction and low parasitic stiffness. A multi-resolution adaptive frequency-domain iterative learning control (MRA-FD-ILC) algorithm is further developed. This algorithm integrates one-third-octave-band error evaluation with narrowband high-resolution spectral updating to effectively suppress stochastic variance disturbances and overlearning, thereby enabling stable convergence in random vibration spectral-shaping control. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system reproduces an adjustable random vibration spectrum from VC-C to VC-A over the 0.5–100 Hz frequency band. The root-mean-square spectral tracking error remains below 0.8 dB. The system also maintains stable spectral-shaping capability in the ultra-low-frequency range. The proposed method can provide important technical support for the performance evaluation of ultra-precision vibration-isolation systems.

title: End-to-end prediction and inverse identification of gear grinding and EOL performance based on physics-informed neural networks
abstract: Existing open-loop quality control paradigms and traditional dynamic models are inadequate for actively suppressing high-frequency whine and ghost noise in electric vehicle (EV) gears, primarily due to unmodeled boundary uncertainties and time-varying transfer functions. Furthermore, purely data-driven methods are inherently constrained by causal feature leakage and insufficient out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization capabilities. To overcome these fundamental bottlenecks, this paper proposes an end-to-end differentiable gray-box framework based on physics-informed integration, which rigorously decouples the forward physical deduction process from the inverse parameter identification process. During the forward prediction phase, the compensation network (NNgrind) exclusively processes remote machine tool vibrations to reconstruct the microscopic three-dimensional (3D) surface waviness. Facilitated by a differentiable smooth relaxation operator, the inverted waviness formulation subsequently drives a 16-degree-of-freedom (16-DOF) gearbox ordinary differential equation (ODE) model. Concurrently, the state-dependent neural operator (NNdyn) strictly extracts transient physical states (i.e., displacement and velocity) to autonomously compensate for nonlinear dynamic residuals, thereby mathematically mitigating the computational overhead and convergence instabilities associated with implicit algebraic loops.During the inverse identification phase, empirical end-of-line (EOL) vibration data serves uniquely as the ground-truth supervision label. Driven by automatic differentiation, the spectrum error gradient backpropagates directly through the ODE solver, achieving the closed-loop calibration of the dual operators with zero causal feature leakage. Blind bench test validations demonstrate that the predicted vibration root mean square error (RMSE) is reduced to 0.052 g. Crucially, this framework strictly complies with cross-axis kinematic conversion laws, precisely resolving the mapping of non-integer ghost frequencies (e.g., accurately tracing a 3.1st-order machine tool excitation to a 26.87th-order macroscopic response on the input shaft). Finally, process sensitivity analysis confirms that actively reshaping the waviness topology can sever its geometric coupling with the line of action, thereby suppressing the ghost noise amplitude by up to 79% directly at the manufacturing source.

title: Parallelized computation of quasi-periodic solutions for finite element problems: A Fourier series expansion-based shooting method
abstract: High-dimensional nonlinear mechanical systems admit quasi-periodic solutions that are essential for the understanding of the dynamical systems. These quasi-periodic solutions stay on some invariant tori governed by complex PDEs in hyper-time. Here, we propose a Fourier series expansion-based shooting method (FSE-Shooting) for the parallelized computation of quasi-periodic solution with $d$ base frequencies ($d \ge 2$). We represent the associated $d$-torus as a collection of trajectories initialized at a ($d-1$)-torus. We drive a set of ODEs that hold for any of these trajectories. We also derive a set of boundary conditions that couple the initial and terminal states of these trajectories and then formulate a set of nonlinear algebraic equations via the coupling conditions. We use Fourier series expansion to parameterize the ($d-1$)-torus and shooting method to iterate the Fourier coefficients associated with initial torus such that the coupling conditions are satisfied. In particular, the terminal points of these trajectories are parallelized computed via Newmark integration, where the time points and Fourier coefficients are transformed to each other by alternating Frequency-Time method. A straightforward phase condition is devised to track the quasi-periodic solutions with priori unknown base frequencies. Additionally, the by-product of the FSE-Shooting can be also directly used to compute the Lyapunov exponents to assess the stabilities of quasi-periodic solutions. The results of three finite element systems show the efficiency and versatility of FSE-Shooting in high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems, including a three-dimensional shell structure with $1872$ DOFs.

title: Fault propagation pathways and decoupling analysis of non-circulating bearing electrical erosion in integrated electric drive units
abstract: With the evolution of electric drive units (EDUs) toward high-voltage integration, bearing electrical erosion damage (BEED) has emerged as a prominent fault mode. However, weak incipient BEED signatures are deeply embedded in high-energy multi-source excitations. Current closed-loop electromechanical modeling and systematic decoupling strategies remain insufficient, thereby obscuring cross-domain modulation mechanisms and hindering effective early diagnosis. To address this, a unified electromechanical-control coupled model is established, integrating motor electromagnetics, gear dynamics, and BEED-induced excitations within a closed-loop framework. A numerical decoupling strategy is then proposed to quantify the independent contributions of multi-source excitations to system responses. Results indicate that electromagnetic torque and gear meshing forces are dominated by motor-side regulation and gear-originated excitation, respectively, demonstrating limited sensitivity to incipient faults. Although bearing vibration exhibits directional heterogeneity, its spectral fault features remain deeply masked by strong rotational harmonics. In contrast, the q-axis stator current provides a more distinguishable electrical-domain indicator. Driven by electromechanical modulation, the BEED-related difference-frequency component fBPFO-fe is approximately 11 dB higher than the direct fault-frequency component fBPFO, indicating better distinguishability for early BEED identification. This study clarifies the cross-domain manifestations of BEED and provides a mechanistic basis for condition monitoring and early fault diagnosis in integrated EDUs.

title: A nature-inspired hybrid wind energy harvester based on a fish evasive maneuvering mechanism
abstract: This study introduces a nature-inspired hybrid wind energy harvester (HWEH) for micro-scale wind energy harvesting under complex airflow conditions. Conceptually motivated by the wake-mediated flow phenomena observed during the C-start escape maneuver of fish, the proposed system exploits the coupled interaction between transverse and rotational wake galloping to harvest wind energy. Unlike conventional systems, which are constrained by fixed obstacles, the HWEH incorporates dynamic self-adjusting rotational bodies and elastically restrained obstacles to facilitate coupling between passive wake tracking and flow–structure interaction, which broadens the ranges of its energy-harvesting modes and operating conditions. Experimental and numerical results demonstrate that the proposed system achieves a low critical wind speed of 1.55 m/s, which contributes to improved harvesting initiation under low-wind-speed conditions. A systematic optimization of its spatial configuration and bluff-body geometry allows the HWEH to attain an interval-averaged power output of 20.39 mW, which is competitive with respect to similar small-scale wind energy harvesters. A flow-field analysis indicates that the C-start-inspired configuration promotes vortex interaction and aerodynamic instability, thereby improving the system’s electrical output performance. Additionally, a multiple-time-delay model is developed to characterize the dynamic coupling between wake evolution and rotational motion. Finally, a dual-source energy-harvesting system integrated with heterogeneous voltage management circuitry is developed to demonstrate the HWEH’s utility for emergency lighting applications. The results highlight the potential of nature-inspired wake interference strategies for facilitating low-threshold wind energy harvesting, providing useful insights for powering distributed sensors and microelectronic devices.

title: A piezoelectric-electromagnetic integrated suspension energy harvester with a variable-ratio lever mechanism for vibration self-sensing
abstract: In conventional fixed-ratio lever-type piezoelectric energy harvesters, the constant transmission ratio creates an inherent trade-off, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve a high excitation amplification effect and a large allowable input stroke. Furthermore, few existing non-intrusive suspension-mounted energy harvesters can extract vibration information from output signals to realize vibration self-sensing. To solve this problem, this work introduces an integrated piezoelectric–electromagnetic suspension energy harvester (SPEH), where a variable-ratio lever mechanism couples the piezoelectric power generation unit (PPGU) with the electromagnetic self-sensing unit (ESSU). The device was investigated through theoretical analysis, transient finite element simulations, and experiments on a prototype. The results indicate that the PPGU performs best in a sliding hinge configuration using two piezoelectric plates connected in series. This configuration can withstand 30 mm of input displacement and generates a peak-to-peak output voltage of 85.3 V at a frequency of 7 Hz, which is 54.8% higher than the output voltage of a fixed 1:1 transmission ratio configuration under the same displacement conditions. At 90 kΩ load, the peak output power reaches 11.4 mW. Regarding vibration self-sensing, the period of the ESSU’s output waveform can be used to estimate excitation frequencies in the 1–8 Hz range with an error of less than 5%. At each fixed excitation frequency, the ESSU’s peak-to-peak voltage exhibits a good linear relationship with the vibration amplitude, with an average coefficient of determination of 0.9663. These results demonstrate that the proposed SPEH, featuring a non-intrusive mounting structure, enables the integration of piezoelectric energy harvesting and vibration self-sensing, offering a feasible structural solution for self-powered suspension vibration sensing nodes.

title: An unsupervised deep learning method for extracting weak reflections from strong guided waves in array data
abstract: The separation of overlapping wavefields in array sensor measurements is a fundamental challenge in acoustic and vibration diagnostics, with critical applications from structural health monitoring to subsurface imaging. A particularly challenging scenario occurs when extremely weak target signals (e.g., geological reflections from fractures) are completely masked by strong guided-wave interference in borehole acoustic reflection imaging. Traditional methods inadequately suppress guided waves, resulting in residual interference that obscures the weak reflections. Furthermore, supervised deep learning methods face practical constraints due to the limited availability of labeled data in field applications. To address these limitations, we propose a novel unsupervised approach that integrates the time-frequency network (TF-GridNet) with a Multi-Frame Wiener Filter (MFWF). Our approach exploits the distinct kinematic properties of guided waves and reflections in array data to achieve separation without requiring labeled training sets. Comprehensive validation on both simulated and field data from complex geological lithologies demonstrates our method’s superiority. On simulated data, it achieves a lower separation residual (L2-norm) than conventional F-K and Multichannel Singular-Spectrum Analysis (MSSA) methods. Crucially, on field data, it enables the reliable extraction of weak reflections, producing significantly clearer images of high-dip-angle fractures and fracture networks with enhanced continuity and reduced artifacts. This work presents a robust, label-free solution for extracting weak signals from strong interference in waveguide structures, as demonstrated in borehole acoustics. The method shows strong potential for advancing structural health monitoring applications that rely on guided-wave sensing.

title: Editorial Board
VA-TFSC-Focusgram: a multi-candidate collaborative framework for industrial gearboxes weak fault diagnosis based on vibration-acoustic cross-modal guidance
abstract: Early detection of weak faults is vital for the reliable maintenance of rotating machinery. However, diagnostic methods based on single-modal vibration or acoustic signals are susceptible to interference from background noise, and blind demodulation indexes face the challenge of distinguishing between periodic impulses, random impulses, and meshing harmonics. To address this issue, this paper proposes a multi-candidate collaborative search method driven by cross-modal physical guidance and decision fusion. A novel blind metric, termed the improved enhanced cyclostationary sparsity index (IECSI), is developed as the key criterion for optimal demodulation frequency band (ODFB) selection. It combines the sparsity of the Gini index with the quantification of cyclostationarity via autocorrelation spectrum entropy. By further introducing an impulse penalty operator, IECSI effectively suppresses interference from meshing harmonics and random noise. This framework first achieves reliable coarse localization of ODFB through vibration-acoustic time–frequency spectral correlation (VA-TFSC). Building on this physical anchoring, an adaptive ternary tree search strategy is developed to construct Focusgram. Finally, a Top-P multi-candidate extraction strategy, together with cross-modal joint score and adaptive arbitration, is introduced to identify physically consistent frequency pairs and intelligently select high-quality diagnostic channels. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the VA-TFSC-Focusgram significantly enhances weak fault feature extraction robustness, maintaining a stable diagnostic boundary even under extreme low-SNR conditions.

title: Maintenance optimization for systems with heterogeneous multi-unit functional subsystems
abstract: Practical engineering systems often incorporate functional subsystems to ensure reliable and stable operation. This study investigates reliability modeling and maintenance decision-making for a system comprising two distinct types of functional subsystems, along with a key subsystem responsible for performing the primary system function. Each functional subsystem consists of heterogeneous component types, with the deterioration of each component represented by discrete degradation states. The different component types contribute to the subsystem’s comprehensive health index with varying importance levels, thereby affecting the key subsystem’s degradation rate and susceptibility to shock damage. Degradation interactions also exist between the functional subsystems, further complicating system reliability. A system reliability model is developed and evaluated using mathematical modeling and Monte Carlo simulation. Based on this model, a maintenance strategy is developed for the system, incorporating cost-saving opportunities from simultaneous maintenance activities at both the subsystem and component levels. Multiple thresholds are defined in terms of the operating time of the key subsystem, functional subsystem health indices, and inter-component degradation states, thereby increasing the optimization complexity as the number of control parameters grows with the number of components and their associated states. To address this complexity, a hybrid approach combining genetic algorithms and Monte Carlo simulation is employed. Case studies based on real-world wind turbine data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The proposed approach is compared with an alternative optimization method and validated against benchmark maintenance strategies. Sensitivity analyses further identify the dominant factors among critical parameters and provide guidance for practical industrial applications.

title: Modeling of unbalanced magnetic pull and nonlinear dynamic analysis of rotor systems for radial permanent magnet eddy current couplers under dynamic eccentricity
abstract: Permanent magnet eddy current couplers (PMECCs), which enable non-contact torque transmission and speed regulation, are widely used in industrial equipment. Most existing research on PMECC has focused on torque transmission, while studies on radial vibration remain limited. This is because, under dynamic eccentricity, unbalanced magnetic pull (UMP) is intricately coupled with rotor motion and varies over time during rotation, significantly increasing the complexity of modeling. In this paper, an analytical model for the UMP of radial PMECCs under dynamic eccentricity is developed by combining the magnetic equivalent circuit method with the Maxwell stress tensor method, and validated by finite element analysis. A dynamic model of the rotor system is further established by incorporating multiple excitation sources, including mass imbalance, nonlinear bearing forces, gravity, and UMP. Through numerical integration of the established model, the radial vibration characteristics of the radial PMECC rotor system were quantitatively investigated in this paper. A comparison with the mechanical coupling (MC) rotor system indicates that the radial PMECC exhibits superior radial vibration reduction performance and more effectively suppresses vibrations induced by parallel misalignment. This advantage becomes increasingly significant as the staic eccentricity (ec) increases. Comparative experiments performed on a test rig validated the proposed UMP and rotor dynamic models. The results further demonstrated that the radial PMECC provides superior vibration reduction performance relative to the MC under parallel misalignment conditions. The findings provide theoretical and experimental support for analyzing the dynamic characteristics of radial PMECCs in complex rotor systems and offer guidance for engineering applications.

title: The combined use of the Hilbert–Huang Transform and the Multiple Scale Method for the parameter identification of nonlinear dynamical systems
abstract: A technique for identifying the parameters of nonlinear mechanical systems is proposed here. Time series of the system response are generated either by non-trivial initial conditions or by the action of harmonic force in conditions of external resonance. The proposed procedure combines the use of the Hilbert Huang Transform (HHT) with the Multiple Scale Method (MSM). In particular, the acquired system response is processed by the HHT, and the output is used to identify the parameters by means of a pseudo-inversion of the Amplitude Modulation Equations provided by the MSM. The procedure is applied to discrete nonlinear systems with one or two degrees of freedom, and then extended to a continuous system, consisting of a beam with geometric and material nonlinearities. Finally, as validation of the procedure, first a real-time simulation on a 1 degree of freedom nonlinear oscillator is performed, and then an experimental application on a clamped–clamped beam is carried out.

title: Physics-informed dual digital twin for online friction updating and decoupled wear identification in robots
abstract: Joint friction is influenced by reversible variations in temperature and load and by irreversible degradation caused by wear. This leads to challenges in friction identification, including operating condition coupling, strong nonlinearity, and poor long-term stability. We present a Physics-Informed Dual Digital Twin (PIDT) framework to overcome these issues. This framework comprises a baseline digital twin trained offline and an evolving digital twin updated online. They enable accurate friction modeling, robust online updating, and decoupled wear monitoring under varying operating conditions. The baseline digital twin uses a ResNet based hybrid deep kernel to learn nonlinear features of temperature and load coupling, and then constructs the kernel function. A multi output sparse variational Gaussian process (SVGP) provides a probabilistic friction model and quantifies predictive uncertainty. The evolving digital twin performs mini batch incremental learning while keeping part of the structural parameters fixed and enforcing physics constraints. Taking the difference between the evolving digital twin and the baseline digital twin suppresses reversible fluctuations and extracts wear related drift. Experiments on the JAKA MiniCobo show that the baseline digital twin reduces RMSE by at least 16.1% compared with conventional methods. The online updating process further improves accuracy and refines uncertainty estimates. The estimated wear related health indicator (HI) correlates with the simulated HI with r = 0.996. The framework remains stable during long duration experiments on the real robot.

title: Vibration of airfoil panel under aerodynamic load: Experimental verification and theoretical research
abstract: The wing is a critical aerodynamic component of aircraft, necessitating in-depth investigation into its dynamic behavior under supersonic flow. However, a unified analytical framework for effectively solving its resonant response, flutter, and limit-cycle oscillations (LCOs) remains lacking. To address this research gap, this study simplifies the outer wing model of Lockheed Martin unmanned aerial vehicle to an airfoil panel model and systematically investigates the nonlinear vibrations of the graphene-reinforced porous composite (G-RPMC) sandwich airfoil panel under combined thermal environment, aerodynamic loads and external transverse excitations. The sandwich panel rests on a Winkler-Pasternak elastic foundation (W-PEF), simulating insulation or damping tape, while its connection to the fuselage is modeled via elastic springs to represent arbitrary support boundaries. The effective material properties of the G-RPMC are derived based on the Halpin-Tsai micromechanical model. The aerodynamic load model of the airfoil panel is obtained by the first-order piston theory. The geometric modeling of the airfoil panel is achieved via a four-node coordinate transformation scheme in conjunction with the chain rule. The governing equations of motion are subsequently formulated as a set of nonlinear ordinary differential equations with multiple degrees of freedom using Lagrange’s equations. The accuracy of the proposed methodology is rigorously verified by comparing the present theoretical results with both finite element simulations conducted in ANSYS and experimental modal tests, showing excellent agreement. Additional validation is provided through linear frequency-sweeping experiments, which further corroborate the reliability of the model. These results unequivocally demonstrate that graphene reinforcement not only improves stiffness but also actively mitigates nonlinear vibration phenomena, offering a novel and validated framework for designing advanced composite airfoil panels with superior dynamic performance in supersonic environments.

title: AWT-DDFN: an end-to-end adaptive wavelet transform-dual domain fusion network for bearing fault diagnosis
abstract: Deep learning has been widely used in intelligent fault diagnosis of rolling bearings. Existing fault diagnosis methods usually use multi-scale wavelet transforms to convert raw 1D vibration signals into time–frequency representations as model inputs. However, such preprocessing brings high computational cost, inevitable information loss and tedious manual parameter tuning, which hinders real end-to-end diagnosis. To overcome these drawbacks, we propose an adaptive wavelet transform–dual domain fusion network (AWT-DDFN), a complete end-to-end framework that directly processes raw vibration signals without manual preprocessing. AWT-DDFN adopts a learnable wavelet convolution layer to replace fixed wavelet transforms, realizing joint optimization of feature extraction and fault diagnosis. Meanwhile, the network uses a dual-branch structure to capture complementary discriminative features: a frequency-domain branch based on pointwise convolution and a time-domain branch combining grouped convolution and dilated convolution. This structure effectively reduces model complexity and parameters, making the model lightweight and robust to noise and trivial signal variations. The features of the two branches are fused by element-wise addition before being sent to the classifier for fault identification, forming a seamless end-to-end diagnosis pipeline. Experiments on PU and CWRU datasets show that AWT-DDFN achieves superior diagnosis performance and stronger noise robustness than state-of-the-art methods, with fewer parameters and lower computation cost. By discarding handcrafted preprocessing, the proposed framework provides a lightweight, end-to-end and deployable intelligent diagnosis solution with strong practical value for industrial scenarios under complex working conditions and strong noise.

title: Cross-radius independent dictionary sparse method for blade vibration reconstruction
abstract: Aircraft engine blades are critical components, and Blade Tip Timing (BTT) is widely used due to its non-contact measurement capability. However, conventional BTT can only measure a single point at the blade tip, making it difficult to capture higher-order modes such as torsional modes. In addition, due to the under-sampling characteristics of BTT signals, increasing the number of measurement points would require a substantial increase in the number of probes. To address these issues, this paper proposes a sensor installation scheme in which probes are mounted on the casing with an inclination angle, so that different probes measure points at different radial positions along the blade leading edge. To address the fact that signals at different measurement points share the same frequency but have different amplitudes and phases, a cross-radius independent dictionary and coupled constraint (CR-IDCC) method is proposed. Based on this method, the amplitudes and phases at multiple radial positions are estimated, enabling reconstruction of the blade vibration mode shapes. This method requires only one probe at each radial position, using a total of five probes, and leverages the cross-radial coupling to recover the blade mode shapes. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, numerical simulations constrained by finite element modal data are conducted, and the estimated mode shapes are compared with the finite element results. Finally, experimental validation is performed on a test rig, and the results are compared with strain gauge measurements. The error analysis further supports the feasibility of the proposed method.

title: Directional coupling analysis and vibration control for transport vehicles with air suspensions based on a matrix decomposition framework
abstract: Coupling effects among the cargo, cab, suspension, and tires fundamentally govern the vibration responses of transport vehicles. However, these coupling interactions are typically embedded within system equations, obscuring their individual contributions and hindering a mechanistic understanding of vibration energy transfer. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes an integrated dynamic modeling and decoupling analysis framework for transport vehicles with air suspensions. A novel matrix decomposition technique is introduced to explicitly extract coupling terms traditionally concealed within system matrices. Furthermore, a Directional Coupling Factor Index (DCFI) is formulated to quantify asymmetric energy transfer and elucidate underlying transmission mechanisms. The established dynamic model is rigorously validated by two tests. First, component-level air spring bench tests verify the model’s accuracy in capturing the amplitude-frequency dependent dynamic stiffness and hysteretic loop properties. Second, full-vehicle road tests under Class B random excitations at constant speeds (40 km/h and 60 km/h) confirm its high global fidelity, with the relative error of the Power Spectral Density (PSD) peak magnitudes strictly controlled within 10% and overall RMS deviations below 15%. Analytical results reveal that the dominant coupling path critically depends on the specific performance objective, whether prioritizing cargo safety, ride comfort, or overall vehicle response. A consistent negative correlation is identified between subsystem coupling strength and overall vibration levels. The body-suspension interaction exerts the strongest influence (coupling factor up to 0.69), followed by the body-cargo (0.48), and body-cab (0.23) interactions. These findings provide a systematic methodology for interrogating interaction mechanisms and establish a new paradigm for passive vibration control via structural coupling design, shifting the engineering focus from isolated component-level parameter tuning to strategic coupling manipulation.

title: Flow-induced vibrations in tandem square cylinders: machine learning analysis of structural response and energy harvesting under variable size and spacing ratios
abstract: Flow-induced vibrations (FIV) provide an effective mechanism for renewable energy harvesting, with potential applications in powering autonomous sensors, smart infrastructures, and low-power electronics. In tandem bluff-body configurations, wake interactions play a key role in modifying the structural response, leading to nonlinear and spacing-dependent vibration characteristics. This study experimentally investigates the performance of piezoelectric energy harvesters (PEHs) employing tandem square cylinders. Five configurations were tested at three spacings (S = 4, 8, and 12 cm) and flow velocities ranging from 2.4 to 13 m/s. The results show that the tandem arrangement significantly modifies both vibration amplitude and electrical output through wake-interaction effects. Depending on the size ratio and spacing, the system exhibits either enhanced or constrained oscillatory behavior. In particular, when a 4 cm cylinder is placed upstream of a 5 cm cylinder (Case 3), increased displacement and RMS voltage are observed compared with the isolated case, with maximum improvements of 356.5% in displacement and 171.9% in voltage. However, the response is strongly dependent on spacing, and no single configuration remains optimal across all flow conditions. This variability is addressed through the introduction of an integrated energy metric combined with normalized power comparison, enabling consistent evaluation across the full velocity range. To complement these findings and capture the nonlinear coupling among flow parameters, structural response, and harvested power, a CatBoost-based machine learning (ML) framework was developed and optimized using 10-fold cross-validation, incorporating an out-of-fold residual filtering step to suppress measurement noise and refine model accuracy. The combined experimental-ML approach enabled accurate prediction and facilitated the interpretation of trends associated with wake interference, achieving R2 = 0.98 for displacement and 0.85 for power, and demonstrates the potential of such tandem configurations within the investigated operating conditions for flow-adaptive energy harvesting systems and self-powered sensing applications.

title: FRP-M2DA: cross-modal multi-source domain adaptation via frequency-domain recurrence and multi-level adversarial alignment for cross-condition bearing fault diagnosis
abstract: In complex variable operating-condition scenarios, bearing fault diagnosis faces two coupled challenges: pronounced distribution shift and insufficient discriminative information from a single view. To address these issues, this paper proposes FRP-M2DA, a frequency-domain recurrence plot (FRP)-guided multimodal multi-source adversarial domain adaptation framework for robust cross-domain diagnosis. FRP transforms one-dimensional spectral sequences into a two-dimensional structured representation that explicitly captures recurrence structures and global correlations associated with fault-induced impulsive components. A heterogeneous dual-stream encoder is then constructed, where a Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT) extracts multi-scale global texture semantics from FRP, and a multi-scale CNN (MSCNN) models local transients from the raw vibration sequence, enabling complementary “global–local” representation learning via feature fusion. To handle multi-source transfer, FRP-M2DA introduces multi-level multi-source adversarial alignment by placing domain discriminators in both modality-specific subspaces and the fused space, thereby enforcing domain invariance at multiple representation levels and mitigating insufficient alignment and negative transfer. Moreover, a bidirectional cross-view contrastive regularization (InfoNCE) is incorporated to enhance semantic consistency across heterogeneous views, promoting intra-class compactness and inter-class separability on the unlabeled target domain. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks (JNU cross-speed and PU cross-load) and an engineering test-rig dataset with coupled speed–load shifts demonstrate that FRP-M2DA consistently outperforms representative baselines and state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods, achieving superior generalization, balanced class-wise performance, and reliable fault detectability under composite operating-condition variations.
keywords: Bearing Fault Diagnosis under Variable Operating Conditions

title: Micro-textured cage for enhanced tribo-dynamics in rolling bearings: Experiments and fluid–structure modelling
abstract: Precision rolling bearings, such as those used in spacecraft attitude control systems and high-speed motorized spindles, demand exceptionally high standards for cage dynamic stability and operational reliability. Friction and instability at the cage-guiding surface remain critical challenges. This study proposes a novel approach by fabricating micro-topological textures on the guide surface of an integral polyetheretherketone (PEEK) cage to simultaneously mitigate friction and suppress cage whirling instability. A comprehensive investigation integrating tribological tests, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and dynamic experiments was conducted. Four typical texture configurations: circle, square, honeycomb, and herringbone groove, were designed and fabricated via picosecond laser machining. Tribological results identified that square and circular micro-pits optimally reduce the coefficient of friction, particularly under oil and high-speed grease lubrication. CFD simulations revealed the underlying hydrodynamic mechanism, where the honeycomb texture geometry promotes more effective pressure generation, especially in small clearance. Textures with sharp corners, such as square, induced significant vortex generation and higher flow resistance, which may reduce lubrication efficiency. Dynamic tests on a high-speed bearing test rig quantitatively demonstrated that the textured cages, especially those with circular and herringbone patterns, effectively reduce the whirling radius and cage whirling speed deviation under oil lubrication. The synergistic improvement in both tribological and dynamic performance validates the efficacy of micro-textures as a surface engineering solution for precision bearing cages. This work provides a valuable design strategy for enhancing the performance and service life of high-precision bearings in demanding aerospace and industrial applications.

title: Guided wavefield damage imaging method for metal plates based on 2D sparse multi-frequency wavenumber spectrum reconstruction
abstract: Although significant progress has been made in ultrasonic guided wavefield damage imaging, its engineering application remains constrained by the requirement for high-density sampling. Compressed sensing technology can break through the limitation of Nyquist sampling law and reconstruct data from a small amount of data samples. Based on compressed sensing technology, this paper proposes a guided wavefield damage imaging method for metal plate via two-dimensional multi-frequency sparse wavenumber spectrum reconstruction. This method enables imaging through the reconstruction of only a selected set of frequency components. This strategy alleviates the computational burden caused by reconstructing all the frequency components, thereby improving the computational efficiency. Firstly, the sparse sampling method is selected to ensure the uniformity and randomness of the sparse sampling process, the pulse laser is used for point-by-point excitation and the sparse wavefield is obtained by the piezoelectric ceramic sensor. Then, a dictionary matrix is constructed based on the two-dimensional ultrasonic guided waves propagation physical model, and the sparse representation of the wavefield is obtained through the two-dimensional orthogonal matching pursuit (2D-OMP) algorithm, enabling the reconstruction of complete multi-frequency wavefield from a limited set of known wavefield data. Furthermore, the reconstructed multi-frequency wavefield data can be used to compute the multi-frequency two-dimensional wavenumber spectrum. Finally, the frequency wavenumber filtering method is used to extract the damage information in the multi-frequency wavenumber spectrum, and the filtered multi-frequency wavefield is subjected to root mean square(RMS) processing to achieve defect imaging. The proposed method is verified in simulation and experiment respectively. The experiment and simulation results show that the method can well realize the reconstruction of frequency wavenumber spectrum and damage imaging in aluminum plate.

title: Hysteretic modeling and experimental validation of a metal-rubber dynamic vibration absorber for aero-engine stator support structures
abstract: Aero-engine stator support structures often exhibit multiple response peaks under broadband, multi-order excitation, whereas conventional linear tuned vibration absorbers are narrow-band and sensitive to structural frequency drift. This study proposes a metal-rubber dynamic vibration absorber (MRDVA) for passive broadband suppression. The MRDVA consists of two absorber mass rings and three metal-rubber layers: MR1 connects the primary structure to the first mass ring, MR2 couples the two mass rings, and MR3 connects the second mass ring to the primary structure, forming a closed nonlinear auxiliary inertial branch. A composite restoring-force model is established for system-level dynamic analysis. The quasi-static loading–unloading tests characterize the nonlinear elastic skeleton and force path, while the rate-dependent terms are treated as equivalent design coefficients in the coupled model. Coupling the MRDVA with a multi-modal primary structure yields steady-state frequency responses through direct time-domain integration and harmonic amplitude extraction. Under harmonic excitation, the MRDVA achieves a global peak reduction ratio of approximately 55.3% and attenuates multiple peaks over a broad frequency range. When the three cubic rate coefficients are varied over 50%–150% of their baseline values, the global peak-reduction ratio remains between 50.43% and 60.67%, indicating that the principal attenuation result is retained over the investigated parameter range. The calculated force–displacement loops and signed cycle-work analysis identify MR1 and MR3 as the principal dissipative paths near the primary response peak. Half-sine impact simulations indicate faster residual energy decay after impact. Full-stator structural excitation tests covering 13,000–15,000 rpm and three installed-unbalance levels further show reduced local output responses. Under the representative condition of 14,500 rpm and a 16 g installed unbalance mass, the dominant spectral component at the bearing-housing measurement point is reduced by 28.31%. These results demonstrate that the MRDVA supports passive broadband vibration attenuation in aero-engine stator support regions through dual-mass inertial coupling and the combined nonlinear restoring and dissipative actions of the metal-rubber connections.

title: A kriging-based data-driven approach for localization of simultaneous impacts in composites
abstract: Detection of simultaneous low-velocity impacts in composite structures involve fundamental challenge as the uniqueness of time-difference-of-arrival (TDoA) features is compromised by guided wave superposition. This challenge becomes significantly more pronounced in the presence of simultaneous multiple impacts. We propose an artificial neural network (ANN)-based framework for both single and multiple impact localization on laminated composite plates employing TDoA features enhanced through singular value decomposition (SVD) for mitigating indeterminacy of source due to wavefield superposition. The effectiveness of the proposed methodology in localizing single and simultaneous impacts without explicit signal separation and densification of sensors has been demonstrated. The ANN trained solely on finite-element simulation data has been shown be robust enough when tested on unseen numerical and experimental datasets, including unequal energy levels and time delays between impacts. The robustness is further enhanced through a kriging-based post-processing correction without retraining. For dual impacts, the proposed framework exhibits 90% probability-of-detection between 24.01and 38.65 mm.

title: System-dynamics-oriented design of electromagnetic active suspension via physics-informed modeling
abstract: Electromagnetic active suspension (EAS) performance is fundamentally governed by actuator dynamics, where the thrust saturation and ripple of permanent magnet linear synchronous motors (PMLSMs) directly affect the ride comfort under random road excitations. In conventional FEA-driven actuator design, the pathway linking electromagnetic design variables to system-level vibration responses is not explicitly revealed, which renders performance-oriented optimization computationally prohibitive. This study proposes a physics-informed modeling and optimization framework that establishes an explicit knowledge pathway from suspension dynamics to electromagnetic actuator design. An analytical Optimal Equivalent Radius-Maxwell Stress Tensor (OMST) formulation is developed to characterize the electromagnetic thrust, and embedded together with Maxwell equations into a physics-informed neural operator (PIMNO) built upon an enhanced Fourier Neural Operator. This enables accurate magnetic field and thrust prediction with substantially reduced data requirements. A MORIME scheme is further introduced to synergize with the PIMNO-OMST model for efficient design exploration. More importantly, device performance requirements are derived directly from system-level vibration simulations using a dual-condition robust weighting strategy, allowing actuator optimization to be guided by vibration and signal-domain indices rather than purely electromagnetic criteria. Experimental results demonstrate that the designed actuator yields suspension vibration responses, power spectral density characteristics, and ride comfort performance nearly identical to those obtained using FEA-driven optimization, while reducing computational cost by over 99%. The proposed framework provides a computationally efficient and physically consistent method for system-dynamics-oriented force performance design in EAS, bridging electromagnetic field-to-force modeling and mechanical system vibration analysis.

title: MSEEN-LightGBM via IDTCWPT for noise-robust fault diagnosis of industrial equipment
abstract: Fault evolution in industrial equipment is reflected in vibration signals through complex nonlinear and chaotic dynamics. However, traditional diagnosis methods are inherently limited in capturing such complexity and are highly sensitive to noise interference. To address these issues, this paper proposes a fault diagnosis method MSEEN-LightGBM that integrates Multiscale Sparse Energy Entropy (MSEEN), and LightGBM with an enhanced loss function. First, an Improved Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform (IDTCWPT) is proposed to address frequency aliasing and translation sensitivity. Then, a Multiscale Sparse Energy Entropy (MSEEN) is developed by integrating IDTCWPT with non-convex sparse regularization to capture multiscale fault characteristics and enable adaptive sparse feature selection. In addition, sparse energy features and multi-domain statistical features are fused and then classified using LightGBM with an enhanced loss function. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, a multi-equipment case study was conducted. The proposed method achieved 97.42% accuracy and 97.38% F1 score, with a false positive rate of 0.4% and F1 exceeding 97% across all four equipment types, while maintaining robust performance under strong noise. These results demonstrate its advantages in diagnostic accuracy, noise robustness, and generalization capability.

title: Acoustic dynamic modal analysis through Bayesian inference with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method
abstract: Aerodynamic acoustic radiation is present throughout an aircraft’s flight. Identifying the dynamic modes of such noise is crucial for understanding the mechanisms of sound generation within the airflow and its propagation. However, the validity of the mode parameters identified by modal decomposition methods faces significant challenges due to the inherent random nature of aerodynamic noise sources. Moreover, the limited number of sensors in experiments constrains high-resolution spatial measurements of the noise. This paper proposes a Bayesian data-driven modal decomposition method, based on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, for the valid and high-resolution identification of aerodynamic noise modes, with applications to microphone array measurements. This Bayesian framework for dynamic mode decomposition is constructed using Koopman eigen-decomposition theory. Subsequently, analytic gradient expressions, which serve as driving forces for the Markov chains, are derived for the mode parameters. The posterior distributions of these parameters are then estimated using the HMC sampler. Finally, the set of mode parameters is iteratively updated based on the relationship between the Koopman eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, significantly reducing computational complexity. The reconstruction of transient dynamics in the noise-driven Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation shows that the proposed method attains a root mean square error below 15%, reflecting its effectiveness in modal decomposition. Further computational aeroacoustic simulations and non-synchronous wind tunnel measurements were conducted on the trailing-edge noise of the NACA 0012 airfoil to obtain the acoustic modes. The results show that this method can effectively visualize the dynamic behavior of sound waves, offering a novel perspective for exploring the mechanisms of aerodynamic noise generation and propagation.

title: Drift-controlled IMU-only displacement estimation for flexible structures using EKF and UKF
abstract: Estimating displacement from inertial measurements without external references is challenging due to integration drift, sensor bias, unmodeled excitation, and nonlinear coupling between attitude and gravity. This paper investigates inertial measurement unit (IMU)-only displacement estimation for a flexible vertical structure using a reduced-order bending model and nonlinear Bayesian filtering. A dominant-mode structural model is augmented with an explicit mean-reverting latent forcing state, so that persistent low-frequency acceleration residuals are represented probabilistically rather than being absorbed into displacement. Extended Kalman filter (EKF) and unscented Kalman filter (UKF) implementations are compared under identical noise assumptions, and the results show that, once latent forcing is introduced, the EKF is more robust than the UKF across the tested IMU-only parameter sweep. We further examine Gaussian-process pseudo-measurements and offline Switching-EM+RTS smoothing as supporting correction and calibration mechanisms. Numerical simulations demonstrate that explicit latent-forcing modeling reduces displacement RMS error by more than an order of magnitude relative to a baseline EKF and substantially improves posterior coverage. The results indicate that reliable IMU-only displacement estimation in GPS-denied settings requires not only nonlinear attitude-gravity modeling, but also explicit stochastic representation of unmodeled low-frequency forcing and uncertainty calibration.

title: Full-field full-stress-tensor identification of base-excited structures
abstract: Identifying the full-stress tensor over the surface of a vibrating structure is essential for design validation and vibration-fatigue-life estimation, yet current experimental methods provide only pointwise or incomplete stress data. Infrared cameras can provide non-contact, full-field surface-stress measurements on vibrating structures via the thermoelastic effect; however, they measure only the first stress invariant ( i.e. , the sum of the normal stresses at the free surface: σ x x + σ y y ). The individual stress components ( σ x x , σ y y , τ x y ) required for a complete characterisation of the surface-stress state remain inaccessible from a single thermoelastic measurement. This article introduces a method that recovers the full-field, in-plane-stress power spectral density (PSD) field from thermoelastic camera data on a base-excited structure, demonstrated for thin, isotropic, metallic, plate-like structures under adiabatic conditions. First, a characterisation measurement identifies the hybrid stress-mode shapes containing all the plane-stress components by merging thermoelastic camera data with a simplified FE model through SEMM. Then, during operation under broadband random base excitation, the camera response is projected onto these mode shapes and expanded to the full-stress-tensor PSD. The method is validated experimentally on a clamped aluminium plate, identifying spatially resolved stress PSDs for all three in-plane components ( σ x x , σ y y , τ x y ). The full-field first invariant σ x x + σ y y is measured experimentally; the individual components σ x x , σ y y and τ x y are reconstructed through an experimentally corrected modal expansion informed by an FE stress basis, which supplies the inter-component ratios.

title: Physics-guided broad learning (PhyBL) for model updating using incomplete modal data
abstract: Finite element model updating (FEMU) is crucial for developing reliable reference models that reproduce the actual dynamic behavior of monitored structures for structural integrity assessment. This paper proposes a Physics-guided Broad Learning (PhyBL) framework that accelerates FEMU by learning a surrogate mapping from noisy and incomplete modal data to stiffness correction factors (SCFs). PhyBL integrates the Broad Learning System (BLS) with a physics-guided learning (PGL) strategy to enable rapid updates and efficient retraining while improving the generalization, robustness, and physical interpretability. The flat BLS architecture supports rapid training and network expansion without retraining the entire network. The output weights are initialized by ridge regression and subsequently refined by minimizing an objective function that incorporates an eigen-equation constraint. The proposed framework is evaluated through numerical studies of a three‑span continuous bridge and the Canton Tower, followed by a field application using monitoring data from the Canton Tower. Comparisons with baseline methods, an ablation study, and a sensitivity analysis are performed. The results show that PhyBL offers superior performance and computational efficiency, providing an efficient and reliable approach to FEMU.

title: The shock isolation performance of high-performance wire rope isolators in floating raft isolation systems
abstract: Traditional wire rope isolators (WRIs) are commonly employed in floating raft isolation systems (FRIS) for aerospace and naval shock protection. However, they are susceptible to strand loosening from asymmetric winding and damping attenuation under large deformations. Moreover, their all-metal construction offers poor high-frequency filtering, failing to meet stringent shock isolation requirements. This study proposes a high-performance wire rope isolator (HP-WRI) by vulcanizing viscoelastic materials into conventional WRI. Mechanical tests show that the HP-WRI increases the average stiffness by up to 4.35 times and the energy dissipation by 248% compared to conventional WRI. A circular ring equivalent geometric model for preliminary design and a rate-dependent composite model integrating modified Bouc-Wen hysteresis, nonlinear damping, and Maxwell elements for precise dynamic analysis are established and experimentally validated, effectively capturing the rate-dependent and displacement-dependent mechanical behavior of the isolator. Parametric analysis of FRIS reveals that reducing the stiffness ratio and mass ratio, or increasing the damping ratio, effectively lowers the isolation coefficient. Free-fall shock tests confirm that, in the FRIS configuration, the HP-WRI maintains an isolation coefficient below 0.1 across all loading conditions, corresponding to over 90% acceleration reduction, whereas the conventional WRI experiences bottoming out under severe shocks. These findings provide valuable insights for the shock-resistant design of FRIS in aerospace and naval applications.

title: Interpretation and mitigation of high-frequency cable vibrations in a cable-stayed bridge: Effects of boundary condition and damper configuration
abstract: High-frequency vibrations have been observed in cables equipped with dampers on a cable-stayed bridge. Long-term monitoring of wind conditions and cable accelerations indicate that these vibrations exhibit the characteristic wind speed–frequency correlation and limited amplitude of typical vortex-induced vibrations (VIVs). Nevertheless, their occurrence differs significantly between two cable types with distinct boundary conditions and damper configurations. For auxiliary cables with an external damper near the girder and a high-damping-rubber (HDR) damper near the tower, such VIVs frequently occur in modes whose first node is located near the external damper. In contrast, such vibrations are seldom observed in stay cables equipped with an external damper and HDR dampers installed inside the guide tubes at both ends. To interpret these differences and guide the mitigation of vibration, a generalized dynamic model of the cable-damper system is developed. Multimode damping analysis shows that an HDR damper installed away from the external damper near the tower end provides negligible damping and therefore cannot suppress the observed high-frequency VIVs. In contrast, an HDR damper located near the girder end can act synergistically with the external damper to effectively suppress high-frequency vibrations when the external damper coincides with a modal node. Based on these findings, a Stockbridge damper (SD) is designed for auxiliary cables that are connected to the girder by pinned joints and guide tubes to install HDR dampers are unavailable. The vibration mitigation performance of the SD is validated through laboratory experiments and further evaluated by theoretical analysis using the identified damper parameters. It is suggested that the required SD mass can be reduced if it is installed above rather than below the external damper. After installing the SDs on the auxiliary cables, field monitoring under normal wind conditions and during two typhoon events confirms the practical effectiveness.

title: Sequential multiple importance sampling for robust and efficient (possibly high-dimensional) reliability estimation
abstract: This study proposes a sequential multiple importance sampling (SeMIS) method for the robust and efficient estimation of small failure probabilities. Unlike conventional sequential methods that force the final importance sampling density (ISD) to approximate the optimal ISD, SeMIS constructs a sequence of intermediate ISDs − comprising an expanded initial distribution followed by adaptively determined truncated distributions − to maximize overall sampling effectiveness. This cooperative strategy utilizes variance inflation to enhance the exploration of complex failure domains and hybrid truncation to minimize computational expenditure. Furthermore, the uncertainty of the SeMIS estimator is quantified through an innovative uncertainty propagation-based method, which enables the coefficient of variation to be predicted from a single simulation run. The performance of the algorithm is demonstrated through a series of low- and high-dimensional benchmark problems and two synthetic engineering applications. The results indicate that SeMIS provides more accurate and stable failure probability estimates than conventional sequential methods, characterized by reduced bias, lower deviation, and improved computational efficiency.

title: A Frequency-Aware Residual Decomposition Network for Extracting Incipient Fault Signatures in Rotating Machinery
abstract: Signal decomposition is an important task in Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) of mechanical transmission systems characterized by nonlinear and non-stationary vibration responses. However, conventional signal processing methodologies are often constrained by fixed basis functions and manual parameter tuning, which compromise noise robustness and limit their ability in capturing transient signatures of incipient faults. Leveraging the paradigm of signal processing-informed neural networks, this paper proposes an interpretable Frequency-Aware Residual Decomposition Network (FARCD-Net), which unfolds iterative filtering into a learnable framework to reduce reliance on manually designed optimization objectives. Specifically, a Generalized Adaptive Decomposition Module (GADM) is constructed via residual learning to generalize the conventional filtering operator, preserving the underlying decomposition principle. To enhance feature extraction in noisy environments, a data-driven Frequency Masking Layer (FML) is introduced. The layer learns adaptive spectral weights, enabling the network to dynamically localize transient signatures within resonance bands. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on a run-to-failure benchmark and a high-speed train bogie system demonstrate effective extraction of fault-induced transients, with physical interpretability supported by intermediate network representations.

title: High-fidelity wear simulation of gas foil bearing-rotor systems in hydrogen fuel cell air compressors using a physics-guided neural network
abstract: A Gas Foil Bearing (GFB)-rotor system is critical to a hydrogen fuel cell air compressor, yet highly susceptible to wear under frequent start-stop operations. Existing simulation models rarely consider wear and lack simulation accuracy, inadequately assessing lubrication performance and frictional power loss of GFB-rotor systems. To address this issue, this study proposes a high-fidelity dynamic model for a GFB-rotor system based on a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), coupling a physics-based GFB-rotor dynamic model with a neural network used for model error compensation. The GFB-rotor dynamic model incorporates wear-induced gas film thickness variation, Reynolds equation, foil structural dynamics, and rigid rotor motion equations. To compensate for deviations from theoretical simplifications, the neural network embeds a learnable model discrepancy term into the GFB-rotor dynamic model. The model parameters and neural network weights are then iteratively optimized via experimental calibration. The simulated results of the proposed high-fidelity model match well with experimental data, with relative errors below 5.73% across all operating conditions. Parametric analyses demonstrate that wear significantly deteriorates gas film lubrication performance. Increased wear depth and worn region reduce minimum gas film thickness, raise maximum gas film pressure, and shift the pressure field from single-peak to dual-peak concentration. Wear amplifies viscous shear dissipation via reduced gas film thickness and elevated gas film pressure, increasing frictional power loss of the GFB-rotor system by up to 44.5% under 20,000 rpm. The proposed high-fidelity model enables accurate condition monitoring of GFB-rotor systems, ensuring stable performance and optimal efficiency of hydrogen fuel cell air compressors.

title: TF-RefineNet: A deep time–frequency refinement network and its application to tacho-less order tracking
abstract: Existing deep time–frequency analysis (TFA) methods have alleviated the parameter sensitivity and time–frequency (TF) energy dispersion of traditional methods, but their mainstream amplitude mapping paradigm is still centered on pixel-wise Mean Squared Error (MSE). Its optimization objective is closer to image restoration than TF-ridge awareness for instantaneous frequency (IF) extraction, making it prone to residual background noise and spurious ridge components that interfere with ridge tracking and degrade IF extraction accuracy. This study redefines deep TFA from the optimization perspective by transforming full-image regression into TF-ridge-aware mask estimation. An ideal binary time–frequency mask (IBTFM) and Dice loss are used to make the network aware of foreground TF ridges and background TF noise, producing a clean TF representation with only ridges retained. For sparse TF ridges, fast Fourier convolution (FFC) is embedded into a residual encoder-decoder (RED) to form a local–global cross-scale fusion module, capturing both local ridge details and global ridge trends. Results show that the proposed method can adaptively represent complex non-stationary signals with closely-spaced and crossing IFs, providing a reliable basis for accurate IF extraction and enabling tacho-less order tracking (TLOT) for variable-speed fault feature extraction.

title: Physics-informed online intelligent discharge state identification for high-energy electrical discharge milling: Theory and methods
abstract: High-energy electrical discharge milling (HEDM) offers considerable potential for high-efficiency machining of difficult-to-machine materials in aerospace and other advanced manufacturing sectors. However, compared with conventional electrical discharge machining (EDM), HEDM is characterized by substantially higher single-pulse energy, greater fluctuations in discharge behavior, and lower process stability. To address the limitations of purely data-driven models in terms of physical interpretability and cross-condition generalization, this paper proposes a physics-informed semi-supervised learning framework for online HEDM discharge state identification. First, a time-threshold-based semi-automatic labeling method is developed to generate discharge state labels and identify key pulse-level physical information. Second, an empirical model for estimating the equivalent plasma channel radius is established based on high-energy single-pulse discharge experiments. The estimated radius is then combined with the actual single-pulse input energy and equivalent short-circuit conduction to construct a multi-level physical supervision framework. These three quantities characterize the spatial scale of thermal effects, heat input intensity, and short-circuit-related conduction behavior, respectively. By jointly optimizing the pulse-level classification loss and the window-level physical consistency loss, the proposed framework enables the model to learn discriminative features while constraining its predictions using discharge-related physical quantities. Comparative and ablation experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves an identification accuracy of 99.17 ± 0.75% under the new operating conditions and improves both cross-condition generalization and physical consistency. Real-time validation further confirms its capability for online HEDM monitoring, thereby providing a theoretical and technical basis for future intelligent control of HEDM processes.

title: Synergy effect of stacked assembly errors and temperature fields on the dynamic characteristics of assembly rotor
abstract: Stacking assembly errors and temperature fields are two critical parameters that influence the geometry, mass distribution and consequently dynamic characteristics of assembly rotors, particularly in non-uniform temperature operation scenarios. Clarifying the dynamic characteristics of assembly rotor induced by the two parameters is essential for enhancing rotor reliability and performance. However, the current investigations rarely focus on the synergy effect of two parameters, making it challenging to accurately predict the rotor dynamic response. Herein, a systematic investigation is performed to dig out the synergy effect of two parameters on the dynamic characteristics of assembly rotor. First, given that stacking assembly errors and temperature fields would induce both stiffness weakening and mass center shifting, the two parameters can be modeled as equivalent to assembly error excitation force and thermal excitation force, respectively. Subsequently, using the established model, the dynamic response of rotor is analyzed, with emphasis on the key influencing factors including assembly phase, temperature gradients and their synergy effects. Last, the high accuracy of model is experimental validated, presenting a feasible avenue for predicting assembly rotor performance under thermo-elastic coupling conditions.

title: Physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for sound field estimation
abstract: The sound field estimation method based on a physics-informed neural network (PINN) integrates physical prior information, which not only significantly reduces dependence on the size of the training set but also improves the accuracy of sound field estimation.
