Compressive sensing (CS), which enables sub-Nyquist sampling by leveraging signal sparsity, presents a potential solution. However, its application to track irregularities, which are characterized by broad bandwidth, stochasticity, and stringent requirements for high-fidelity reconstruction in both spatial and frequency domains, faces unique obstacles, and thus remains underexplored. This study systematically analyzes the applicability of most compatible sparse representation bases, including Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), and Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), to track irregularity signals. Through sparsity analysis and multi-dimensional performance evaluation (e.g., NRMSE, R2, PAE, SPD), it is demonstrated that the DFT provides the most effective sparse representation. The DFT-based CS framework enables compression ratios of track irregularity data up to 50% while maintaining high fidelity. Nevertheless, DFT-based reconstruction involves higher computational cost than its DCT counterpart. Accordingly, DCT is a practical choice for efficiency-oriented applications, as validated by train-track dynamic simulations. This work establishes a practical and efficient CS-based solution for large-scale track irregularity data management.

title: Structural modal identification based on motion magnification and improved subpixel edge detection algorithm
abstract: Modal identification is essential to structural health monitoring (SHM). The use of computer vision (CV) for modal identification offers several advantages compared to conventional approaches. However, most existing CV technologies require the installation of artificial targets and are limited to scenarios with significant vibration amplitudes. Therefore, this paper proposes a target-free modal identification approach integrating the broad-band phase-based video motion magnification (BPVMM) technique with an improved subpixel edge detection technique. The BPVMM technique is employed to amplify the low-amplitude vibrations and the improved subpixel edge detection algorithm based on partial area effect (PAE) is applied to extract displacement from the amplified video. The data-driven stochastic subspace identification (Data-SSI) method is then used to identify the frequencies and mode shapes of the structure. Finally, the performance of the developed technique is evaluated through laboratory and field tests to verify its accuracy. The results show that the mode shapes identified by the proposed technique are in good agreement with the reference mode shapes, and the MAC value is above 0.9843. This study provides a convenient, no-target, and low-cost method for structural modal identification.

title: Parameter-identification-based time-varying aeroelastic modeling framework and wind-tunnel tests for a folding-wing model
abstract: This paper presents a time-varying aeroelastic modeling framework for folding wings undergoing large, continuous morphing, with an emphasis on parameter identification. In the framework, the time-varying stiffness of the actuation system is identified from time-domain responses by extracting instantaneous frequencies and minimizing the discrepancy between identified and simulated frequencies at each time step. The identified stiffness is then incorporated into a time-varying structural dynamics model formulated using the floating frame of reference. The structural model is coupled with an unsteady vortex lattice method to simulate the transient aeroelastic responses under arbitrary flow conditions. A simulation example verifies the accuracy of the stiffness identification strategy. The wind-tunnel experiments validate and characterize the nonstationary vibration characteristics during the morphing process. The comparison between simulations and experiments demonstrates that the proposed framework accurately captures the time-varying aeroelastic behavior of the folding wing. The results reveal that the folding and unfolding processes exhibit opposite aeroelastic responses. In addition, the morphing rate plays a critical role in determining dynamic stability. The primary contribution of this work lies in integrating frequency-based system identification with a parametric, time-varying aeroelastic modeling framework, providing a practical, experimentally grounded approach to analyzing and predicting the stability of morphing wing systems.

title: Sensing limit in blade tip timing measurement and underlying theory
abstract: Blade Tip Timing (BTT) is a promising non-contact technique for measuring blade vibrations in rotating machinery due to its minimal hardware intrusion and long service life. However, the inherent mismatch between the high vibration frequencies of the blades and the relatively low sampling rates achievable in practice leads to severe undersampling, thereby hindering accurate parameter identification—an essential task for blade health monitoring. Although numerous advanced parameter identification methods have been proposed, their performance strongly depends on the probe layout, and a unified, intuitive theory for evaluating and optimizing layouts remains lacking. In this paper, we develop a sensing limit theory based on the Delay Sampling Theorem (DST), providing fundamental insights into the capabilities and limitations of BTT measurement. Furthermore, recognizing that sampling jitter arising from tip vibration and rotational speed fluctuations is inevitable in practice, we extend the theory to account for such uncertainties and introduce the concept of a robust sensing limit. For practical applications, we derive a straightforward formula to compute the robust sensing limit for any given layout and present guidelines for layout evaluation and optimization. The strong agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental results validates the correctness and applicability of the proposed theory. Overall, the robust sensing limit theory offers a foundational framework for advancing BTT-based vibration measurement.

title: Dynamic modeling of high-speed helical gear transmission system with multiple geometric deviations and non-uniform contact
abstract: Existing helical gear dynamic models remain limited in providing a unified state-dependent description of the combined effects of multiple geometric deviations on non-uniform contact. To address this problem, this study develops a dynamic model in which pitch, profile, and helix deviations are mapped as normal perturbations into a common time-varying backlash field and coupled with the dynamic transmission error to determine the instantaneous contact state and load-bearing configuration. The improved mesh element is directly coupled with the shafting, bearings, and casing, establishing a consistent pathway from geometric deviations to system vibration response. The results show that pitch deviation changes the tooth-pair load-bearing sequence and mainly enhances rotational-frequency sideband components around the gear mesh frequency (GMF). Helix deviation enhances sideband modulation through contact position migration along the face width direction, whereas profile deviation primarily increases the GMF main-peak energy by changing the local stiffness of the main load-bearing region. As gear accuracy grade deteriorates, sideband related indices show higher sensitivity to accuracy degradation than the GMF main peak alone. Experimental validation shows good agreement between simulation and experiment in terms of time-domain amplitude, GMF main peak energy, and rotational-frequency sideband components. These results provide a practical basis for linking operational vibration features with geometric deviation related manufacturing accuracy assessment, assembly quality control, and sideband-based condition monitoring.

title: Closed-form optimal design of passive switching dampers for stay cables
abstract: Near-anchor linear viscous dampers for stay cables are constrained by the small local motion available for energy dissipation. This study proposes a passive switching damper that mechanically alternates between high- and low-damping states according to motion direction, without sensors, controllers, or external power. A first-harmonic reduction separates the non-smooth switching force into equivalent viscous and displacement-related components. Combined with complex-eigenvalue analysis, this representation yields the first-harmonic equivalent added modal damping ratio and a closed-form optimum for the high-state damping coefficient at a prescribed near-anchor location, while recovering the classical linear viscous damper (LVD) limit when the two damping states coincide. A detailed A10 stay-cable model is used to assess the analytical design against the fixed classical target-mode LVD under free decay, primary resonance, multi-frequency excitation, and stochastic aerodynamic loading. Without parameter retuning, the proposed damper reduces the maximum full-cable peak-displacement envelope by 26.67% under the prescribed three-frequency excitation. Across ten stochastic realizations, it reduces the mean mid-span RMS response by 31.40% relative to the LVD. Component tests at five excitation frequencies demonstrate passive two-state switching. A globally calibrated two-state force model achieves a mean normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) of 5.5%, compared with 14.6% for the linear viscous baseline. These component tests characterize local switching and force behavior rather than full-scale cable performance.

title: Remaining useful life prediction under noisy conditions via adaptive degradation modeling incorporating memory effects
abstract: Accurate modeling of degradation processes is fundamental to reliable remaining useful life (RUL) prediction for mechanical systems. However, practical degradation processes are often affected by measurement uncertainty, non-Markovian degradation characteristics, and evolving degradation mechanisms, which may limit the prediction performance of existing methods. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an adaptive degradation modeling framework that jointly considers measurement uncertainty, memory effects, and online model adaptation. The proposed method first constructs an initial degradation model using the training units, with the model parameters estimated via maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). An improved cumulative sum (CUSUM) procedure is then employed to detect structural variation points by comparing the model predictions with online monitoring data. Once a structural variation is detected, the degradation model is adaptively updated using the newly available observations while retaining the stochastic degradation structure. An enhanced particle filtering (PF) algorithm is employed to recursively estimate the latent degradation state. For RUL prediction, the first hitting time (FHT) concept is adopted to derive an approximate probability density function (PDF) based on the adaptively updated degradation model. Experimental results obtained under both the internal data partitioning strategy and the official C-MAPSS training/testing protocol demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves improved predictive performance compared with the benchmark methods.

title: Experimental investigation, mechanism analysis and mitigation solutions for tire hop during snap start of vehicles
abstract: During rapid vehicle startup on low-adhesion road surfaces, stick-slip friction between the tires and the pavement triggers self-excited vibration of the vehicle driveline system. This vibration induces drive shaft torque fluctuation, accompanied by powertrain and seat track vibration, a phenomenon formally defined as tire hop. Existing research lacks high-precision testing methods for transient drive shaft torque under tire hop. The influences of road conditions, driving modes and powertrain layouts on tire hop characteristics have not been systematically explored. Moreover, the formation mechanism of multi-frequency vibration peaks during tire hop remains unclear, and few studies consider the nonlinear features of powertrain mounts to analyze vibration characteristics or propose targeted suppression solutions. This paper presents several distinct innovations for tire hop research. Firstly, a wireless telemetry-based testing method is proposed to achieve high-precision measurement of transient drive shaft torque under tire hop conditions. Secondly, vehicle snap start experiments are conducted to systematically analyze how road surface states, different driving modes and diverse powertrain layout configurations affect key tire hop parameters. The parameters include oscillation of wheel speed and drive shaft torque, vibrations of powertrain vibration and seat track. Thirdly, a refined vibration model is established by taking the nonlinear force-displacement characteristics of powertrain mounts into account, which successfully uncovers the formation mechanism of multi-frequency vibration peaks. The relationship between powertrain output torque and inherent natural frequencies is also quantitatively investigated. Finally, a targeted optimization strategy is put forward by optimizing mount mechanical performance, quantity and arrangement to reduce tire hop-caused vibrations of powertrain mounts and seat tracks.

title: A novel bridge damage indicator based on vehicle-induced instantaneous frequency characteristic function
abstract: Accurate structural damage identification is significant for bridge health monitoring and safety maintenance. However, current damage identification practices often struggle with the incompleteness of structural response monitoring or suboptimal signal-to-noise ratios in measurements. Regarding these challenges, this paper proposes a novel bridge damage identification framework based on the monitoring of vehicle-bridge system’s instantaneous frequency. The framework integrates traffic load monitoring with vehicle-bridge interaction analysis, detecting structural damages via the characteristic function of the instantaneous frequency along the bridge during vehicle traversal, i.e., the vehicle-induced instantaneous frequency characteristic function (VIFCF). Derived from the VIFCF, two damage indicators are proposed to address small and big data-driven scenarios, corresponding to the damage identification using standard vehicles and ambient vehicles, respectively. Through numerical simulation and experiments, the proposed indicators have been proven to effectively detect the overall performance degradation and local damage of bridges. The proposed framework shows potential for long-term bridge monitoring and damage localization with limited bridge-mounted sensing.

title: Self-recovered phase reference and structured phase evidence aggregation for bearing degradation transition detection under nonstationary conditions
abstract: Degradation-related changes in rolling bearings can reorganize the phase structure of resonance-band responses before pronounced vibration-energy growth. Extracting this information under nonstationary conditions requires a cyclic coordinate that follows the signal and a scoring rule that consolidates phase changes distributed across bands and descriptors. This paper proposes SRR-SPEA, which combines a self-recovered phase reference with structured phase evidence aggregation for bearing degradation transition detection. Baseline records determine the harmonic reference family, cyclic orders and normalization statistics, after which records are processed chronologically using fixed descriptor directions, resonance bands and aggregation settings. Controlled tests covered three nonlinear mechanism families, four noise levels and matched transition and null sequences. In the mixed amplitude-phase benchmark, self-recovery increased the median phase-score Spearman coefficient from 0.340 for a fixed reference to 0.783. In the equal-RMS benchmark, the calibrated phase-score rule detected 60/60 prescribed transitions, produced false alarms in 3/60 null sequences and yielded a median lead of 19.5 segments relative to the prescribed transition center. On full-resolution NASA IMS2-B1, the continuous SRR-SPEA score achieved a Spearman coefficient of 0.838, compared with 0.812 for RMS and −0.082 to 0.188 for the implemented cyclostationary scalar baselines. A sensitive SRR-SPEA event occurred at record 373 before the corresponding RMS event at record 533, whereas a conservative calibration placed the phase-score alarm at record 619. The later IMS bearings and the UPB B01 case further showed that trend coherence and alarm timing depend on degradation trajectory, monitoring resolution and baseline composition. SRR-SPEA therefore provides an interpretable means of detecting and tracing phase reorganization, with its alarm behavior explicitly characterized by calibration and operating conditions.

title: A self-powered and self-sensing multi-joint wearable energy harvester with lightweight edge-deployable CNN for real-time lower-limb kinematics and motion mode recognition
abstract: With the global aging population, continuous monitoring of daily activities is increasingly important for rehabilitation and health assessment. However, conventional wearable devices are plagued by insufficient energy self-sufficiency, limiting their practical application in long-term activity monitoring. In this work, we propose a self-powered and self-sensing multi-joint wearable energy harvester capable of simultaneously harvesting negative mechanical work from both the hip and knee joints during human locomotion. The harvested biomechanical energy is converted into electrical power (0.39 W per device) to support embedded computing and wireless communication modules, enabling intermittent energy-autonomous operation. Meanwhile, the generated electrical signals are directly utilized for motion sensing without additional sensors. To achieve real-time motion analysis on resource-constrained embedded platforms, a lightweight convolutional neural network optimized via multi-objective optimization is developed for edge deployment. The proposed framework simultaneously estimates hip and knee angular velocities and recognizes seven motion modes. Experiments involving five participants demonstrated accurate lower-limb kinematics estimation with a mean absolute error of 0.05±0.01, root mean square error of 0.09±0.02, and correlation coefficient of 0.96±0.01, while achieving a motion recognition accuracy of 98.7%. This work establishes a new paradigm integrating biomechanical energy harvesting, self-sensing, and embedded artificial intelligence for sustainable wearable rehabilitation and daily activity monitoring.

title: Online algebraic identification–based trial-weight-free modal balancing of asymmetric rotor–bearing systems
abstract: Asymmetric rotor–bearing systems exhibit parametric excitation and complex vibration behavior due to unequal stiffness along their principal axes, which significantly complicates conventional balancing procedures. Most existing methodologies require trial weights and multiple rotor runs to achieve acceptable vibration levels. A modal balancing method for asymmetric rotors that eliminates the need for test masses is proposed and experimentally validated in this work. The approach is based on an online algebraic identification model that estimates modal unbalance directly from vibration measurements acquired at a single point and at constant rotational speed. A Finite Element model of a multiple-degree-of-freedom asymmetric rotor–bearing system was developed and transformed into a pseudo-modal representation to allow mode-by-mode unbalance identification. The proposed algebraic identifier operates independently of initial conditions and requires only a short time window of the fundamental (1×) vibration component as input. The identified modal unbalance is then used to compute a modal mass arrangement using classical modal balancing principles. The methodology was validated using an experimental test rig comprising an asymmetric shaft with three inertial disks and two supports. Modal unbalance was accurately identified near the first and second critical speeds with errors below 10%, using only 5 s of vibration data. A single balancing run achieved vibration amplitude reductions exceeding 80% in the first mode and between 50% and 80% in the second mode across the operating range of 0–6000 rpm. For comparison, a classical influence-coefficient-based balancing procedure combined with modal balancing required seven experimental runs, including trial-weight runs, to balance the two modes and produced comparable vibration-reduction levels, although with greater variability among measurement locations. These results demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve comparable balancing performance with substantially lower experimental effort, while eliminating trial weights and reducing the number of rotor runs required.

title: Progressive Cross-Model distillation with heterogeneous synergistic classifier for Few-Shot bearing fault diagnosis
abstract: In industrial scenarios, current signals are easier to collect than vibration signals, with more flexible sensor deployment. To address the challenges of source-free constraints, weak fault features, and limited fault samples in current signals for bearing fault diagnosis, and to achieve flexible fault diagnosis under complex working conditions, this paper proposes a progressive cross-model distillation method with heterogeneous synergistic classifier (PCMD-HSC) for few-shot bearing fault diagnosis. In this approach, a vibration-trained source model serves as a knowledge provider, guiding the target model to progressively align the response patterns of current features. Different from the knowledge transfer of conventional distillation methods, this approach transfers the inductive biases of the vibration modality to the target model in the form of response patterns, realizing cross-model response patterns learning and significantly enhancing the diagnostic performance of the target model on the current modality. The proposed heterogeneous synergistic classifier integrates the advantages of prior knowledge and metric learning, and performs synergistic decision-making via an inverse-uncertainty balancing fusion mechanism. It effectively addresses the problem of performance degradation of single classifier under few-shot conditions and improves the generalization ability and noise robustness of the model. Extensive experiments conducted on two bearing datasets covering multimodal data fully demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior diagnostic accuracy and generalization in cross-condition scenarios.

title: Real-time spectral signal processing for robust thickness monitoring during wafer thinning
abstract: Wafer thinning, as a key step in 3D integration using through-silicon via (TSV), highly relies on precise in-situ thickness monitoring to control accurate endpoint and avoid overgrinding or undergrinding. For ultra-thin wafers, conventional contact-based techniques become increasingly limited due to insufficient accuracy and surface damage. Spectral interferometry has been employed for in-situ thickness measurement. However, its application during wafer grinding is challenged by mechanical vibration, cooling flow, silicon debris, and variations in surface conditions, which may lead to incorrect endpoint detection, increasing the risk of wafer scrap. In this study, a compact water-guided optical probe is developed to maintain a stable optical path and reduce contamination from slurry and debris. Meanwhile, a Fourier transform thickness extraction algorithm is combined with a Z-score quality-factor criterion and a dynamic thickness tracking strategy to identify invalid measurements and suppress outliers during continuous thinning. This approach minimizes misjudgments while maintaining a high valid data rate during real-time acquisition. The proposed method was validated over a wide thickness range and achieved accurate endpoint control down to 3 μm. Static comparison with the F50 showed absolute deviations below 0.5 μm within the designed range of 3–400 μm, while valid data rates remained above 80 % across all thinning tasks. Reliable monitoring was further verified for ultra-thin wafers below 10 μm, demonstrating the robustness of the proposed method under practical grinding conditions.

title: Reconfigurable interlocking mechanical metamaterials for tunable vibration mitigation and energy absorption
abstract: A reconfigurable mechanical metamaterial featuring topological interlocking in a modular architecture enables integrated vibration mitigation and energy absorption. This design enables adhesive-free assembly and disassembly and offers potential for repeated use. An integrated experimental and numerical investigation is conducted, combining acceleration-transmissibility measurements, compressive stress estimation, and a Bayesian optimization-Gaussian process regression (BO-GPR) surrogate model to characterize both dynamic and quasi-static mechanical responses. The results demonstrate that the metamaterial produces an elastic wave bandgap within the specific frequency range, and substantial vibration mitigation is validated by acceleration-transmissibility measurements. The bandgap characteristics are governed by the geometric parameters of the re-entrant arcs. Under cyclic compressive loading, the metamaterial retains a considerable proportion of its initial energy absorption capacity after multiple deformation cycles accompanied by substantial dimensional recovery, indicating potential for repeated use under the tested conditions. A parametric mapping relationship between the re-entrant arc geometry and the performance metrics of vibration bandgap and specific energy absorption (SEA) is established. The results reveal that SEA varies non-monotonically with arc length, decreasing to a minimum at a certain length before increasing markedly, whereas it generally increases with arc thickness. SEA also varies non-monotonically with arc width, exhibiting a local minimum at a particular width. A performance design framework is constructed to improve the bandgap width (BW) and SEA, yielding a topological parameter combination that synergistically improves both properties. This mechanical metamaterial integrates vibration mitigation and energy absorption through topological interlocking and offers a tunable design paradigm for multifunctional structural protection.

title: Early anomaly detection in wind Turbines by Causality-based graph attention networks
abstract: Early anomaly detection is a key issue for ensuring reliability, availability and efficiency in Wind Turbines (WTs) operation. Traditional condition monitoring techniques struggle to identify anomalies because of: i) the strong interconnections among the subsystems of a WT, which induce complex spatio-temporal dependencies in the measured signals and can enable the cascading propagation of the effects of anomalies, ii) the variability of the operating conditions, which can affect the anomaly signatures, and iii) the presence of control systems that can mask the anomalies signatures. To address these challenges, this work proposes a novel anomaly detection method employing a Graph Neural Network (GNN) autoencoder. GNN is selected for its capability in modeling the interconnected nature of subsystems and capturing the spatio-temporal dependencies in operational signals. A key contribution is the use of the Granger causality test to generate the GNN functional graph. By leveraging the causal relationships among turbine signals, the obtained graph ensures that the learned topology reflects the underlying physical dependencies rather than spurious correlations, as it may occur in traditional graphs. To handle variability of the operating conditions, graph attention layers adaptively weight sensor relationships, while gated recurrent units process the temporal dynamics. The proposed method is validated on synthetic data simulated using a high-fidelity WT model and applied to SCADA data collected from real WTs. Results demonstrate a 4% increase in recall and a 45% reduction in detection delay compared to state-of-the-art methods.

title: Rolling-bearing lubrication state identification using order-domain cumulative spectral centroid curves and identity-preserving adaptive modulation
abstract: Rolling-bearing lubrication degradation rarely produces stable fault-characteristic frequencies and instead manifests as weak and distributed spectral-energy redistribution, making cross-speed identification challenging. Lubrication-state identification is formulated as order-domain signal representation followed by one-dimensional curve classification. A cumulative spectral centroid curve (CSC) is constructed by progressively expanding the cumulative order range and evaluating the normalised first spectral moment at each cumulative endpoint, thereby encoding the migration of the spectral centroid. After resampling and sample-wise standardisation, the CSC and its first-order difference form a two-channel input to a one-dimensional residual network (ResNet1D) equipped with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM). The difference curve also provides a local-transition prior to an identity-preserving Adaptive Step-Aware modulation (AStA) module through bounded learnable modulation initialised at zero. Experiments were conducted on a three-speed rolling-bearing dataset with five controlled grease-quantity conditions ranging from 4 g to 0 g. Generalisation to unseen rotational speeds was evaluated using leave-one-speed-out splits. Under the same plain ResNet1D backbone, single-channel CSC achieved 89.55% mean Macro-F1, compared with 49.37% for a conventional cumulative energy curve (CEC), showing that CSC provides substantially stronger cross-speed discrimination than the matched zeroth-order cumulative-energy representation. The complete CSC-CBAM-AStA framework then achieved 96.91% mean accuracy and 96.58% mean Macro-F1 across the three held-out speeds. In the reduced-label setting, Macro-F1 reached 87.40% with 2% labelled data and 95.05% with 5%, while the 0.33%–1% regime exhibited substantial seed-to-seed variability. The representation-level contribution of CSC and the additional effects of CBAM feature recalibration and AStA differential-prior modulation are quantified through controlled comparisons and gate-response analyses.

title: Power Bond graph-embedded causal flow-aware graph neural network for fault localization of electro-hydraulic systems
abstract: To achieve precise fault localization for electro-hydraulic systems of mechanical, a Causal Flow-aware Graph Neural Network (CFAGNN) is proposed, which integrates power bond graph topology with deep learning. A power bond graph model is constructed to characterize energy transfer mechanisms and clarify dynamic coupling relationships among subsystems, providing quantifiable physical constraints and edge-node attributes. To accommodate real-time operating conditions, learnable edge attributes are constructed with embedded dynamic correction parameters. These physical priors are embedded into the Causal Flow Attention (CFA) mechanism, where physical regularization and causal direction loss are utilized to constrain attention coefficients to conform to energy transfer laws, thereby enabling accurate tracking of fault propagation paths. Validation on a real engineering machinery dataset demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art models. The results indicate that CFAGNN balances diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency effectively, providing a reliable solution for the fault diagnosis of complex electro-hydraulic systems.

title: Multistage health state estimation and uncertainty quantification for bearing remaining useful life via graph-guided representation learning
abstract: Bearing degradation follows stochastic and nonlinear trajectories, which makes the accurate prediction of remaining useful life (RUL) a critical challenge in industrial prognostics. Recent deep learning-based methods have achieved promising performance in bearing RUL prediction. However, they have limited ability to explicitly account for changes in degradation behavior during the prognostic process. Health-stage information has been employed to characterize degradation progression, but it is typically used only for stage estimation rather than guiding degradation representation learning or RUL prediction. To address this limitation, we propose the Stage-Aware Graph-guided Embedding-Uncertainty Quantification (SAGE-UQ) framework. The proposed framework consistently leverages health-stage information through degradation representation learning and uncertainty-aware RUL prediction. Specifically, graph-guided spectral representation learning and stage-aware temporal contrastive learning were employed to jointly estimate health-stage information. This estimated stage information is further exploited to learn degradation representations that capture health-stage transition characteristics. It is then leveraged to guide uncertainty-aware RUL predictions. The proposed framework explicitly incorporates health-stage transition ambiguity into predictive uncertainty. Experimental results demonstrate that SAGE-UQ consistently outperforms representative baselines and recent state-of-the-art methods. It achieves an average root-mean-square error (RMSE) reduction of approximately 17.4%. The lightweight architecture and low inference latency enhance its practicality for online prognostic applications.

title: Laser beams target-based monocular vision measurement system self-calibration and localization method for boom-type roadheader in large-scale underground complex scene
abstract: The monocular vision measurement system is an effective approach to obtain accuracy and reliable pose estimation for underground tunneling, especially with a specially designed laser beams targets for the far-distance and large-scale scene localization in the tunneling face. However, the conventional manual off-line calibration with a total station is complex and difficulty resulting unsuitable for the automatic underground excavation. This article presents a novel online self-calibration method for the monocular vision measurement system based on the double laser beams targets, in which one is as the benchmark target, the other is as the movable target. The double 3D targets-based monocular vision geometric constraint model is established to connect the 3D targets spatial distribution and the laser beams image points and lines features, considering explicitly the 2D-3D correspondences between laser beams image and object coordinates of the double 3D targets. On this basis, we perform the extrinsic parameters self-calibration to reconstruct the laser beams spatial vector of the movable target from its multi-view image sequences. With no need to gain explicit knowledge of object space coordinates, the movable target multi-station online self-calibration can be performed with known initial benchmark target as well as the multi-view image sequences. The experimental results demonstrated the proposed self-calibration approach to be effective and the accuracy of the fuselage pose estimation has increased by 67.7%, meeting the far-distance localization requirements for underground excavations in coal mine.

title: Surface roughness prediction and process parameter optimization based on grinding force signals in end face grinding of quartz glass
abstract: Grinding wheel wear continuously changes the wheel–workpiece contact condition, grinding force, and surface formation during end face grinding of hard and brittle materials. This study presents an integrated method for surface roughness prediction and process parameter optimization in the end face grinding of quartz glass using a diamond grinding wheel. First, a grinding force model considering abrasive wear is established from single abrasive grain wear and force analyses and validated through full-life grinding experiments. Normal grinding force signals and surface topography profiles are then collected under different process conditions. After drift compensation, steady-state extraction, and frequency-domain analysis, the maximum and mean amplitudes of the force spectrum are mapped to the corresponding features of the surface-topography spectrum. A frequency-domain surface model combining a chi-square distribution, exponential decay, and random disturbance is constructed, and the surface profile is reconstructed using the inverse discrete Fourier transform. Particle swarm optimization identifies the decay coefficient, enabling surface roughness prediction directly from grinding force signals. Finally, a random forest surrogate model and Bayesian optimization are used to maximize grinding efficiency subject to a surface roughness constraint. The results show that the proposed framework supports effective roughness monitoring and identifies efficient parameter combinations while satisfying surface quality requirements. This study provides a mechanism-informed approach for intelligent monitoring and adaptive optimization in the end face grinding of hard and brittle quartz glass.

title: Effective vibration length identification and cable tension estimation of stay cables based on UAV video: Integrating multi-order mode-shape consistency constraints and SSD-CEEMDAN drift separation
abstract: Cable tension is a key indicator for safety assessment and maintenance decision-making of cable-supported bridges. Effective vibration length identification is essential for improving the accuracy of vibration-based cable tension estimation; however, existing methods rely on multi-point accelerometer measurements, resulting in high deployment costs and low field efficiency. To address this issue, this study proposes a UAV-photography-based framework for effective vibration length identification and high-accuracy cable tension estimation, establishing a complete procedure consisting of video acquisition, cable segmentation, vibration extraction, UAV drift suppression, multi-order mode-shape-consistency-constrained fitting, effective vibration length identification, and cable tension calculation and validation. First, a semantic segmentation model is used to extract the cable and marker regions, and the marker centroids are then tracked to generate multi-point displacement time histories. Subsequently, a spectral-morphology-driven adaptive drift separation method, namely SSD–CEEMDAN, is adopted to suppress UAV drift interference while enhancing the distinguishability of dominant spectral peaks. Under the condition that only amplitude information is available, a joint least-squares model constrained by multi-order mode-shape consistency is constructed to identify the effective vibration length of the cable. Field tests on four cables of an actual bridge show that the relative errors of cable tension calculation using the identified effective vibration length are 1.69%, 1.07%, 3.70%, and 2.85%, respectively. Compared with the results obtained using the geometric cable length, the errors were reduced by 7.36, 6.79, 9.18, and 5.88 percentage points, respectively. The results verify the necessity of effective vibration length identification and the engineering feasibility of UAV-based non-contact measurement, providing a new approach for rapid, efficient, and high-accuracy monitoring of bridge cable tension.

title: Lightweight pavement-adaptive TimesNet for road preview information correction in preview model predictive control of active suspensions
abstract: Accurate road-preview information is essential for active suspension systems to achieve effective and high-performance control. However, in real-world driving scenarios, sensor noise and environmental disturbances can cause severe perceptual errors, degrading controller performance. To address this issue, this paper proposes a pavement-adaptive TimesNet, termed P-TimesNet, for road-preview correction in preview model predictive control of active suspensions. The proposed network reconstructs road preview information by fusing biased preview inputs with vehicle dynamic responses. The reconstructed preview sequence is then incorporated into the prediction and optimization process of the model predictive control (MPC) controller, forming an integrated P-TimesNet-MPC framework for active suspension control under perceptual errors. Two typical perceptual error scenarios are constructed to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method: when the road grade perceived by the visual preview is lower than the actual grade, the root mean square values of vehicle body acceleration, suspension dynamic deflection, tire dynamic load, and actuator force are reduced by 4.30 %, 6.36 %, 2.36 % and 2.48 % compared with MPC without information correction; when the perceived road grade is higher than the actual grade, the corresponding reductions are 45.86 %, 62.50 %, 27.55 % and 65.35 %. These results demonstrate that the proposed P-TimesNet-MPC framework effectively improves active suspension performance under road-preview perceptual errors. In addition, experimental results on a quarter-car active suspension platform further verify the effectiveness of the proposed P-TimesNet-MPC under two typical perceptual error scenarios.

title: Tail-dependence-based up-crossing analysis for extreme value prediction
abstract: Extreme value prediction based on up-crossing analysis is widely used for reliability assessment of engineering structures. However, existing approaches for non-Gaussian processes often rely on Gaussian dependence assumptions through memoryless translation models, which may be inadequate when the upper-tail dependence between consecutive observations differs from that of a Gaussian copula. This study develops a tail-dependence-based up-crossing framework for extreme value prediction of non-Gaussian dependent random sequences. The Ledford–Tawn representation is incorporated to characterize the joint upper-tail behavior of consecutive observations, leading to an explicit formulation of the up-crossing rate in terms of the marginal distribution and tail dependence parameters. A sensitivity analysis is further conducted to quantify how variations in tail dependence parameters affect return-level estimates. Numerical examples and measured wind speed records demonstrate that the proposed method accurately reproduces up-crossing rates and extreme-value exceedance probabilities, while revealing the potential bias caused by inappropriate Gaussian dependence assumptions.

title: Strong–weak modal coupling in finite structures with antinode-concentrated resonators
abstract: Dynamic vibration absorbers (DVAs) and locally resonant metamaterials share a common physical foundation: subwavelength resonators coupled to a host structure. The two paradigms, however, have developed along parallel lines. DVA design on continuum hosts traditionally proceeds mode by mode, relying on modal truncation and iterative tuning. Metamaterial design rests on Bloch analysis of infinite periodic arrays, whose assumptions do not transfer to bounded structures with a finite number of resonators. As a result, neither paradigm captures the host–resonator interaction in such finite systems within a single governing relation. In this work, a unified closed-form framework is proposed for bounded continuum hosts equipped with a finite number of antinode-concentrated resonators. The host dynamic stiffness is expressed in a rational closed form, and the infinite modal sum is captured exactly. The optimal placement, tuning, and damping of all resonators follow simultaneously from a single characteristic equation, eliminating the iterative design process of conventional DVA theory. Within this single framework, a strong–weak mode coupling mechanism is identified. It reveals how a small number of finite resonators concentrated at antinodal positions can broaden the practical stopband well beyond the predictions of infinite-periodic metamaterial theory. The framework is validated against finite element analyses and beam experiments across a broadband range. The resulting closed-form expressions provide a practical, metamaterial-inspired design tool for broadband vibration suppression in finite continuum structures.

title: Calibration-light multi-point displacement measurement for railway bridge monitoring via a differential-form projection model
abstract: This study proposes a calibration-light framework for practical multi-point displacement monitoring of railway bridges using a single high-resolution video camera (and, when needed, two synchronized cameras for 3D reconstruction) with a wide-angle lens. The method enables synchronous displacement estimation during train passage without requiring full on-site calibration of external parameters. A differential-form projection model was developed to relate pixel movement to physical displacement increments in a bridge-fixed coordinate system, incorporating perspective-effect compensation via the pixel-to-displacement mapping (Eq. (15)), radial lens distortion correction, and camera-to-target distance estimation. Laboratory experiments demonstrated that the proposed method achieved accurate displacement estimation even under wide-angle imaging. Field applications to four railway bridges demonstrated the method’s practical applicability: Bridge A showed accurate vertical displacement consistent with velocimeter data; Bridge B revealed resonance and vibration modes across three spans; Bridge C demonstrated long-distance measurement (over 100 m) with span-specific modal characteristics; and Bridge D achieved 3D displacement estimation using two synchronized cameras consistent with laser Doppler velocimeter results at the same location. These results highlight the method’s practical applicability for bridge monitoring under diverse structural and environmental conditions.

title: Global optimization with structural reliability analysis methods
abstract: Bayesian theory-based stochastic search methods transform optimization problems into Bayesian updating problems by introducing a parameter T, but optimization performance and efficiency are highly sensitive to T, and its repeated calibration is costly. This paper reformulates the optimization problem as an augmented reliability analysis problem by introducing an auxiliary limit-state function, and proposes a global optimization framework based on structural reliability analysis (GO-SR). In GO-SR, unconstrained optimization problems require one reliability analysis, while constrained problems require two. By linking the auxiliary limit state function with T, a failure probability-based criterion is developed to guide the selection of T, thereby reducing the need for iterative calibration. The resulting framework provides a reliability-sampling interface for global optimization and is broadly compatible with sampling-based reliability simulation methods that can generate representative failure-domain samples, or provide equivalent weighted sample representations. For efficient implementation in this study, an improved adaptive Subset Simulation method with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling is developed. Owing to the high acceptance rates, low sample correlation, and a new adaptive parameter updating scheme for HMC, the method explores feasible and optimal regions more effectively and achieves higher accuracy and stability than traditional MCMC-based Subset Simulation. The framework is validated by two numerical optimization examples and two reliability-based optimization problems involving stochastic dynamic systems.

title: Physics-constrained neural parameter calibration of a Bouc-Wen hysteresis model for bolted joint assemblies
abstract: Bolted joints are characterized by friction-induced hysteresis and response dependence on excitation and tightening conditions, which complicates the calibration of reduced-order nonlinear models. A physics-constrained neural framework is introduced for calibrating a Bouc-Wen model using mean vibration records obtained under varying tightening torques. For each torque, a bounded neural generator proposes admissible model parameters, and a differentiable forward solver integrates displacement, velocity, and the model-internal hysteretic state. Calibration relies exclusively on measured velocity and measurement-derived displacement, while additional excitation levels are reserved for evaluating the torque-specific calibrated ensembles. Multiple independent calibration paths are maintained according to a prescribed convergence criterion and are organized using loss-informed empirical Gibbs weighting. Complete joint parameter vectors are then propagated to obtain time-domain, receptance, and hysteresis summaries. The results indicate torque-conditioned parameter organizations, consistent convergence behavior across most calibration paths, and close agreement with measured resonance locations. Propagation at excitation levels excluded from calibration further demonstrates that the calibrated ensembles can reproduce the principal amplitude-dependent response trends. The proposed framework thus offers a systematic approach for neural parameter calibration and empirical variability propagation, while preserving the prescribed Bouc-Wen dynamics throughout the inverse problem. • Physics-constrained neural calibration of Bouc-Wen bolted-joint parameters. • Mean-response calibrations are performed independently at two torques levels. • The unobserved hysteretic state is integrated using a measured-only loss. • Converged optimization paths form loss-informed joint empirical ensembles. • Frozen ensembles are propagated to amplitudes excluded from calibration.

title: TimeXer-based main bearing temperature prediction and Bayesian fault early warning for offshore wind turbines via transfer learning
abstract: Main bearing failures are a primary driver of offshore wind turbine unplanned downtime, yet data-driven monitoring methods lack cross-turbine generalization and probabilistic fault detection. This study proposes an integrated framework combining the TimeXer model, transfer learning, and a two-stage Bayesian fault early warning system for main bearing temperature prediction. The TimeXer model applies patch-level tokenization to endogenous variables and cross-variable attention to exogenous SCADA inputs, capturing temporal dependencies and inter-variable coupling. Fault early warning sequentially applies a three-sigma threshold, Bayesian posterior probability estimation, and a three-step persistence criterion to suppress false alarms. A two-phase transfer learning protocol adapts the source-domain model to target turbines using limited data. Validated on 41,906 ten-minute SCADA samples from Yangjiang, China, the model achieves R2 = 0.9898, RMSE = 0.3172 °C, and MAE = 0.1636 °C on the 58# 8.3 MW source turbine, surpassing Transformer, LSTM, and XGBoost baselines by up to 42.1% in RMSE. Transfer to the 24# 6.8 MW and 33# 8.3 MW target turbines yields R2 = 0.9851 and 0.9840, with RMSE below the source baseline. The early warning system attains a step-level false alarm rate of 2.1% with a 94.4% detection rate, and component-wise ablation, prior sensitivity analysis and residual normality testing are reported to substantiate each design choice. Normalized error analysis further shows that the lower target-domain RMSE reflects the reduced temperature variability of the target machines rather than an accuracy gain. The framework provides a scalable pathway for offshore wind turbine predictive maintenance.

title: Ultrasonic imaging modalities enabled by laser diffuse ultrasonic phased arrays
abstract: To perform a full matrix capture (FMC) with a laser-induced ultrasonic phased array, both the generation and detection lasers must be independently scanned to acquire signals from all combinations of source and receiver positions. In contrast, a laser diffuse ultrasonic phased array (LDUPA) enables rapid acquisition of an equivalent FMC dataset by scanning only a detection laser while ultrasound is generated from a fixed transducer. This FMC dataset is subsequently reconstructed by applying a diffuse correlation technique to the raw receive dataset. While the reconstructed FMC dataset is used for total focusing method (TFM) images, the early, coherent raw receive dataset can also be used directly to form images via a receive-only focusing method (RFM). This study compares ultrasound images generated from both the raw receive datasets and the reconstructed FMC datasets across various inspection configurations, including different transmitter positions and incident wave angles. Results from simulations and experiments show that the RFM images exhibit excellent detection capability within the incident wave’s illumination area, providing 2–5 dB higher signal to peak noise ratio compared to TFM images. In contrast, TFM images demonstrate good detection across the entire receiver aperture. The results also highlight the flexibility in transmitter positioning and incident wave angle, facilitating inspections that can adapt to accessibility constraints.

title: Low-frequency broadband acoustic transmission through air–water interface using sonic black hole-based metasurface
abstract: Acoustic transmission across the air–water interface is limited by the extreme impedance mismatch between two media. Although recent acoustic metamaterials have enabled cross-interface transmission, their performance is typically restricted to high frequencies or narrow bandwidths. To address this challenge, we propose a sonic black hole (SBH) metasurface for compact, low-frequency, and broadband acoustic transmission across the air–water interface. A transfer-matrix method and finite-element simulations are developed to analyze the transmission characteristics and underlying mechanism. The results show that the metasurface substantially enhances transmission and reduces the transmission loss of the bare interface over a broad low-frequency band. In particular, a pronounced transmission band is predicted near 870 Hz, while the thickness is only 0.0418 m, corresponding to λ/9.34 in air. An effective-parameter inversion is introduced to reveal continuous impedance variation and strong terminal pressure amplification through slow-wave compression. Thermoviscous analysis indicates that dissipation remains well controlled. Experiments validate this concept, showing a maximum transmitted-level enhancement of 18.7 dB at 1070 Hz and significant transmission from 549 to 1319 Hz. These results demonstrate that SBH metasurface provides a feasible route for compact, low-frequency, and broadband acoustic air–water transmission, with potential applications in cross-medium communication, sensing, and energy transfer.

title: A geometric data augmentation and mechanism modeling framework for class-imbalanced wind turbine fault diagnosis
abstract: With the growing deployment of wind energy, reliable fault diagnosis of wind turbines (WTs) is increasingly important for sustainable operation and maintenance. However, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system data are often characterized by severe class imbalance and complex correlations among multi-source features, which hinder accurate fault recognition. To address these challenges, this study proposes a geometric visibility augmentation-mechanism supervision graph (GVA-MSG) framework for imbalanced fault diagnosis of WTs. At the data level, GVA integrates visibility-based neighbor filtering, Voronoi-based boundary constraints, and density-adaptive directional filling into the synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) to generate minority samples within class manifolds and alleviate imbalance. At the model level, MSG captures temporal dependencies and introduces mechanism supervision based on the wind speed-power relationship. A mechanistic consistency loss aligns model decisions with physical principles, while a latent-space graph adaptively learns cross-channel feature relationships for fault recognition. Comparative, ablation, and generalization experiments are conducted on real SCADA datasets. GVA-MSG achieves a Macro-Accuracy, Macro-F1, and Macro-Gmean of 98.57 %, 96.42 %, and 97.75 %, respectively. Compared with the best-performing data generation baseline, these metrics improve by 1.29, 3.55, and 2.94 percentage points; compared with the best-performing diagnostic baseline, they improve by 0.17, 0.44, and 0.28 percentage points. These results demonstrate that GVA-MSG improves class balance, the quality of generated samples, and mechanism-supervised feature characterization. Moreover, the cross-wind-farm validation results indicate that GVA-MSG maintains stable performance under the tested distribution shifts, demonstrating promising transfer stability and application potential under the current validation conditions.

title: Mechanism-data hybrid-driven model for spatial thermal error prediction of horizontal machining center
abstract: Thermal error is one of the main factors affecting the machining accuracy of machine tools. Existing thermal error prediction methods mainly focus on local components and have limited ability to characterize spatial thermal errors (STE) across the machining space. To address this problem, a mechanism-data hybrid-driven model, named thermal perception physics-constrained xRFM (TPC-xRFM), is proposed for spatial thermal error prediction of machine tools. A transient finite element model (FEM) is first established to obtain the temperature field and thermal deformation field of the machine tool, and the simulated temperature data are fused with measured data to provide mechanism-based prior information for model training. A temperature-weighting strategy based on the average gradient outer product (AGOP) is then introduced to identify and enhance thermally sensitive variables, while thermal error consistency and delay constraints are incorporated to improve physical consistency and temporal stability. In addition, a rapid STE measurement scheme is designed to acquire multi-position thermal errors in the machining space. Experimental results show that TPC-xRFM significantly outperforms the baseline models in different directions, providing an effective and interpretable solution for spatial thermal error prediction of machine tools.

title: Implementation of multimodal laser ultrasonic F-SAFT algorithm for cylinders based on the cylindrical phase shift migration theory
abstract: Ultrasonic methods are widely used in industry to ensure the reliable operation of cylindrical components. Traditional transducers need special designs to adapt to curved geometries. In contrast, laser ultrasonic (LU) method is well-suited for this scenario because it enables remote, noncontact evaluation of components with complex geometries. To further enhance defect detectability, the frequency domain synthetic aperture focusing technique (F-SAFT) is introduced to provide intuitive defect visualization. In this study, cylindrical phase shift migration (CPSM) method, a form of F-SAFT, is implemented and systematically evaluated for LU inspection of small internal defects in high curvature cylinders. High-frequency, broadband, and multimodal ultrasonic signals are used for CPSM imaging, providing mutual validation of the defect indication from LL and SS wave reconstructed results. Polynomial fitting and adjacent wave subtraction are used to suppress the strong thermoelastic displacement produced by co-located pump and probe beams and extract weak defect echoes for CPSM imaging. The influences of practical spatial separation between the pump and probe beams are also systematically analyzed. Beam separation reduces thermoelastic interference but violates the co-located excitation and reception assumption of CPSM, causing a predictable angular shift of approximately half the separation angle. The radial position remains nearly unchanged, although image distortion increases with separation. Finite element simulation and real LU experimental data are used to validate the reliability of the proposed imaging method. Images are reconstructed for the minimum tested defect diameters of 0.2 mm in simulation and 0.6 mm in experiment. Across the tested configurations, the maximum absolute errors in buried depth are 5.60% in simulation and 4.00% in experiment.
keywords: Frequency domain synthetic aperture focusing technique (F-SAFT)

title: Feature–label similarity-aware hypergraph attention network: A semi-supervised fault diagnosis method for machinery under extremely low label rate scenarios
abstract: Label propagation algorithms (LPAs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) are semi-supervised learning models that have yielded satisfactory results in machinery fault diagnosis under limited labeled data conditions. However, LPAs consider only label similarity, while GNNs primarily focus on feature similarity, and both encode pairwise connections that inherently fail to capture high-order correlations, consequently limiting the ability to make full use of scarce labeled and massive unlabeled data. To address the above limitations, this paper proposes a novel semi-supervised learning model, named feature–label similarity-aware hypergraph attention network, to jointly model high-order feature and label similarities for machinery fault diagnosis under extremely low label rate scenarios. Firstly, a hypergraph of all samples is constructed to encode their high-order correlations beyond pairwise connections. Then, a hypergraph attention network is constructed, in which a cross-attention mechanism is employed to adaptively learn the importance weights of node–hyperedge interactions, facilitating propagation and aggregation of class-specific features along hyperedges from both labeled and unlabeled samples. Subsequently, a hypergraph LPA is integrated into the proposed framework, propagating label information from labeled samples to their neighbors, to fully exploit scarce label information. Finally, the semi-supervised fault diagnosis model is jointly optimized by imposing supervised constraints on classifier predictions and propagated labels for labeled samples, along with a consistency constraint between them for unlabeled samples. Experimental results on three machinery fault diagnosis datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior diagnostic accuracy compared with the state-of-the-art approaches, especially when the label rate is as low as 1 %. The related code was released at https://github.com/yushi1006/FLSHGAT-for-semi-supervised-fault-diagnosis.

title: Online unbalance vibration suppression of large rotating machinery using a pneumatic liquid automatic balancing system with adaptive sealing
abstract: Traditional offline dynamic balancing techniques can no longer satisfy the vibration suppression requirements of large rotating equipment because of the required shutdown, long balancing cycles, and limited balancing accuracy. Therefore, a pneumatic liquid automatic balancing system with adaptive sealing (PLABS-AS) is proposed and developed, capable of performing online rotor unbalance compensation during operation. First, based on a multi-degree-of-freedom rotor dynamic model, the steady-state frequency-domain response of the rotor system considering compensating forces was derived, thereby elucidating the automatic balancing mechanism. Furthermore, to address the long-interval intermittent operating characteristics of the actuator, an adaptive sealing mechanism was developed. The mechanism adaptively adjusts the contact state of the sealing ring, allowing it to remain disengaged from the rotor during idle periods, thereby achieving nearly zero wear and significantly extending its service life. A coupled mathematical model describing the force–clearance–leakage behavior of the sealing ring was established and solved using a two-level nested iterative algorithm. Sealing performance tests demonstrated that, under a gas injection pressure of 0.5 MPa and a sealing back pressure of 0.15 MPa, the air-chamber pressure reached at least 0.23 MPa, thereby meeting the pressure requirement for balancing-fluid transfer. The proposed system was successfully implemented in a forced-draft fan of a 600 MW power generation unit. Within approximately 33 s, the unbalance vibration was reduced from 0.56 mm/s to 0.13 mm/s, corresponding to a 76.8% reduction. These results demonstrate the excellent balancing performance, rapid response, and engineering applicability of the proposed system, providing a reliable technical solution for the online automatic balancing of large rotating equipment.

title: A novel low-complexity amplitude estimation ESPRIT algorithm for blade feature parameter identification based on BTT signals
abstract: Blades, as critical components in rotating machinery, play a vital role in ensuring stable operation, making condition monitoring imperative. Blade Tip Timing (BTT), an advanced non-contact measurement technique, enables simultaneous health monitoring of all blades. However, BTT suffers from severe under-sampling issues. ESPRIT, as a signal subspace algorithm, can solve this problem to a certain extent by utilizing the rotational invariance of the signal subspace. However, the recognition effect of feature parameters is easily affected by noise and sensor angles, and the vibration amplitude cannot be recognized. To address the aforementioned issues, this paper proposes a novel low-complexity amplitude estimation ESPRIT algorithm for blade feature parameter identification based on BTT signals, termed AE-ESPRIT. Firstly, the single sensor signal is analyzed and smoothed to ensure that the frequency can be directly extracted from the frequency domain; Secondly, a special unitary matrix is proposed to directly process real valued signals, reducing the computational complexity of recognition and ensuring reliable extraction of amplitude signals; Finally, based on subspace rotation invariance, the blade feature parameters are accurately identified by combining the fuzzy frequency under dual sensors and the precise aliasing frequency under single sensor. The efficacy and robustness of the AE-ESPRIT are demonstrated through both numerical simulations and experimental tests on rotating test rig.

title: Broadband performance optimization of arrayed piezoelectric energy harvesters via inclination-angle tuning of mass blocks
abstract: Adjusting the mass-block inclination angle can improve the power generation performance of an arrayed piezoelectric energy harvester (APEH). However, determining how to adjust the mass-block inclination angle for different frequency bands to achieve optimal power generation performance remains a challenge. To address this issue, a mass-block inclination-angle optimization method is proposed. By changing the positions of the mass blocks along the cantilever beams, the resonance frequencies of the APEH are redistributed to maximize its power generation performance. First, a bidirectionally coupled electromechanical theoretical model accounting for variations in the mass-block inclination angle was established, and the relationships among the inclination angle, resonance frequencies, and output power were analyzed. Second, considering the dynamic variation characteristics of excitation frequencies in practical environments, a two-stage mass-block inclination-angle optimization algorithm was proposed, together with a performance evaluation metric based on the target band power area. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed method was validated through finite-element simulations and experiments. The results demonstrate that appropriate adjustment of the mass-block inclination angle can effectively improve the power generation performance of the APEH and that an optimal inclination angle exists for each excitation frequency band. Compared with the APEH at a mass block inclination angle of 0°, the proposed method improves the power generation performance by 0.25-19.43 times. Furthermore, the method can be readily extended to APEH with different numbers of beams, providing a new approach for improving the broadband performance of APEH.

title: A nonlinear transient dynamic model for the shaft system of mixed-flow pumps integrating transient head theory: a speed conversion case
abstract: To address the strongly nonlinear and nonstationary characteristics of shaft vibration (SV) observed in mixed-flow pump (MFP) during speed conversion, this study investigates the transient dynamic mechanisms governing the rotor system response. A shaft system dynamic model (SSDM) is established using the lumped parameter method, in which the axial hydraulic thrust (AHT) is dynamically corrected by incorporating transient head (TH) theoretical calculation model (THTCM). The differential equations of motion are solved using nonlinear numerical methods, and the model is systematically validated against experimental data. The results indicate that the proposed THTCM can effectively describe the dynamic evolution of TH during speed conversion process, with good agreement between calculated and experimental results. Deviations in both speed rise and speed drop processes are controlled within ± 10 %. The established SSDM successfully reproduces the main characteristics of SV in both the time and frequency domains. Good consistency is achieved between the simulated and experimental testing signals in terms of amplitude levels and the evolution of the dominant frequency. The discrepancies remain within reasonable limits under both steady-state and transient operating conditions. Comparative analyses performed with and without the proposed THTCM-corrected AHT demonstrate that the introduction of AHT into the SSDM reduces the prediction error by 1.17 %-25.62 % under different speed conversion conditions, thereby improving the simulation accuracy of transient SV responses. A representative comparison with a fluid structure interaction model based on the finite element method indicates that the proposed SSDM involves a substantially smaller computational scale and has the potential to support efficient evaluation of transient SV responses. The findings provide reliable theoretical support for SV mechanism analysis and operational optimization of MFPs under transient conditions.

title: A rotor dynamic balancing method without trial weights based on multi-sensor feature fusion with an attention mechanism
abstract: Accurate identification of unbalance parameters lies at the core of rotor dynamic balancing technology. In this paper, a deep learning approach is integrated with rotor dynamic balancing theory, and a multi-sensor feature fusion dynamic balancing method without trial weights based on the attention mechanism is proposed. First, considering the unique nature of the dynamic balancing process, a rotor model with varying unbalance parameters was established, and the dataset for model training was augmented by adding bandpass noise. Subsequently, a neural network model for unbalance identification based on the multi-head attention mechanism was designed, and ablation experiments were conducted to verify its superiority over single-sensor models and the feature fusion model without attention. Finally, both a finite element simulation model and an experimental model of a triple-disk rotor system were established for dynamic balancing validation. The simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed dynamic balancing method can substantially reduce the vibration amplitudes of the rotor across all critical speed regions. Moreover, compared with the influence coefficient method (ICM), the proposed method requires only a single run-up process to complete the dynamic balancing procedure, significantly improving the balancing efficiency and achieving superior balancing performance across all critical speed regions.

title: A new partitioned component mode synthesis via variable condensation
abstract: In dual assembly component mode synthesis, interconnecting forces between substructures are represented by Lagrange multipliers that are augmented to the displacement vector as additional variables. Compared with the primal assembly, this force-based coupling is better suited to non-matching interfaces and yields the interconnecting forces explicitly. However, this augmentation entails additional degrees of freedom (DOFs), leading to a null space in the system matrix. Furthermore, such a null space has the potential to induce numerical instability. To eliminate these augmented DOFs, this study adopts the variable condensation originally developed for the displacement-partitioned equation of motion and applies it within flexibility-based component mode synthesis, condensing the Lagrange multipliers and frame nodes, thereby removing the null space they introduce and constructing a numerically stable model. Unlike conventional interface reduction methods, which improve compactness at the expense of accuracy, the proposed condensation markedly reduces the model size while retaining accuracy comparable to, or marginally better than, that of the original model. Consequently, the method substantially enhances numerical robustness and compactness without compromising accuracy. An iterative extension is also introduced to account for higher-order dynamic effects, yielding additional accuracy improvements while preserving model compactness. The proposed models are verified through a series of plate examples in terms of the eigenfrequency accuracy, the mode shape consistency, and the computational cost.

title: Local linearization modeling and coefficients identification of five-axis milling force considering size effect and radial runout
abstract: In the five-axis machining of complex curved surfaces, the cutter-workpiece engagement geometry fluctuates dramatically with the change of cutting parameters, making it difficult for traditional mechanical models to achieve a balance between the identification efficiency and the real-time prediction accuracy. To address this issue, a local linearized milling force model and its corresponding milling force coefficients identification method are proposed, while also taking into account the size effect and radial runout. By parameterizing the instantaneous undeformed chip thickness and the engagement state between the cutter and the workpiece, a five-axis milling force parametric model related to parameters such as the tool orientation, radial runout, and feed rate was established. By extending the size effect law of the single edge element to the entire cutting edge, and statistically describing the mapping relationship between the equivalent force coefficient of the cutting edge and the average undeformed chip thickness, a local linearized five-axis machining force model was further obtained. In this model, the milling force was explicitly expressed as a function of the cutting force coefficient, radial runout and geometric operator. The latter (geometric operator) is determined by the distribution of the cutting edge on the cutter surface and is modeled as a parameter of the tool rotation angle. The proposed method can achieve linear modeling of milling force under different rotation angles. With a small amount of monitoring data, the model could support online updates of force coefficients and radial runout parameters, effectively reducing the prediction errors caused by changes in cutting parameters and cutter wear. Milling experiments were conducted with different tool orientations, different rotational speeds, and different feed rates. The experimental results showed that the prediction error of the proposed method was less than 9.2 %, which was 6.6 % lower than that of the method without considering the time variation coefficient. This study lays the foundation for intelligent process optimization in aerospace manufacturing and online monitoring of advanced milling equipment based on digital twins.

title: A mag-boost-enabled vibration energy harvester for argo-like ocean floats under low-frequency and low-acceleration excitations
abstract: Argo-like floats are important mobile platforms for long-term ocean observation, yet their endurance is fundamentally constrained by limited onboard energy. Harvesting wave-induced vibration offers a potential route toward sustainable power supply, but the available input is typically characterized by ultra-low-frequency, low-acceleration, and weak vertical motion, which makes efficient energy harvesting particularly challenging. To address this issue, this work proposes a Mag-Boost-enabled vibration energy harvester (MB-VEH). The device employs a single-degree-of-freedom spring-mass system to capture weak wave-induced vertical vibration of the float and utilizes non-contact magnetic coupling to efficiently convert low-frequency mechanical input into high-frequency motion of the generating unit. Experiments show that the MB-VEH operates effectively at 0.5–1 Hz and 0.18–0.22 g, boosting a 0.5 Hz input to power magnet (PM) oscillations above 20 Hz. Under 0.5 Hz and 0.2 g excitation, the MB-VEH achieves a maximum peak power of 710 mW at 60 Ω and a maximum average power of 12.5 mW at 150 Ω. Moreover, within 10 h, the MB-VEH delivers 118 mWh to a 350 mAh lithium battery, enabling intermittent operation of a self-powered wireless ocean monitoring system and demonstrating its feasibility for powering sensing nodes on marine floats. This work provides a new route toward long-term self-powered operation of Argo-like floats under ultra-low-frequency and low-acceleration wave-induced vibration, and offers useful insight into efficient energy harvesting and system integration under weak-vibration conditions.

title: A general closed-form second-moment framework for probabilistic updating of damped MDOF systems
abstract: Probabilistic updating of damped structural systems lacks closed-form expressions for operator statistics, leaving iterative numerical methods or implicit auxiliary variable formulations that obscure analytical uncertainty propagation. This work develops a closed-form second-moment framework for simultaneous updating of mass, damping, and stiffness matrices under combined eigenvalue, eigenvector, and modal damping uncertainty, a combination for which explicit operator statistics were previously unavailable. The formulation exploits a sequential property of weighted Frobenius norm minimisation subject to modal orthogonality constraints, whereby the three updates are obtained in three successive convex steps. Stiffness updating depends only on measured frequencies, damping updating depends only on measured modal damping, and mass updating is deduced from the measured modal mass matrix through Berman’s incomplete-mode correction. Gaussian moment closures give exact mean operators, and Fréchet derivative-based perturbation expansions give Kronecker-structured sensitivity matrices that map modal uncertainty to physical-space operator covariance without auxiliary variables or nonlinear solvers. The cross-covariances between the identified modal quantities are retained throughout. Numerical verification on a non-proportionally damped benchmark confirms close analytical-Monte Carlo agreement for mean and covariance predictions, with cross-correlation inclusion yielding order-of-magnitude improvement over independence assumptions.
