Their relevance is assessed through a finite element model formulated within an explicit dynamic framework, accounting for geometric nonlinearities and for hysteretic material behavior via a visco-elasto-plastic constitutive law. Three configurations with different boundary and initial conditions are investigated, while focusing on responses dominated by the first vibration mode. The proposed energy-based damping measures are systematically compared with the structural damping ratio obtained from the logarithmic decrement. The close agreement observed between these approaches confirms the consistency of the proposed energy-based identification. A parametric study is then conducted to examine the influence of cable tension and added mass on the natural frequency and dynamic damping of the structure, in connection with stiffness and dissipation mechanisms identified at the material scale. Finally, the methodology is extended to the second vibration mode, thereby demonstrating its applicability beyond first-mode-dominated responses.

title: Local spectral submanifold modeling of fundamental and higher-order periodic responses in flexible bevel gear dynamical systems
abstract: Driven by time-varying mesh parameters and backlash nonlinearity, gear systems exhibit multi-periodic responses. However, the high dimensionality of full-order models impedes efficient local-branch tracking and dynamical-structure identification. A local spectral submanifold (SSM) framework is therefore proposed for flexible gear systems. Initially, the flexibility of shaft and gear is characterized using Timoshenko beam theory and component mode synthesis (CMS). A flexible bevel gear model is formulated by coupling these substructures with bearing elements and nonlinear mesh elements incorporating time-varying mesh stiffness, transmission error, and backlash. Through nonlinear frequency sweeps, bifurcation analysis, and Poincaré sections, 1 T, 2 T, and 3 T periodic branches and local modeling intervals are identified, where T denotes the meshing period. Subsequently, a unified non-autonomous state-space interface is constructed between the dynamic model and local SSM. Local trial spaces and closure models are then established for 1 T responses with one recurring Poincaré point, 2 T responses with two alternating points, and 3 T responses with a three-point cycle. Results indicate that all models satisfy periodic closure conditions and yield locally stable periodic solutions, with forward and backward sweeps exhibiting excellent agreement. The 2 T and 3 T models preserve their alternating and cyclic state sequences. Finally, the approach is validated via rolling inspection, modal and gearbox vibration tests. The study reveals that as periodic order increases, local SSM modeling shifts from single-section parameterization to multi-phase coordination, providing a methodological foundation for low-dimensional characterization and stable tracking of multi-periodic branches in flexible gear dynamics.

title: Honeycomb metamaterial panel with core grid of wire-masses resonators for tuneable vibration and sound radiation bandgap
abstract: Controlling flexural vibrations and sound radiation in thin-walled structures subjected to time-varying tonal excitations remains a major engineering challenge. While acoustic metamaterials have demonstrated significant potential for vibration attenuation, most tuneable designs rely on complex architectures that hinder practical implementation. This study proposes a lightweight composite panel integrating a simple honeycomb-core elastic metamaterial capable of generating a continuously tuneable flexural vibration bandgap. The proposed concept consists of a tensioned wire routed in a continuous zigzag path through the honeycomb cells, with concentrated masses attached at the centre of each cell. Each wire–mass subsystem acts as a base-excited resonator whose natural frequency is controlled by the wire tension. The resulting periodic array of identical resonators enables continuous tuning of the resonance frequency and the associated flexural vibration stopband without modifying the structural layout. The design methodology is presented and validated through simulations and experimental testing of a prototype panel. The results demonstrate the formation of both flexural vibration and sound radiation stopband with maximum attenuations of 25 dB and 20 dB respectively. By varying the wire tension, the stopband can be shifted over a frequency range of approximately 300 Hz, allowing adaptive suppression of time-varying tonal disturbances. The proposed metamaterial combines structural simplicity, low mass, ease of implementation, and robust, broadband-tuneable dynamic behaviour, providing an effective strategy for adaptive vibration and noise control in lightweight engineering structures operating under variable excitation conditions, including aerospace, automotive, marine, and industrial applications.

title: Impact damage localization in woven CFRP laminates using laser-ultrasonic wavefields and a masked spatiotemporal reconstruction network
abstract: Barely visible impact damage (BVID) can compromise the structural integrity and service reliability of composite structures. Laser-ultrasonic full-wavefield analysis provides an effective nondestructive evaluation approach for such damage, as it can capture the spatiotemporal evolution of guided-wave propagation. However, existing data-driven wavefield analysis methods generally rely on costly damage annotations and are often limited to two-dimensional spatial image analysis, thereby insufficiently exploiting the spatiotemporal information contained in laser-ultrasonic wavefields. To address these limitations, this study proposes a self-supervised three-dimensional spatiotemporal anomaly localization method for impact damage detection in woven carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) laminates. The proposed method uses only undamaged wavefield data during training. Random spatiotemporal masking is applied to local wavefield clips, and a masked 3D reconstruction network is trained to learn the normal spatiotemporal propagation patterns of guided waves. During testing, anomaly heatmaps are generated through multiple random masked reconstructions of the inspected wavefield and spatiotemporal aggregation of the resulting reconstruction residuals, thereby characterizing local scattering that deviates from normal propagation patterns and enabling effective damage localization. Experimental results on woven CFRP specimens with single and multiple impact damage sites demonstrate that the proposed method can generate concentrated damage-related anomaly responses for most damage sites. Compared to conventional energy imaging techniques, the proposed method presents more distinct damage-related hotspots and does not produce obvious concentrated damage-like responses on the undamaged specimen. These results suggest that self-supervised spatiotemporal reconstruction based on normal wavefield learning provides a feasible framework for label-free laser-ultrasonic localization of impact damage in composite laminates.

title: A multimodal fusion network guided by environmental semantics for reconstructing missing bridge strain trends
abstract: Long term bridge strain trends describe the gradual evolution of structural responses under environmental actions and operational loads, providing important information for structural health monitoring and condition assessment. However, communication interruptions, sensor abnormalities, and unstable data transmission can lead to missing strain data, which affects the completeness of monitoring records and the reliability of subsequent analysis. This study proposes an environmental semantics-guided multimodal fusion network for reconstructing missing bridge strain trends. The network mainly consists of an environmental semantic modulation module and a temporal reconstruction module. The environmental semantic modulation module encodes environmental textual descriptions into semantic representations and introduces environmental contextual information through feature-wise semantic modulation. The temporal reconstruction module uses a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN) to extract local trend variation features and a modified Transformer encoder to model long-range temporal dependencies, enabling environment-aware strain trend reconstruction. Based on strain data obtained from a real bridge field monitoring experiment, this study constructs several typical missing scenarios and validates the proposed method through comparison with multiple baseline methods. The results show that the proposed model can effectively recover the original strain trends under different missing conditions and outperforms the compared methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy and robustness. Ablation experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of the environmental semantic modulation and temporal reconstruction modules.

title: Vibration signal AM-FM models and spectral characteristics for rotate vector reducer fault diagnosis: an insight into multiple modulations and fault feature analysis
abstract: Rotate vector (RV) reducers need to undertake cyclic heavy load, and therefore are prone to faults. However, they feature highly intricate kinematics, due to their complex structure, simultaneous multiple point contacts and coupled spin–revolution of cycloidal and planetary gear stages. This leads to high vibration complexity, and poses a great challenge to vibration based fault diagnosis. To address the above issue, we derive the fault characteristic frequency equations for the main components in both cycloidal and planetary gear stages, including the sun, planets, cycloids and pinwheel. Considering the multiple modulation effects on meshing vibration (including the amplitude modulation and frequency modulation effects due to localized fault, and the extra amplitude modulation effects caused by time-varying measurement angle and vibration transfer path), we establish analytical vibration signal models for the localized fault case of each main component. These analytical signal models provide an insight into the multiple modulation nature of vibrations, and justify the presence of gear rotating and fault characteristic frequencies in vibrations from kinetics perspective. In order to extract fault symptoms from multiple modulation signals, we further derive the explicit equations of Fourier and envelope spectra, thus revealing the fault vibration characteristics explicitly. Such explicit spectral signatures provide a guidance for vibration based fault diagnosis. The above theoretical derivations are validated experimentally. The localized fault of both cycloidal and planetary gear stages is successfully diagnosed.

title: Cost-sensitive active learning for rotating machinery fault diagnosis under data imbalance
abstract: Data-driven fault diagnosis has become an important approach for ensuring the reliability and safety of rotating machinery. However, practical deployment is often hindered by severe data imbalance and label scarcity. Active learning (AL) mitigates label scarcity by selecting the most informative samples for annotation to improve model performance. Nevertheless, conventional AL strategies typically optimize for overall accuracy and treat all misclassifications equally. Consequently, they fail to account for the asymmetric operational costs of diagnostic errors, particularly the greater losses caused by missed detections and severity underestimation. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a cost-sensitive active learning (CS-AL) framework tailored for highly imbalanced fault distributions. In this framework, raw vibration signals are first transformed into two-dimensional time–frequency representations via continuous wavelet transform (CWT). A Bayesian convolutional neural network, integrated with a convolutional block attention module, is developed to extract fault-sensitive features, while epistemic uncertainty is quantified through Monte Carlo (MC) dropout. To explicitly penalize high-risk errors during sample selection, an asymmetric diagnostic cost matrix is constructed to formulate a cost-sensitive acquisition score based on the expected pairwise misclassification cost. To optimize annotation efficiency, a diversity-aware clustering mechanism selects representative prototypes from this high-risk candidate pool. Experimental validations on the CWRU bearing and MCC5-THU gearbox datasets demonstrate that the CS-AL framework achieves enhanced diagnostic performance and significantly reduces high-cost misclassification risks compared to representative AL baselines. The results confirm the effectiveness of CS-AL in accurately allocating limited labeling resources to rare, safety-critical faults while minimizing total operational risk under imbalanced conditions.

title: Adaptive and uncertainty-aware surrogate modeling for reliability analysis of nonlinear dynamic systems
abstract: Reliability analysis of nonlinear inelastic dynamic systems under uncertainty remains a critical challenge, owing to the path-dependent, high-dimensional nature of the problem. To this end, this paper proposes an adaptive and uncertainty-aware surrogate modeling framework comprising three synergistic components. The first component is the aLSTM–SNGP surrogate model, an uncertainty-aware surrogate for nonlinear dynamic systems that integrates an attention-enhanced LSTM (aLSTM) encoder with a Spectral-normalized Neural Gaussian Process (SNGP) predictor, jointly optimized through end-to-end co-training. The aLSTM encoder processes excitation sequences and system parameters together, capturing temporal dependencies while implicitly reducing dimensionality; the SNGP predictor provides scalable uncertainty-aware prediction through random Fourier feature approximation. The second component develops two surrogate-based failure probability estimation methods: Method I (aLSTM-SNGP-MCS) based on direct Monte Carlo simulation, and Method II (aLSTM-SNGP-IS) based on importance sampling with an adaptively constructed proposal density that concentrates sampling effort in failure-prone regions. The third component is an adaptive exploration–exploitation refinement strategy that iteratively refines the surrogate model by combining active learning with an alternating training scheme of full training and local fine-tuning. The framework is validated under stochastic seismic excitations through two examples: a numerical example based on a six-story nonlinear inelastic shear building model with Bouc-Wen hysteresis, and a practical engineering example based on a nine-story SAC steel frame represented by a nonlinear finite element model. Results demonstrate that both methods yield accurate failure probability estimates while significantly reducing the number of evaluations to the simulation model relative to crude Monte Carlo simulation, with Method II outperforming Method I.

title: Modeling of AMR magnetic encoder signals for instantaneous angular speed and vibration separation
abstract: Magnetic encoder signals are susceptible to distortions caused by small transverse vibrations and dynamic misalignments, particularly in off-shaft configurations. A novel anisotropic magnetoresistive (AMR) encoder coupling model is established, capturing both torsional and transverse displacements to reveal how dynamic vibrations affect signal formation. Based on this model, a dual-sensor reconstruction method is developed to estimate instantaneous angular speed (IAS) and transverse vibration. Simulation and experimental validation under varying encoder resolutions and multi-source vibration conditions confirm the method’s robustness and high accuracy, achieving high correlation coefficients and low normalized root mean square error (NRMSE). The approach enables accurate IAS measurement with fewer sensors and facilitates its integration into practical condition monitoring systems.

title: Influence of localized failures on the vibration characteristics of gear-rotor-bearing system considering gear lead crown relief
abstract: The Gear-Rotor-Bearing (GRB) system plays a critical role in the transmission chains of high-end equipment systems. However, existing research on failure mechanisms tends to neglect the intrinsic coupling effects of key components, leading to inaccuracies in failure modeling and dynamic response prediction. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel Analytical-Finite Element Method (AFEM)-based approach for calculating the Time-Varying Meshing Stiffness (TVMS) of gear pair with spalling faults and lead crown relief. Meanwhile, a 32-Degree-of-Freedom (DOF) closed-loop iterative dynamic model is proposed, incorporating nonlinear factors such as time-varying backlash and rotor misalignment. This aims to capture the bidirectional coupling mechanism between localized bearing failures and gear surface load distribution. The study reveals the internal load transfer and contact stress variation law within the GRB system under localized failure, providing a theoretical foundation for analyzing failure mechanisms and vibration control in complex transmission systems.

title: Hybrid testing of wind turbine components using Kane’s method
abstract: Hybrid testing combines numerical simulations with physical experiments to evaluate large mechanical systems, such as wind turbines, that are impractical to test at full scale. While hybrid testing has been widely applied in structural dynamics, its extension to complex multibody dynamic systems remains challenging due to nonlinear kinematics and strongly coupled degrees of freedom. Although Kane’s method underpins widely used wind turbine simulation tools, hybrid testing frameworks that directly integrate Kane-based multibody formulations and interface force coupling remain largely unexplored. Here, a stepwise hybrid testing framework is presented in which the equations of motion are formulated using Kane’s method, enabling a systematic treatment of multibody dynamics within hybrid testing. Interface forces are identified from free-body diagrams and incorporated into the equations of motion through the principle of virtual power, allowing consistent coupling between numerical and physical substructures. The framework is demonstrated in a pseudo-dynamic hybrid test of a 13-degree-of-freedom simplified wind turbine rotor system, where a pitch bearing is tested as a physical substructure under force-controlled bi-axial bending and displacement-controlled pitch rotation. A virtual hybrid test validates the formulation and coordination algorithm, while the physical hybrid test demonstrates stable mixed-mode coupling under experimental feedback. The results show that the framework can couple a Kane-based multibody model with a physical wind turbine component and capture its influence on the system-level rotor response.

title: Control-Based Continuation for self-oscillating systems: Application to flow induced vibrations
abstract: An enhanced version of Control-Based Continuation (CBC) is proposed to carry out experimental continuation on self-sustained systems, whose working frequency is not known a priori . Our approach combines three main stages: an online frequency tracking algorithm using an embedded phase-locked loop, an online noninvasive CBC stabilization loop using adaptive filters, and a derivative free arc continuation algorithm. As a proof of concept, it is implemented to study an elementary aero-vibro-acoustical model of buzzing lips that exhibits self-sustained oscillations with a wide range of fundamental frequency. The model relies on interactions between an acoustical resonator (the air column) and an oscillating valve (the lips) through a nonlinear flow. The Control-Based Continuation is implemented without taking advantage of the modeling equations, mimicking a real experiment. This results in a pseudo-experimental bifurcation diagram, showing strong accordance with virtual open-loop testing and numerical continuation, which proves robustness of our method.

title: Adaptive backstepping-based swing suppression control for tower crane with obstacle avoidance
abstract: Obstacle avoidance in tower cranes is a significant challenge due to underactuation, strong nonlinearities, and uncertain dynamics. To address this challenge, an adaptive backstepping-based obstacle-avoidance control method is proposed for tower crane systems. The proposed control method simultaneously addresses obstacle avoidance, positioning overshoot constraint, payload swing suppression, and uncertainty compensation. Specifically, a locally activated obstacle-avoidance barrier term that accounts for the payload swing envelope is first incorporated into the controller to achieve closed-loop obstacle avoidance. Next, based on the activation state of the obstacle-avoidance term, a dynamic scheduling mechanism coordinates obstacle avoidance with positioning overshoot constraints. Then, by exploiting the inherent dynamic coupling of the tower crane, the payload swing angular velocities are fed back into the actuated channels to construct a damping term for swing suppression. Furthermore, a generalized fuzzy hyperbolic model is introduced to compensate for lumped uncertainties, including uncertainties in payload mass, rope length, and friction. The stability and asymptotic convergence of the proposed control system are theoretically proven using Lyapunov stability theory. Finally, experimental results on a tower crane prototype demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method over comparative approaches in positioning, payload swing suppression, and obstacle avoidance.

title: A multiband magnetic quasi-zero-stiffness vibration isolator-energy harvester
abstract: Most reported vibration-isolation energy-harvesting devices remain constrained by narrow harvesting bandwidths and poor alignment between the energy-harvesting and vibration-isolation regions. To address this issue, this paper proposes a multiband magnetic quasi-zero-stiffness vibration isolator-energy harvester (MB-MQZSI-EH), which enables multiband energy harvesting and dual-functional performance in the middle-frequency band. Quasi-zero stiffness is realized through repulsive magnetic interaction, while multiband harvesting is achieved through the coordinated responses of isolation and absorber PZT cantilevers. An electromechanically coupled model is established using Lagrange’s method and solved by the harmonic balance method. The influences of structural, damping, and electrical parameters are analyzed, and a prototype is fabricated for experimental validation. The results show that the MB-MQZSI-EH achieved three distinct energy-harvesting bands while maintaining effective vibration isolation in the middle-frequency band. The maximum output power reached 1.12 mW, and the low-frequency output power was improved by 26.7% compared with the MQZSI-EH. The isolation onset frequency was reduced to 7.27 Hz, which was 48.2% lower than that of the linear isolator. The harvested energy was also sufficient to power a low-power temperature-humidity sensor. The proposed design offers a compact route for integrating low-frequency vibration suppression with multiband energy conversion.

title: A fully-enclosed torsional galloping electromagnetic wind energy harvester
abstract: Most galloping wind energy harvesters (WEHs) are based on transverse galloping, whereas very few utilize torsional galloping. Adopting a fully-enclosed structure to protect components vulnerable to harsh external environmental conditions can improve the stability and reliability of WEHs. The existing fully-enclosed WEHs need two spring-mass systems, and the frequency mismatch between them reduces the stability of electrical output. This paper proposes a fully-enclosed torsional galloping electromagnetic wind energy harvester (TGEWEH) with the torsion movement caused by the aerodynamic torque on bluff body. It only has one spring-mass system and does not involve frequency matching, thus potentially improving the stability. Based on the quasi-steady assumption, a mathematical model of TGEWEH is presented. Experiments show that sealing the bluff body shell’s opening with a flexible film has an acceptable impact on the cut-in wind speed and electrical outputs. The simulated voltages agree well with the experiments, indicating that the proposed model meets the requirement of TGEWEH design. The harvester with the bluff body side ratio of 1.5 achieves the maximum output power of 4.41 mW and power density of 36 μW/cm3 at 15 m/s, which are higher than existing torsional galloping WEHs and semi- or fully-enclosed WEHs. It can stably drive a wireless sensor node in the wind speed range from 4.14 to 15 m/s. For the improved stability of fully-enclosed WEHs with one spring-mass system, and the high power density and wide wind speed range of torsional galloping WEHs, more relevant research is worth conducting in the future.

title: Physics-informed identification of dynamic propeller excitations via EM-based Kalman filtering
abstract: Accurate identification of propeller-induced hydrodynamic loads is crucial for vibration control and structural reliability in propeller propulsion systems. However, direct measurement of propeller excitation is infeasible due to the harsh operating environment and inherent structural constraints, which necessitates indirect identification approaches such as Kalman filtering. While these methods enable online estimation external inputs, the conventional random-walk assumption fails to represent the colored nature of hydrodynamic excitations, leading to spectrum mismatch and potential instability. To address this limitation, this study proposes an adaptive identification framework that integrates a scaled spherical simplex filter (S3F) with a physics-informed latent force model. The latent model combines an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process with a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) system to simultaneously capture the broadband attenuation and hump-resonance features of propeller loads. Furthermore, to mitigate the difficulty of filter parameter tuning, an adaptive expectation–maximization (EM) strategy is incorporated to update noise covariances directly from structural response measurements, thereby enhancing robustness against uncertain prior settings. Numerical simulations and experimental validations confirm that, compared with the random-walk assumption, the proposed method significantly suppresses low-frequency drift, improves estimation accuracy, and maintains stability under varying noise conditions. These results highlight the method’s potential as a reliable strategy for indirect hydrodynamic load identification in propeller propulsion systems.

title: Gudermannian-based Active Impulsive Noise Control Algorithm: Design and performance analysis
abstract: In active noise control (ANC) systems, the conventional filtered-x least mean square (FxLMS) algorithm suffers from performance degradation in impulsive-noise environments. To address this problem, a robust filtered-x least Gudermannian (FxLGD) algorithm is proposed by incorporating a Gudermannian-based nonlinear saturation transformation that compresses the residual noise into the FxLMS framework. Based on the Gaussian-mixture model to characterize the impulsive noise, we analyze the mean-square transient evolution of the FxLGD algorithm and obtain a closed-form to predict its steady-state behavior. To further improve performance in both convergence speed and residual error, a variable-parameter FxLGD algorithm is developed by taking advantage of the logarithmic mapping with respect to the residual error. Simulation results under various impulsive-noise scenarios have verified the proposed theoretical analysis as well as that the proposed algorithms achieve faster convergence, lower residual error, and better robustness than the compared algorithms. In addition, the experiment on a real single-channel pipeline ANC system further confirms their effectiveness.

title: Comparative study of sound transmission loss enhancement in double-leaf walls using inertial amplifier and resonator
abstract: This paper investigates the sound transmission loss (STL) characteristics of double-leaf walls incorporating different mechanical impedance elements within the cavity, including a spring, a spring–mass–spring (SMS) resonator, and an inertial amplifier (IA). This study presents a novel investigation of cavity-integrated spring–mass–spring resonators and inertial amplifiers for enhancing the sound transmission loss of double-leaf walls, together with their systematic optimization under an equal-mass constraint. A theoretical model is developed and validated through impedance tube experiments performed on baseline single-leaf and double-leaf walls, together with modified double-leaf configurations containing a spring, a SMS and an IA resonator in the air gap. A genetic algorithm-based optimization is further carried out to identify the optimal resonator parameters for the different configurations while maintaining a constant total mass of the wall and inserted mechanism. The results show that all mechanical insertions significantly enhance the STL relative to the baseline double-leaf wall. The optimized spring, SMS resonator, and IA configurations provide net STL improvements of 30%, 37.4%, and 40.3%, respectively. Although the IA yields the highest improvement, its advantage over the SMS resonator is found to be marginal, while both configurations exhibit superior sound insulation to the spring configuration. A parametric investigation reveals that increasing spring stiffness improves STL in the cavity-controlled region, whereas increasing the SMS auxiliary mass enhances low-frequency performance but introduces a pronounced resonance peak. For the IA configuration, increasing the inclination angle between the rod and spring reduces STL, while increasing spring stiffness produces the opposite effect. The increase in auxiliary mass improves STL in the mid-frequency range, but this benefit diminishes in the pre-coincidence region due to the dominance of plate impedance. The study highlights the effectiveness of embedded mechanical impedance elements for enhancing acoustic insulation and provides guidance for the optimal design of lightweight double-leaf wall systems.

title: Mechanism of skidding-induced IAS fault characteristic order shifts in tapered roller bearings considering electromechanical coupling
abstract: Under practical operating conditions, skidding is inevitable in tapered roller bearings, causing complex internal dynamics and significant shifts in instantaneous angular speed (IAS)-based fault characteristic orders, thereby degrading the accuracy of condition monitoring and early fault diagnosis. Existing research has yet to elucidate the underlying mechanism of skidding-induced fault characteristic order shifts and their relationship with skidding severity. To address this issue, an electromechanically coupled dynamic model of a faulty tapered roller bearing is developed by integrating multi-source nonlinear contact-friction interactions with a PI speed feedback control mechanism for dynamic torque regulation. Based on the proposed model, the mechanism of skidding-induced fault characteristic order shifts is systematically investigated, and the relationship between skidding severity and order shift is revealed. The results show that the proposed model comprehensively captures the transient angular speed response and nonlinear skidding evolution of the bearing. Crucially, skidding induces shifts in opposite directions in the fault characteristic orders depending on fault location: the fault characteristic order of outer-ring faults shifts toward lower orders, whereas that of inner-ring faults shifts toward higher orders. Furthermore, the absolute magnitude of the characteristic order shift is approximately proportional to the skidding rate, regardless of whether the fault is located on the inner ring or the outer ring. These findings highlight the necessity of incorporating skidding-induced kinematic deviations into IAS-based fault diagnosis frameworks for rolling bearings operating under complex conditions.

title: A multi-domain degradation signal feature extraction and adaptive feature fusion regression method for state of health prediction in lithium-ion batteries
abstract: This paper proposes a multidimensional feature extraction and adaptive feature fusion regression method for state-of-health (SOH) prediction in lithium-ion batteries. This method addresses the high dimensionality and redundancy of raw charge–discharge data and the difficulty of balancing prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. First, based on the two-stage degradation process of charging and discharging, feature curve clusters are constructed in the time, state-of-charge (SOC), and differential response domains. Parameters including the response centre, response width, main inflection point location, and slope contrast are extracted to form 52-dimensional candidate health features. These features are jointly evaluated and filtered by considering correlation, stability, foresight, and stage sensitivity, yielding nine key health features. Furthermore, an adaptive feature fusion regressor (AFFR) is developed to achieve accurate SOH prediction through adaptive sparse filtering, active subset refinement, and structural relaxation refitting. To validate the effectiveness and generalisation capability of the proposed method, this paper conducts experiments using two public datasets from NASA and MIT and performs comparative analyses across multiple battery samples and different training-ratio conditions. The results demonstrate that the proposed method predicts SOH with high accuracy and robustness across different degradation trajectories. The RMSE for typical battery samples is as low as 0.0020, and the overall predictions agree well with the actual SOH degradation trends. These results indicate that the proposed method improves SOH prediction accuracy and computational efficiency while maintaining the physical interpretability of the features and provides a reliable basis for practical online battery health management applications.

title: Improving low-wind-speed aero-elastic responses by peanut-shaped auxetic structure for galloping energy harvesting
abstract: The galloping energy harvester (GEH) is a promising wind energy harvesting solution for powering the Internet of Things (IoT) and wireless sensor networks (WSNs). However, conventional GEHs face bottlenecks such as high critical wind speeds and low energy-harvesting efficiency under weak wind conditions. This work introduces a peanut-shaped auxetic structure into the GEH system, proposing a novel peanut-shaped auxetic galloping energy harvester (AGEH). The proposed design enhances energy conversion performance through two mechanisms: reducing the stiffness of the cantilever beam and modifying the aerodynamic flow field characteristics around the bluff body. The vibration response and energy harvesting behavior of a plain galloping energy harvester (PGEH) with a cuboid bluff body (PGEH-Cuboid), an AGEH with a cuboid bluff body (AGEH-Cuboid), and an AGEH with a peanut-shaped profiled bluff body with porosity K = 0.4 and shape coefficient M = 8.5 (AGEH-(K = 0.4, M = 8.5)) are evaluated numerically and experimentally. Compared to the PGEH-Cuboid, the AGEH-Cuboid initiates vibration at 2.4 m/s, and increases the maximum root mean square voltage (Vrms) by 332.96%. The peanut-shaped bluff body further increases the overall average output power (OAOP) by 100.23% relative to the cuboid bluff body. Three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (3D-CFD) simulations elucidate the flow mechanism through which the peanut-shaped bluff body enhances aerodynamic forces by increasing wake vortex size and accelerating boundary layer separation. Application tests confirm that the proposed AGEH can serve as a reliable alternative power source for low-power electronic devices.

title: Sound field shaping in thermoacoustic cells via a synergistic hybrid tuning framework: Symmetry breaking, active excitation and impedance tuning
abstract: Sound field shaping, particularly in the contexts of acoustic focusing and cloaking, remains one of the most challenging tasks in modern wave manipulation, necessitating precise control over energy distribution and propagation paths. However, conventional passive methods frequently have fundamental limitations in tunability and dynamic response, resulting in inefficient manipulation under complex boundary conditions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a synergistic hybrid tuning framework for thermoacoustic cells that achieves a sound-pressure-level control range of ΔLp = 189 dB by jointly combining temperature-gradient-driven symmetry breaking, active acoustic excitation, and general impedance boundary tuning. Each mechanism, applied in isolation, is inherently bounded: symmetry breaking cannot inject energy, active excitation cannot reconfigure the modal landscape, and impedance tuning operates within a passive design space. Their coordinated integration, however, yields a control authority that far exceeds the sum of their individual contributions. To realize this framework computationally, a spectral improved-Fourier-Galerkin method is developed for solving the linear thermoacoustic governing equations under full thermo-viscous coupling, enabling efficient free-modal and forced-response analyses with general impedance boundary conditions. A preliminary experimental validation, carried out on a thermoacoustic cell with one rigid and one open termination, confirms the predicted onset frequencies to within 1.6 %. Free-modal analysis reveals that the temperature gradient shifts the first eigenfrequency upward by 18.8 % and induces topological twists in eigenvector trajectories, thereby breaking the spatiotemporal separability of the sound field. In forced response, the boundary auxiliary function autonomously adapts its spectral weights to boundary impedance variations, confirming its capacity for dynamic boundary reconfiguration without reformulating basis functions. A parametric study across the three control degrees of freedom quantitatively demonstrates that only their synergistic coordination reaches the full 189 dB control range; any subset of mechanisms yields substantially narrower dynamic ranges. This control range is a theoretical upper bound obtained under linear conditions. The framework provides a theoretical foundation for high-authority sound field control in thermoacoustic systems, with direct implications for the design of adaptive thermoacoustic actuators and controllable acoustic waveguides.

title: A multi-scale progressive fusion method for predicting the remaining useful life of gears guided by a control-equation-compatible a priori cascade
abstract: Gears are core transmission components of high-end equipment in aerospace, rail transit and other key fields. Accurate remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of gears is critical for equipment prognostics and health management (PHM), to ensure operational safety and reduce maintenance costs. Aiming at key limitations of existing data-driven gear RUL prediction methods, including strong data dependency, insufficient physical interpretability, low mapping accuracy and weak cross-condition generalization, this paper proposes a novel progressive multi-level feature fusion RUL prediction framework guided by cascaded control equation compatibility priors. Taking gear vibration time-domain signals as the sole input, the framework sequentially adopts three customized modules: Governing Equations Auto-Encoder (GEAE) to extract physically consistent robust degradation features, Multi-scale Fusion Network (MsNet) to construct health indicators for degradation characterization, and Dual Temporal Constraints Network (DTCNet) to achieve accurate RUL mapping. Systematic validation on two heterogeneous datasets demonstrates that the framework reduces RMSE by up to 40.6% and improves R2 by 25.0% over end-to-end methods, while significantly enhancing HI monotonicity and trendability. Cross-seed statistical tests confirm its robustness (coefficient of variation ≤ 1.9%). The method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches and exhibits strong cross-scenario generalization.

title: Nonlinear vibrations of a marine propulsion shafting rotor system considering bolt loosening and interface friction coupling
abstract: As a critical component of marine propulsion shafting, bolted joints are prone to loosening under the influence of alternating loads and vibration impacts, leading to reduced connection stiffness and potentially inducing thrust bearing misalignment as well as mechanical-magnetic coupling faults. Moreover, under low-speed and heavy-load conditions, bolt loosening exacerbates interface friction in the stern bearing, severely compromising the safe operation of the power system. In response to the issues, a dynamic modeling method for bolt loosening based on the equivalent crack theory is proposed. This method accurately captures the periodic opening and closing behavior of the connection interface during bolt loosening through the breathing effect of the crack. Furthermore, by comprehensively considering the frictional excitation of the stern bearing and the misalignment effect of the permanent magnet thrust bearing, a coupled shafting rotor dynamic model integrating friction and bolt loosening faults is established. Through numerical simulation and experimental validation, the effects of bolt loosening, thrust bearing misalignment, and stern bearing stiffness on the nonlinear vibration response of the shafting are investigated. The vibration response characteristics and evolution laws of bolt loosening faults are characterized, and the dominant excitation sources governing the vibration response at different fault stages are identified, providing support for bolt loosening state recognition based on vibration characteristics.

title: Sensitivity-driven model updating for bridge structures using operational modal analysis and enhanced batched Thompson sampling-based Bayesian optimization
abstract: This paper proposes a robust and effective finite element model updating (FEMU) framework for inverse parameter identification of bridge structures by integrating operational modal analysis (OMA) and variance-based global sensitivity analysis (GSA) with an enhanced batched Thompson sampling-based Bayesian optimization (ETS-BO) method. Specifically, a Gaussian process (GP) model is constructed to approximate the nonlinear relationship between uncertain structural parameters and the corresponding modal responses. Leveraging the trained GP model, the variance-based GSA identifies the most influential parameters governing the dynamic behavior of the bridge, thereby significantly reducing the dimensionality of the FEMU problem and improving computational efficiency. Building upon the reduced parameter space, the ETS-BO method is developed by integrating an adaptive trust-region selection strategy with an enhanced batched Thompson sampling (ETS) method to efficiently solve the FEMU problem. The adaptive trust-region selection evaluates the improvement potential at the regional level, guiding the search toward promising regions of the parameter space while avoiding over-exploration of less promising ones. The trust region method is then applied to perform local optimization, whereby each trust region is adaptively expanded or contracted based on its observed improvement history, and local optimization runs exhibiting greater potential for further improvement are selectively continued. Within the selected trust regions, the ETS method is employed to determine the optimal updating parameters by iteratively selecting batches of candidate solutions sampled from the posterior distributions of the corresponding independent GP models. The effectiveness of the proposed ETS-BO is validated through a real-world case study of a bridge structure equipped with wireless accelerometers for vibration monitoring. Ambient vibration responses recorded under normal traffic conditions are analyzed using OMA to identify modal parameters, which subsequently serve as targets for updating the finite element (FE) model developed to represent the structural behavior of the bridge. The results demonstrate that the proposed ETS-BO requires substantially fewer FE evaluations than conventional optimization methods while achieving rapid convergence toward the optimal solution. Furthermore, the updated FE model closely reproduces the experimentally identified modal parameters, including natural frequencies and mode shape correlations, thereby providing a reliable numerical representation of the in-service dynamic behavior of the bridge and demonstrating the potential of the proposed framework to support long-term structural health monitoring of large-scale civil infrastructure systems.

title: Energy transfer and modal coupling in coated composite spatial shells under thermal loading
abstract: To address the vibration prediction and suppression requirements of fiber-reinforced composite spatial shells with protective coating (PC-FRCSSs) in thermal environments, this study develops an integrated framework combining dynamic modelling, coating preparation, thermal protection testing, and experimental validation. A theoretical model of PC-FRCSSs assembled from cylindrical and toroidal substructures is established by introducing virtual springs, spatial corner coupling, temperature-dependent material properties, and a higher-order shear deformation displacement field. The modal strain energy ratios and a degeneracy-sensitive coupling index are further proposed to quantify energy transfer and modal coupling. Then, the convergence analysis, literature verification, and finite element comparisons demonstrate the accuracy of the proposed model for coated and uncoated spatial shells. The coating preparation process is presented, and the thermal protection performance of the protective coating is evaluated under continuous heating at 473.15 K. Experimental results show that the maximum frequency errors of the uncoated and coated specimens are 3.96 % and 4.03 %, respectively, and the response prediction error remains within 10.91 %. The displacement responses of the coated specimens decrease by 23.5 % and 29.3 % at 299.15 K and 373.15 K, respectively. Finally, parametric results further reveal the effects of laying angle, spatial corner, and thickness-radius ratio on mode degeneracy and high-response regions.

title: Physics-informed DeepONet with modal coordinate encoding for predicting dynamic responses of unseen motor housings
abstract: This study proposes a unified physics-informed machine-learning (PIML) framework for predicting the dynamic responses of traction motor housings under unseen geometric conditions. The framework incorporates three key forms of physical priors into a neural network. First, an observation bias is introduced through modal coordinate encoding, which embeds both geometric characteristics and excitation-dependent modal contributions into the neural network. Second, an inductive bias is incorporated by deploying a separable deep operator network architecture, which effectively learns nonlinear operator mappings and generalizes them to unseen housing geometries. Third, a learning bias is enforced by embedding the governing equations of structural dynamics into the training process to ensure physically consistent predictions. Novel training strategies are also employed to enhance convergence and numerical stability during physics-informed training. Quantitative evaluations and ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving a mean MAPE of 3.32 % across the full test set and outperforming conventional neural networks. A design-optimization application further confirms that the proposed framework improves computational efficiency compared with conventional finite element analysis. Overall, this study establishes a robust framework for accelerating AI-driven design optimization and advancing intelligent structural engineering methodologies.

title: Accurate in-situ sensing and condition monitoring of bearings using embedded conformal piezoelectric sensors
abstract: Rolling bearings are critical components that carry loads in rotating machinery. However, conventional sensors mounted outside the bearing are susceptible to signal attenuation along complex transmission paths, variations in mounting conditions, and environmental interference. To enable in situ perception close to the excitation source, this study develops an intelligent bearing that integrates a thin, flexible, and conformal PVDF-TrFE piezoelectric sensor into a local recess in the bearing outer ring. The sensor is fabricated by depositing a functional PVDF-TrFE layer onto a patterned copper clad polyimide substrate using a flexible electronics spray coating system developed in house. A systematic design strategy was adopted to integrate sensor geometry, electrode patterning, conformal installation on the outer ring, mechanical compatibility, and fault sensing evaluation within a unified framework. Finite element analysis demonstrated that adapting the recess geometry to the sensor profile markedly reduces the local structural disturbance caused by sensor integration. Under the conservative static loading condition considered, the optimized numerical configuration shallow recess retained approximately 82.5 % of the apparent local radial stiffness of the intact outer ring. Bearing experiments conducted at rotational speeds from 1800 to 3000 r/min demonstrated that the embedded sensor simultaneously captured high frequency impacts induced by faults and low frequency responses associated with rolling element passage. The relative phase between these components varied with the circumferential position of the outer race defect, providing preliminary information about the fault location. Under identical experimental conditions, the embedded sensor also exhibited consistently higher signal to noise ratios for fault related components and higher normalized fault amplitudes than the external acoustic emission sensor and accelerometer. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating conformal piezoelectric sensing into a bearing component that carries load and provide a practical route toward condition perception close to the excitation source in intelligent bearings with integrated sensing capabilities.

title: A single-sided inverse absolute nodal coordinate formulation for large-deformation shape sensing of slender structures
abstract: Shape sensing reconstructs structural displacement fields from discrete strain measurements and is important for monitoring flexible slender structures. For large-deformation cases, existing inverse strain-based methods often require back-to-back measurements and prescribed sensor locations, limiting their use when only one surface is accessible or installation conditions are constrained. This paper proposes a single-sided strain-to-shape reconstruction framework for slender structures, termed SS-iANCF, based on inverse absolute nodal coordinate kinematics. Unilateral surface strain is converted into curvature information and embedded in a nonlinear least-squares inverse problem. An inextensibility penalty and an inter-element curvature-continuity constraint are introduced to stabilize reconstruction without opposite-side strain data. The influence of intra-element sampling location on accuracy and Hessian conditioning is also examined. Numerical simulations and experiments using a weak-FBG/OFDR sensing system confirm that SS-iANCF achieves high-fidelity reconstruction for both unidirectional large-deformation and reverse-bending configurations. Across the experimental cases, the mean absolute reconstruction error remains below 5 mm, with a maximum mean normalized displacement error of 1.22 × 10−2 occurring in the reverse-bending case with curvature reversal.

title: Multidirectional hybrid pendulum-magnetic quasi-zero-stiffness isolator: modeling, analysis and experimental validation
abstract: Multidirectional quasi-zero-stiffness vibration isolation remains challenging owing to the low dynamic stiffness, static stability, coupled rigid-body motion, and the weak linearity of conventional negative-stiffness mechanisms. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a hybrid pendulum-magnetic quasi-zero-stiffness (HPM-QZS) isolator combining a four-point flexible suspension with a centralized magnetic negative-stiffness (MNS) module. It employs separated positive–negative stiffness combinations in the horizontal and vertical directions, respectively. Horizontally, the pretensioned suspension provides positive pendulum stiffness, while the elevated payload mass center introduces an inverted-pendulum effect that reduces the effective horizontal stiffness through translation-rotation coupling. Vertically, the suspension springs act in parallel with the MNS module, whose force is transmitted to the moving frame through a compliant rod. A closed-form linearized six-degree-of-freedom model is derived from suspension-point kinematics and incremental force and moment relations. The model provides an analytical basis for stability, modal, and transmissibility analyses and guides suspension-parameter selection. In order to improve stiffness linearity within the working stroke, an unequal-size three-stator-two-mover MNS is further developed. In addition, static calibration and passive modal tests are conducted to confirm the accuracy of the analytical model. Finally, supplementary absolute-velocity feedback is introduced to suppress residual low-frequency resonance, and passive/active-assisted transmissibility tests demonstrate effective attenuation in all three translational directions. The experimental results demonstrate that the HPM-QZS isolator combines separate horizontal and vertical stiffness-regulation mechanisms, exhibits excellent stiffness linearity in the vertical direction, and offers superior vibration isolation performance, indicating its potential for low-frequency vibration isolation in fields such as precision manufacturing and metrology.

title: A physics prior spectral embedding network expansion method for domain-incremental fault diagnosis under variable working conditions
abstract: Key rotating components such as bearings and gears operate under complex and variable working conditions, which significantly increases their risk of failure and directly compromises the reliability of the mechanical system. Existing methods for solving fault diagnosis under variable conditions, such as transfer learning, struggle to achieve satisfactory performance across both previously learned and newly encountered domains. As a result, models tend to suffer from severe catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired knowledge when adapting to new domains. To address this issue, this paper proposes a domain-incremental fault diagnosis method based on a Physical Prior Spectral Embedding Network Expansion framework (PPSENE). First, a Physical Prior Spectral Embedding Network (PPSEN) is developed. Specifically, global instance compression is employed to normalize time-domain signals, thereby reducing distribution discrepancies across different domains. Then, a real-valued Fast Fourier Transform is applied to transform signals from the time domain to the frequency domain, facilitating physically interpretable spectrum input. A logarithmic magnitude compression mechanism is introduced to mitigate the adverse effects of extreme amplitudes on feature learning. Meanwhile, frequency domain instance normalization is utilized to alleviate the scale drift of spectral energy across domains, enabling effective physical prior modeling of vibration signals. Finally, a multi-layer perceptron is adopted for deep feature extraction, yielding discriminative fault representations. Based on this, a Physical Prior Spectral Embedding Network Expansion framework is constructed for domain-incremental fault diagnosis. By expanding the spectral network, parameter isolation across different domains is achieved, which enhances the stability of the model during incremental learning. In addition, a knowledge distillation loss is introduced to align the output distributions between the new model and the old model. The proposed method is validated on a comprehensive gear transmission test rig dataset and a high-speed railway wheelset bearing dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively alleviates catastrophic forgetting in domain-incremental fault diagnosis scenarios while maintaining superior diagnostic performance under varying working conditions, the average accuracy exceeds 98 % on both datasets.

title: Differential graph spectral modulation and its application in bearing fault feature identification
abstract: Reliable identification of incipient bearing faults remains challenging in industrial scenarios involving complex operating conditions and intense noise interference. To address this issue, a Differential Graph Spectral Modulation (DGSM) method is developed to improve fault feature extraction performance. A dual-order screening model based on the differential order and reconstruction order is designed to dynamically enhance the signal spectrum, thereby improving the signal-to-noise ratio and adaptivity. The introduced differential order decomposes the signal into frequency-domain representations with energy concentrated in different frequency bands. By exploiting the spectral clustering characteristics of the Laplacian matrix, fault-related information is concentrated within a compact range of graph spectral reconstruction orders, enabling targeted reconstruction of fault-sensitive resonance components while suppressing noise and interference. Harmonic spectral kurtosis is designed to quantify feature information in different graph spectral orders, allowing accurate and effective selection of the resonance frequency band while eliminating noise interference. Validation using both simulation and experimental cases demonstrates that the proposed method effectively strengthens fault-related information. Compared with existing techniques, the proposed method achieves better feature enhancement performance and higher diagnostic reliability under complex interference conditions.

title: Complex-amplitude design of dynamic acoustic holography via physics-assisted neural network
abstract: Acoustic holography promises diverse applications, including high-resolution imaging, water–air communication, and in-vivo tissue/organ printing. While complex-amplitude design of acoustic holography yields superior performance in resolution and information content for sophisticated acoustic fields, but most holograms are spatially and temporally static once fabricated. This dilemma may be addressed by introducing the incident wavefront modulation as an additional degree of freedom, and dynamic holography would be realized by tuning the incident wavefronts via electrically switching a transducer array. Here, we propose a physics-assisted neural network optimization framework for the complex-amplitude design of dynamic acoustic holography, which enables joint optimization of multiple incident amplitude and phase profile. The framework embeds an angular-spectrum propagation model into neural network and introduces amplitude-binarization regularization to enable dynamic control through an electrically switched partitioned transducer. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits remarkable versatility, supporting the phase modulations in either continuous or binary manner and even cascaded configuration. As a proof-of-concept demonstration, it successfully achieves the dynamic display of three-frame animations and 26 alphabetic letters, creating compelling “acoustic movies”. Quantitatively, the proposed method outperforms traditional designs both numerically and experimentally, which reduces mean squared error by 24.1% and 32.1%, respectively. We believe this work would greatly advance acoustic holography and imply unprecedented opportunity for broad acoustics.

title: An adaptive internal model and linear active disturbance rejection hybrid control algorithm for helicopter cabin noise suppression
abstract: Active structural acoustic control is effective for suppressing gearbox noise in helicopter cabins. The conventional filtered-x least mean square (FxLMS) algorithm has obvious limitations in complex vibro-acoustic environments. First, rotor speed fluctuations and load variations cause the noise to exhibit non-stationary features including frequency drift and drastic amplitude fluctuations, leading to algorithm iteration lag, control performance degradation, and even divergence. Besides, reference signals can only be indirectly obtained through accelerometers, resulting in poor quality and reduced noise reduction performance. Therefore, this paper draws on the idea of active disturbance rejection control (ADRC) in modern control theory and extends it to helicopter cabin noise control, proposing a hybrid control algorithm. It reconstructs reference signals online based on the internal model principle for high-precision harmonic suppression, and adopts an ADRC controller to estimate and compensate system disturbances in real time for improved robustness. Further, unlike existing studies that mostly use simple plate and beam structures for experiments, this paper constructs panel excitation and gearbox excitation experimental systems. The former simulates a simplified vibro-acoustic environment to verify the algorithm performance under controllable conditions, while the latter reproduces the characteristics of helicopter gear meshing noise to evaluate the algorithm’s engineering applicability in complex environments. Experimental results show that the algorithm achieves stable and efficient noise reduction in both environments. Under steady-state excitation of the gearbox, the target frequency band noise reduction reaches 33.2 dB and 21.7 dB, respectively. Under time-varying conditions, the algorithm can stabilize within 4 s with no significant decline in noise reduction effect.

title: Multi-resonance peak distribution and broadband frequency zoning of flexible substrate-flexible equipment (FSFE) vibration isolation systems
abstract: To address the complex broadband multi-resonance peak distribution in flexible substrate–flexible equipment (FSFE) vibration isolation systems, which cannot be effectively described by classical rigid-body isolation theory, this study investigates the multi-resonance peak distribution characteristics and broadband frequency-zoning behavior of FSFE systems. Based on the four-terminal parameter method, an analytical FSFE model with single-point mounting is established, and a vibration isolation effectiveness ratio based on the total kinetic energy of the substrate is defined as the performance criterion for broadband vibration isolation. On this basis, it is revealed that each modal interval exhibits an alternating three-zone pattern, namely the first vibration-isolation operation zone (VIOZ I), the resonance amplification zone (RAZ), and the second vibration-isolation operation zone (VIOZ II), thereby forming a periodically evolving zoning structure over a broad frequency range. The formation mechanism of VIOZ I is further clarified from the perspective of impedance phase relations, showing that it originates from the in-phase superposition of the substructure stiffness and the isolator stiffness. The influences of isolator stiffness and damping are then analyzed through quantitative indices such as the broadband energy integral. Finally, free-free dual-beam suspension excitation experiments are conducted to examine the theoretically predicted multi-resonance peak distribution characteristics and frequency-zoning behavior. The results can provide a reference for the broadband analysis and parameter design of flexibly coupled vibration isolation systems.
